teaching_concepts.explanation: Most impurity in these chapters is temporary and morally innocent, and the rites of restoration teach dependence on God's provision for cleansing.
The clean and unclean categories marked Israel out among the nations and dramatized that death and disorder cannot approach the living God.
These are the exact laws in view when Jesus declares foods clean and Peter is sent to Gentiles, so the New Testament treats them as a school that pointed toward a fuller cleansing.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the difference between being unclean and being guilty in Leviticus, and describe what the purity laws were training Israel to remember about God.

comprehension_check.question: What are the clean and unclean rules of Leviticus 11-15 for?
options: They wove God's holiness into Israel's everyday embodied life
They shielded the nation's health from infection and unsafe food
They marked out which members of Israel were guilty of sin
They proved Israel's customs superior to those of the nations
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 11:44-45 grounds the rules in God's own holiness and his rescue of Israel from Egypt.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 11:44-45 again. Notice the reason God himself attaches to the food rules.

comprehension_check.question: Most uncleanness in Leviticus 12-15 comes from childbirth, disease, or the body's ordinary flows. What does that show about what uncleanness is?
options: A punishment tracing every affliction back to hidden sin
A temporary condition met by God's own provision for cleansing
A sign of God's displeasure with the body and its processes
A lasting status shutting certain Israelites permanently outside the camp
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 14:2 opens the law for the day a defiled person is cleansed, so the system itself expects restoration.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 12:6-8 and Leviticus 14:1-9 again. Notice how each case of uncleanness ends.

connections.reason: Jesus 'declared all foods clean' — a direct ruling on these chapters.
Peter's vision of the sheet of unclean animals reworks Leviticus 11 to open the door to Gentiles.

nodes.title: The Day of Atonement
nodes.summary: Once a year the high priest enters the innermost sanctuary with blood, and a scapegoat carries the nation's sins into the wilderness — the Old Testament's most detailed ritual portrait of atonement. Yom Kippur is the ritual heart of the Torah and the backbone of Hebrews' argument about the cross.
nodes.discussion_prompt: One goat dies at the sanctuary and one carries the nation's sins into the wilderness, out of sight. Why might God give his people such a vivid, physical picture of sins being dealt with and removed, and what would it mean to believe your own failures could be carried that far away?
assessment_questions: What does the high priest do with each of the two goats on the Day of Atonement?
The high priest enters the Most Holy Place only once a year, and only with blood. What does the ritual's extreme caution communicate about sin and about access to God?
The scapegoat carried sins away where no one could retrieve them. What guilt do you keep retrieving, and what would trusting God's cleansing on that point change?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The slain goat shows sin paid for at the sanctuary while the scapegoat shows it carried out of the community's presence, so atonement deals with guilt in both directions.
One man, one day a year, only with blood: the ritual's restrictions teach how serious it is for sinful people to stand before a holy God.
The high priest bears the people's burden into God's presence on their behalf, a role Hebrews later reads as the pattern Christ fulfills once for all.
The chapter's promise 'you shall be clean before the LORD' is declared by God himself, so the day's hope rests on his provision rather than human effort.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the Day of Atonement ritual with its two goats, and explain what each goat pictures about how God deals with sin.

comprehension_check.question: Leviticus 16 uses two goats, one slain before the LORD and one sent away alive. What does the double ritual say about sin?
options: Forgiveness means God sends sin away without any cost being paid
The people secure their own cleansing by the day's fasting and self-denial
Atonement reaches the priests fully but the people only in part
Its guilt is paid for and also carried far from the people
comprehension_check.why: Blood goes before God in Leviticus 16:15 and the sins are carried off in Leviticus 16:21-22, so the day both pays and removes.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 16:15-22 again. Notice what happens with each goat in turn, and what each act deals with.

comprehension_check.question: Only the high priest enters the inner sanctuary, only once a year, and never without blood. What do the restrictions of Leviticus 16 teach?
options: Entering God's presence is grave, and the way is his gift
God would rather keep his distance from the people he saved
Entry turns on the high priest's own superior moral character
The rules aim to make Israel too fearful to seek God
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 16:2 bars even Aaron from entering at will, and the same chapter appoints the one way in.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 16:1-3 again. Notice what makes entering dangerous, and what Aaron must bring to come in.

connections.reason: Hebrews reads Christ's death as the final Day of Atonement, entered once for all.
Paul's word for Christ as the 'place of atonement' (hilasterion) is the Greek name for the mercy seat of Leviticus 16.

nodes.title: The Holiness Code: Loving Your Neighbor
nodes.summary: Holiness moves from ritual to ethics: sexuality, justice for the poor, honest scales, care for the immigrant — and the command Jesus called the second greatest, 'love your neighbor as yourself' (19:18). Holiness in Leviticus is as much about how you treat people as how you worship.
nodes.discussion_prompt: In a single chapter, Leviticus moves from honest scales to leaving harvest for the poor to loving your neighbor as yourself. What does it mean that God treats money, speech, and sex as matters of holiness, and which of those areas would his holiness confront first in you?
assessment_questions: What command in Leviticus 19 did Jesus call the second greatest, and what kinds of everyday situations surround it in the chapter?
The refrain 'be holy, for I am holy' anchors these chapters. What does it mean that Israel's ethics are grounded in God's own character?
Leviticus 19 commands leaving the edges of the field for the poor and the foreigner. What margin could you build into your money or time that exists purely for someone else's need?

teaching_concepts.explanation: How Israel treats workers, neighbors, and strangers is as much a holiness matter as anything done at the altar.
The blood rule of Leviticus 17:11 declares that life itself is sacred and God-owned, which grounds the code's reverence for life and worship.
The command Jesus called the second greatest sits inside concrete acts of justice, so love in Leviticus means honest scales, paid wages, and welcomed strangers.
The code's rules for sexuality and family draw lines that guard persons and community life from exploitation and harm.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Leviticus 19 connects holiness to everyday justice, and give two concrete examples from the chapter.

comprehension_check.question: Leviticus 19 mixes commands about the altar with honest scales, paid wages, and care for the stranger. What does the mixture claim about holiness?
options: Just dealings can take the place of the altar entirely
True holiness means withdrawing from ordinary daily affairs
Right treatment of people is as much holiness as right worship
The love command reaches kin and countrymen but never the outsider
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 19:2 sets God's own character over every command that follows, workplace and altar alike.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 19:9-18 again. Notice what kinds of commands sit side by side beneath the call of Leviticus 19:2.

comprehension_check.question: The command to love your neighbor sits in Leviticus 19 among rules about wages, courts, and grudges. What does its placement say about love?
options: Love is chiefly an inward warmth the law cannot regulate
Love takes shape in concrete acts of fairness toward people
Love replaces the surrounding rules for anyone who means well
Love is owed to neighbors only as far as they earn it
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 19:18 caps a run of commands about wages, verdicts, and grudges, so love means doing a neighbor concrete right.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 19:11-18 again. Notice what the commands just before the love command are about.

connections.reason: Jesus pairs Leviticus 19:18 with the Shema as the two commands on which everything hangs.
James calls 'love your neighbor as yourself' the royal law and applies it against favoritism.

nodes.title: Sacred Time: Feasts, Jubilee, and Covenant Sanctions
nodes.summary: Israel's calendar — Sabbath, Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles — plus the radical economics of the Jubilee year, when debts release and land returns. Chapter 26 lays out covenant blessings and curses, the script the prophets will later read Israel's history by.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Israel's calendar rehearses rescue every year, and the Jubilee resets debt and land every fifty years so no family stays crushed forever. What do these rhythms say about what God wants time and money to do, and which of them would be hardest for you to live by?
assessment_questions: What are the major feasts in Israel's calendar, and what happens to land and debts in the Jubilee year?
Chapter 26 sets the promise 'I will walk among you and be your God' alongside blessings and curses. What do the covenant sanctions reveal about how seriously God takes the relationship?
The Jubilee assumes possessions are held on loan from God. What would you handle differently this month if you treated your money and time as leased rather than owned?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Sabbath and the feasts give Israel a calendar of remembrance, so the year itself keeps retelling what God has done.
Because the land belongs to God, debts release and land returns every fiftieth year, protecting the poor from permanent ruin.
Chapter 26 spells out the covenant's consequences in advance, and the prophets later read Israel's whole history by this script.
The covenant's promised blessing peaks at 'I will walk among you,' echoing Eden and showing that restored fellowship with God is the point of it all.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the Jubilee year and explain what Israel's calendar of feasts was designed to keep the nation remembering.

comprehension_check.question: Leviticus 23 orders Israel's year around sabbaths and appointed feasts. What is the calendar for?
options: It keeps the nation rehearsing what God has done for them
It secures good harvests by honoring the seasons' turning points
It rewards the diligent with rest they have earned by work
It marks certain days as holy by their very nature
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 23:42-43 has Israel live in booths so every generation will know the exodus story.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 23:42-43 again. Notice the reason God gives for the Feast of Booths.

comprehension_check.question: In the Jubilee year of Leviticus 25, debts release and land returns to its family. What conviction drives the arrangement?
options: Wealth itself is a danger the law periodically strips away
Each generation must start over so none inherits an advantage
The poor earn their release through the years they have served
The land belongs to God, so ruin can never be final
comprehension_check.why: Leviticus 25:23 says the land may never be sold beyond reclaim, since it is God's and Israel lives on it as his guests.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Leviticus 25:23-28 again. Notice whose land it is said to be, and what that makes every sale.

connections.reason: Jesus announces his ministry as 'the year of the Lord's favor' — Jubilee language from Leviticus 25 via Isaiah 61.

nodes.title: The Census: Israel Arrayed Around the Presence
nodes.summary: Numbers opens with counting: the fighting men tribe by tribe, then the camp laid out in ranks with the tabernacle at dead center and the Levites ringed around it as a guard. The lists read dry until their design appears, a nation being shaped into marching order with God's dwelling in the middle and every tribe assigned its place and its load. The Levites are counted separately, taken in place of Israel's firstborn and given the sanctuary's care, so that nearness to holiness protects the camp instead of destroying it.
key_themes: Levites in place of the firstborn
nodes.discussion_prompt: Every tribe in this camp knows exactly where it stands, and every position is defined by its relation to the tent at the center. If someone mapped your week the way Numbers 2 maps the camp, what would sit at the center of the layout, and how did it get there?
assessment_questions: Who gets counted in the census of Numbers 1, who is left out of it, and what different assignment are the uncounted given?
The same people are counted like an army and arranged like a congregation around God's tent. What is that double identity preparing Israel to be?

Every Israelite in these chapters has an assigned place and an assigned burden, down to who carries which pole. What place and load have been given to you in your family or community, and what would carrying them the way chapter 4 describes look like?

teaching_concepts.concept: A census in service of promise
teaching_concepts.explanation: The count musters the people God multiplied in Egypt for the march to the land he swore, so even a muster roll is covenant bookkeeping, promise turned into organization.
The camp's geometry preaches: God's dwelling in the middle, every tribe oriented toward it, and all order flowing outward from the holy.

teaching_concepts.concept: The Levites as substitutes and shield
teaching_concepts.explanation: Taken in place of the firstborn God claimed at the exodus, the Levites absorb the danger of nearness and keep wrath from the people, service framed as protection.
The careful wrapping and carrying rules of chapter 4 treat the holy things as lethal to casual contact, teaching reverence through procedure rather than sentiment.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the census and camp layout of Numbers 1-2 are for, and describe the double role the Levites play between the tabernacle and the tribes.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 1-2 spends two chapters on head counts and camp positions. What are the lists doing?
options: Preserving the tax and supply records of the wilderness years
Proving the exodus account with verifiable population figures
Ranking the twelve tribes by the honor each had earned
Forming a people into an ordered camp around God's dwelling
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 2:2 gives the design: every tribe camped under its own banner around the Tent of Meeting, a nation taking its shape from the presence at its center.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 2:1-2 and Numbers 2:17. Notice where the Tent travels when the whole camp moves.

comprehension_check.question: Why are the Levites pulled out of the military census and camped in a ring around the tabernacle?
options: They replace the firstborn and shield the camp from wrath
They form an elite corps holier than the other tribes
They are exempted so that worship never pauses for war
They earn the position by stricter obedience to the law
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 3:12-13 and Numbers 1:53 give both halves: God takes the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn, and their camp keeps wrath from the congregation.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 3:11-13 for whose place the Levites take, then Numbers 1:53 for what their position prevents.

nodes.title: The Camp Consecrated and the March from Sinai
nodes.summary: Before Israel can march, the camp must be fit for the God at its center: purity regulations, restitution for wrongs, and the Nazirite vow press holiness into ordinary relationships. At the heart of the section God puts his own name on the people in the priestly blessing, and the tribes answer with twelve days of identical offerings for the altar's dedication. Passover is kept, with provision made for the unclean and the far away to keep it late, and when the cloud lifts, Israel finally moves out from Sinai behind the ark with the trumpets sounding.
key_themes: a camp fit for God's presence
nodes.discussion_prompt: The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 asks God to bless, keep, shine, be gracious, turn his face, and give peace, spoken over people about to walk into a wilderness. Why do you think Israel is given these words at this moment, and which line would you most need spoken over you this week?
assessment_questions: What does God instruct Aaron and his sons to do for Israel in Numbers 6:22-27, and what does he say the act places on the people?
Numbers 7 records the identical offering twelve times over when a single summary would have done. What might the repetition be saying about the tribes and the altar?

Israel's travel schedule in Numbers 9:15-23 has no fixed itinerary, only a cloud that lifts or settles. Which decision in front of you right now most needs that posture of readiness to wait or move, and what would practicing it look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The section moves holiness out of the sanctuary into the camp's relationships, wrongs repaid and vows kept, insisting that life around God's dwelling answers to him in its details.
Numbers 6:27 says the spoken blessing puts God's own name on Israel, so the people's security rides on who God is, pronounced over them again and again.
Chapter 7 records the same offering twelve times over, giving every tribe identical standing at the altar and showing that God receives each giver singly rather than in bulk.
The cloud, the trumpets, and the ark going ahead make God himself the itinerary, so Israel's only schedule is attentiveness.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what the priestly blessing asks and what Numbers 6:27 says it places on Israel, and explain how the cloud and the trumpets governed the march from Sinai.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 5-9 fills the space between the census and the departure with purity rules, vows, blessing, and offerings. What is this material doing there?
options: Setting conditions Israel must meet to earn the land
Making the camp fit to carry God's presence on the road
Recording miscellaneous laws with no bearing on the story
Teaching sound hygiene for a large camp in a harsh wilderness
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 5:3 states the logic at the outset: the camp must be kept clean because the LORD himself dwells in the middle of it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 5:1-4 and notice the reason given at the end of the paragraph for moving the unclean outside.

comprehension_check.question: What does the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:22-27 actually give Israel?
options: A formula whose recitation guarantees safety on the march
A prayer priests may speak only over the deserving
God's own name and favor, set on the people
A privilege kept for the priests and their households
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 6:27 explains the gift beneath the words: the blessing puts God's name on the Israelites, and God himself does the blessing.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 6:22-27 to the last verse. Notice who acts once the priests have finished speaking.

nodes.title: Rebellion at the Edge of the Land

comprehension_check.question: Ten spies and two see the same land, the same cities, the same giants (Numbers 13). What actually divides the two reports?
options: Whether the land is as rich as the promise claimed
Whether Israel's forces need more training before an assault
Whether God's promise gets any weight in the assessment
Whether the giants are as large as the majority insists
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 14:8-9 grounds the minority report in the LORD's presence and pleasure, the factor the ten never mention.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 13:30-33 and 14:6-9 again. Notice what Caleb and Joshua bring up that the ten never do.

comprehension_check.question: In Numbers 14 God pardons the people at Moses' plea, yet that generation still dies outside the land. How do the two outcomes fit?
options: Forgiveness stands while the refusal still carries its cost
The pardon was withdrawn again at the very next complaint
Moses won only a stay of execution rather than pardon
The people were spared and only the ten spies punished
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 14:20-23 places the word of pardon and the closed door side by side in a single reply.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 14:20-23 and 14:34 again. Notice what God grants Moses and what he still swears.

nodes.summary: Grumbling escalates to catastrophe: twelve spies scout Canaan, ten spread fear, and the people refuse to enter. The generation of the Exodus is sentenced to die in the wilderness — forty years for forty days of faithless scouting.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Twelve spies walk the same land and come back with two different verdicts. What lets Caleb and Joshua look at the same giants and see promise where the other ten see doom, and what would trusting God's promise over your fear cost you today?
assessment_questions: What do the twelve spies report about Canaan, and how do the people respond?
Moses pleads for Israel by quoting God's own words about his slow anger and steadfast love. Why does his intercession appeal to God's character instead of the people's record?

The people talk themselves into believing slavery in Egypt was better than the risk of trusting God. Where do you romanticize an old comfort instead of stepping toward what God has put in front of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Israel's refusal to trust God's promise at Kadesh costs an entire generation the land, showing that faith is a decision with stakes.
God hears Moses' intercession and pardons the people, yet the consequences of their refusal still stand, so forgiveness and discipline belong to the same God.
Moses intercedes for the very people who exhaust him, and God spreads the load onto seventy elders, showing that spiritual leadership is weight-bearing work.
The grumbling people remember Egypt as a place of free fish rather than slavery, showing how fear distorts the past to excuse distrust in the present.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of the twelve spies and explain why that one refusal at Kadesh cost the Exodus generation the promised land.

connections.reason: Hebrews 3-4 turns the Kadesh refusal into the standing warning: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.'
Psalms 95 and 106 retell this rebellion as Israel's cautionary self-portrait.

nodes.title: Korah's Revolt and the Contested Priesthood

comprehension_check.question: Korah's slogan in Numbers 16:3 sounds true, since the whole congregation is holy. Why does the story treat it as rebellion?
options: It denies that ordinary Israelites carry any holiness at all
It insults Moses, and insulting God's servant is punished
It demands that the priesthood be abolished for everyone
It uses a shared truth to grab a God-given role
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 16:11 names the real target, a company gathered against the LORD who assigned the priesthood.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 16:8-11 again. Notice whom Moses says the company has actually banded against.

comprehension_check.question: After the revolt, the unit turns to a preserved staff, priestly duties, and the red heifer's ashes (Numbers 17-19). What is this material for?
options: Replacing worship at the tent with tighter crowd control
Settling who mediates, and keeping a death-marked camp near God
Rewarding the tribe of Levi with income for its loyalty
Teaching that death no longer defiles those inside the covenant
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 17:10 keeps the staff to end the grumbling, and Numbers 19:9 keeps cleansing ready where death keeps touching.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 17:10 and 19:9 again. Notice what each kept object is for once the crisis passes.

nodes.summary: Korah leads a revolt against Moses and Aaron — 'all the congregation is holy, why do you exalt yourselves?' — and the earth swallows the rebels. Aaron's staff buds to settle whose priesthood God has chosen, and the red heifer rite addresses death's contamination.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Korah's slogan sounds almost right: the whole congregation is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron stand above it? What does the story suggest went wrong in how he used that truth, and how do you tell the difference between serving God and grasping at a role God has not given you?
assessment_questions: What happens to Korah and his followers, and how does God then settle whose priesthood he has chosen?
When the plague breaks out, Aaron runs into the middle of it with incense and stands between the dead and the living. What does that scene teach about what a mediator is for?

Korah was already a Levite with real, God-given work to do, yet he wanted more. Where does envy of someone else's role creep into your life, and what would contentment with your own calling look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The earth swallowing Korah shows that defying the order God has established is a serious matter rather than a mere leadership dispute.
Aaron's staff budding overnight settles the priesthood question with a sign from God, so the community can trust that its mediators serve by appointment rather than ambition.

teaching_concepts.concept: God supplies the remedy for death
teaching_concepts.explanation: The red heifer rite treats contact with death as real defilement and shows that only God can provide the cleansing for it.
The tassels commanded in Numbers 15 turn obedience into a daily visual habit, keeping God's commands in view rather than leaving them to memory alone.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Korah's revolt and its outcome, and explain how Aaron's budding staff and his stand between the dead and the living answer the question of who mediates for Israel.

connections.reason: Jude cites 'Korah's rebellion' as a byword for defying God-given authority.

nodes.title: The Bronze Serpent and Balaam

comprehension_check.question: In Numbers 21:8-9 the cure for the serpent bites is a look at the bronze serpent on the pole. What is the passage teaching through that arrangement?
options: Healing comes through trusting the remedy God appoints
The bronze image held a power Israel could keep using
The serpent's own spirit had to be ritually appeased
God healed the few whose faith was already strong
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 21:8 promises life to any bitten person who looks, so the power sits in God's word behind the sign.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 21:8-9 again. Notice what the bitten must do, and how little it is.

comprehension_check.question: Balak's hired curses fail across Numbers 22-24, yet Israel is devastated in Numbers 25. What does that sequence reveal?
options: The blessings lapsed once the seer was paid and gone
Moab's gods proved stronger at Peor than on the heights
No outside curse can do what Israel's own sin can
God's protection ended when Moses struck the rock in anger
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 23:8 shows the hired curse powerless, and Numbers 25:1-3 shows the wound arriving from inside the camp.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 23:8 and 25:1-3 again. Notice where the real damage finally comes from.

nodes.summary: Moses strikes the rock and forfeits the land; a bronze serpent lifted on a pole heals all who look at it; and the pagan seer Balaam, hired to curse Israel, can only bless — prophesying a star from Jacob. Victory sours at Peor when Israel curses itself through idolatry.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Everyone bitten by the serpents was offered the same cure: look at the bronze serpent lifted on the pole and live. Why do you think God chose a remedy that asked for nothing except a look of trust, and what does that say about how rescue from sin works?
assessment_questions: What does Moses do at the rock in Meribah, and what consequence does God announce for him?
Balaam is hired to curse Israel and finds he can only bless. What does his story reveal about whether God's purposes can be bought or turned aside?

Israel survives every enemy army in these chapters and then falls to temptation at Peor. Why is quiet compromise often more dangerous than open opposition, and where does that warning land in your life?

teaching_concepts.concept: Leaders answer for how they represent God
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses strikes the rock in anger instead of speaking as commanded, and the cost of misrepresenting God before the people is losing entry to the land.

teaching_concepts.concept: A saving sign that points forward
teaching_concepts.explanation: The bronze serpent heals everyone who simply looks in trust, and Jesus later names it as the picture of his own lifting up on the cross.

teaching_concepts.concept: Blessing that cannot be hired away
teaching_concepts.explanation: Balaam's oracles show that God's commitment to bless his people overrides money, kings, and professional curses.
The failure at Peor shows that a people no army could defeat can still defeat itself by embracing idolatry and immorality.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the bronze serpent episode and explain both why Moses was barred from the land and what Balaam's oracles reveal about God's unstoppable blessing.

connections.reason: Jesus makes the bronze serpent the picture of his own lifting up: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness…' (John 3:14).
Balaam's 'star out of Jacob' stands behind the star the magi follow.

nodes.title: The Second Census and the Succession
nodes.summary: After the plague at Peor, a new census counts a new Israel: the generation born in the wilderness, mustered on the plains of Moab for the land their parents refused. The count settles how the land will be divided, and its fairness is immediately tested when the five daughters of Zelophehad claim their dead father's portion and God rules in their favor. Moses, told he will see the land only from a mountain, asks God for a shepherd to replace him, and Joshua is commissioned in public before the priest and the whole assembly.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses hears he will die outside the land, and his first recorded response in Numbers 27:15-17 is a request that the people not be left leaderless. What does that moment reveal about Moses, and what would wanting your work to outlive you that way look like in practice?
assessment_questions: What does Numbers 26:64-65 record about who from the first census is still present in the second, and why?

The daughters of Zelophehad bring a case no existing law covers, and God says their claim is just. What does the way their case is received and answered show about the character of the law being given?

Moses hands his authority to Joshua in public, hands laid on him before the priest and the assembly in Numbers 27:22-23. What is worth imitating in how Moses lets go of his life's work, and where might you be holding something God is asking you to hand on?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The second census counts a nation that did not exist at Sinai, quiet proof that judgment on the parents did not cancel the covenant with the children.
Unlike the first muster, this count is expressly for dividing the land, so the list works like a title deed written in advance, promise treated as fact.
The Zelophehad ruling shows Israel's law able to hear an uncovered case and correct toward justice, with God himself affirming the claim of the overlooked.
Moses asks for a successor in shepherd language and commissions Joshua publicly, modeling authority that seeks the flock's good beyond its own tenure.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what makes the second census different in purpose from the first, and describe how the Zelophehad ruling and Joshua's commissioning each prepare Israel for the land.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 26 repeats the census of chapter 1 with a new generation. What is the second count for?
options: Fixing each tribe's share of the land ahead
Measuring the nation's decline across the wilderness years
Confirming the army's recovery after the plague at Peor
Replacing muster records lost during the forty years
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 26:52-56 draws the conclusion straight from the count: the land is to be apportioned among these names, larger and smaller by their numbers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 26:52-56, the instruction that follows the counting. Notice what the totals are immediately used for.

comprehension_check.question: What does the scene of Numbers 27:12-23 establish about leadership in Israel?
options: Authority passes by seniority to the eldest qualified elder
Each leader should name his own son to guard the legacy
The office ends with Moses, since no one could replace him
God appoints the shepherd, and the handover happens in the open
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 27:18-23 has God name Joshua and Moses commission him before Eleazar and all the congregation, succession given from above and sealed in public.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 27:15-23. Notice who chooses the successor and who is watching when authority changes hands.

connections.reason: Joshua's commissioning here is the hinge into the conquest narrative.

nodes.title: The Offerings Calendar and the Law of Vows
nodes.summary: With the land in view, God fixes Israel's calendar: the daily offerings morning and evening, then Sabbaths, new moons, and the festival cycle from Passover to Tabernacles, each with its prescribed gifts. The rhythm is relentless on purpose, a nation's time claimed hour by hour and season by season for the God it serves. Chapter 30 then turns from public worship to private speech, binding vows and oaths with rules for when a word must stand and who can release it, because a people whose worship is ordered must also mean what it says.
nodes.discussion_prompt: This calendar starts with two offerings every single day before it ever reaches a festival, and the great feasts stand on top of that steady base. Looking at how your own weeks and years are patterned, what does your calendar say you are devoted to, and what would a daily base layer of devotion change?
assessment_questions: What offering opens the calendar in Numbers 28:3-8, and what is its schedule?
The festival list piles daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly rhythms on top of one another. What is a calendar like this designed to do to a people's sense of time?

Numbers 30 treats a spoken vow as something that binds, releasable only through defined relationships and never through convenience. What promise are you currently tempted to quietly downgrade, and what would this chapter's seriousness about words ask of you there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The calendar builds devotion into time itself, daily offerings under weekly, monthly, and yearly feasts, so covenant loyalty becomes a practiced pattern rather than a periodic burst.
Everything festal rests on the morning and evening offering that never lapses, teaching that extraordinary worship grows out of ordinary constancy.
Numbers 28:2 has God call the offerings and their times his own, framing the year as a series of appointments God himself has set.
Numbers 30:2 binds a person to his word because Israel's God keeps his, and the chapter's careful release rules treat spoken words as weighty enough to need law at all.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the layers of Israel's worship calendar from daily to yearly, and explain what Numbers 30 teaches about the weight of a spoken vow.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 28-29 schedules offerings for every day, week, month, and feast of the year. What is the calendar for?
options: Funding the sanctuary's needs through a predictable stream of gifts
Securing good harvests by keeping God continually satisfied
Claiming the whole shape of Israel's time for the LORD
Testing the nation's obedience through sheer ritual demand
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 28:2 sets the frame: these are the LORD's offerings at the LORD's appointed times, so the calendar belongs to him before it belongs to Israel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 28:1-2 and Numbers 29:39. Notice whose appointed times the whole list keeps calling these.

comprehension_check.question: Why does the law of vows in Numbers 30 sit beside the offerings calendar?
options: So worshipers would know which offerings each kind of vow requires
Words offered to God bind like offerings brought to him
It quietly steers Israel away from ever making vows
Private promises outrank the public duties of the feasts
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 30:2 gives a vow the same seriousness as an altar gift: what leaves the lips for God must be carried out.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 30:1-2 right after Numbers 29:39-40. Notice how the subject shifts from what Israel offers to what Israel says.

nodes.title: Last Acts in Moab: Midian, Transjordan, and the Map of the Land
nodes.summary: The wilderness account closes with unfinished business and forward motion: vengeance on Midian for Peor, a hard chapter that refuses to soften Israel's story, then the Transjordan tribes winning their request on the condition that they fight for their brothers first. An itinerary recounts the whole road from Egypt stage by stage. Then the land not yet entered is bounded, allotted, and legislated, with towns for the Levites, refuge for the accused, and a final ruling for Zelophehad's daughters, so that Numbers ends with a map of promises drawn as if the crossing were already done.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Numbers 33 walks back through roughly forty stops on the road from Egypt, most of them places where nothing recorded happened. Why do you think Israel was told to keep the whole list, and what would your own list of stops look like if you wrote out the last decade that way?
assessment_questions: What condition do Reuben and Gad accept in Numbers 32 before they may settle east of the Jordan?

Chapters 34-36 spend their energy on boundaries, Levite towns, and refuge cities for a land Israel has not entered. What does legislating in advance say about how this generation is meant to regard the promise?

Moses warns in Numbers 32:23 that walking away from their brothers' battles would be sin with a way of catching up to them. Where does your own comfort tempt you to settle early while others still fight for theirs, and what would keeping the Numbers 32 bargain look like for you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Transjordan grant binds settlement to solidarity, the first tribes seated only on condition that they arm for the rest, making inheritance a shared project.
The cities of refuge put due process into geography, shielding the accidental killer from vengeance until trial, so mercy and justice are zoned into the land before Israel arrives.
Numbers 35:34 grounds the land law in God's own dwelling among the Israelites, so how they treat blood, boundaries, and neighbors is a matter of hosting his presence.
The itinerary of chapter 33 fixes the whole wilderness road in Israel's memory, each stage a receipt of survival, before the command to take the land in Numbers 33:53.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the condition attached to the Transjordan settlement, what the cities of refuge are for, and why Numbers ends by mapping and legislating a land not yet entered.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers ends with boundary lines, city lists, and inheritance rulings for territory still across the river. What does that ending assert?
options: The coming conquest will succeed through Israel's military readiness
The wilderness generation finally earned the land by patience
Careful planning will keep Israel from losing heart again
The grant is certain enough to be surveyed unseen
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 33:53 rests the whole section on God's word: the land is given, therefore Israel is to take possession and settle it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 33:50-54 and Numbers 34:1-2. Notice how the LORD speaks of the land before anyone has crossed the river.

comprehension_check.question: Why does the law of Numbers 35 set aside cities of refuge in the middle of the tribal allotments?
options: So bloodshed is weighed at trial, ahead of the avenger
So killers of any kind can purchase asylum from the Levites
So the Levite towns gain standing and support among the tribes
So violent men can be banished without more blood being shed
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 35:12 states the purpose: the cities shield the accused from the avenger until he stands before the congregation for judgment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 35:9-15 and Numbers 35:24-25. Notice who the refuge protects and what must happen before any case is settled.

nodes.title: Moses Retells the Journey
nodes.summary: On the plains of Moab, Moses preaches the past: the failure at Kadesh, the wilderness years, the first victories — and warns the new generation that their God is a consuming fire who tolerates no idols. Deuteronomy is the Torah as sermon.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses spends four chapters retelling a story most of his hearers were too young to remember. Why does he treat remembering as a survival skill for faith, and what practices help you keep hold of what God has done before you forget it?
assessment_questions: What failure at Kadesh does Moses retell, and what did it cost the previous generation?

Moses reminds Israel that at Horeb they saw no form of God, only heard a voice, and must therefore make no carved image. What is the connection between how God revealed himself and how he insists on being worshiped?
Moses warns against forgetting slowly, not only rebelling suddenly. What do you quietly rely on for security that could take God's place, and how would you catch that drift early?

teaching_concepts.concept: Faithful in covenant, just in consequence
teaching_concepts.explanation: God keeps his promise of the land while still judging the generation that refused to trust him, so his faithfulness never cancels his justice.
Moses insists the commands be kept in the heart and passed to children, because faith that is never rehearsed and never taught dies in one generation.
Because Israel heard a voice and saw no form at Horeb, any attempt to reduce God to an object misrepresents who he is.
The spies' generation had all the information and still refused to trust, showing that faith turns on trust in God's character rather than on evidence alone.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Moses retells the wilderness story to a generation that did not live it, and summarize the warning of Deuteronomy 4 against idols in your own words.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 4:9 commands Israel to remember what they saw and to teach it to their children. Within Moses' sermon, what work is all this remembering meant to do?
options: It preserves an accurate record for the nation's archives
It earns the next generation the credit their parents forfeited
It keeps trust alive where their parents' trust collapsed
It guarantees the coming conquest by rehearsing the old victories
comprehension_check.why: Moses ties memory to loyalty: the story is retold so the children hold to the God their parents doubted at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 4:9).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 4:9 again, right after the retelling of Horeb. Notice who the remembering is for.

comprehension_check.question: At Horeb Israel heard a voice out of the fire and saw no shape. Why does Moses build the idol ban on that detail in Deuteronomy 4:15-16?
options: An image would misrepresent the God who spoke there
Seeing is a less reliable way of knowing than hearing
The fire made any likeness too dangerous to attempt
Israel might mistake their own carvings for Canaan's gods
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 4:12 stresses that Israel received words and saw no form, so a shape would claim to show what God did not reveal.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 4:12-16 again. Notice what Israel received at Horeb and what they did not.

nodes.title: The Shema: Love the LORD Your God
nodes.summary: The Ten Commandments restated, then the center of Israel's faith: 'Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Love the LORD your God with all your heart.' Jesus called this the greatest commandment; these chapters are also where he draws all three answers to the tempter in the wilderness.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The command at the center of these chapters is to love God with all your heart, soul, and strength. What does it mean for love to be commanded at all, and what would loving God with everything you have change about an ordinary Tuesday for you?
assessment_questions: What does the Shema declare about God, and what does Moses tell parents to do with these words at home and on the road?
Moses warns that the real danger will come after Israel eats and is satisfied in the land. Why does prosperity threaten their memory of God more than hardship did?
Jesus answered temptation with this section's words: man does not live by bread alone. Which appetite in your life most needs that sentence spoken over it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The commandments open with the God who brought Israel out of slavery, so obedience is a response to rescue rather than a way of earning it.
Israel's central confession is that the LORD is one and is to be loved with heart, soul, and strength, making whole-person devotion the core of the covenant.
The commands are to be talked about at home, on the road, at bedtime and morning, so ordinary family conversation becomes the main carrier of faith.
Moses warns that full stomachs and fine houses make people forget the God who provided them, so gratitude has to be practiced deliberately.

nodes.completion_criteria: Recite or paraphrase the Shema, and explain why Moses ties loving God to teaching children and to remembering him in prosperity.

comprehension_check.question: Before any command is given, Deuteronomy 5:6 names God as the one who brought Israel out of slavery. What does that opening establish about the law?
options: Obedience earns the favor God is offering Israel
Obedience answers a rescue that has already happened
Obedience repays a debt Israel owes for Egypt
Obedience completes a rescue that is still unfinished
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 5:6 puts redemption before command, so the law is given to a people God has already saved.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 5:6 again. Notice what God has already done before the first command arrives.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 6:4-7 stands at the center of Israel's faith. What do these verses make the covenant's core demand?
options: Faithful recitation of the words at set times
Complete separation from all the surrounding peoples
Exact obedience to each of the ten commands
Undivided love carried into every corner of life
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 6:5 calls for love with all the heart, soul, and strength, making whole-person devotion the covenant's center.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 6:4-7 again. Notice which single verb the commands gather around.

connections.reason: All three of Jesus' replies to Satan in the wilderness are quotations from Deuteronomy 6-8.
Jesus names the Shema as the first and greatest commandment.

nodes.title: Worship in the Land: One Altar, Festivals, and Release
nodes.summary: The covenant code opens where the Shema pointed: one God will be worshiped at one chosen place, on his own terms, and every rival shrine and homemade cult must go. From there the code moves through the tests of enticing prophets and kin, the clean and unclean table, and a tithe that becomes a feast before the LORD. The rhythm of release follows, debts canceled and slaves freed in the seventh year with open-handedness commanded, and the section closes with the pilgrim festivals, all Israel traveling to appear before God, each bringing what his blessing allows.
nodes.discussion_prompt: This worship code keeps commanding joy: households told to rejoice before the LORD at the altar, at the tithe feast, and at the festivals, with servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows pulled into the celebration. What picture of worship is being painted when joy is legislated and the guest list is that wide, and how does it compare with yours?
assessment_questions: What does Deuteronomy 12:2-7 tell Israel to do about the existing shrines in the land, and where is worship to happen instead?

Deuteronomy 15 concedes that poverty will persist in the land, yet still commands lending freely and giving without a grudging heart. What understanding of ownership and blessing sits underneath a law like that?

Deuteronomy 16:17 measures each worshiper's festival gift by how the LORD has blessed him. If your giving this year were measured by that standard, blessing received against hand opened, what would it show, and what would you change first?

teaching_concepts.concept: One altar against a thousand shrines
teaching_concepts.explanation: Centralizing worship at the chosen place guards Israel from absorbing Canaan's cults and keeps the one God from being reimagined locally, unity of worship protecting truth of worship.
Chapter 12 closes by warning against everyone worshiping as he personally sees fit, making revelation rather than preference the rule of approach to God.
The seventh-year cancellation of debts and freeing of servants translates Israel's own rescue from Egypt into policy, generosity commanded because redemption was received.
Three annual pilgrimages gather the scattered tribes to one place to rehearse the exodus and the harvests together, so Israel's identity is renewed by shared, scheduled joy.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the code begins with the demand for one place of worship, and describe how the release year and the festivals each turn Israel's redemption from Egypt into practice.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 12 orders Canaan's shrines destroyed and worship gathered to the one place the LORD will choose. What is this law protecting?
options: The revenue a single sanctuary would concentrate for the priests
The purity of Israel's worship from the pull of local cults
The holy site itself, since God can be present only there
The land's peace, by ending rivalry between tribal shrines
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 12:4 and 12:30-31 give the reason: Israel must not serve the LORD in the ways the nations served their gods, so the chosen place guards the covenant.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 12:29-31 at the chapter's end. Notice what Israel is warned against asking about the nations' worship.

comprehension_check.question: Chapter 15 commands open hands toward the poor and freed servants sent away loaded with gifts. Where does the law anchor that demand?
options: In the shame a stingy household would bring on its town
In a bargain where generosity purchases the LORD's continued blessing
In the assurance that poverty is about to disappear
In Israel's own memory of being freed and provided for
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 15:15 grounds the command in Israel's own story of slavery and redemption, which is why the freed servant leaves loaded with provisions.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 15:12-15. Notice the reason attached to the command about how a freed servant leaves.

nodes.title: Israel's Offices: Judge, King, Priest, Prophet
nodes.summary: In a few tight paragraphs the code constitutes a nation's public life: judges in every town charged to pursue justice without bribes or favoritism, a king permitted but stripped of the usual engines of royal power and set to daily reading of this law, priests and Levites given service in place of territory, and the promise of a prophet like Moses through whom God will keep speaking. Every office faces the same direction, standing under the covenant word rather than over it, and even prophecy is given a test to keep it honest.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Israel's king is denied the tools ancient kings ran on, war horses, a harem of alliances, and heaped-up gold, and is assigned daily reading of the covenant instead. What is this law trying to make a ruler into, and what would its equivalent look like for the kinds of power you see up close?
assessment_questions: What is Israel's future king commanded to do with this law in Deuteronomy 17:18-20, and what three things is he forbidden to multiply?
Judges, king, priests, and prophet are each defined by limits and duties before God. Taken together, what vision of power do the four offices add up to?

Deuteronomy 18:21-22 anticipates the question of how to tell a true word from a false one and gives Israel a test. Where do you currently take in voices claiming authority, and what tests do you actually apply before trusting them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The section opens by seating courts in every town and binding them to impartiality, making everyday local justice the ground the other offices stand on.

The law strips the throne of harem, treasury, and war machine and chains it to a handwritten copy of the covenant, an inversion of ancient kingship that Israel's later story keeps measuring its kings against.
Priests and Levites live from the offerings and hold no tribal territory, their support woven into worship so that the teachers of the law depend on the people they teach.
God promises to keep speaking through a prophet he will raise up, with listening as the command and fulfillment as the test, a promise the New Testament applies to Jesus.

nodes.completion_criteria: List the four offices of this section with the main limit or duty attached to each, and explain what the promise of a prophet like Moses adds to Israel's future.

comprehension_check.question: The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14-20 forbids the usual royal accumulations and prescribes daily reading instead. What is the design?
options: A ruler kept humble and governed by the covenant
A throne kept weak so that priests hold the real power
A test proving whether Israel deserves a king at all
A king made in the image of the nations' emperors
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 17:19-20 gives the aim: daily reading so the king learns to fear the LORD and stays level with his brothers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 17:16-20. Notice what the king is denied, what he must produce by hand, and what the reading is said to prevent.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 18:9-22 bans the nations' divination and then promises a prophet like Moses. How do the ban and the promise fit together?
options: Israel may use only divination its own priests supervise
Israel must wait without revelation until the prophet arrives
God's own speech replaces the nations' hidden arts
Israel replaces the pagan seers with a hereditary office
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 18:14-15 draws the contrast itself: the dispossessed nations listen to diviners, while Israel will listen to the prophet the LORD raises up.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 18:14-18. Notice the word about listening that links what the nations do with what Israel must do.

connections.reason: Stephen cites Deuteronomy 18's 'prophet like Moses' promise of Jesus (Acts 7:37), as Peter does in Acts 3:22.
Peter's temple sermon identifies Jesus as Deuteronomy 18's 'prophet like Moses.'

nodes.title: Life Together: Justice, Warfare, Family, and Mercy
nodes.summary: The code now walks through common life: cities of refuge and the law of witnesses, rules that restrain war, and a dense weave of household and neighbor cases, marriage wronged, property strayed, wages withheld, gleanings left for the poor. Under the variety runs one refrain, Israel told again and again to remember its own slavery, so that mercy to the vulnerable becomes the nation's signature. The code then closes in liturgy: firstfruits offered with the wandering-Aramean confession, and Israel and the LORD each declaring the other their own.
nodes.discussion_prompt: These chapters legislate small mercies, a cloak returned by sunset, wages paid the same day, sheaves left where they fell, a mother bird let go. Why do you think a national law code descends to details this small, and which small structural mercy could you build into your own routines?
assessment_questions: According to Deuteronomy 24:17-22, which three groups keep reappearing in these protections, and what memory is Israel told to attach to them?

The code ends its long run of cases with the firstfruits liturgy and the mutual declarations of Deuteronomy 26:16-19. What does closing hundreds of laws with worship and belonging say about what all the laws were for?

The gleaning law provides for the poor by telling owners what to leave rather than what to hand out. What is the difference between those two kinds of giving, and where could you leave an edge of your field this month?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Refuge cities, multiple witnesses, and proportionate penalties build restraint into the system itself, so the innocent are protected from mobs and courts alike.
Chapter 20 and its companions put limits, exemptions, and obligations around warfare, refusing to let necessity or victory suspend Israel's accountability to God.
The code keeps grounding protections for the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow in Israel's own years as slaves, making compassion an act of remembering.
The code closes with gratitude spoken over a basket of firstfruits and covenant declarations exchanged, revealing obedience as the shape of a relationship rather than a ledger.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe three concrete protections this section builds for the vulnerable and the memory each is tied to, and explain how chapter 26 turns the whole code into covenant commitment.

comprehension_check.question: Laws about cloaks, wages, and gleanings keep citing Israel's years in Egypt. What work is that memory doing in the code?
options: It warns that disobedience could send Israel back to slavery
It ranks the redeemed nation above the foreigners among them
It dates the laws to the generation that left Egypt
It makes Israel's own rescue the measure of its mercy
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 24:18 attaches the reason directly to the command: Israel remembers slavery and redemption, and treats the vulnerable accordingly.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 24:17-22. Notice the sentence that repeats after the commands and what it asks Israel to recall.

comprehension_check.question: After chapters of case law, the code ends in Deuteronomy 26 with a confession over firstfruits and mutual declarations. What does the ending reveal?
options: The rituals of chapter 26 outrank the case laws before them
The laws aim at a people bound to God in love
The whole code was recited yearly at the firstfruits ceremony
The closing confession earns blessings the laws alone could not
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 26:17-19 seals the code with a mutual pledge, Israel declaring the LORD its God and the LORD declaring Israel his treasured people.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 26:16-19. Notice who makes a declaration in these verses and what each party declares.

nodes.title: Blessing, Curse, and the Choice of Life
nodes.summary: Covenant blessings for obedience, devastating curses for rebellion — up to and including exile — and then, astonishingly, a promise beyond the curse: God will circumcise hearts and bring his scattered people home. 'Choose life.' The prophets and Paul both build on these chapters.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses lays out blessing and curse, predicts that Israel will fail, and then promises that God will circumcise their hearts so they can finally love him. What does that sequence suggest about where the power to obey actually comes from, and what would asking God for a changed heart mean for you?
assessment_questions: What two paths does Moses set before Israel at the end of chapter 30, and what does he beg them to choose?
Before Israel has even entered the land, chapter 30 already assumes exile and promises return. What does it mean that restoration is written into the covenant from the very start?
Moses says the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so obedience is within reach. Which choice in front of you right now is really a choice between life and death in slow motion?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The blessings and curses declare that covenant choices carry real outcomes, up to and including exile from the land.
The covenant addresses the whole nation while summoning each Israelite to choose, so no one can hide inside the crowd or stand outside the community.
God promises to gather his scattered people when they return to him, so failure is anticipated and mercy is already prepared on the far side of it.
Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that God himself will change hearts so that love for him becomes possible, pointing forward to inward renewal rather than mere rule-keeping.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the choice Moses sets before Israel in Deuteronomy 30, and describe what the promise of a circumcised heart adds to the blessings and curses.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy 30:1-3 promises return and regathering, placed directly after the curse chapters. What does that placement reveal?
options: The covenant already carries mercy for its own breaking
The curses were warnings God never intended to enforce
Israel will avoid exile if this generation stays faithful
Repentance can cancel the curse before it ever lands
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 30:1 assumes the curse will actually fall and still promises regathering beyond it, so mercy is written into the covenant from the start.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 30:1-3 again. Notice which events Moses treats as certain before the return is promised.

comprehension_check.question: The command is to love God with the whole heart, yet Deuteronomy 30:6 promises that the LORD himself will circumcise Israel's heart. What does that promise admit?
options: Wholehearted love is a goal reached by steady practice
Covenant obedience requires a change only God can give
God rewards the love Israel first works up itself
Israel's failure came from laws that asked too much
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 30:6 has God performing the circumcision so that love for him follows, locating the deepest obedience in his gift.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 30:6 again. Notice who performs the circumcising and what it is meant to produce.

connections.reason: 'Cursed is everyone hanged on a tree' (Deut 21) and the curse of the law (Deut 27) anchor Galatians 3.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30's 'the word is near you' as the voice of righteousness by faith.
The exile to Babylon is the Deuteronomy 28 curse executed in history.

The great confession of Nehemiah 9 retells Israel's whole history in Deuteronomy's blessing-and-curse categories — and the closing failures show why Deuteronomy 30's promised heart-circumcision is still outstanding.

nodes.title: The Death of Moses
nodes.summary: Moses commissions Joshua, teaches Israel a witness-song predicting their future failure and God's faithfulness, blesses the tribes, and dies on Mount Nebo overlooking a land he will never enter. 'No prophet like him has arisen since' — a deliberate cliffhanger the New Testament answers.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses climbs Nebo, sees the land he spent forty years walking toward, and dies without entering it. What do these chapters say about a faithful life that ends with promises still open, and how does that change what you would count as a successful life?
assessment_questions: Where does Moses die, who buries him, and what does the closing tribute say made him unlike any prophet since?
God has Moses teach Israel a song that predicts their unfaithfulness before it happens. Why would God give a people a witness-song against themselves?

Moses tells Joshua that the LORD goes before him and will never leave him or forsake him. What task feels too big for you right now, and how would taking that promise seriously change the way you step into it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses commissions Joshua before he dies, showing that the covenant work continues on God's faithfulness rather than on any one leader.

teaching_concepts.concept: The word made public and memorable
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses has the law written down and read aloud to everyone, so covenant faith is preserved as a shared possession that each generation can hear.
The Song of Moses announces both Israel's future failure and God's faithfulness, standing as a testimony the people carry in their own mouths.

teaching_concepts.concept: Even the greatest servant is mortal
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses dies with the promise still ahead of him, leaving a deliberate cliffhanger that keeps hope fixed on God and on the prophet still to come.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the death of Moses on Nebo, and explain what the Song of Moses and Joshua's commissioning each say about God's faithfulness beyond one leader's life.

comprehension_check.question: In Deuteronomy 31:16-21 God predicts Israel's apostasy before Moses even dies, then commissions a song about it. What does this pairing say about the covenant's future?
options: The covenant will lapse once the apostasy arrives
The next generation may yet escape the prediction
God regrets the covenant he made at Horeb
Israel's coming failure is foreseen and already answered
comprehension_check.why: In Deuteronomy 31:21 God commissions the song precisely because he knows what Israel will do, so provision outruns the failure.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 31:19-21 again. Notice when the song is written relative to the sin it concerns.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy ends with Moses dead outside the land and a note in Deuteronomy 34:10 that no prophet like him has risen. What kind of ending is that?
options: A closed ending, the Torah's story finished at Moses' grave
An open ending that keeps Israel waiting on God's promise
A cautionary ending about trusting any single human leader
A quiet ending meant to honor Moses above the law
comprehension_check.why: Deuteronomy 34:4 shows the promise still ahead and Deuteronomy 34:10 leaves the prophet's place unfilled, so the book closes leaning forward.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Deuteronomy 34:4 and 34:10 together. Notice what Moses sees and what the final verses say has not yet come.

connections.reason: Moses finally stands in the promised land at the Transfiguration, beside the prophet greater than he.

nodes.title: Crossing into the Land
nodes.summary: Joshua takes command, Rahab the Canaanite hides the spies and joins Israel, and the Jordan parts like a second Red Sea. The promise made to Abraham back in Genesis finally touches ground.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Rahab is a Canaanite in a doomed city, yet she is the one who declares that Israel's God rules heaven and earth. What do her faith and Joshua's courage each show about how a person steps into what God is doing, and what step like that is in front of you right now?
assessment_questions: What happens when the priests carry the ark into the Jordan, and what are the twelve stones taken from the riverbed for?
God tells Joshua three times to be strong and courageous, and each time the reason is that the LORD will be with him. Why does the command rest on God's presence instead of Joshua's qualifications?
Rahab risked her life on what she had only heard about Israel's God. What have you learned about God secondhand that is now asking for a firsthand decision from you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The crossing into Canaan is the promise to Abraham finally landing, showing that God's word holds across centuries and generations.
Joshua is told to be strong because the LORD is with him wherever he goes, so courage comes from who is beside you rather than what you can do.
Rahab the Canaanite trusts Israel's God on the strength of what she has heard, and she is rescued and folded into God's people.
The memorial stones, the circumcision at Gilgal, and the Passover all mark God's saving acts so that future generations can ask and be told.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the Jordan crossing and Rahab's story, and explain why the memorial stones at Gilgal mattered for the generations to come.

comprehension_check.question: The memorial stones get their meaning in Joshua 4:21-24, where the Jordan crossing is set beside the Red Sea. What are the stones meant to keep saying?
options: The exodus God is the same God acting now
The new generation has now matched their parents' faith
Israel's army crossed with a skill worth remembering
The river gave way to the priests' obedient courage
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 4:23-24 links the Jordan to the Red Sea so that every generation and all peoples recognize the same mighty hand at work.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 4:21-24 again. Notice which older story the stones are tied to and who is meant to hear about it.

comprehension_check.question: Rahab's speech in Joshua 2:9-11 comes before Israel has won a single battle in the land. What does her rescue show about how someone comes under this God's protection?
options: She acted from political fear of a stronger army
The spies owed her protection as payment for hiding them
Faith in Israel's God mattered more than her ancestry
Her kindness earned her family an exemption from judgment
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 2:11 records Rahab confessing that Israel's God is God of heaven and earth, and that trust is what brings her house through.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 2:9-11 again. Notice what Rahab says she has heard and where her conclusion lands.

connections.reason: Rahab appears in Jesus' genealogy — the Canaanite convert becomes an ancestor of the Messiah.
Rahab and the walls of Jericho both appear in Hebrews' roll call of faith.
Joshua's commissioning here is the hinge into the conquest narrative.

nodes.title: Jericho and Ai
nodes.summary: Jericho's walls fall to trumpet blasts, but Achan's hidden theft brings defeat at Ai — one man's sin costs the whole camp. Victory in this book runs on obedience, not military strength.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jericho falls without Israel swinging a sword, and Ai defeats them the moment one man hides stolen treasure. What do those two battles together teach about where Israel's strength actually comes from, and what hidden thing would you have to bring into the open to live that way?
assessment_questions: How does Jericho fall, and what causes Israel's defeat at Ai?
God says Israel cannot stand against its enemies because of one man's hidden theft. Why does the story treat Achan's private sin as the whole camp's problem?
Achan confesses only after he is exposed. What would it look like to deal with a hidden compromise in your own life before it costs you and the people around you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Marching around a wall for seven days is military nonsense, and Jericho falls anyway, because the battle runs on God's word rather than Israel's tactics.
Achan's secret theft brings defeat on the whole camp, showing that within God's people sin is never a purely private matter.

teaching_concepts.concept: Dealing with sin restores the mission
teaching_concepts.explanation: Once the hidden sin is confronted and removed, God sends Israel back to Ai with the promise of victory, so honesty reopens the way forward.
After Ai, Joshua builds an altar and reads the whole law aloud, because winning the land matters only if Israel lives rightly in it.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Israel wins at Jericho and loses at Ai, and what Achan's story shows about the cost of hidden sin to a community.

comprehension_check.question: Seven days of silent marching is no way to take a city. What is Jericho's strange battle plan teaching Israel?
options: Patience and repetition are the highest military virtues
Worship rituals can be weaponized when armies are outmatched
God tests obedience with commands that make no sense
The land will be won by trusting God's word
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 6:2 hands the city over as already delivered before the first lap, so the marching is trust acting on a promise.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 6:2 again, before the instructions start. Notice the tense of what God says about Jericho.

comprehension_check.question: One man stole from Jericho, yet Joshua 7:1 says anger burned against Israel, and the whole army fails at Ai. What is the story insisting on?
options: Sin inside the covenant community is never purely private
Every military setback signals some hidden sin somewhere
The theft mattered mainly because it shorted the LORD's treasury
God's presence abandons Israel whenever any member sins
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 7:11 charges all Israel with breaking the covenant over one hidden theft, because the camp stands before God as one body.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 7:1 and 7:11 again. Notice who the text says sinned and who the text says is charged.

nodes.title: The Southern and Northern Campaigns
nodes.summary: The Gibeonites trick their way into a treaty, the sun stands still over Gibeon, and the conquest sweeps south then north. These chapters raise the Bible's hardest ethical questions about the herem ('devoted to destruction') warfare texts.
nodes.tradition_notes: All major traditions have wrestled with the conquest's ethics rather than splitting along confessional lines: readings range from straightforward divine judgment on Canaanite practice, to ancient Near Eastern hyperbole (fortified military centers, not total populations), to typological readings (the church fathers often read the conquest as spiritual warfare). The graph notes the difficulty; it does not resolve it.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Israel swears an oath to the Gibeonites without asking God first, then keeps it even though it was won by trickery, and God himself fights to defend Gibeon. What does that whole episode show about how seriously God's people should take their word, and what promise are you tempted to treat as optional?
assessment_questions: How do the Gibeonites obtain a treaty with Israel, and what happens when their trick is discovered?

The text notes that Israel did not inquire of the LORD before the Gibeonite treaty, yet God later throws his power behind defending Gibeon. What does that sequence suggest about how God regards the commitments his people make?

These chapters raise hard questions about God's judgment on Canaan that faithful readers still wrestle with. How do you handle a part of Scripture that troubles you without ignoring it and without walking away from it?

teaching_concepts.concept: Oaths bind even when gained by deception
teaching_concepts.explanation: Israel honors the Gibeonite treaty because it was sworn in the LORD's name, showing that a promise made before God stays serious even when you were fooled into it.
The hailstones and the long day at Gibeon present the victories as God's own intervention, so the conquest is his act rather than Israel's military achievement.
The text presents the ban as God's judgment on centuries of Canaanite practice rather than ethnic conquest, and every major tradition still wrestles honestly with how to read it.

teaching_concepts.concept: Hard texts drive us to humility
teaching_concepts.explanation: Passages like these are meant to be studied with prayer and with the church rather than solved with quick answers or quietly skipped.

nodes.completion_criteria: Summarize the southern and northern campaigns, and explain why Israel honored the Gibeonite treaty even though it was obtained by deception.

comprehension_check.question: Hailstones outkill swords, the sun stands still, and kings fall in a sweep. What do these chapters want Israel to conclude about the conquest?
options: Their army had become the strongest force in Canaan
The land was a gift and God the giver
Bold tactics plus favorable weather explain the sweep
Total war was now Israel's permanent divine calling
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 10:14 and 10:42 credit the campaign to the LORD fighting for Israel, so the land is received before it is achieved.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 10:14 and 10:42 again. Notice who the narrator says was doing the fighting.

comprehension_check.question: Israel is tricked into the Gibeonite treaty, discovers the fraud, and keeps the treaty anyway in Joshua 9:18-19. What carries that decision?
options: Mercy toward Gibeon outweighed the command about the land
Breaking treaties would have provoked the remaining kings
An oath sworn in the LORD's name stays binding
Gibeon's cleverness earned them a place in Israel
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 9:19 shows the leaders bound by their own oath before the LORD, so his name outweighs their blunder.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 9:14-19 again. Notice what step Israel skipped, and what the leaders say they cannot undo.

nodes.title: The Tribal Allotments
nodes.summary: Seven chapters distribute the land tribe by tribe: the Transjordan grants first, then Judah and the Joseph tribes at Gilgal, then the seven remaining tribes surveyed and allotted at Shiloh. Caleb, eighty-five and undimmed, claims the hill country promised him forty-five years earlier, while Joshua has to rebuke seven tribes still camped instead of possessing. The boundary lists read like a deed of title, the promise to Abraham parceled out in named towns and borders, yet the text keeps admitting how much land remains untaken.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Caleb asks for the Anakim's hill country at eighty-five, while seven whole tribes sit at Shiloh until Joshua asks how long they will put off possessing what God has given. What separates receiving a promise from possessing it, and which of those two postures looks more like yours right now?
assessment_questions: What does Caleb ask for in Joshua 14:12, and what question does Joshua put to the seven waiting tribes in Joshua 18:3?

The section opens with God telling an old Joshua that much land remains, then records the whole country as allotted. Why does the book present the gift as settled in the lists while admitting the taking is unfinished?

Caleb claims his mountain at eighty-five; seven tribes need a rebuke before they move. Where has God's faithfulness already given you ground you have not yet walked onto, and what would claiming it look like this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The boundary lists record God's faithfulness parcel by parcel, working like a signed title so that every tribe and generation can point to what the promise delivered.
The land is given by promise yet must still be possessed, and Joshua 13:1 and 18:3 hold God's grace and Israel's responsibility in a single frame.
Forty-five years of waiting have not loosened Caleb's grip on what God said; he asks for the hardest hill country while younger tribes hesitate at Shiloh.
