Each tribe's life is framed by assigned boundaries, duties, and shared memory, so belonging to God's people means living within what he apportions rather than grabbing what you can.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the book devotes seven chapters to boundary lists, and what Caleb's claim and Joshua's rebuke each show about possessing what God has given.

comprehension_check.question: Joshua 13-19 spends seven chapters on borders and town lists. Within the book, what are those lists doing?
options: Recording each tribe's portion as proof the promise was delivered
Preserving tax and census districts for the later monarchy
Ranking the tribes by the quality of land each received
Mapping battle lines for campaigns still ahead in the book
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 14:1-2 presents the allotment as the LORD's own distribution, commanded through Moses, so the lists document a promise being kept parcel by parcel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 14:1-2 again. Notice whose command stands behind each tribe's assigned portion.

comprehension_check.question: Joshua 13:1 and 18:3 both admit that land remains untaken even as it is being allotted. What is that tension teaching?
options: The conquest failed and the lists paper over that failure
The gift stands secure while possessing it remains Israel's calling
God withdrew parts of the grant when tribes proved slow
Each tribe was granted only the ground its obedience earned
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 18:3 lays the delay at the tribes' feet, never the promise's: the land is already given by God and waits to be entered.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 18:3 again. Notice who Joshua says the delay belongs to, and what he says God has already done.

nodes.title: Cities of Refuge and the Levites' Towns
nodes.summary: With the territories drawn, Israel appoints the six cities of refuge commanded through Moses, where anyone who killed without intent can flee the avenger of blood and stand trial. The Levites then receive forty-eight towns scattered through every tribe, since their inheritance is the LORD's service rather than a region of their own. The section closes with the narrator's sweeping verdict: the LORD gave the land, gave rest on every side, and let not one of his good promises fall.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The refuge cities mean that even in a land of blood avengers, an accidental killer is never far from due process. What does it say about God that he builds mercy into the map itself, and where could your community use a structure of mercy instead of relying on good intentions?
assessment_questions: Who may flee to a city of refuge according to Joshua 20:2-3, and from whom does the city protect him?
The Levites receive towns inside every other tribe's territory instead of a region of their own. What does that scattering accomplish for Israel, and what does it say about the Levites' inheritance?

The narrator declares that not one good promise failed, right after founding institutions that assume Israel will keep sinning. How do you hold God's faithfulness and your community's ongoing failure together, and what would building refuge for someone look like for you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The refuge city shields the accidental killer from the avenger until a fair hearing, honoring both the seriousness of blood and the difference intent makes.
The Levites' scattered towns place servants of the sanctuary within reach of every tribe, and the LORD himself, rather than any acreage, is their inheritance.
Joshua 21:43-45 closes the conquest with a threefold claim, land given, rest granted, promises kept, the conclusion the whole allotment has been building toward.
Refuge cities and Levitical towns build faithfulness into structures, so that mercy and worship in Israel do not depend on anyone's mood or memory.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what the cities of refuge were for and why the Levites received scattered towns, and explain the claim Joshua 21:45 makes about God's promises.

comprehension_check.question: What understanding of justice do the refuge cities of Joshua 20 build into Israel's land?
options: Bloodshed can be settled privately once tempers have cooled
Killing done without intent deserves protection and a hearing
Any killer who reaches sacred ground escapes all judgment
Vengeance belongs to the family until the courts mature
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 20:3 shelters the one who killed unintentionally, and Joshua 20:6 still requires him to stand trial before the assembly.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 20:3-6 again. Notice which kind of killer the city receives, and what still has to happen at the gate.

comprehension_check.question: After all the allotments, Joshua 21:43-45 declares that nothing God promised failed. What is that verdict doing at this point in the book?
options: Sealing the lists as evidence that God's sworn word held
Claiming every enemy inside the land had been destroyed
Promising Israel that its rest could never again be lost
Crediting Israel's armies with finishing the whole conquest
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 21:43-45 states the conclusion the boundary lists were compiled to prove: the LORD gave, Israel received, and every word stood.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 21:43-45 again. Notice who the verbs belong to in all three verses.

nodes.title: Choose This Day: Covenant at Shechem
nodes.summary: An altar misunderstanding nearly sparks civil war, Joshua delivers his farewell, and at Shechem the tribes formally choose: 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.' The book ends with the covenant renewed — and a warning that Israel may not keep it.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Joshua tells the tribes to choose this day whom they will serve, and when they answer confidently he warns them they may not be able to keep that promise. What makes serving the LORD costlier than the crowd's quick yes suggests, and what would that choice cost you today?
assessment_questions: What nearly causes civil war over the eastern tribes' altar in chapter 22, and how is the crisis resolved?
When the people promise to serve the LORD, Joshua pushes back and says they cannot. Why does he challenge their easy commitment instead of simply accepting it?
Joshua says that as for him and his house, they will serve the LORD. What competing loyalty would you have to put away to say that honestly?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Joshua will not let Israel drift into loyalty; he makes them name their God out loud, because covenant faith is chosen rather than inherited.
The eastern tribes build their altar as a witness for future generations, and Joshua retells Israel's whole story at Shechem, because forgetting what God did is the first step to leaving him.

teaching_concepts.concept: Divided loyalty is the real threat
teaching_concepts.explanation: Joshua's warnings target the foreign gods still in Israel's midst, since quiet syncretism can undo a people that open war never could.
The altar crisis nearly becomes civil war until the tribes send a delegation and hear the explanation, showing how covenant community handles suspicion with words before weapons.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the covenant renewal at Shechem and explain why Joshua warns the people about the seriousness of the promise they are making.

comprehension_check.question: With the land at rest, Joshua's last act in Joshua 24:15 is making Israel say out loud whom they will serve. What does the scene teach about covenant faith?
options: It must be renewed by each generation's own decision
It is a private preference each household selects freely
It was secured for good by the fathers at Sinai
It is guaranteed by living inside the promised land
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 24:15 puts the choice to households who already belong, because covenant loyalty lives only where it is freshly chosen.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 24:14-19 again. Notice what Joshua says when the people answer too quickly.

comprehension_check.question: A second altar nearly starts a civil war, until the eastern tribes explain themselves in Joshua 22:24-27. What was their altar actually for?
options: Worship, so the eastern tribes could sacrifice closer to home
Defense, marking a border the western tribes must respect
Rivalry, an eastern shrine built to compete with Shiloh
Witness, so future generations kept their place in Israel
comprehension_check.why: Joshua 22:27 makes the altar a testimony between the tribes so that coming generations still claim their share in the LORD.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joshua 22:24-27 again. Notice what the builders say their children might one day be told.

connections.reason: Judges opens by replaying Joshua's death — and then showing the generation that did not choose.

nodes.title: The Unfinished Conquest and the Cycle
nodes.summary: Israel fails to finish what Joshua began, a generation arises that 'did not know the LORD,' and chapter 2 lays out the book's tragic loop: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, relapse. The cycle is the thesis; everything after is evidence.
nodes.discussion_prompt: A whole generation grows up that does not know the LORD or what he did for Israel. How do these chapters show that happening one small compromise at a time, and what is your own generation at risk of forgetting?
assessment_questions: What repeating pattern does chapter 2 describe in Israel's life after Joshua's generation dies?
Israel drifts from God gradually, starting with the failure to drive out its neighbors. Why does the book treat partial obedience as the seed of the whole tragedy?
The cycle begins when memory fails. What practices keep the story of what God has done alive for you, and which ones have you let slide?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Israel finishes most of the conquest and tolerates the rest, and that leftover compromise becomes the snare that pulls the nation into idolatry.
Chapter 2 lays out the loop of sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and relapse, and the whole book is that loop turning over and over.
Even while judging Israel's unfaithfulness, God is moved by their groaning and keeps raising deliverers, so his patience runs through the whole sad story.
The disaster starts with a generation that never learned what God had done, which makes passing on the story a matter of survival for God's people.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the judges cycle from Judges 2 in your own words, and explain how partial obedience set it in motion.

comprehension_check.question: Before a single judge appears, Judges 2:11-19 lays out a whole pattern of rebellion, oppression, crying out, and rescue. What is that preview for?
options: It summarizes troubles finished before the judges ever arose
It gives the frame every following story will keep proving
It promises each judge will leave Israel a little stronger
It shows the pattern broke as soon as Israel understood it
comprehension_check.why: Judges 2:19 already notes that each relapse sinks deeper than the one before, the downward spiral the rest of the book documents.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 2:16-19 again. Notice what happens every time a judge dies, and which direction each new round moves.

comprehension_check.question: Israel cries out and God delivers, round after round. What does Judges 2:18 reveal about why the rescues keep coming?
options: Each round of crying out proves Israel has truly repented
The judges' own merits persuade God to grant the victories
Israel's suffering completes the punishment its sin had earned
God cannot bear the misery his own people are in
comprehension_check.why: Judges 2:18 grounds each rescue in the LORD's own compassion at what oppression was doing to his people.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 2:18-19 again. Notice the motive the text gives God, and what it never says about Israel.

connections.reason: Judges opens by replaying Joshua's death — and then showing the generation that did not choose.

nodes.title: Deborah and Gideon
nodes.summary: The early deliverers: Ehud's left-handed assassination, Deborah and Jael breaking Canaanite power, and Gideon's three hundred routing Midian with torches and trumpets — God saving through the weak so no one can boast. Gideon's story already shows the rot: he ends by making an idol.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God cuts Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred so that Israel cannot claim the victory for itself. Why does God insist on winning through weakness, and where might your own sense of being under-equipped be exactly the place God wants to work?
assessment_questions: How does God reduce Gideon's army, and how is Midian defeated?
God tells Gideon the army is too large in case Israel boasts that her own hand has saved her. What does that reason reveal about the point of these victories?
Gideon ends his story by making an ephod that becomes a snare to his family and to Israel. How can a good gift or a real victory turn into an idol in your own life?

teaching_concepts.explanation: A left-handed assassin, a woman with a tent peg, and a fearful farmer become Israel's deliverers, because salvation is God's work rather than a reward for human merit.
Three hundred men with torches and trumpets rout an army, making it unmistakable that the strength belongs to God.
The narrative includes deception and rough violence without pausing to approve them, showing God working his purposes through a messy, sinful world.
Gideon refuses a crown and then builds an ephod that Israel worships, proving that even a faithful deliverer can plant the seeds of the next relapse.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Gideon's story from his call to the ephod, and explain why God shrank his army to three hundred.

comprehension_check.question: A left-handed loner, a woman with a tent peg, a farmer hiding from Midian, an army cut to three hundred. Why does Judges keep choosing deliverers like these?
options: To keep the saving unmistakably God's, with no room for boasting
To celebrate the underdog cunning of Israel's folk heroes
To show any weapon becomes holy once the cause is just
To prove Israel's enemies were feebler than they appeared
comprehension_check.why: Judges 7:2 explains the shrinking of Gideon's army, God removing every ground for Israel to credit itself with the rescue.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 7:2 again. Notice the danger God names before the battle, which has nothing to do with Midian.

comprehension_check.question: Gideon turns down the crown and points Israel to the LORD's rule (Judges 8:23), then makes an ephod that Israel worships (Judges 8:27). What is that ending showing?
options: Proof that his refusal of kingship settled Israel's loyalty
Blame for the people alone while Gideon's hands stay clean
The next relapse starting inside the deliverer himself
A veteran's reward of gold his triumph had fairly earned
comprehension_check.why: Judges 8:27 counts Gideon and his own family among the ephod's victims, seed of the idolatry the next cycle will reap.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 8:22-27 again. Notice how quickly the man who refused to rule produces something Israel serves.

connections.reason: Gideon and Barak appear in Hebrews 11's catalogue of faith.

nodes.title: Abimelech and Jephthah: Deliverers Gone Dark
nodes.summary: Gideon's son Abimelech murders his seventy brothers to be king, and Jephthah's rash vow costs him his daughter. The deliverers are now nearly as broken as the oppression they end — the book is deliberately darkening.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jephthah tries to secure God's help with a vow he never stops to weigh, and it costs him his daughter. What does his story teach about the difference between trusting God and trying to bargain with him, and where do you catch yourself bargaining instead of trusting?
assessment_questions: How does Abimelech become ruler, and how does his reign end?
Jotham's fable pictures Abimelech as a bramble reigning over the trees. What is the fable saying about the kind of leadership Israel has chosen?
Jephthah's vow was rash speech aimed at guaranteeing an outcome. What commitments do you make carelessly, and what would sober, weighed speech look like instead?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Abimelech murders seventy brothers to seize power, and his violent rise produces tyranny and ruin for everyone under him.
With no king and failing judges, God still repays Abimelech's wickedness, showing that moral order holds even when human structures collapse.
Jephthah's hasty promise brings grief that careful, honest speech would have avoided, and readers across traditions still debate exactly how his vow was fulfilled.
Even in this dark stretch, God cannot bear Israel's misery, so his mercy keeps working underneath the nation's decay.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Abimelech's rise and fall and Jephthah's vow each show the deliverers themselves going dark.

comprehension_check.question: Abimelech murders seventy brothers, rules three years, and dies under a dropped millstone. What does the narrator want seen in that arc (Judges 9:56-57)?
options: Violent men naturally destroy themselves without any divine hand
Israel being punished for flirting with the idea of kings
A tyrant's fall restoring Israel's faith for a generation
God's justice at work where every human institution failed
comprehension_check.why: Judges 9:24 says the strife came so the crime against the seventy would be answered, and Judges 9:56 confirms God repaid it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 9:23-24 and Judges 9:56-57. Notice who the narrator says stood behind the falling-out and the reckoning.

comprehension_check.question: The Spirit of the LORD comes on Jephthah before he ever opens his mouth to vow (Judges 11:29-31). What does that order of events suggest about the vow?
options: It was the act of faith that qualified him to win
It bargained for a victory God was already giving
It secured a greater triumph than the Spirit alone would
It was the standard price every deliverer paid for victory
comprehension_check.why: Judges 11:29 has the Spirit on Jephthah and his campaign moving before the vow of Judges 11:30-31 is ever spoken.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 11:29-31 in order. Notice what has already happened before Jephthah starts making conditions.

nodes.title: Samson
nodes.summary: A lifelong Nazirite with supernatural strength and no self-control, Samson fights Philistines mostly over personal grievances — and wins his greatest victory blind, in chains, at the cost of his life. The strongest judge is the weakest man; Israel needs something better than heroes.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Samson has every advantage: a calling from before birth, the Spirit's power, unmatched strength. He loses it all chasing what he wants in the moment. What does his story show about the gap between gifting and character, and which of the two are you actually building?
assessment_questions: What vow sets Samson apart from birth, and how does he finally lose his strength?
The saddest line in the story says Samson did not know that the LORD had left him. How did he reach the point of not even noticing?
Samson's gifts outran his self-control. Where does your own strength or talent tempt you to skip the slow work of character, and what would guarding your heart look like this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Samson is set apart from the womb and empowered by the Spirit, yet he remains ruled by appetite, so God's choosing of a person is no guarantee of their character.

teaching_concepts.concept: Outward vows cannot replace an inward heart
teaching_concepts.explanation: Samson keeps the external marks of a Nazirite for years while breaking its spirit at every turn, showing that consecration on the surface can hide sin underneath.
Samson's choices cost him his eyes, his freedom, and finally his life, because divine empowerment never removes personal responsibility.

teaching_concepts.concept: God works through a broken instrument
teaching_concepts.explanation: Samson's dying prayer is answered and his greatest deliverance comes at the end, so even a squandered life is never beyond God's purpose or mercy.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Samson's life from the birth announcement to the temple of Dagon, and explain what his story says about a squandered calling.

comprehension_check.question: Shorn and seized, Samson assumes he will shake free as always (Judges 16:20). What had he failed to understand about his own strength?
options: It was the LORD's presence with him, now departed
It lived in the hair itself, a charm now cut away
It was a natural gift that betrayal had finally broken
It depended on Israel's prayers, which had long ceased
comprehension_check.why: Judges 16:20 explains the failure by the LORD's departure, and in Judges 16:28 Samson finally asks God himself for strength.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 16:20 and Judges 16:28. Notice what the narrator says Samson did not know, and where he turns at the end.

comprehension_check.question: Samson's last prayer asks strength to avenge his own two eyes (Judges 16:28), yet his death brings the greatest blow yet against Philistia (Judges 16:30). What is the story saying?
options: One noble death can redeem a whole squandered life
His regrown hair restored the power the razor took
God's purpose works even through a deliverer this broken
Israel's repentance finally released the help God had withheld
comprehension_check.why: Judges 13:5 promised this man would begin Israel's deliverance, and Judges 16:30 shows God keeping that word through a deeply flawed final act.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 16:28-30 next to Judges 13:5. Notice whose stated purpose gets carried out, and through what kind of prayer.

nodes.title: No King in Israel
nodes.summary: Two appalling epilogues — a bootleg shrine with a hired priest, and a crime at Gibeah that ignites civil war — under the book's tolling refrain: 'In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.' The stage is set for Samuel and the monarchy.
nodes.discussion_prompt: These chapters show what happens when every person becomes his own standard of right. What do the two epilogues reveal about where that road leads, and what standard outside yourself do you actually answer to?
assessment_questions: What does Micah set up in his house, and what happens to his shrine and his priest?
The refrain says there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. How do these two stories work as the book's closing argument?
Micah's religion was homemade and self-serving, yet he expected God's blessing for it. Where might your own faith be shaped more by preference than by God, and how would you find out?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Scripture records these atrocities to indict them, letting the horror of the outcomes deliver the verdict that the narrator never states outright.
Micah builds a shrine, an idol, and a hired priesthood out of sincere-sounding piety, showing how faith detached from God's word bends toward whatever we want.
When Israel abandons its covenant norms, the vulnerable are the first to suffer, and one crime spirals into civil war that nearly erases a tribe.

teaching_concepts.concept: The refrain points to a needed king
teaching_concepts.explanation: The repeated line about no king in Israel diagnoses the chaos and sets up the longing for righteous rule that the books of Samuel will take up.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the refrain about no king in Israel means in these chapters, and how the two epilogues prepare for the monarchy.

comprehension_check.question: The last chapters of Judges pile up idols, outrage, and civil war with almost no editorial comment. How does the book deliver its verdict?
options: By declining to judge people who meant well in chaos
By its refrain and the horror of the outcomes themselves
By recording the era as bare history needing no verdict
By blaming the Levites alone for corrupting a sound nation
comprehension_check.why: Judges 21:25 closes the book with its diagnosis, no king and every person a law to himself, and the stories display the cost.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 17:6 and Judges 21:25. Notice the sentence that frames these stories from both ends.

comprehension_check.question: Micah has a shrine, an idol, a hired Levite, and high confidence that blessing must now follow (Judges 17:13). What is his story exposing?
options: A sincere seeker whom God rewarded with lasting prosperity
Worship acceptable in substance though housed at the wrong shrine
A poor man's piety that the established priesthood refused
Homemade religion that borrows God's name to serve its owner
comprehension_check.why: Judges 17:13 shows Micah counting his arrangements as leverage on God, and Judges 18:24 shows gods that were made being simply carried away.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Judges 17:13 and Judges 18:24. Notice what Micah expects his setup to earn, and what finally becomes of it.

connections.reason: The demand for a king in 1 Samuel 8 is the direct answer to Judges' closing refrain.

nodes.title: Ruth: Loyal Love in the Days of the Judges
nodes.summary: A Moabite widow binds herself to her broken mother-in-law — 'your people will be my people, your God my God' — and is folded into Israel through Boaz, the kinsman-redeemer. Set in the era of Judges' chaos, it's a small story of hesed (loyal love) that ends by naming King David's great-grandmother.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Naomi comes home calling herself bitter and empty, and by the end the neighborhood women are naming her grandson. Nothing miraculous happens in between, just Ruth's loyalty and Boaz's generosity. What does that show about how God's providence usually works, and whose emptiness are you positioned to help fill?
assessment_questions: What does Ruth promise Naomi on the road to Bethlehem, and how does Boaz redeem the family in chapter 4?

Boaz prays that Ruth will be repaid by the God under whose wings she has taken refuge, and then he himself becomes the answer to that prayer. What does the book teach about God working through human faithfulness?
Ruth binds herself to a bitter widow who has nothing to offer her. What would loyal love like that cost you, and who in your life is asking for it right now?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Ruth's vow to Naomi models self-giving covenant loyalty that goes far beyond duty, and that kind of love drives everything good in the story.
God never speaks or performs a miracle in this book, yet gleaning laws, harvest timing, and faithful people quietly deliver his redemption.
Boaz uses Israel's law of the go'el to rescue a destitute family, and his costly, willing redemption becomes a pattern the rest of Scripture builds on.
A Moabite widow becomes the great-grandmother of King David, showing that God's grace reaches past ethnic boundaries and writes outsiders into his central story.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Ruth's story in your own words, and explain what a kinsman-redeemer is and why the closing genealogy matters.

comprehension_check.question: God never speaks and no miracle interrupts the story of Ruth. How does the book show him at work?
options: Through chance events the story leaves unexplained
Through signs that guide each character's next step
Through rewards paid out as each kindness earns them
Through gleaning law, harvest timing, and kept promises
comprehension_check.why: Ruth 2:12 prays for the LORD's repayment, and the book delivers it through ordinary fields, laws, and faithful people.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ruth 2:3 and Ruth 2:12 again. Notice how the narrator frames her arrival at that field, and how Boaz frames it.

comprehension_check.question: Ruth closes with a formal genealogy running from Perez to David. What is that list for?
options: To carry the family's quiet faithfulness into Israel's kingship
To certify Boaz's legal claim to Elimelech's land
To prove the family kept its bloodline records intact
To anchor the story firmly in the judges' era
comprehension_check.why: Ruth 4:22 ends the list at David, revealing the quiet story as part of how God prepared Israel's king.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ruth 4:18-22 again. Notice where the list chooses to stop.

connections.reason: Ruth the Moabite stands in Jesus' genealogy alongside Rahab — outsiders written into the messianic line.
The closing genealogy hands the story to David, whom Samuel will anoint.
Boaz calls Ruth a 'woman of valor' — the only narrative character given Proverbs 31's exact title; in the Hebrew ordering Ruth follows Proverbs directly.

nodes.title: Hannah's Prayer and the Call of Samuel
nodes.summary: Childless Hannah pours out her grief at Shiloh, vows her son to the LORD, and names the answered prayer Samuel; her song of reversal, the poor raised from the dust, becomes the theology of the whole book. The boy grows up beside Eli's corrupt sons, who treat the offerings and the worshipers with a contempt the old priest will not restrain. One night the LORD calls the child by name, and by morning the word that ends Eli's house has begun making Samuel a prophet all Israel will recognize.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Hannah's answer to years of anguish is a son she gives away, and her song celebrates a God who overturns human rankings. What does her willingness to hand back the very thing she begged for reveal about what she was really asking God for, and what would praying that freely cost you?
assessment_questions: What does Hannah vow before Samuel is born, and what does she do in 1 Samuel 1:27-28 once he is weaned?

Hannah's song celebrates a God who raises the poor and breaks the mighty, right before the story turns to Eli's privileged, corrupt sons. How does the song's pattern frame what happens to Eli's house and to Samuel?

Samuel's first prophetic word is a hard message for Eli, the man who raised him, and Eli tells him to hold nothing back. When has faithfulness asked you to say something costly to someone you love, and what do Samuel and Eli each model for that moment?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Hannah's anguished vow and answered prayer show God responding to a sincere heart in his own time, and her keeping of the vow turns gratitude into worship.
Hannah's song announces the pattern the books of Samuel will follow, where barren women sing and the mighty fall, and Mary will later borrow its melody.
Eli's sons serve at the altar while despising the LORD's offering, and the judgment on their house shows God holding sacred office strictly to account.
The night call shows revelation returning to Israel through a listening servant, and Eli, for all his failure, still teaches Samuel how to answer.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Hannah's vow and Samuel's night call, and explain how Hannah's song announces the reversal pattern that Eli's fall and Samuel's rise both follow.

comprehension_check.question: Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2:1-10 ranges far beyond her own story, to armies, thrones, and a king. What is the song doing there?
options: Announcing the reversals God is about to work through the book
Thanking God for a private mercy in fitting poetic language
Predicting that her own son will one day take Israel's throne
Teaching that the humble always end up richer than the proud
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 2:10 ends the song with the LORD judging the earth and strengthening his king, the story the books of Samuel are about to tell.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 2:4-10 again. Notice how far past Hannah's own situation the song has reached by its final line.

comprehension_check.question: In 1 Samuel 3, the LORD's first word to Samuel is a judgment on Eli's house. What does the chapter present as the mark that Samuel is truly a prophet?
options: He hears an audible voice no one else in Shiloh hears
He is raised in the sanctuary from his earliest childhood
He replaces Eli's sons in the priestly line of service
He delivers the hard word entrusted to him, and it stands
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 3:19-20 seals it: the LORD let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground, and all Israel knew him as a prophet.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 3:17-21 again. Notice what Samuel does with the message, and what the narrator says the LORD did with Samuel's words.

connections.reason: Mary's Magnificat is modeled on Hannah's song; Luke writes Jesus' infancy against Samuel's.

nodes.title: The Ark Among the Philistines and Israel's Return
nodes.summary: Losing to the Philistines, Israel hauls the ark into camp like a weapon and loses it; Eli's sons die, the old priest falls dead at the news, and a dying mother names Israel's condition Ichabod, the glory gone. Yet in Philistine country the captured ark needs no army: Dagon falls on his face, plague strikes city after city, and the trophy is shipped home with guilt offerings. A generation later Samuel calls Israel to put away its gods at Mizpah, and the stone he raises, Ebenezer, marks what repentance recovered that presumption had lost.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Israel carries the ark into battle expecting victory and loses it; the Philistines keep it as a trophy and cannot get rid of it fast enough. What is the difference between having God's presence and trying to use it, and where does your own faith drift toward the ark-in-the-camp move?
assessment_questions: Why do the elders send for the ark in 1 Samuel 4, and what happens to it, to Eli's sons, and to Eli?
In Philistine cities the ark humiliates Dagon and spreads plague without a single Israelite soldier nearby. What is the story saying about whose defeat the battle of chapter 4 actually was?

At Mizpah, Israel fasts, confesses, and puts away its foreign gods before God routs the Philistines, and Samuel raises the Ebenezer stone. What would putting something away and raising a marker look like in your own return to God?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The ark's capture exposes Israel's superstition, since God's presence calls for covenant trust and never works as a talisman to control outcomes.
Dagon prostrate before the ark shows the LORD needing no defenders; Israel lost the battle at Aphek, and God did not.
One name mourns the glory departed and the other marks help received, and what stands between them in the story is Israel's repentance at Mizpah.
Beth-shemesh learns that the ark endangers presumptuous Israelites as surely as Philistines, and its question, who can stand before this holy God, hangs over the books that follow.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the ark's capture and its solo victory in Philistia each reveal, and what changed at Mizpah that the elders of chapter 4 had gotten wrong.

comprehension_check.question: When the elders bring the ark to the battlefield in 1 Samuel 4:3, what does the story expose in that move?
options: A sincere faith that God punishes on a technicality
A bid to command God's power without seeking God
A wise instinct betrayed by the corrupt priests carrying it
A forgivable error God overlooks once the ark returns
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 4:3 has the elders treating the ark as a device that will save them, while the LORD himself is never consulted at all.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 4:3 again. Notice who the elders talk to about the plan, and who they never address.

comprehension_check.question: What do the ark's months in Philistine territory in 1 Samuel 5-6 establish before Israel's story resumes?
options: The plagues show the ark is dangerous cargo for any nation
The LORD needed to reach his own land to act freely
The LORD's defeat was never real; only Israel's was
Philistine religion was too weak to hold a stronger god
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 5:3-4 puts Dagon on his face before the ark; with no Israelite in sight, the LORD vindicates his own name.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 5:1-7 again. Notice what happens to Dagon overnight with no army anywhere near.

nodes.title: Israel Demands a King
nodes.summary: Samuel's sons take bribes, and the elders seize the moment to demand a king to judge them like all the nations; the LORD tells Samuel the rejection is of God himself, and grants the request anyway. Saul is anointed in private, chosen by lot in public, and vindicated when he rescues Jabesh-gilead, silencing his doubters. In his farewell Samuel puts the whole transaction under the covenant: king and people alike will stand or fall by whether they fear and serve the LORD, and he will not stop praying for them.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God calls the demand for a king a rejection of himself, grants it, and then keeps sending warnings, victories, and Samuel's prayers into the new arrangement. What does that sequence show about how God works inside choices he grieves, and where might you be living in a granted request rather than a surrendered one?
assessment_questions: What reasons do the elders give for wanting a king in 1 Samuel 8, and what does the LORD tell Samuel the demand really means?

Samuel warns exactly what a king will take, the people insist, and God then provides Saul with real gifts and a real victory. How can the monarchy be both Israel's rebellion and God's provision at the same time?

In his farewell, Samuel tells the people who pushed him aside that he will keep teaching them and praying for them. What would it look like for you to keep serving faithfully inside an outcome you argued against?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Israel's demand for a human king reveals distrust of God's rule, and the whole monarchy begins under that shadow.
God gives the people the king they ask for while spelling out the cost through Samuel's speech about what a king will take.
Saul's anointing, the Spirit's rush, and the Jabesh-gilead rescue are genuine gifts, showing God working good within an arrangement born of distrust.
Samuel's farewell sets king and people together under the covenant, with the prophet remaining as teacher and intercessor, the shape Israel's politics will keep.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the demand for a king counts as rejecting God, how God nonetheless provides in Saul, and what terms Samuel's farewell sets for the monarchy.

comprehension_check.question: Deuteronomy had long anticipated Israel having a king. What makes the demand in 1 Samuel 8 land as rebellion?
options: Wanting any human ruler at all is an insult to God
They seek a king to replace the God who rules them
They ask through elders instead of through God's prophet
They rush the timing God had appointed for the monarchy
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 8:7 gives the LORD's own reading of the demand: they have rejected me as their king.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 8:5-7 and 8:19-20 again. Notice whose job description the people want the new king to take over.

comprehension_check.question: Samuel's farewell in 1 Samuel 12 closes the transition to monarchy. On what does he say Israel's future now depends?
options: On whether king and people together fear and serve the LORD
On the new king's skill in judging and leading Israel's wars
On Israel keeping a prophet stationed over its kings
On how faithfully Israel brings its sacrifices and offerings
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 12:14-15 lays down one condition covering both king and people: follow the LORD, or his hand turns against you.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 12:13-15 and 12:20-25 again. Notice who is included in the condition Samuel lays down.

connections.reason: The demand for a king in 1 Samuel 8 is the direct answer to Judges' closing refrain.

nodes.title: Saul Rejected
nodes.summary: Under Philistine pressure Saul offers the sacrifice he was told to await, and hears that his kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after his own heart. Jonathan's daring faith cracks the Philistine lines while his father's rash oath nearly kills him, and at Amalek Saul keeps the best of what was devoted and calls it worship. Samuel's verdict gives the books of Samuel their center: obedience is better than sacrifice, and rejecting God's word costs Saul the crown.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Saul never stops sacrificing, building altars, and invoking God's name, and it is exactly his religion that keeps going wrong. What separates Jonathan's risky trust in chapter 14 from his father's rash oaths and salvaged offerings, and which pattern does your own devotion resemble under pressure?
assessment_questions: What does Saul do at Gilgal in chapter 13, and again with Amalek in chapter 15, that Samuel names as disobedience?

Both times Saul dresses his disobedience in religious language, a forced sacrifice, animals spared for offerings. Why does Samuel's answer in 1 Samuel 15:22-23 treat that as worse than no worship at all?

Saul explains each failure by pointing at circumstances and the people around him. Where are you currently explaining away a clear obedience, and what would obeying without the explanations look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Samuel's verdict makes obeying God's voice the true measure of worship, and no volume of religious performance can substitute for it.
Saul executes most of the Amalek command and treats the remainder as negotiable, and the text counts that remainder as rejection of God's word.

teaching_concepts.concept: A man after God's own heart
teaching_concepts.explanation: The announcement of 1 Samuel 13:14 measures kings by inward orientation to God, the criterion that will pass over Saul's stature for a shepherd.

teaching_concepts.concept: Faith and rashness side by side
teaching_concepts.explanation: Jonathan's few-against-many trust and Saul's oath in the same battle set living faith against zeal that performs, and the army can tell the difference.

nodes.completion_criteria: Recount Saul's two acts of disobedience and explain, in the sense of 1 Samuel 15:22, why his religious framing of them made things worse rather than better.

comprehension_check.question: Saul's sacrifice at Gilgal in 1 Samuel 13 looks like piety under pressure. Why does it cost him so much?
options: He sacrificed at Gilgal rather than at the appointed shrine
He abandoned the word he was given when fear pressed
He rushed a ritual that only lacked Samuel's official presence
He led the army to worship before securing the battlefield
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 13:13-14 names the offense as failing to keep what the LORD commanded, a king who would not wait on God's word.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 10:8 and 13:8-14 again. Notice what instruction Saul was under, and what he says pushed him to act.

comprehension_check.question: When Samuel says obedience is better than sacrifice in 1 Samuel 15:22, what claim is he making?
options: Sacrifices belong to an older stage of Israel's worship
Moral effort earns what ritual observance never could
Worship offered out of disobedience has stopped being worship
God prefers private devotion to public ceremony and ritual
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 15:22-23 weighs Saul's spared animals against the voice of the LORD; what God asked for was the obeying itself.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 15:19-23 again. Notice what Saul says the animals were for, and what Samuel says the LORD delights in.

nodes.title: David Anointed; Goliath Falls
nodes.summary: God sends Samuel past seven impressive brothers to a shepherd boy — 'the LORD looks on the heart' — and David fells Goliath with a sling and a stone in the Bible's most famous underdog scene. Saul's jealousy turns lethal; Jonathan's friendship becomes David's shield.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Samuel nearly anoints the tall oldest brother before God says he looks on the heart, and then David faces Goliath with nothing that would impress anyone. What do these chapters teach about where real strength comes from, and where would relying on it change how you face what scares you?
assessment_questions: How does David defeat Goliath, and in whose name does he say he comes?
David is anointed king in chapter 16, yet he spends these chapters serving Saul and running for his life. What does the gap between anointing and throne reveal about how God's promises unfold?
Jonathan hands David his robe and sword even though David's rise threatens Jonathan's own claim to the throne. What would friendship that loyal require of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God passes over every impressive brother for the overlooked shepherd, showing that his choices rest on inward character rather than outward appearance.
David's sling against Goliath's armor shows God accomplishing his purposes through unlikely people so the glory belongs to him.
David is chosen long before he reigns, and the delay teaches that God's calling often includes years of waiting and hardship.
Jonathan's loyalty to David at real personal cost models a faithful, sacrificial love that holds firm amid political danger.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the Goliath story and explain what 'the LORD looks on the heart' means for how God chooses people.

comprehension_check.question: In 1 Samuel 16:6-7, even Samuel is certain Eliab must be the LORD's anointed. What is the scene teaching through the prophet's mistake?
options: Even prophets must wait for signs before they judge
God's choice works by a measure human judgment cannot supply
Israel deserved a second imposing king and nearly got one
Eliab hid a flaw of heart that his stature concealed
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 16:7 corrects the prophet mid-scene, the LORD seeing the heart where man sees only height and face.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 16:6-7, then 1 Samuel 10:23-24. Notice what Israel's first king had going for him, and what Samuel notices first here.

comprehension_check.question: In 1 Samuel 17:45-47, David tells Goliath what the day will prove. What, for David, is the fight actually about?
options: Whether the God of Israel's armies can be defied
Whether courage can outweigh training and heavy armor
Whether Israel's shepherds were braver than its soldiers
Whether Saul's kingdom or Philistia's would hold the valley
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 17:46-47 stakes the duel on the whole earth learning there is a God in Israel, whose battle it is.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 17:45-47 again. Notice what David says the whole earth will know by the day's end.

connections.reason: Ruth's genealogy delivered this shepherd from Bethlehem — the town now enters the Bible's center stage.

nodes.title: The Fugitive in Judah: Sparing the LORD's Anointed
nodes.summary: David runs: holy bread at Nob, feigned madness at Gath, the cave of Adullam where the desperate gather to him, and a terrible price paid by Nob's priests for helping him. Twice the hunt hands Saul to David defenseless, in the cave at En-gedi and asleep at Hachilah, and twice David refuses to touch the LORD's anointed, staking his future on God's timing. Between the two refusals, Abigail's swift wisdom stops him from avenging himself on Nabal, the near miss that shows what his restraint is protecting.
nodes.discussion_prompt: David will not take Saul's life, yet he is one insult away from slaughtering Nabal's household until Abigail talks him down. What do the spared king and the near massacre together reveal about where restraint really comes from, and who plays Abigail's role in your life?
assessment_questions: What does David do, and refuse to do, when Saul is delivered into his hands at En-gedi and again at Hachilah?

Between the two sparing scenes, David nearly wipes out Nabal's house over an insult until Abigail intervenes. What does that near miss show about David's restraint toward Saul, and about what Abigail's speech gives him?

David leaves his claim on the throne to God's timing while armed men urge shortcuts. Which promised or deserved thing are you tempted to seize by your own hand, and what would David's kind of waiting require of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: David refuses to harm the LORD's anointed even when killing Saul would end his suffering, trusting God to settle the matter in his own time.
David's logic rests on God's right to install and remove kings, so seizing the throne by force would deny the very anointing his own hope depends on.
Her speech names bloodguilt before it happens, and David blesses the discernment that kept his future kingship clean of avenged insults.
Hunted through Keilah, Ziph, and En-gedi, David is preserved scene by scene, and even his compromises cannot derail where God is taking him.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell one scene where David spares Saul, and explain how the Nabal episode shows what his refusal to avenge himself protects.

comprehension_check.question: Twice David stands over a helpless Saul and refuses to strike. What reasoning does the text put in his mouth?
options: Killing a king would turn the army and tribes against him
Saul's office belongs to God, who alone may end it
Mercy shown now will purchase mercy when he is king
Jonathan's covenant binds him to protect his father Saul
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 26:10-11 spells out David's logic: the LORD himself will strike Saul, or his day will come, so David's hand must stay.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 24:6 and 26:9-11 again. Notice whose title for Saul keeps appearing in David's refusals.

comprehension_check.question: The Nabal story sits between the two scenes of David sparing Saul. What does its placement let the reader see?
options: David's patience with Saul had hardened into indifference to insult
Nabal's fate shows that David's enemies always end up destroying themselves
David's restraint is real yet fragile, kept alive by wise intervention
Abigail's marriage secures David an alliance among Judah's clans
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 25:32-33 has David bless the God who sent Abigail to keep him from bloodshed, naming how close he came.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 25:21-33 again. Notice what David has already sworn to do before Abigail reaches him.

connections.reason: Multiple Book I psalms (34, 52, 54, 56, 57, and more) carry superscriptions locating them in these fugitive chapters.

nodes.title: Ziklag and Gilboa: The End of Saul
nodes.summary: Convinced Saul will finally kill him, David crosses into Philistine service and plays a double game from Ziklag, raiding southern peoples while telling Achish otherwise. The narrative interleaves him with Saul's last night: silence from the LORD, a desperate seance at Endor, and a word of defeat that comes true on Mount Gilboa. When Amalekites burn Ziklag, David, at the edge of being stoned by his own men, finds strength in the LORD his God and recovers everything; Saul, forsaken and wounded, falls on his own sword as the Philistines take the field.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Both men in these chapters hit bottom: Saul meets silence at every door he tries, and David comes home to a burned town and talk of stoning. One goes to a medium, the other to the LORD. What decides which way a desperate person turns, and which direction is your own desperation currently facing?
assessment_questions: Why does David move to Philistine territory in 1 Samuel 27, and what does Saul do at Endor when the LORD will not answer him?

The story cuts back and forth between David's crisis at Ziklag and Saul's on Gilboa. What is the contrast between how each man meets abandonment, and what does it reveal about where their strength lay?

David's worst season includes real compromises, yet at Ziklag he still turns to God first. When your own record is mixed, what does 1 Samuel 30:6 suggest is still possible, and what would finding strength in God look like this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Saul's seance at Endor tries to force an answer God has withheld, and the word it obtains only confirms the judgment he refused to hear.
At Ziklag David turns to God before he turns to strategy, and the inquiry that follows reverses everything Saul's night at Endor got wrong.
David lies and plays double agent through these chapters and remains the chosen man, even kept from marching against Israel by a providence he did not arrange.

teaching_concepts.concept: The promise arrives without David's hand
teaching_concepts.explanation: Saul's death on Gilboa is a tragedy the narrative mourns, and it is also the door to the kingdom opening exactly as David refused to force it.

nodes.completion_criteria: Contrast Saul at Endor with David at Ziklag, and explain how the interleaved endings bring David to the throne's edge without his hand touching Saul.

comprehension_check.question: What does Saul's visit to the medium in 1 Samuel 28 mean within his own story?
options: A grieving man's pardonable reach for comfort at the end
A ruler prudently gathering intelligence before a great battle
A last resort that proves God had hidden truth from him
A final grasp at God's voice on forbidden terms
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 28:6-7 sets the order plainly: the LORD does not answer, and Saul immediately seeks out what he himself had outlawed.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 28:3 and 28:6-7 again. Notice what Saul had done to the mediums earlier, and when he decides to seek one.

comprehension_check.question: At Ziklag in 1 Samuel 30, with his men talking of stoning him, what turns David's crisis?
options: He finds strength in his God and inquires of him
He rallies his men with the confidence a leader projects
He recalls the anointing that guarantees his own survival
He channels his grief into swift and decisive action
comprehension_check.why: 1 Samuel 30:6-8 moves from David strengthening himself in the LORD straight to inquiry, and the pursuit follows God's answer.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Samuel 30:6-8 again. Notice what David does before he gives a single order to his men.

nodes.title: David Takes the Throne; the Ark Comes Home
nodes.summary: David laments Saul rather than gloating, is crowned over Judah and then all Israel, takes Jerusalem, and dances the ark into his new capital. City, king, and divine presence converge — Zion is born.
nodes.discussion_prompt: In one chapter Uzzah dies for touching the ark, and soon after David dances before it with all his might. What do those two scenes together teach about approaching a holy God with both reverence and joy, and which of the two comes harder for you?
assessment_questions: How does David respond to the news of Saul's death, and what city does he capture and make his capital?
The ark's journey stops for three months after Uzzah dies, and something changes before it enters Jerusalem. What does the episode teach about handling what is holy on God's terms instead of our own?
David composes a public lament honoring the king who hunted him for years. What would honoring someone who wronged you actually require, and why might it matter?

teaching_concepts.explanation: David's rise runs through civil war, assassinations, and hard politics, showing God establishing his purposes inside flawed human events.
David's lament for Saul and Jonathan models mourning that refuses to gloat, treating even a fallen enemy with dignity.
Uzzah's death is a hard reminder that God's presence is never casual, and that zeal for God must be ordered by obedience to his word.
When the ark enters Jerusalem, worship, kingship, and God's dwelling come together in one place, and Zion becomes the Bible's great symbol of God with his people.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe how city, king, and ark come together in Jerusalem, and explain what the Uzzah episode teaches about God's holiness.

comprehension_check.question: After David is crowned and takes Jerusalem, the story climaxes with the ark entering the city. What does that arrival accomplish in the narrative?
options: It joins God's presence to king and city
It shields the young capital from any Philistine reprisal
It repays David's long faithfulness with a crowning honor
It relocates worship to a setting worthy of it
comprehension_check.why: With the ark set in David's new capital, God's dwelling and the kingship now share one place (2 Samuel 5:12, 2 Samuel 6:17).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 5:12 and 2 Samuel 6:15-17 again. Notice what David understands about his kingdom, and what he brings into his city next.

comprehension_check.question: Uzzah dies when the ark first sets out, yet three months later David dances it into Jerusalem with all Israel. What changed in between?
options: God's anger had simply faded with the passing months
The ark was moved on God's own terms this time
A larger, more careful escort prevented another stumble
The ark grew safe as it neared the holy city
comprehension_check.why: The second attempt goes with bearers carrying the ark and sacrifice marking the journey (2 Samuel 6:13).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 6:3 and then 2 Samuel 6:13 again. Notice how the ark travels on each attempt.

connections.reason: Reading Samuel's warts-and-all account beside the Chronicler's curated one teaches how biblical historiography works.

nodes.title: The Davidic Covenant
nodes.summary: David offers to build God a house; God answers that he will build David a house — a dynasty, a throne established forever, a son who will be to God a son. This single chapter is the taproot of the Bible's messianic hope: 'Son of David' means this promise.
nodes.discussion_prompt: David plans to build God a house, and God turns the offer around and promises to build David one instead. What does that reversal show about how grace works, and where might God be asking you to receive what you were busy trying to achieve?
assessment_questions: What does God promise David through the prophet Nathan in this chapter?
God promises David's throne will stand forever, yet also says he will discipline David's son when he does wrong. How can the promise be unbreakable while the kings remain accountable?
David's response is to sit before the LORD and ask, 'Who am I?' How does receiving a promise you did nothing to earn change the way a person prays and plans?

teaching_concepts.explanation: David's building project is set aside so God can give rather than receive, showing that the covenant rests on God's generosity and never on human achievement.
God promises David a dynasty that will never finally fail, a commitment the rest of Scripture keeps returning to.
God pledges to be a father to David's heir, binding steadfast love to responsible rule and correction.
The everlasting throne reaches past Solomon toward the messianic hope, which is why the New Testament calls Jesus the Son of David.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words what God promises David in 2 Samuel 7 and why 'Son of David' carries this promise through the rest of the Bible.

comprehension_check.question: David proposes to build God a house, and God responds with a promise instead. What is the shape of the exchange?
options: God rebukes the plan as presumption on David's part
God postpones the temple until David earns the right
God reverses the offer, making himself the builder
God accepts, assigning the work to a worthier heir
comprehension_check.why: The oracle turns David's plan around: the LORD declares that he will establish a house for David (2 Samuel 7:11).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 7:5 and 2 Samuel 7:11 again. Notice who ends up building a house for whom.

comprehension_check.question: God promises David a house and throne established forever. In the Bible's long story, what does this chapter become?
options: The taproot of the Bible's hope for the Messiah
A pledge that Solomon's temple would satisfy and complete
A conditional grant that exile finally proved forfeit
A tribute to David that his successors squandered away
comprehension_check.why: The promise of a throne established forever is what later scripture keeps reaching for in the title Son of David (2 Samuel 7:16).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 7:12-16 again. Notice how long the promised house and throne are said to stand.

connections.reason: Gabriel's words to Mary — 'the throne of his father David… his kingdom will never end' — quote this covenant.
Psalm 2's begotten king enthroned on Zion is this promise set to music.
Hebrews 1 cites 'I will be to him a father' from this chapter as fulfilled in Christ.

nodes.title: The Kingdom Established
nodes.summary: David's wars secure the borders the patriarchs were promised, and his kindness to Mephibosheth — Jonathan's disabled son, seated at the king's table — shows covenant loyalty exercised from the throne. The kingdom at its brief best.
nodes.discussion_prompt: At the height of his power, David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house so he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake, and he seats a disabled man at the king's table for life. What does it mean to use power that way, and who could you seek out to honor a promise no one would force you to keep?
assessment_questions: Who is Mephibosheth, and what does David do for him?
The narrator repeats that the LORD gave David victory wherever he went. What does that refrain say about the real source of the kingdom's success?
David's kindness to Mephibosheth flows from an old covenant with Jonathan. What commitments have you made that still claim something from you today, and how will you keep them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: David's military success is credited to the LORD giving him victory, so kingship is portrayed as stewardship under God rather than raw human achievement.
David lavishes grace on Mephibosheth because of a past promise, modeling loyalty that seeks out the vulnerable instead of waiting to be asked.
David administers justice and equity for all his people, sketching what right rule under God is supposed to look like.
War, diplomacy, and administration fill these chapters, and the narrative asks whether authority serves God's aims or the ruler's own.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the Mephibosheth story and explain how it shows covenant loyalty exercised from the throne.

comprehension_check.question: At the height of his power David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house, and seats lame Mephibosheth at the royal table. What is the search showing?
options: A public mercy staged to adorn the new reign
A repayment of debts owed to Jonathan's household
An amends for deaths that cleared his way to power
Promise-keeping kindness that goes looking for the weak
comprehension_check.why: David starts the search unprompted, seeking someone to receive kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 9:1).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 9:1-7 again. Notice who begins the search, and whose name supplies the reason for the kindness.

comprehension_check.question: The war records keep repeating that the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. What is the refrain doing?
options: Certifying that every campaign David ever fought was just
Crediting the kingdom's success to God rather than David
Teaching that obedient kings will never lose their battles
Preserving David's tactics as a pattern for his successors
comprehension_check.why: The conquests are framed as the LORD giving the victories, so the empire is received before it is achieved (2 Samuel 8:6).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 8:6 and 2 Samuel 8:14 again. Notice who is named as acting whenever David wins.

nodes.title: Bathsheba and Nathan's Parable
nodes.summary: David takes Bathsheba and murders her husband to cover it, and the prophet Nathan corners the king with a story about a stolen lamb: 'You are the man.' The Bible's model king is exposed as an adulterer and murderer — and the model penitent.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Nathan tells the king a story about a rich man stealing a poor man's lamb, and David condemns the thief in fury before realizing the thief is him. Why do we see other people's sins so much more clearly than our own, and who have you given permission to speak that honestly into your life?
assessment_questions: How does David try to cover up what he did with Bathsheba, and what finally happens to Uriah?
God forgives David the moment he confesses, yet the child dies and the sword stays in his house. How do forgiveness and consequences fit together in this story?
David's fall unfolds in small steps: staying home, looking, asking, sending. Which early step of a temptation do you most need to interrupt, and how?

teaching_concepts.concept: Secret sin grows into public harm
teaching_concepts.explanation: One private act of lust spirals into adultery, deceit, and murder, showing how quickly hidden sin multiplies its victims.
Nathan's parable is God's kindness in disguise, bringing David to see his sin so that confession and restoration become possible.
God pardons David's confessed sin, yet the earthly fallout still comes, teaching that divine forgiveness does not erase every temporal cost.
The king after God's own heart commits the Bible's most infamous royal sin, so God's choice of a servant is never a certificate of moral perfection.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Nathan's parable and explain how 'You are the man' brings David to genuine repentance.

comprehension_check.question: Nathan confronts the king with a story about a stolen lamb instead of a direct accusation. What does the parable accomplish?
options: It cushions a rebuke no king could hear plainly
It draws David into sentencing his own deed unawares
It cloaks the charge so only David would understand
It protects Nathan from a king who removes inconvenient men
comprehension_check.why: David's fury at the rich man becomes the verdict Nathan turns back on the king himself (2 Samuel 12:5-7).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 12:1-7 again. Notice what David does in verse 5, before he learns who the rich man stands for.

comprehension_check.question: Nathan tells David the LORD has put away his sin, and in the same oracle announces lasting trouble for his house. What is the passage holding together?
options: A pardon left incomplete until suffering repays it
Evidence that David's repentance fell short of sincerity
A judgment postponed for a season rather than truly forgiven
Genuine pardon beside the lasting earthly cost of sin
comprehension_check.why: One oracle carries both words, the sin taken away and the sword staying in the house (2 Samuel 12:10, 2 Samuel 12:13).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 12:10-14 again. Notice which things Nathan says are ended and which he says will remain.

connections.reason: Psalm 51's superscription places it here: David's own prayer after Nathan's confrontation.

nodes.title: The Sword in David's House: Absalom
nodes.summary: Nathan's sentence — 'the sword shall never depart from your house' — unfolds in slow motion: Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's revenge, rebellion, and death in the oak, leaving David wailing 'O Absalom, my son, my son.' Sin forgiven still bears bitter fruit.
nodes.discussion_prompt: David burns with anger when Tamar is violated, and then does nothing. Trace what his silence costs his family across these chapters. Why is failing to act against injustice so destructive, and where might silence be doing damage around you?
assessment_questions: What does Absalom do to avenge Tamar, and how does his rebellion against David end?
Nathan warned that the sword would never depart from David's house. How do these chapters show that sentence coming true through the family's own choices rather than through lightning from heaven?
David weeps 'O Absalom, my son, my son' over the son who tried to kill him. What does his grief teach about loving people whose choices break your heart?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Amnon's crime, Absalom's revenge, and the civil war that follows show one unaddressed sin multiplying into national ruin.
David's anger without action after Tamar's rape leaves the vulnerable unprotected and hands the story to vengeance.
Nathan's sentence and the family's own passions unfold as one story, holding God's judgment and human responsibility together without dissolving either.

teaching_concepts.concept: A father's grief and a king's duty collide
teaching_concepts.explanation: David's wail over Absalom shows the agonizing tension between political necessity, justice, and a parent's love for a rebellious child.

nodes.completion_criteria: Trace the chain from Amnon's crime to Absalom's death, and explain how it fulfills Nathan's words after the Bathsheba affair.

comprehension_check.question: Nathan said the sword would never leave David's house. How do these chapters show that sentence being carried out?
options: Through direct blows from heaven that bypass human hands
Through foreign enemies raised up against the throne
Through the family's own choices, which no one restrains
Through a fate that runs on regardless of anyone's acts
comprehension_check.why: The oracle located the coming trouble inside David's own house, and there it rises (2 Samuel 12:11).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 12:11 and then 2 Samuel 13:21-22 again. Notice where the trouble comes from, and what the king fails to do about it.

comprehension_check.question: After Tamar's rape, David burns with anger and does nothing. What does the narrative trace to that silence?
options: The revenge that fills the space justice left empty
An ambition in Absalom that nothing could have curbed
The withdrawal of God's covenant promise from the house
comprehension_check.why: Absalom's hatred festers for two years over the crime his father's anger never answered (2 Samuel 13:21-22).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 13:21-23 again. Notice the two years that pass between the king's fury and anyone acting.

connections.reason: Psalm 3 is superscribed 'when David fled from Absalom his son.'

nodes.title: Epilogue: The King Assessed
nodes.summary: A non-chronological closing portfolio: famine and war records, David's great psalm of deliverance, his last words, his mighty men — and the census that ends with an altar on the threshing floor where the temple will one day stand.
nodes.discussion_prompt: At the threshing floor David refuses a free gift, saying he will not offer to God what costs him nothing. Looking back over this closing portrait of his whole reign, why does worship that costs something matter, and what would it cost you?
assessment_questions: What does David buy at the threshing floor, and what does he do there?
The epilogue places David's psalm of deliverance and last words between records of famine, war, and a sinful census. What verdict on David's reign does this arrangement suggest?
After a lifetime of danger, David calls the LORD his rock, fortress, and deliverer. Which line of a testimony like that could you honestly say today, and which one are you still waiting to?

teaching_concepts.explanation: David's great song reads his whole story of danger and rescue as God's work, modeling thanksgiving as the right response to deliverance.
The census shows a king's pride exposing his people to judgment, and true leadership responding with confession and repair.
David insists on paying for the threshing floor because an offering that costs nothing says nothing, and that altar site becomes the future temple.
The roll of mighty men honors loyalty and sacrificial service, showing that God's work through David ran through committed friends.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the census ends at a threshing floor altar, and what David's 'I will not offer what costs me nothing' says about worship.

comprehension_check.question: Araunah offers David the threshing floor, the oxen, and the wood without charge. Why does David insist on paying?
options: A gift that costs the giver nothing is no offering
A king must never stand in the debt of a subject
Only land lawfully purchased could carry an altar
A freely given site could be claimed back later
comprehension_check.why: David refuses to offer the LORD burnt offerings that cost him nothing, so he buys the floor and the oxen (2 Samuel 24:24).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 24:22-25 again. Notice the reason David gives when he declines the free gift.

comprehension_check.question: The epilogue sets David's long song of rescue beside records of famine, war, and a costly census. What does the song do there?
options: It grants the reign's brighter years their equal share
It marks the point where the kingdom's wars ended
It restores the reputation the census chapter cost David
It reads the reign's escapes as the LORD's rescue
comprehension_check.why: The song is sung to the LORD on the day of deliverance from all his enemies, a lifetime read as rescue (2 Samuel 22:1).
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Samuel 22:1-4 again. Notice whom the song credits, and what span of David's life its heading covers.

connections.reason: The threshing floor David buys in chapter 24 becomes the temple site Solomon builds on.

nodes.title: Solomon Secured; Wisdom Granted
nodes.summary: Amid deathbed intrigue David names Solomon king, and the young ruler asks God not for wealth or long life but for a discerning heart — receiving wisdom that draws the world to his court. The famous split-the-baby judgment shows it in action.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Offered anything he wanted, Solomon asks for a discerning heart to govern God's people. What does his request reveal about what wisdom is actually for, and if God asked you the same question tonight, what would your honest answer be?
assessment_questions: What does Solomon ask God for at Gibeon, and what does God give him beyond his request?
In the dispute between the two mothers, Solomon has no witnesses and no evidence. How does his ruling show what a discerning heart looks like in practice?
Solomon asked for wisdom to serve people rather than for things that would serve himself. What decision are you facing where asking for discernment first would change what you do?

teaching_concepts.concept: God keeps the Davidic promise through messy politics
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon reaches the throne amid intrigue and rivalry, yet God's covenant with David moves forward exactly as promised.

teaching_concepts.concept: Wisdom is a gift to ask for
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon receives discernment because he asks God for it in humility, and the story treats that request as the best prayer he ever prayed.
The judgment between the two mothers shows that real wisdom defends the vulnerable instead of impressing an audience.
God ties continued blessing to obedience in David's charge, since even a God-given gift like wisdom needs a heart that stays true.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Solomon asked for at Gibeon and how the judgment between the two mothers shows that wisdom in action.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Kings 1 is all palace intrigue: rival feasts, hurried alliances, a rushed anointing. What is the chapter showing about God's promise to David?
options: Only Nathan's quick maneuvering saved a promise that had failed
The promise passes to whichever son proves the boldest claimant
The promise moves forward even through court scheming and rivalry
The promise was suspended until Solomon could earn the throne
comprehension_check.why: Solomon is crowned because David keeps an oath sworn by the LORD in 1 Kings 1:29-30, so the succession lands where the promise pointed.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 1:29-30. Notice what David appeals to when he finally settles who will reign.

comprehension_check.question: All Israel hears the verdict between the two mothers and stands in awe (1 Kings 3:28). What has the judgment shown them?
options: God's gift of wisdom in their king works to do justice
Their king can outwit any liar who enters his court
A ruler may bend the truth whenever a case demands it
Fear of the throne will now keep order in Israel
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 3:28 says the awe came from seeing God-given wisdom applied to justice, the gift Solomon had asked for in 1 Kings 3:9.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 3:9 and 1 Kings 3:28 together. Notice what Solomon asks the gift for, and what Israel concludes from the verdict.

connections.reason: Proverbs presents itself as the deposit of the Solomonic wisdom granted here.

nodes.title: The Temple
nodes.summary: Solomon builds the temple, the ark enters, and the glory-cloud that once filled the tabernacle fills the house — while Solomon's dedication prayer already anticipates exile and pleads that God hear the penitent 'toward this place.' The tabernacle's portable Eden becomes stone and gold on Zion.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Solomon builds God a magnificent house and then prays that even the highest heaven cannot contain him. How can both be true at once, and what difference does it make to know that the God you pray to is both near and beyond every place built for him?
assessment_questions: What fills the temple when the priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary, and how do the priests respond?
Solomon says heaven itself cannot contain God, yet he asks God to hear every prayer made toward this house. What does his prayer teach about how God chooses to meet his people?
Solomon's dedication prayer keeps returning to forgiveness for people who sin and then turn back. What would it look like for your own prayers to lean that confidently on God's readiness to forgive?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The temple completes what God promised David, showing that God's commitments hold across generations and delays.

teaching_concepts.concept: The temple as the place of God's presence
teaching_concepts.explanation: The glory-cloud filling the house marks the temple as the place where God chooses to dwell among his people.
Solomon confesses that no building can hold the Creator, so the temple points beyond itself to a God greater than any sign of him.
Solomon's prayer models worship that mixes praise with honest confession and counts on God's mercy when people fail.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what happens when the ark enters the temple, and explain how Solomon's prayer holds together God's presence in the house and God's greatness beyond it.

comprehension_check.question: In his dedication prayer Solomon says even the highest heavens cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27). What does that make of the temple he just built?
options: The one place on earth where God may now be found
A meeting place God chose that points beyond itself to him
A house whose rituals guarantee the nation's lasting security
A tribute whose splendor earns God's attention to its prayers
comprehension_check.why: In 1 Kings 8:29-30 Solomon asks the God who dwells in heaven to keep his Name and his ear turned toward this house.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 8:27-30. Notice where Solomon says God dwells, and what he asks the building to be for.

comprehension_check.question: Solomon's long dedication prayer keeps imagining failure: defeat, drought, famine, even exile (1 Kings 8:33-50). Why fill a dedication with disasters?
options: Solomon privately doubts the value of the house he built
Listing the dangers wards them off before they can arrive
The disasters threaten only nations that have no temple
The temple is where penitent failures turn to find forgiveness
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 8:30 sets the pattern of the whole prayer, heaven's ear open toward this place whenever failed people turn back to plead.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 8:46-50. Notice what Solomon asks God to do when the people have sinned and been carried far away.

connections.reason: 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' presents Jesus as the true temple — glory in a human body.
