Chronicles retells the temple construction with its own post-exilic emphasis.
The threshing floor David buys in chapter 24 becomes the temple site Solomon builds on.

nodes.title: The Glory and Fall of Solomon
nodes.summary: The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon and leaves breathless — then the same king amasses horses, gold, and seven hundred wives, and his heart turns to other gods. The wisest man in the world breaks every rule in Deuteronomy's law of the king, and God tears the kingdom in two.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The wisest man alive drifts into worshiping other gods, one marriage and one alliance at a time. What do these chapters show about how a heart turns, and what small compromise in your own life would look exactly like this if it kept growing?
assessment_questions: What draws the queen of Sheba to Jerusalem, and what does she conclude after seeing Solomon's court?
The narrator says Solomon's heart was not fully devoted to the LORD in his old age. Why does the story locate his fall in his heart rather than in his circumstances?
Solomon's gifts and success did not protect his devotion. Where in your life could success itself become the thing that pulls you away from God, and what guard would you put in place?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God renews his promise to Solomon while tying continued favor to obedience, so privilege never cancels responsibility.

teaching_concepts.concept: Success is no shield for the heart
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon's fame and wealth coexist with a slow turn away from God, proving that gifts and devotion are two different things.
Solomon's accumulating wives and alliances pull his worship after their gods, showing how small accommodations grow into open unfaithfulness.
God tears the kingdom in judgment yet preserves David's line and one tribe, holding justice and promise together.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Solomon's reign moves from the queen of Sheba's praise to God's announcement of judgment, and name what turned his heart.

comprehension_check.question: The king who received wisdom straight from God ends 1 Kings 11 building shrines for other gods. What does his fall teach about God's gifts?
options: A gift never substitutes for a heart kept devoted
The wisdom God gave must have faded as Solomon aged
His celebrated wisdom had been courtly legend, never God's gift
Wealth that great proves God's favor never left him
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 11:4 locates the collapse in an aging king's divided heart, while 1 Kings 9:4 had conditioned blessing on integrity before God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 9:4-5 and 1 Kings 11:4. Notice the condition God states, and what the narrator says eventually happened inside Solomon.

comprehension_check.question: God's sentence on Solomon tears the kingdom away yet leaves one tribe and a lamp for David (1 Kings 11:11-13, 11:36). What is the sentence doing?
options: Reducing the loss to a warning that never takes effect
Proving the covenant with David has now been revoked
Holding real judgment and the promise to David together
Letting politics run its course without any divine involvement
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 11:36 preserves David's line and city even while the kingdom is torn, covenant faithfulness working inside real judgment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 11:11-13. Notice what God says he will take, what he will keep, and for whose sake.

connections.reason: Jesus invokes this scene: 'the queen of the South came to hear Solomon — and something greater than Solomon is here.'
The Teacher's persona — a king of unmatched wisdom and wealth who tried everything — is Solomon's biography turned into an argument.

nodes.title: The Kingdom Divided
nodes.summary: Rehoboam's arrogance splits the nation: ten tribes follow Jeroboam north (Israel), two stay with David's line in Jerusalem (Judah). Jeroboam's golden calves at Bethel and Dan institutionalize idolatry, and king after king 'walked in his sin' — the drumbeat of both books of Kings.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jeroboam builds golden calves because sending worshipers to Jerusalem feels politically risky. When has convenience quietly reshaped what worship or obedience looks like in your world, and how would you recognize it happening?
assessment_questions: Why do the ten northern tribes break away from Rehoboam, and who becomes their first king?

Jeroboam sets up calves at Bethel and Dan and says these gods brought Israel out of Egypt. Why does the story treat his practical religious solution as the sin that defines every northern king after him?
Rehoboam rejects the elders' counsel for the advice of his young friends. Whose counsel do you actually weigh when you make decisions, and what would taking wise counsel seriously change?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Rehoboam's refusal to listen to wise counsel costs him ten tribes, showing how arrogant leadership brings communal disaster.
Jeroboam's calves look like practical religion, and the story exposes them as apostasy that cuts a nation off from God.
Prophets keep interrupting royal plans in these chapters, and ignoring their warnings consistently invites judgment.
God keeps his commitment to David's line while still judging each king by covenant faithfulness, so mercy never erases responsibility.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how the kingdom split under Rehoboam, and explain why Jeroboam's golden calves become the measuring stick for every northern king.

comprehension_check.question: At the moment Rehoboam refuses to listen, the narrator points behind the scene to the LORD's own word (1 Kings 12:15). What is that note claiming?
options: Rehoboam bears no blame since the outcome was fixed
God abandoned the whole nation to its political fate
The kingdom fell to chance the narrator dresses in piety
The split executes the judgment God had already announced
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 12:15 ties the disaster to the word spoken through Ahijah, the judgment announced in 1 Kings 11:11 now arriving on schedule.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 11:11 and then 1 Kings 12:15. Notice whose earlier sentence the narrator says this moment fulfills.

comprehension_check.question: Jeroboam sets up the golden calves only after some anxious arithmetic in his heart (1 Kings 12:26-28). What does the story expose in his new religion?
options: A sincere reform God accepted although its style was irregular
Worship engineered to protect a throne, whatever God had commanded
A forgivable compromise that later kings quietly walked back
An honest guess at worship by a king without guidance
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 12:26-27 shows the calves born of political fear about pilgrims returning to Jerusalem, and 1 Kings 13:34 names the result sin.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 12:26-28. Notice what Jeroboam is worried about before he ever says a word about worship.

connections.reason: Kings covers the same era with both kingdoms in view; Chronicles deliberately keeps only Judah in frame.

nodes.title: Elijah vs. Baal
nodes.summary: Against Ahab and Jezebel's state-sponsored Baal cult, Elijah shuts the sky, calls down fire on Mount Carmel, then collapses into despair and meets God not in wind or earthquake but a low whisper. Naboth's stolen vineyard shows what the fight is about: kings who devour their own people.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Elijah asks the people how long they will waver between two opinions. Where in these chapters does God prove himself with fire, where does he speak in a whisper, and what would it mean for you to stop wavering between two loyalties this week?
assessment_questions: What happens on Mount Carmel when Elijah and the prophets of Baal each prepare a sacrifice?

Right after the fire falls at Carmel, Elijah collapses into despair, and God passes by in a low whisper rather than in wind, earthquake, or fire. What does that scene teach about how God meets a discouraged servant?
Naboth dies so a king can have a vegetable garden, and God sends Elijah to name the crime. What injustice near you needs someone willing to speak, and what holds you back?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Elijah is fed by ravens and a starving widow, showing that God sustains his servants in surprising ways when he calls them into conflict.
Carmel puts Baal to a public test and fire answers only the LORD, so worship is a real decision between rival claims rather than a mood.
At Horeb God meets Elijah's despair with food, rest, a whisper, and a new assignment, treating exhaustion with care instead of rebuke.
Naboth's vineyard shows God taking the side of the powerless, since no crown puts a person above the covenant.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the contest on Mount Carmel and explain what Elijah's encounter with God at Horeb adds to the picture of who God is.

comprehension_check.question: On Carmel, Elijah gives Baal's prophets every advantage and all day (1 Kings 18:21-39). What is the contest built to settle?
options: Whether the LORD or Baal is God, ending Israel's hedging
Whether prayer works better when it is loud and desperate
Whether Baal deserves a lesser place under the LORD
Whether Israel's drought came from angering the storm god
comprehension_check.why: 1 Kings 18:24 makes an answered altar the deciding test between rival gods, and 1 Kings 18:39 records Israel's verdict.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 18:21. Notice the question Elijah puts to the people before any altar is built.

comprehension_check.question: After Carmel's triumph, Elijah flees to Horeb asking to die (1 Kings 19:4). How does God handle his collapsed prophet?
options: With a public rebuke that shames him into returning
With agreement that Israel's apostasy is now past remedy
With food, rest, his own presence, and further work
With silence until the prophet's despair burns itself out
comprehension_check.why: The angel feeds him twice in 1 Kings 19:5-7, and in 1 Kings 19:15-16 God entrusts him with new assignments.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Kings 19:5-8 and 1 Kings 19:15-18. Notice what God provides before asking anything, and what work still waits.

connections.reason: Elijah stands with Moses at the Transfiguration — the prophets personified beside the law.
James holds up Elijah's prayer that shut the sky as the model of effective righteous prayer.
Paul cites God's 'seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal' as the pattern of the faithful remnant.

nodes.title: Elisha: Double Portion
nodes.summary: Elijah ascends in a whirlwind amid chariots of fire and Elisha inherits a double portion of his spirit: oil that doesn't run out, a Shunammite's son raised, Naaman the Syrian general healed of leprosy in the Jordan. Grace keeps leaking across Israel's borders to outsiders.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Naaman almost misses his healing because the instruction is too simple and the river too ordinary. What do Elisha's miracles keep showing about the kinds of people God helps and the means he uses, and where might you be despising a simple obedience God has put in front of you?
assessment_questions: What does Elisha ask for before Elijah is taken up, and how does he receive it?
Naaman is a foreign general with leprosy, and a captive Israelite servant girl points him to the prophet. What does his healing say about how far God's mercy reaches?

Gehazi turns Naaman's healing into a chance for personal profit and walks away carrying the leprosy. What does his story warn about using sacred things for private gain, and where does that temptation touch you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Elisha's double portion marks God carrying the same Spirit-empowered ministry forward after Elijah, so the mission outlives the man.
Elisha's signs multiply a widow's oil, raise a dead boy, and cleanse a leper, showing God's power directed at ordinary and desperate people.
Naaman the Syrian is healed through humble obedience in the Jordan, proof that God's mercy was never fenced inside Israel.
Gehazi's greed shows that closeness to God's work is no license to exploit it, and signs must be matched by character.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the healing of Naaman and explain what it, together with Elisha's other miracles, reveals about who God's mercy is for.

comprehension_check.question: Naaman nearly walks away from his healing in 2 Kings 5. What does the story treat as the real obstacle?
options: The prophet's distance, since Elisha would not meet an enemy commander
His own expectation of a cure as grand as his standing
Israel's king, who read the request as a pretext for war
His people's gods, whom he had to renounce before the cure
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 5:11-14 shows the healing waiting only on humble obedience to the simple word the prophet sent.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 5:10-14 again. Notice what Naaman says he expected, and what finally happens instead.

comprehension_check.question: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit in 2 Kings 2. Within these chapters, what does the request turn out to mean?
options: The firstborn heir's share, carrying the same ministry forward
A standing above his master, proved by mightier public wonders
A guarantee that Israel would never lack a miracle worker
A private gift of power for the hardest cases ahead
comprehension_check.why: In 2 Kings 2:15 the watching prophets recognize that the spirit of Elijah now rests on Elisha, the heir carrying his master's work forward.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 2:9-15 again. Notice what the watching prophets conclude when Elisha strikes the water.

connections.reason: Jesus cites Naaman and the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth — God's pattern of blessing outsiders — and nearly gets thrown off a cliff for it.

nodes.title: Jehu's Purge
nodes.summary: A young prophet from Elisha's circle anoints Jehu in secret, and the purge that follows is swift and total: Joram shot on Naboth's ground, Ahaziah of Judah caught in the sweep, Jezebel thrown from her window, seventy sons of Ahab beheaded, and the Baal temple turned into a latrine. The narrator counts each blow as the fulfillment of Elijah's word against Ahab's house, and God grants Jehu four generations on Israel's throne. Yet the verdict is double: Jehu destroys Baal and walks on in Jeroboam's calf worship, zeal against evil without a heart careful for God's law.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God commends Jehu for carrying out everything that was in his heart against Ahab's house, and the same paragraph says Jehu was not careful to follow God's law with all his heart. What is the difference between being zealous against evil and being devoted to God, and where could that gap open in your own life?
assessment_questions: What is Jehu anointed to do in 2 Kings 9:6-7, and what has happened to Ahab's house and to Baal worship by the end of chapter 10?

The narrator keeps pausing the violence to note that each blow fulfills words spoken through Elijah. Why does the account insist the purge is the LORD's sentence rather than Jehu's ambition, and what does 10:29-31 add to that picture?

Jehu tears down what is evil with total energy and never builds wholehearted obedience of his own. Where are you more defined by what you are against than by devotion to God, and what would careful attention to his instruction look like there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Elijah's sentence from Naboth's vineyard is executed detail by detail, presenting the prophetic word as history written in advance.
Jehu carries out judgment without being righteous himself, and the text holds divine justice and human violence in real, unresolved tension.
Destroying Baal's temple coexists with keeping the state calves at Bethel and Dan, so being against idolatry still falls short of seeking God.
God rewards the obedience Jehu did render, and the limit set on the promise quietly announces that instruments of judgment are also judged.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Jehu's purge fulfills, and why the narrator's final verdict on him is double rather than simple praise.

comprehension_check.question: The narrator repeatedly ties each death in Jehu's purge back to words spoken through Elijah. What is that framing establishing?
options: The prophets held the real political power in Israel
Jehu's ambition conveniently matched an old prophecy
The purge executes a sentence God had already passed
Israel's dynasties always ended in prophetic bloodshed
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 9:7 gives the commission before a single blow falls: strike down the house of Ahab so the LORD may avenge his servants' blood.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 9:6-10 again. Notice whose words define Jehu's task before he acts, and whose blood is being answered for.

comprehension_check.question: How does 2 Kings 10:28-31 finally weigh Jehu?
options: A flawed king whose zeal fully atoned for his sins
A failure whose obedience God refused to acknowledge
A king too violent for God to ever use again
God's instrument who still withheld his heart
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 10:30-31 grants Jehu four generations for work well done, then records that he was not careful to follow the LORD wholeheartedly.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 10:28-31 again. Notice what Jehu destroys, what he keeps, and what the LORD says about each.

nodes.title: Two Kingdoms Sliding toward Assyria
nodes.summary: Athaliah slaughters the royal seed and rules Judah until the priest Jehoiada, having hidden the infant Joash in the temple for six years, crowns him and renews the covenant. From there the story alternates north and south through a century: Joash repairs the temple and then buys off Aram with its treasures, Jehu's line runs four generations to Jeroboam II's prosperous hollow reign, and after Zechariah the north churns through assassinations while Assyria's shadow lengthens. It ends with Ahaz of Judah stripping the temple and copying a Damascus altar to please his new master, a vassal remodeling the house of the LORD.
key_themes: the promise kept by a thread
nodes.discussion_prompt: In the middle of the collapse, the narrator says the LORD was gracious to Israel because of his covenant with Abraham and was unwilling to destroy them. As coups, buy-offs, and vassal deals pile up in these chapters, what difference does that one sentence make to how you read the era, and to how you read your own worst seasons?
assessment_questions: How does the Davidic line survive Athaliah in 2 Kings 11, and what covenant does Jehoiada make when Joash is crowned?
The narrator credits Israel's survival to the covenant with Abraham even while kings fail on both sides of the border. How do 2 Kings 13:23 and the era's steady decline fit together?

Ahaz answers a military threat by calling himself Assyria's servant and refitting God's altar to match Damascus. When pressure comes, what do you reshape to please the powers you fear, and what would trust have looked like instead?

teaching_concepts.explanation: One hidden infant is all that remains of David's line under Athaliah, and God's promise proves stronger than a palace massacre.
Jehoiada's covenant makes king and people the LORD's people again, a renewal that flows out of the sanctuary rather than the throne.
The narrator's aside in 2 Kings 13:23 credits the covenant with Abraham for Israel's survival, mercy underwriting even the north's final century.
Ahaz's Damascus altar shows political fear redesigning the sanctuary itself, a surrender of trust that feeds the very power it courts.

nodes.completion_criteria: Trace how David's line survives Athaliah, and explain what 2 Kings 13:23 and Ahaz's altar each reveal about the era's real struggle.

comprehension_check.question: What is at stake in the hiding and crowning of Joash in 2 Kings 11?
options: Whether the priesthood can overrule a reigning queen
Whether Judah will copy the north's rotating dynasties
Whether a child king can hold power over his elders
Whether God's promise to David survives the massacre
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 11:1-3 leaves one hidden son between Athaliah and the extinction of the royal line God had pledged himself to.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 11:1-4 again. Notice how much of David's house is left, and where the survivor is kept for six years.

comprehension_check.question: Amid the coups and losses of these chapters, 2 Kings 13:23 explains why Israel is not simply erased. What does it credit?
options: The repentance each new king briefly displayed
The LORD's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
Elisha's continued intercession for the northern kings
Israel's value to Assyria as a buffer state
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 13:23 says the LORD was gracious and turned toward Israel because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 13:22-23 again. Notice the reason the narrator gives for Israel's survival, and how old that reason is.

nodes.title: Samaria Falls: The Covenant Autopsy
nodes.summary: Samaria falls to Assyria in a few verses, and then the narrator stops the history to explain it: Israel sinned against the God of the exodus, walked in the nations' customs, ignored every prophet, and stiffened its neck until the LORD removed it from his presence. The chapter is the interpretive key of Kings, reading the exile of 722 BC as the covenant's own sanctions executed rather than an accident of empire. It closes with Assyria's resettled peoples learning a hybrid worship, fearing the LORD while serving their own gods, the seedbed of the later Samaritans.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The autopsy says God warned Israel through every prophet and seer, generation after generation, before the end came. If a narrator wrote this kind of honest postmortem about your community's drift, what would it name, and which warnings are currently being tuned out?
assessment_questions: According to 2 Kings 17:7-18, what reasons does the narrator give for Israel's exile, and what happens in the land afterward?

The chapter reports the fall in two verses and spends dozens explaining it. Why does the writer care more about the why than the how, and what does that priority say about how Kings understands history?

The resettled peoples feared the LORD while serving their own gods, an arrangement the chapter refuses to bless. Where does that both-and pattern show up in your own life, and what would undivided loyalty require?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The exile of 722 BC lands exactly where Deuteronomy said unfaithfulness would lead, so God's warnings prove to be history in advance.
God keeps sending messengers for centuries before the end comes, so the fall testifies to long-refused mercy rather than a short temper.
The narrator orders the evidence like a covenant lawsuit, writing theology as history so the reader cannot mistake the cause of the catastrophe.
The settlers' mixed devotion, fearing the LORD while serving their gods, names the exact compromise Israel itself had died of.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain, using 2 Kings 17, why the northern kingdom fell, and what the chapter's closing picture of mixed worship warns about.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Kings 17 halts the story to explain Samaria's fall at length. What explanation does the narrator rule out by writing it?
options: That God's patience had run out too quickly
That exile was the fate of every small kingdom
That the fall was ordinary imperial politics
That Israel's sin was too recent to deserve exile
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 17:7 opens the explanation with a cause no empire supplies: all this happened because Israel sinned against the LORD their God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 17:7-8 again. Notice what the narrator names as the cause before any army is mentioned.

comprehension_check.question: What role do the prophets play in the autopsy of 2 Kings 17:13-14?
options: They are the evidence that God warned before he judged
They are the leaders who should have replaced the kings
They are the last resort God tried once judgment began
They are proof that some in Israel stayed faithful
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 17:13 records the standing appeal through all his prophets and seers, turn from your wicked ways, sent long before the end.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 17:13-15 again. Notice when the warnings come in the story, and how the people answer them.

connections.reason: Hosea preached into exactly this collapse; the two texts narrate the same catastrophe from prophet's and historian's angles.
The Samaritans of Jesus' day descend from chapter 17's resettlement — the backstory of the woman at the well.

nodes.title: Hezekiah and the Assyrian Siege
nodes.summary: Hezekiah trusts the LORD like no king before him, removes the high places, and rebels against Assyria; Sennacherib's field commander answers beneath the walls, mocking every god who failed to save its city. Hezekiah spreads the blasphemous letter before the LORD, Isaiah carries God's answer, and the angel of the LORD empties the Assyrian camp in a night. Two further scenes complicate the triumph: a mortal illness reversed with fifteen added years, and Babylonian envoys shown every treasure, drawing Isaiah's quiet word that Babylon, not Assyria, will one day carry it all away.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Face to face with the empire's propaganda, Hezekiah's move is to spread the letter before the LORD and pray that all kingdoms may know who alone is God. What does his prayer ask for beyond survival, and what would it change to pray about your own crises with that larger goal in view?
assessment_questions: What does Hezekiah do with Sennacherib's letter in 2 Kings 19, and how is Jerusalem delivered from the Assyrian army?

The Rabshakeh's speech lists the gods of conquered cities and files the LORD among them. How does the deliverance answer that taunt, and why does Hezekiah's prayer in 19:19 make the nations' knowledge its goal?
After deliverance and healing, Hezekiah shows Babylon's envoys everything he has. Where does gratitude in your life shade into display, and what would stewarding a blessing humbly look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Hezekiah takes Assyria's threat straight to God, and the deliverance that follows shows prayer as a real act with real consequences.
Assyrian theology treats every god as a local failure waiting its turn, and the emptied camp answers with the difference between idols and the living God.
The same reign that sees Jerusalem saved also awakens Babylon's interest in its treasures, and the book lets the triumph and the seed of exile stand together.

teaching_concepts.concept: Trust as the measure of a reign
teaching_concepts.explanation: 2 Kings 18:5-6 summarizes Hezekiah by his trusting and holding fast to the LORD, the rubric by which every king of Judah is weighed.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how Jerusalem was delivered from Sennacherib, and explain how the Babylonian envoy scene plants the seed of the book's ending.

comprehension_check.question: The Rabshakeh's taunt in 2 Kings 18 files the LORD among the gods that failed their cities. What does the deliverance of chapter 19 answer?
options: Jerusalem's temple made the city impossible to conquer
Assyria's cruelty had finally gone too far for heaven
Kings who trust the LORD are always rescued from enemies
The LORD is no local god; he alone is God
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 19:19 asks deliverance so that all kingdoms may know that the LORD alone is God, and 19:35 gives heaven's answer.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 18:33-35 and 19:19 again. Notice the claim the taunt makes about the LORD, and what Hezekiah asks God to prove.

comprehension_check.question: What does the visit of the Babylonian envoys in 2 Kings 20 contribute to the book?
options: It shows Judah wisely courting a counterweight to Assyria
It proves Hezekiah's faith failed at the very end
It plants the word naming Babylon as the coming exile
It records a routine diplomatic courtesy with no larger meaning
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 20:17-18 turns the tour of treasures into the book's forecast: everything shown will one day be carried off to Babylon.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 20:12-19 again. Notice what Hezekiah shows, and what Isaiah says will happen to exactly those things.

connections.reason: Isaiah 36-39 retells the Hezekiah-Sennacherib crisis nearly word for word; the prophet is a character in it.

nodes.title: Manasseh's Ruin and Josiah's Reform
nodes.summary: Manasseh reverses everything his father built: altars for Baal inside the temple courts, his son through the fire, innocent blood filling Jerusalem, until the LORD announces a judgment that will make both ears tingle. Two generations later the boy king Josiah hears the rediscovered Book of the Law read aloud, tears his robes, and leads the most sweeping reform in Judah's history, from the temple to Bethel's altar to a covenant renewed with all the people. The narrator honors him beyond every king and still records the verdict: the fury kindled by Manasseh does not turn back, and Josiah dies at Megiddo with the end already in motion.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Josiah turns to the LORD with all his heart, soul, and strength, and the narrator says the coming judgment still stands. If obedience cannot be measured by whether it changes the outcome, what is it for, and what would it mean for you to obey like Josiah inside a story you cannot fix?
assessment_questions: What does Manasseh do in 2 Kings 21, and what happens when the Book of the Law is read to Josiah in chapter 22?

Josiah's reform is the most thorough in Judah's history, yet 23:26-27 says the LORD's anger over Manasseh remains. How do the reform and the verdict fit together, and what does Huldah's word to Josiah add?

Josiah tears his robes at words his nation had owned all along and forgotten. What Scripture have you effectively lost through familiarity, and what would letting it read you the way the scroll read Josiah involve?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The revival begins when the lost book is read aloud, showing the word's power to remake first a king and then a kingdom.
Manasseh's generation-deep damage outlasts even Josiah's obedience, teaching that God's patience never makes sin harmless.
2 Kings 23:25 crowns Josiah as the king who turned with all his heart when turning could no longer avert the end, obedience honored apart from outcomes.
The sentence of 2 Kings 21:12-13 stretches Samaria's measuring line over Jerusalem, so the reader watches the reform knowing what is already coming.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Manasseh's reign and Josiah's reform relate, and why the book honors Josiah supremely while judgment still falls.

comprehension_check.question: When the Book of the Law is read to Josiah in 2 Kings 22, he tears his robes. What does his reaction show he understood?
options: The scroll put his nation under unkept covenant terms
The scroll was a lost relic requiring proper ceremonial honor
The scroll had predicted his own coming death at Megiddo
The scroll condemned the generations before his own reign
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 22:13 is Josiah's own reading: great is the wrath against us, because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 22:11-13 again. Notice who Josiah says the book's words are about.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Kings 23 praises Josiah beyond every king, then says the LORD's fierce anger did not turn back. What is the narrative teaching?
options: Reform was pointless once exile had already been decreed
Public displays of reform count less than private repentance
God simply valued Manasseh's offense above Josiah's devotion
Centuries of sin carry weight no reign can lift
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 23:25-26 sets the two facts side by side: a king without equal in turning to the LORD, and a judgment whose causes lay generations deep.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 23:25-27 again. Notice whose deeds the LORD's remaining anger is tied to.

nodes.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
nodes.summary: The end comes in waves: Jehoiakim's revolt, the first deportation with Jehoiachin, Zedekiah's doomed rebellion, and then the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, when the walls are breached, the king's sons are killed before his blinded eyes, and the house of the LORD is burned to the ground. The narrator insists this happened at the LORD's command, the sentence for Manasseh's sin, and follows the survivors through Gedaliah's murder down into Egypt. Then the last four verses lift Jehoiachin from prison to the king of Babylon's table, a Davidic heir alive and eating bread, the book's one small light left burning.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Kings ends with a deposed heir of David eating daily bread at his conqueror's table, and the writer thought that worth recording after the temple burned. Why end there, and what does it teach about the size of hope God's people are sometimes given to live on?
assessment_questions: What happens to Jerusalem, the temple, and the last kings of Judah in 2 Kings 24-25?

The narrator says the catastrophe came at the LORD's command for the sins of Manasseh, even naming innocent blood the LORD would not pardon. What is gained, and what is hard, about reading 586 BC that way?

The book closes on Jehoiachin's small mercy rather than on the flames. When a season of your life ends in real loss, what would it mean to hold the Jehoiachin-sized mercies without pretending the loss is smaller than it is?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The fall executes the sentence announced since Manasseh, so the catastrophe vindicates the word of the LORD rather than defeating it.

teaching_concepts.concept: The temple is not a talisman
teaching_concepts.explanation: The house where the LORD set his name burns like any building once the covenant behind it is dead, the end of a presumption the prophets had long attacked.
Nebuchadnezzar wins no contest of gods; the narrator keeps the LORD as the actor throughout, which is the only reason hope can survive the defeat.
The exiled Davidic king raised to Babylon's table leaves the covenant promise alive, ending the book with a door still ajar.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how 2 Kings presents Jerusalem's fall as the LORD's own act, and name the flicker of hope the book chooses for its final scene.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Kings 24:3 interrupts the invasions to say this came upon Judah at the command of the LORD. What is the narrator securing with that line?
options: That resistance to Babylon was always a doomed policy
That the LORD, not Babylon, governs Judah's fall
That readers should accept imperial rule as God's order
That the LORD had transferred his favor to Babylon
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 24:3-4 roots the catastrophe in the LORD's own sentence on Manasseh's sins, keeping God the actor even in defeat.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 24:2-4 again. Notice who sends the raiders, and for what stated reason.

comprehension_check.question: After the temple burns, the book ends with Jehoiachin freed to eat at Babylon's table. Why close there?
options: To show that surrender to Babylon brought reward
To soften the horror of the fall for future readers
To leave David's line alive and the promise breathing
To record one exile's fortune among the many losses
comprehension_check.why: 2 Kings 25:27-30 lifts a son of David from prison to the king's table, a sign that the covenant line survives the catastrophe.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Kings 25:27-30 again. Notice whose descendant is being kept alive, fed, and honored as the book ends.

connections.reason: Jeremiah's narrative chapters cover the same siege and fall from inside the doomed city.
Lamentations is the poetry of the destruction 2 Kings 25 reports as history.
The exile to Babylon is the Deuteronomy 28 curse executed in history.
The same final century told twice: Kings explains the disaster, Chronicles points past it.

nodes.title: The Genealogies: Adam to the Return
nodes.summary: Nine chapters of names running from Adam to the families resettling Jerusalem after exile — the post-exilic community proving to itself that it is still Israel, still carrying David's line and Aaron's priesthood. Tedious until you see what's at stake: identity after catastrophe.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Nine chapters of names look tedious until you remember who first read them: families back from exile wondering if they were still Israel. Why does a list of ancestors answer that fear, and where do you look when you need proof that you belong to something that survives?
assessment_questions: With whom does the genealogy begin, and with which community does it end in chapter 9?
The Chronicler chooses to open his whole book with family lists tracing kingship and priesthood through the exile. What is he trying to prove to his first readers by arranging names this way?
These lists insist that God did not forget a single generation of his people. When you feel anonymous or disconnected, what would it change to believe your name is kept in a story like this?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The unbroken line from Adam to the returned exiles shows God keeping a people and a promise alive through every catastrophe.
The lists trace David's royal line and Aaron's priestly line through the exile, proving that Israel's God-given institutions survived it.
Recording names is an act of theology, since remembering each family declares that exile could not erase who Israel is.
The Chronicler selects and arranges his sources to make an argument about identity and hope, so the shape of the list is part of its message.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the Chronicler opens with nine chapters of genealogies and what those lists were meant to prove to families returning from exile.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Chronicles opens with nine chapters of names before any story is told. What are the lists doing for the community that first received them?
options: Preserving family records the exile had nearly destroyed
Ranking the tribes by honor within the restored community
Tracing how sin spread through the generations from Adam
Anchoring the returned remnant in Israel's unbroken line
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 9:1-2 lands the whole genealogy on the families resettling their towns, one Israel running from Adam to the return.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 9:1-2 again. Notice where the long line of names finally arrives, and who is living there.

comprehension_check.question: Within the genealogies, Judah with David's line and Levi with Aaron's receive by far the most space. What does that weighting signal?
options: The promises carried by king and priest still stand
The compiler simply used the fullest archives available
The northern tribes had forfeited their place in Israel
Only Judah and Levi kept their lines pure through exile
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 3:17-24 carries David's line beyond the exile, and 1 Chronicles 6 keeps Aaron's, so both offices outlive the catastrophe.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 3:17-24, then skim 1 Chronicles 6:1-15. Notice which two family lines refuse to stop at the exile.

connections.reason: Matthew's opening genealogy works the same way — using a family tree to claim the whole story for its subject.

nodes.title: David Crowned by All Israel
nodes.summary: The Chronicler compresses Saul to a single chapter: his death on Gilboa, read as unfaithfulness, he did not seek the LORD, so the kingdom is turned over to David. Then the account builds David's coronation as a national act of glad consensus: all Israel gathers at Hebron, the mighty men are honored, and long musters count off warriors from every tribe who come with undivided hearts to make David king. For the post-exilic audience the lists argue a thesis: the true king is the one all Israel, seeking God, unites around.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The Chronicler explains Saul's death with a single phrase, he did not seek the LORD, then spends two chapters naming the people who gathered to crown David. Why do you think seeking and gathering are the two measures this historian cares about, and which one is weaker in your own life right now?
assessment_questions: How does 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 explain Saul's death, and what happens at Hebron in chapters 11-12?

The muster lists name warriors from every tribe, including Issachar's men who understood the times, all of one mind to make David king. What are these lists arguing to the Chronicler's post-exilic readers?

Saul's epitaph is about failing to seek the LORD; David's rise begins with a whole people gathering in shared purpose. Where do you need to move from drift to deliberate seeking, and whose kingdom-work needs you to show up the way the tribes did at Hebron?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Saul's one-chapter treatment ends in the verdict of unfaithfulness, announcing the rubric, seeking the LORD or not, that will govern the whole retelling.
The Chronicler's favorite phrase gathers every tribe at Hebron, painting the unity a scattered post-exilic community needed to imagine again.
The musters are anything but military bookkeeping; counting every tribe's volunteers is how the Chronicler proves the kingdom's consensus under God.
Issachar's small company, famous for knowing what Israel should do, models discernment joined to commitment rather than commentary from the sidelines.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how the Chronicler reads Saul's death, and what the Hebron gathering and tribal musters are meant to prove about David's kingship.

comprehension_check.question: The Chronicler gives Saul a single chapter and closes it with a verdict in 1 Chronicles 10:13-14. What is that compression doing?
options: Sparing the returned exiles a painful chapter of national memory
Correcting Samuel's fuller account of Saul's long decline
Setting seeking the LORD as the measure of every reign
Marking the monarchy itself as Israel's great mistake
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 turns Saul's whole story into one lesson, he did not seek the LORD, the standard the Chronicler will apply to every king.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 again. Notice the reason given for the kingdom changing hands, and how little else about Saul is kept.

comprehension_check.question: Chapters 11-12 pile up names and numbers from every tribe coming to Hebron. What is the Chronicler establishing with the lists?
options: That all Israel, wholehearted, stood behind God's chosen king
That David's army was too strong for rivals to resist
That each tribe earned its place by military contribution
That the true records of the kingdom survived the exile
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 12:38 sums the lists up: men of war came to Hebron fully determined, and all the rest of Israel was of one mind to make David king.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 12:38-40 again. Notice the phrase describing the gathered nation's mind, and the mood of the days at Hebron.

connections.reason: Reading Samuel's warts-and-all account beside the Chronicler's curated one teaches how biblical historiography works.

nodes.title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
nodes.summary: David's first great project is bringing the ark up to his new capital, and the first attempt fails at the cost of Uzzah's life: a new cart instead of Levite shoulders, enthusiasm without the prescribed order. Three months at Obed-edom's blessed house later, David tries again the commanded way, Levites carrying, sacrifices offered, the city dancing, and the ark comes to its tent with a psalm of thanksgiving appointed for daily worship. The Chronicler expands this far beyond its Samuel parallel because it is his heart: Israel's life reordered around the presence of God, sought in the way God prescribes.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The same ark that broke out against Uzzah's steadying hand blesses Obed-edom's whole house for three months. As David studies that contrast and changes his approach, what is he learning about God, and what would seeking God in his way rather than in your preferred way look like for you?
assessment_questions: What goes wrong the first time David moves the ark in 1 Chronicles 13, and what does he do differently in chapter 15?

David concludes that the LORD broke out against them because we did not seek him about the proper order. What does the episode teach about the relationship between good intentions and God's instructions in worship?

The appointed psalm of chapter 16 calls Israel to seek the LORD's face always and to give thanks, and it becomes the pattern of daily ministry before the ark. What fixed rhythm of seeking and thanks could you appoint for yourself, and what would it change?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Uzzah's death and Obed-edom's blessing flow from the same presence, teaching that how God is approached matters because of who he is.
1 Chronicles 15:13 locates the failure in unconsulted procedure, and the second procession succeeds by seeking God about the way as well as the goal.
The successful ascent is louder than the failed one, showing that ordered worship and exuberant celebration are allies rather than rivals.
David institutionalizes gratitude, appointing thanksgiving as Israel's regular work before the ark, worship built into the calendar.

nodes.completion_criteria: Contrast the two attempts to move the ark and explain what 1 Chronicles 15:13 identifies as the difference, and what chapter 16 establishes in response.

comprehension_check.question: Between the failed procession of 1 Chronicles 13 and the successful one of chapter 15, what changes?
options: David's enthusiasm gives way to a quieter reverence
The people's hearts are finally ready for the ark
God's anger simply subsides during the three months
Israel seeks and follows God's prescribed way of carrying
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 15:13 names the earlier failure as not seeking God about the proper order, and 15:14-15 shows the Levites carrying as Moses commanded.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 15:11-15 again. Notice who carries the ark this time, and on whose instructions.

comprehension_check.question: David's psalm in 1 Chronicles 16 is appointed for regular ministry before the ark. What does that institution say worship is for?
options: Guarding the ark's holiness from another deadly mistake
Keeping Israel's memory, thanks, and seeking constantly before God
Giving the Levites a role now the carrying is finished
Marking the capital as the kingdom's one lawful shrine
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 16:8-11 sets the appointed work: give thanks, make known his deeds, seek the LORD and his strength, seek his face always.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 16:8-12 and 16:37 again. Notice which verbs the psalm commands, and how often the ministry is to happen.

nodes.title: Covenant, Conquest, and the Chosen Site
nodes.summary: David wants to build God a house, and God answers with the reverse: a promise to build David a house, a son whose throne will be established forever, a covenant David can only sit before in astonished prayer. The wars of chapters 18-20 then give the land rest on every side, and the census David orders over Joab's protest brings plague, an angel with drawn sword, and an altar raised at Ornan's threshing floor, where David refuses to offer what costs him nothing. The Chronicler ends the movement at that floor on purpose: judgment met by mercy has just chosen the temple site.
nodes.discussion_prompt: David plans to give God a building and instead receives a promise reaching generations he will never see. When he prays, who am I, that you have brought me this far, what has he understood about grace, and what would sitting before the LORD with your own version of that question sound like?
assessment_questions: What does David want to build in 1 Chronicles 17, and what does God promise to build instead?

The census ends with plague halted at Ornan's threshing floor, where David buys the site at full price and sacrifice answers judgment. Why does the Chronicler want this exact spot remembered as the place the temple will stand?
David refuses to offer burnt offerings that cost him nothing. Name what your own worship currently costs you, and what a full-price offering, of time, money, or pride, might look like this month.

teaching_concepts.explanation: God's promise to build David a lasting house anchors the whole retelling, and its forever reaches past Solomon toward Israel's messianic hope.

teaching_concepts.concept: A house he will not build
teaching_concepts.explanation: David's plan is denied without his hope being denied, modeling how God redirects devotion without despising it.
The wars of chapters 18-20 secure rest on every side, the condition Israel's law set for establishing central worship, so even the war chapters serve the temple story.
Judgment stayed, mercy received, and full price paid mark the site of the future altar, so the temple's location itself preaches atonement.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what God promises David in 1 Chronicles 17, and how the census story ends by identifying and consecrating the future temple site.

comprehension_check.question: David proposes to build God a house in 1 Chronicles 17. What shape does God's answer take?
options: A refusal until David's wars have made Israel safe
A demand for a costlier site than David had chosen
A promise that God will establish David's house instead
An instruction to wait until the ark's wanderings end
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 17:10-14 turns the offer around: the LORD will build David a house, raising up a son whose throne stands forever.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 17:4 and 17:10-14 again. Notice who ends up doing the building in God's answer.

comprehension_check.question: The census brings plague, and the story ends with an altar at Ornan's threshing floor. Why does the Chronicler close this movement there?
options: To warn kings against numbering what belongs to God
To show Joab vindicated against his king's command
To explain how Jerusalem absorbed its Jebusite population
To ground the future temple where mercy met judgment
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 21:26-27 shows sacrifice answered and the sword sheathed at that floor, the spot the next chapter names as the house of the LORD.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 21:24-27 again. Notice what happens at the floor David buys, and what he declares about the site right after.

nodes.title: David Prepares the Temple and Passes the Crown
nodes.summary: None of this material appears in Samuel: David, told he cannot build because he has shed much blood, pours his final years into preparing what Solomon will finish. He stockpiles gold, silver, iron, and cedar, organizes the Levites, priests, musicians, gatekeepers, and officials into courses, hands Solomon the plans, and charges king and assembly to seek God with a whole heart. The freewill offerings cascade, David prays the doxology that everything in heaven and earth is the LORD's, and Solomon is enthroned; the Chronicler's David dies as the founder of Israel's worship.
nodes.discussion_prompt: David spends his last strength gathering materials, drafting rosters, and blessing a project he is barred from finishing. What does it mean to pour yourself into something you will never personally enjoy, and what is the version of that work sitting in front of you?
assessment_questions: Why can David not build the temple himself according to 1 Chronicles 22:8, and what does he prepare and organize instead?

David's charge in 28:9 tells Solomon to know God and serve him wholeheartedly because the LORD searches every heart. How does that charge reframe all the lists of materials, courses, and duties around it?

In the offering prayer David says everything comes from God and giving only returns what was his. Try restating 1 Chronicles 29:14 in your own words, and name one possession or ability it would change your grip on this week.

teaching_concepts.explanation: David stockpiles materials and organizes ministries for a temple Solomon will build, modeling generosity toward a future he will not see.
The charge of 1 Chronicles 28:9 makes the heart the temple project's true foundation, since the LORD searches every heart and understands every intent.
The doxology of chapter 29 reframes generosity as stewardship, for everything in heaven and earth already belongs to the LORD.
Courses of priests, musicians, and gatekeepers turn devotion into institutions that outlast their founder, the Chronicler's blueprint for his own community.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what David prepares and organizes for the temple, and explain how 1 Chronicles 28:9 and 29:14 give the preparation its theological meaning.

comprehension_check.question: Chapters 23-27 are rosters: Levites, priests, singers, gatekeepers, treasurers, officers. What is the Chronicler doing with them?
options: Preserving personnel records the exile nearly destroyed
Proving David's administration rivaled other ancient courts
Filling narrative space until Solomon can take the throne
Founding the temple's ministry before one stone is laid
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 28:11-13 has David handing Solomon plans for the courses of priests and Levites along with the buildings, one prepared whole.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 28:11-13 and 28:19-21 again. Notice what the plans cover besides architecture, and who stands ready when the charge ends.

comprehension_check.question: In David's prayer over the offerings, what makes the people's giving acceptable?
options: The staggering totals that their generosity finally reached
It completes the vow David made about the temple
It returns to God what was always his, gladly
It offsets the bloodshed that barred David from building
comprehension_check.why: 1 Chronicles 29:14 says it plainly: everything comes from you, and from your own hand we have given to you.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Chronicles 29:14-17 again. Notice whose hand the gifts come from, and what God is said to test in the giver.

nodes.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
nodes.summary: The Chronicler opens Solomon's reign at Gibeon, where the whole assembly seeks the LORD before the Mosaic altar and God appears at night with an open offer: ask what I shall give you. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern a people too great for him, and receives them, plus the riches and honor he never requested. One chapter is all the Chronicler needs to set the reign's terms: the king who begins by asking rightly is the king fit to build the house.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Given one open-ended offer from God, Solomon's request is shaped entirely by the task in front of him: govern this great people. What does the shape of your asking reveal about what you think your life is for, and what would a Solomon-shaped request sound like from you?
assessment_questions: Where does Solomon go to worship in 2 Chronicles 1, and what does he ask for when God says to ask?
God's reply lists everything Solomon did not request, riches, honor, the lives of his enemies, before granting wisdom and more besides. What does that inventory teach about how God weighs requests?

Solomon asks for wisdom because of a responsibility he already carries. Name the biggest responsibility currently on you, and put into one sentence the request for it you would bring to God's open offer.

teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern God's people, and God grants both the request and the wealth he never sought.
God's delight in what Solomon asked, and in what he did not, shows prayers working as diagnostics of what we actually treasure.
Wisdom is requested for governing, so the gift exists for the people's good rather than the king's advantage, the pattern for every good endowment.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Solomon's request at Gibeon and explain why God grants riches and honor that were never asked for.

comprehension_check.question: In 2 Chronicles 1:11-12, God explains why Solomon's request pleases him. What is the reason?
options: Solomon asked humbly rather than presuming on the promise
Solomon asked for the good of the people he must govern
Solomon asked at the lawful altar with the whole assembly
Solomon asked for the one gift God most loves to give
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 1:11 singles out what Solomon did not ask, and honors the request made for governing the people in his charge.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 1:10-12 again. Notice which unmade requests God lists, and what the made request was for.

nodes.title: The Temple Built and Dedicated
nodes.summary: Solomon builds: the Huram correspondence and the conscripted labor, the house on Mount Moriah with its cherubim and veil, the sea, the lampstands, the courts. At the dedication the ark enters, the singers praise, and the glory cloud fills a house Solomon freely admits cannot contain the God of heaven; his great prayer asks that this impossible address become the place where sinners, foreigners, and exiles are heard. Fire falls, the feast is kept, and God answers by night with the Chronicler's signature promise: when judgment falls, if my people humble themselves and pray and seek and turn, I will hear, forgive, and heal.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Solomon builds God a magnificent house while asking out loud how any house can hold him, and God's night answer is about what happens when his people sin and disaster comes. Reading chapters 6-7 together, what do you think the temple is actually for, and what would it mean for your praying that God plans for failure in advance?
assessment_questions: What fills the temple in 2 Chronicles 5:13-14 and again in 7:1-3, and how do the people respond?

Solomon's prayer keeps imagining futures of defeat, drought, and exile, and asks God to hear from heaven when people pray toward this place. What does that make the temple's central purpose, and how does God's answer in 7:12-16 confirm it?
God's night answer gives a sequence, humble, pray, seek, turn, and a promise, hear, forgive, heal. Which step in that sequence is hardest for you, and what situation in your life is waiting on it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Fire and glory answer the dedication, marking the house as the place where God hears his people and they bow in worship.

teaching_concepts.concept: A house that cannot hold him
teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon's question in 2 Chronicles 6:18 keeps the theology honest: God dwells with Israel without being contained by Israel's architecture.
The dedication prayer and God's answer both center on sin, return, and forgiveness, so the temple's core business is mercy for people who fail.
2 Chronicles 7:14 gives the Chronicler's community its blueprint for restoration after judgment, the promise the whole book is arranged around.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what happens at the temple's dedication and explain the sequence and promise of God's night answer in 2 Chronicles 7:13-14.

comprehension_check.question: Solomon asks in 2 Chronicles 6:18 whether God will really dwell with man on earth, since heaven cannot contain him. Standing inside his own new temple, what is he confessing?
options: The temple is God's gracious address, never God's container
The temple project overreached what God had actually commanded
The temple must stay open to the surrounding nations
The temple's holiness depends on the king who built it
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 6:18-21 holds both truths in one prayer: heaven cannot contain God, yet his name and eyes rest on this house to hear.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 6:18-21 again. Notice what Solomon asks God's eyes and ears to do toward the house he cannot live in.

comprehension_check.question: God's night answer in 2 Chronicles 7:13-14 assumes a future of drought, locusts, and plague among his people. What does that assumption reveal about the temple's purpose?
options: It guarantees the land against disaster while worship continues
It warns that the building itself will share in Israel's punishments
It secures the dynasty Solomon's line needs to keep ruling
It stands ready as the road back when his people fall
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 7:13-14 plans for failure in advance: when judgment falls, humbling, prayer, seeking, and turning meet hearing, forgiveness, and healing.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 7:12-16 again. Notice what circumstances God describes, and what he promises to do from heaven when they come.

connections.reason: Chronicles retells the temple construction with its own post-exilic emphasis.

nodes.title: Solomon's Splendor and the Queen of Sheba
nodes.summary: The frame closes: building projects finished, the worship courses keeping David's ordinances at the completed house, the fleet bringing gold from Ophir. The queen of Sheba arrives with hard questions and leaves breathless, blessing the LORD who delighted in Solomon and set him on the throne to do justice and righteousness. The Chronicler ends the reign at its height, wealth beyond every king of the earth and wisdom the world lines up to hear, and omits the fall that Kings records; his Solomon exists to show what Israel looks like when the temple stands at the center.
nodes.discussion_prompt: A foreign queen looks at Solomon's kingdom and reads it correctly: your God loved Israel, so he made you king to do justice and righteousness. When outsiders look at what you have built, what do they conclude about your God, and what would you want them to?
assessment_questions: What does the queen of Sheba come to test in 2 Chronicles 9, and what does she say about the LORD in 9:8?
Kings records Solomon's later idolatry; the Chronicler stops at his splendor. Given the post-exilic audience, what is the Chronicler teaching by ending the portrait at its height?

The queen blesses God because Solomon's throne exists to do justice and righteousness. Where has God positioned you with resources or standing, and what justice-shaped use of them would make an outsider bless him?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Solomon's wealth and the queen's astonishment display God's blessing, while the story insists that favor never replaces faithfulness.
Kings of the earth seeking Solomon's God-given wisdom previews Israel's vocation as a light that draws outsiders toward the LORD.
The queen's blessing defines the throne's purpose: kingship held for the LORD, given because God loved Israel and wants justice done.
The omitted fall is the Chronicler's sermon in silhouette, holding up temple-centered kingship as the model his community should rebuild toward.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the queen of Sheba's visit shows about Solomon's reign, and why the Chronicler ends the portrait without the fall that Kings records.

comprehension_check.question: The queen of Sheba interprets everything she has seen in 2 Chronicles 9:8. Whose achievement does she say the kingdom is?
options: Solomon's, whose own wisdom turned inherited peace into great wealth
David's, whose preparations made the whole reign possible
The LORD's, who enthroned Solomon out of love for Israel
Israel's, whose offerings and labor raised the temple
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 9:8 blesses the LORD who delighted in Solomon, set him on the LORD's own throne, and loved Israel enough to want justice done.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 9:7-8 again. Notice whose throne the queen says Solomon sits on, and why she says he was given it.

comprehension_check.question: Readers of Kings know how Solomon's story ends; the Chronicler stops at the splendor of chapter 9. What is the omission doing?
options: Holding up temple-centered kingship as the pattern to rebuild
Implying the familiar ending has been corrected by better records
Protecting a beloved national hero's reputation for later generations
Suggesting wealth itself proves that a king pleases God
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 8:16 crowns the account, all Solomon's work completed with the house of the LORD finished, the ideal his community is called back to.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 8:12-16 again. Notice what activities fill the Chronicler's summary of the reign, and what the completed house anchors.

nodes.title: Schism to Asa: The Divided Kingdom's First Kings
nodes.summary: Rehoboam takes the young men's counsel and loses ten tribes in a sentence; the Chronicler follows only Judah from here. Shishak's invasion answers unfaithfulness, yet humbling brings partial deliverance; Abijah wins by relying on the LORD; and Asa's long reign becomes the rubric's showcase: reform and peace while he seeks the LORD, then a bought alliance with Aram, an imprisoned seer, and a disease he takes to physicians alone. Two sayings from these chapters carry the book's theology: the LORD is with you while you are with him, and his eyes range the earth to strengthen hearts fully devoted to him.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Asa in his youth faces a vast Cushite army with prayer, and in his old age cannot face a border dispute or an illness without buying human help. What happens to a person between those two points, and what keeps early trust from calcifying into late self-reliance in your own life?
assessment_questions: What splits the kingdom in 2 Chronicles 10, and how do Asa's early years in chapters 14-15 differ from his last years in chapter 16?
Azariah tells Asa the LORD is with you while you are with him, and Hanani says God's eyes seek hearts fully devoted. How do these two sayings interpret everything that happens from Rehoboam to Asa?
Asa's decline shows in where he turns first, treaty before trust, physicians before prayer. Audit your own last hard month: where did you turn first, and what would seeking God first have changed?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Chronicler grades each king on whether he sought the LORD, making covenant faithfulness the real measure of political success.
Rehoboam's response to Shishak shows judgment tempered the moment leaders humble themselves, the temple promise already at work in history.
Asa's bought Aramean treaty wins a skirmish and forfeits the war, exposing where Judah's security actually comes from.
Asa's story warns that a good start does not decide the end, since the seeking rubric keeps being applied to the whole of a life.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the Chronicler's seek-the-LORD rubric using Rehoboam's humbling and the two halves of Asa's reign as evidence.

comprehension_check.question: Asa defeats a huge army by prayer in chapter 14, then buys Aramean help against little Baasha in chapter 16. What does the seer Hanani say Asa's treaty revealed?
options: A kingdom grown too depleted to fight two wars at once
A ruler grown wiser about the limits of miracles
A political skill the Chronicler was unwilling to honor
A heart no longer relying on the LORD who saved him
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 16:7-9 contrasts the Cushite deliverance with the new treaty, and names the eyes of the LORD seeking fully devoted hearts.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 16:7-9 again. Notice what Hanani reminds Asa about the earlier war, and what he says God is looking for.

comprehension_check.question: Azariah's word in 2 Chronicles 15:2, the LORD is with you while you are with him, governs the whole section. What is it claiming?
options: God's presence rewards the nation's ritual exactness
God lets his people choose the nearness they will have
God's faithfulness fluctuates with his people's moods
God remains only with the kings who win their battles
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 15:2 and 15:4 promise that seeking finds and forsaking loses, the covenant dynamic Asa's own two halves then act out.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 15:1-4 again. Notice the conditions in the sentence, and who does the turning in verse 4.

connections.reason: Kings covers the same era with both kingdoms in view; Chronicles deliberately keeps only Judah in frame.

nodes.title: Jehoshaphat: The LORD Fights for Judah
nodes.summary: Jehoshaphat's early reign is the rubric at its best: he walks in the earlier ways of David, sends officials with the Book of the Law to teach in every town, and the fear of the LORD keeps the neighbors at peace. His alliance with Ahab nearly kills him at Ramoth-gilead, where only Micaiah, against four hundred prophets, tells the truth; the seer Jehu's rebuke sends him home to reform the courts. Then a vast coalition marches, and Judah's answer is the book in miniature: fasting, a prayer that ends we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you, and a choir marching before the army while the LORD sets the ambush.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jehoshaphat's battle prayer admits powerlessness and ignorance in front of his whole nation, and the army marches out behind singers instead of shock troops. What kind of confidence makes that possible, and what current fight of yours would look different if it opened with that admission?
assessment_questions: What does Jehoshaphat send through the towns of Judah in 2 Chronicles 17, and how does Judah face the invasion in chapter 20?

The battle liturgy of chapter 20, fasting, prayer, a prophet's word, singers in front, wins without Judah fighting. What is the Chronicler teaching about where the battle is decided, and how does 20:15 say it?

Jehoshaphat's prayer ends with eyes on God rather than a plan. Name the situation where you most need to say we do not know what to do, and decide what fixing your eyes on God would concretely involve this week.

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jehoshaphat's teaching mission sends the Book of the Law through every town, reform by instruction before any crisis arrives.
The word of 2 Chronicles 20:15-17 hands the war to God, and Judah's role becomes standing, believing, and singing.
The choir sings God's enduring love before the victory exists, worship as trust in motion rather than a technique that forces results.
The Ahab venture nearly costs Jehoshaphat his life and draws prophetic rebuke, the counterweight to his reforms in the Chronicler's assessment.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how Judah faces the coalition in 2 Chronicles 20, and explain what the teaching mission and the Ahab alliance each contribute to Jehoshaphat's portrait.

comprehension_check.question: Jehoshaphat puts singers in front of the army in 2 Chronicles 20:21. What does that arrangement express?
options: Trust acting on the promise that the battle belongs to God
A newly discovered ritual technique for unleashing God's power in war
A ceremonial formality Israel's armies had always observed
Confidence that the enemy would flee at loud worship
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 20:15-17 gives the promise before the march, the battle is God's and Judah need only stand, and the singing answers that word with trust.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 20:15-22 again. Notice what Judah is told the battle is, and when the singing begins relative to the victory.

comprehension_check.question: At Ramoth-gilead, four hundred prophets promise victory and Micaiah alone dissents. What does the scene teach about God's word?
options: Prophecy in Israel had decayed beyond recovery
Kings deserve counsel that strengthens their resolve
Majorities of religious voices can be wrong together
God speaks through whichever prophet the king commissions
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 18:13 sets Micaiah's rule, whatever my God says, that I will speak, and the battle's outcome vindicates the lone voice.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 18:12-13 and 18:33-34 again. Notice what Micaiah refuses to adjust, and how the day ends for the king who ignored him.

nodes.title: Athaliah, Joash, and the Line Nearly Extinguished
nodes.summary: The house of David nearly dies: Jehoram murders his brothers and marries into Ahab's house, Ahaziah falls in Jehu's purge, and Athaliah destroys all the royal seed, all but the infant Joash, hidden six years in the temple. Jehoiada's coup crowns the boy, renews the covenant, and while the old priest lives Joash even restores the house of the LORD; when Jehoiada dies, Joash listens to new advisers, abandons the temple, and has Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in its courtyard for saying so. Through it all runs one narrow thread: the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the lamp he had promised.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Joash does right all the days of Jehoiada the priest, then collapses the moment the voice beside him goes silent. What is the difference between a faith held for you by someone else and a faith that is yours, and whose death or absence would expose which one you have?
assessment_questions: How does the royal line survive Athaliah in 2 Chronicles 22-23, and what does Joash do after Jehoiada dies?
The narrator says the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David because of his covenant and promised lamp. How does 21:7 explain why this section's horrors never quite finish the story?

Zechariah dies for saying in public what Joash once knew, that forsaking the LORD forfeits his blessing. When truth-tellers in your life have become inconvenient, how have you handled them, and what would honoring one cost you this week?

teaching_concepts.concept: A lamp that will not go out
teaching_concepts.explanation: 2 Chronicles 21:7 explains the era's survival by God's covenant with David, promise-keeping as the deep plot under the palace horrors.
Joash's righteousness lasts exactly as long as his mentor, warning that secondhand devotion must become firsthand or die.
Jehoiada's covenant that king and people would be the LORD's repeats Israel's pattern of reconstituting national life around loyalty to God.
Zechariah's stoning in the temple court shows a leadership that silences correction, and his dying words hand the case to the God who sees.

nodes.completion_criteria: Trace how close the Davidic line comes to extinction and why it survives, and explain what Joash's rise and fall teach about borrowed faith.

comprehension_check.question: Massacres, coups, and an apostate king fill 2 Chronicles 21-24, yet the line of David keeps surviving. What does the Chronicler say is holding it?
options: The courage of priests who outmaneuver wicked rulers
The loyalty Judah's people keep showing the dynasty
The weakness and rivalries of the usurpers themselves
The covenant lamp God had promised David's house
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 21:7 says it outright: the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David because of the covenant and the promised lamp.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 21:7 again. Notice the reason given for Judah's survival, and how little it has to do with anyone's merit.

comprehension_check.question: Joash restores the temple under Jehoiada, then abandons the LORD once the priest dies. What does his arc expose?
options: His devotion had lived in his mentor, never in him
His reforms had been a political performance from the start
His childhood in the temple had bred quiet resentment
His advisers were the true rulers throughout his reign
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 24:2 ties Joash's doing right to all the days of Jehoiada, and 24:17-18 shows the turn the moment that influence is gone.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 24:2 and 24:17-22 again. Notice the time-limit clause on Joash's obedience, and whose voices replace Jehoiada's.

nodes.title: Amaziah to Ahaz: Decline into the Assyrian Era
nodes.summary: Four reigns run the rubric downhill. Amaziah obeys, but never wholeheartedly, dismissing hired troops at a prophet's word and then bowing to the idols of the nation he defeated; Uzziah prospers as long as he seeks the LORD, until strength breeds the pride that carries him into the sanctuary and out a leper; Jotham walks steadily; and Ahaz completes the collapse, sacrificing his sons, stripping the temple to bribe Assyria, serving the gods that defeated him, and finally shutting the doors of the house of the LORD. The section ends in the dark on purpose: the next chapter opens with those doors.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Uzziah's epitaph could read: he was marvelously helped until he became strong. Why is being helped easier on the soul than being strong, and where has a strength or success of yours started writing checks against humility?
assessment_questions: What does the narrator say about Amaziah's heart in 2 Chronicles 25:2, and what does Ahaz finally do to the temple in 28:24?
Uzziah's success is credited to seeking God, and his fall to pride in the strength success brought. How do 26:5 and 26:16 turn one king's biography into the section's warning?

Ahaz responds to every defeat by serving the gods of his conquerors, reasoning that they must be stronger. When life defeats you, whose help do you instinctively court, and what would it take to resist the Ahaz reflex?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Amaziah's right-but-not-wholehearted epitaph names the divided condition this whole section anatomizes reign by reign.
Amaziah and Uzziah begin well and fall through pride or drift, warning that yesterday's faithfulness does not decide today's.
Uzziah's censer asserts that success confers rights before God, and the leprosy that answers marks presumption as the disease it is.
Ahaz's closed temple is Judah locking out its own healing, the low point Hezekiah's first act will reverse.

nodes.completion_criteria: Use Amaziah, Uzziah, and Ahaz to show the section's descent, and explain why the closed temple doors are its fitting final image.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Chronicles 26 hinges Uzziah's reign on a single turn. What is it?
options: From early priestly guidance to the counsel of military men
From seeking God in weakness to pride in acquired strength
From Jerusalem's interests to his building projects abroad
From public faithfulness to secret personal idolatry
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 26:5 and 26:15-16 draw the arc: success while he sought the LORD, then strength, then the pride that destroyed him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 26:5 and 26:15-16 again. Notice what his success depended on, and what changed when he grew strong.

comprehension_check.question: In his distress, Ahaz sacrifices to the gods of Damascus because they seemed to beat him. What does the Chronicler make of that logic?
options: An understandable experiment that simply came too late
The reasoning of the age that any king would follow
A shrewd diplomatic necessity dressed up in religious clothing
A misreading, since his own God sent the defeats
comprehension_check.why: 2 Chronicles 28:5 and 28:19 attribute Ahaz's defeats to the LORD's own hand, so help lay behind him, never in Damascus.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Chronicles 28:5 and 28:22-23 again. Notice who the narrator says gave Ahaz into his enemies' hands, and whom Ahaz thanks.

nodes.title: Hezekiah's Reformation
