connections.reason: Revelation's merchants weeping over fallen Babylon rework Ezekiel 27's shipwreck lament for Tyre.

nodes.title: Egypt: The Dragon and the Felled Cedar
nodes.summary: Seven dated oracles fall on Egypt, and they keep circling one boast: Pharaoh saying that the Nile is his and that he made it. Ezekiel answers with a great river monster hauled out of its own waters and dumped in the open field. Chapter 31 then hands Pharaoh a history lesson shaped like a cedar, a tree so tall its top stood among the clouds, cut down because it grew proud of its height. The last oracle marches Egypt's horde down to lie with the other fallen nations in the pit, and the light itself goes out over the land.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Pharaoh's boast is that the river is his and that he made it, when the Nile was the one thing in Egypt no king had any hand in making. Where do people take credit for what was simply handed to them, and where do you catch yourself doing the same?
assessment_questions: What boast does God quote back to Pharaoh in Ezekiel 29:3 and 29:9, and what creature is Pharaoh compared to?
Chapter 31 answers a living empire with the story of a cedar that was already cut down. Why argue with Egypt by telling her about somebody else's fall?
These oracles keep saying the outcome God wants is that Egypt will know who he is. What would have to change for one of your own successes to teach you something about God rather than about yourself?

teaching_concepts.concept: The boast that gives itself away
teaching_concepts.explanation: Pharaoh claims to have made the river his whole kingdom depends on, which turns a gift into a possession and becomes the exact charge the oracles answer.
Assyria is held up as a cedar already felled, so Egypt is invited to read her own future in a story she can verify for herself.

teaching_concepts.concept: Even the greatest go down to the pit
teaching_concepts.explanation: Chapter 32 seats Pharaoh's horde among nations that once terrified the living, which quietly erases the difference between empires that all looked permanent.
The refrain about knowing the LORD returns through every oracle, so the goal of the sentence is that Egypt end up understanding who God actually is.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Pharaoh's boast about the Nile is claiming, and describe how the cedar of chapter 31 and the pit of chapter 32 answer it.

comprehension_check.question: God quotes Pharaoh's boast about the Nile back to him more than once. Why is that the line the oracles keep returning to?
options: It takes credit for the one thing Egypt was given rather than built
It insults the God of a small nation that Egypt had already defeated
It denied that Babylon would ever be allowed to defeat Egypt
It proves Pharaoh never understood how the river actually worked
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 29:3 and 29:9 both put the claim that the Nile is his and that he made it at the center of the charge against Pharaoh.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 29:1-9 again. Notice the line God repeats back to Pharaoh, and what he says will become of that river's land.

comprehension_check.question: Chapter 31 answers Pharaoh with a cedar that towered over every other tree and was then cut down. What is the argument?
options: Egypt's empire is younger and smaller than the one being described
Trees and empires alike are subject to natural cycles of decay
Greatness itself was the offense, since God resists every large power
What already happened to a greater power is Egypt's own future
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 31:10-11 says the cedar was handed over because it grew proud on account of its height, and the chapter sets that fall in front of Pharaoh as his own case.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 31:1-14 again. Notice who the tree stands for, and who is told to look at it.

nodes.title: Dry Bones and the Shepherd King
nodes.summary: The city falls, and Ezekiel's message flips to hope: God himself will shepherd the flock his leaders devoured (34), give a heart of stone-for-flesh transplant and his own Spirit (36), and breathe a valley of dry bones back into a living army (37) — 'can these bones live?' Resurrection enters Israel's vocabulary as national hope.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God promises to trade a heart of stone for a heart of flesh and to put his own Spirit inside his people. Why does real change have to start that deep, and what part of your life most needs that kind of transplant?
assessment_questions: What happens in the valley of dry bones, and in what stages do the bones come back to life?
In chapter 34 God condemns the shepherds who fed themselves and promises to shepherd the flock in person. What does that promise reveal about how God views failed leaders and scattered people?
God promises a new heart and his own Spirit as the source of obedience. What have you tried to change by willpower alone, and what would depending on the Spirit look like instead?

teaching_concepts.explanation: After the leaders devour the flock, God promises to search out, feed, and heal his sheep personally, and to raise up a Davidic shepherd over them.
God promises to work change from the inside, replacing a stone heart with a living one and giving his Spirit so obedience becomes possible.
The dry bones show God's power to revive what looks utterly finished, and resurrection enters Israel's vocabulary as real hope.
Chapter 33 renews Ezekiel's commission, so faithful warning and each hearer's responsibility frame all the hope that follows.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the vision of the dry bones and explain what God promises in Ezekiel 36:26-27 and why it matters.

comprehension_check.question: Ezekiel 36:22-23 grounds Israel's restoration in the honor of God's own name rather than in Israel. What does that grounding secure?
options: A restoration payable once Israel's record improves
A restoration designed to shame Israel before the nations
A restoration limited to protecting the divine reputation
A restoration as dependable as God's own character
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 36:22-23 stakes the restoration on God's holy name, a ground Israel's failures cannot pull down.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 36:22-23 again. Notice whose honor the promised action is said to defend.

comprehension_check.question: The vision of dry bones comes with its own interpretation in Ezekiel 37:11. What situation is the vision speaking into?
options: A people declaring their hope dead and themselves finished
A faithful remnant needing courage for the journey home
An army preparing to retake the land by force
A people awaiting word that the temple still stands
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 37:11 names the bones as the whole house of Israel in despair, and the breath answers exactly that death.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 37:11 again. Notice whose voice the bones are given and what that voice says.

connections.reason: Jesus' 'born of water and the Spirit' to Nicodemus draws on Ezekiel 36's clean water and new Spirit.
'I am the good shepherd' takes up Ezekiel 34: God himself, shepherding in person, against the false shepherds.
The Spirit poured out at Pentecost enacts Ezekiel 36-37's promise of God's Spirit within his people.
Ezekiel 34 turns the shepherd image into prophecy: God himself will come to shepherd his flock.

nodes.title: Gog of Magog
nodes.summary: After the restoration, a final enemy: Gog, from the far north, gathers a coalition against a peaceful, regathered Israel — and God destroys the horde without Israel lifting a sword, on the mountains, with fire and hail. A deliberately mysterious oracle of the last battle, written to be recognized rather than scheduled.
nodes.tradition_notes: No major tradition dogmatizes Gog's identity. Readings range from historical empires, to a symbol of every final assault on God's people, to a still-future battle; dispensationalist Protestantism maps it onto modern geopolitics far more confidently than Catholic, Orthodox, or most other Protestant interpreters do.
nodes.discussion_prompt: After every disaster Ezekiel has announced, God promises that the final assault on his people will fail without them lifting a sword. What does this oracle claim about who actually holds history's outcome, and how would trusting that free you from fear about the future?
assessment_questions: Who gathers against the restored and peaceful Israel in these chapters, and how is the invasion defeated?

God says that through this battle he will vindicate his holiness and the nations will know that he is the LORD. What is the oracle's central claim about God, whatever the battle's timing turns out to be?
Readers in every generation have been tempted to map Gog onto the enemies of their own day. How does trusting God's promised victory change the way you face threats you cannot control?

teaching_concepts.concept: God rules even the last assault
teaching_concepts.explanation: The great coalition from the north moves only within God's sovereign purpose, so no gathering of powers can undo his restoration.
Israel never lifts a sword in this battle, which teaches that final deliverance rests entirely on God and never on his people's strength.
The stated goal of the battle is that Israel and the nations come to know the LORD, so the oracle is finally about who God is.
The oracle's deliberate mystery resists confident scheduling, and Christians across traditions read its timing in several ways without any reading being required.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the central promise of the Gog oracle in your own words, and name at least two ways Christians have read its timing without settling the question.

comprehension_check.question: In the Gog oracle Israel never draws a sword; God alone breaks the assault (Ezekiel 39:3). What is that detail teaching about the last battle?
options: Israel's peaceful posture is what disarms its enemies
The regathered nation has outgrown the need for defenses
Final deliverance rests wholly on God's own hand
Victory is promised only to a fully purified people
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 39:3 has God himself striking the weapons from Gog's hands, so the deliverance is his act from start to finish.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 38:21-23 and 39:3 again. Notice who performs every act of the fighting.

comprehension_check.question: Twice the oracle states the point of the whole battle, in Ezekiel 38:23 and 39:7. What outcome is God after?
options: Ending warfare among the nations once and for all
Being known as holy before Israel and the nations
Restoring the full borders promised to Abraham's line
Repaying the nations for the centuries of exile
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 38:23 and 39:7 both land on knowing the LORD, so the battle's real outcome is God's name made known.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 38:23 and 39:7 again. Notice the clause both verses end with.

connections.reason: Revelation 20 names 'Gog and Magog' explicitly for the final rebellion after the thousand years.

nodes.title: The Temple Measured
nodes.summary: Twenty five years into the exile and fourteen years after the city fell, Ezekiel is set down on a very high mountain and handed over to a man who looks like bronze and carries a linen cord and a measuring rod. What follows is a walking tour: east gate, outer court, chambers, inner gates, the sanctuary, and the room the guide names the Most Holy Place. The numbers pile up with almost no commentary, and the tour closes outside with a wall measured all the way around to separate the holy from the common. The instruction given at the door governs everything after it, that Ezekiel is to look, listen, and give his attention to all of it, because that is why he was brought there.
nodes.discussion_prompt: For three chapters Ezekiel is walked through gates and courts while his guide records every dimension and explains almost nothing. What does a people who have lost their land and their temple gain from a set of measurements rather than a speech, and what does that precision communicate that words would not?
assessment_questions: Who meets Ezekiel at the start of the vision, what is he carrying, and what is Ezekiel told to do with everything he is about to see?
The tour ends in Ezekiel 42:20 with a wall measured around the whole area to separate the holy from the common. How does that closing detail explain what all the measuring was for?
Ezekiel is told to look closely and then describe what he saw to Israel. What is something you have genuinely understood but never passed on to anyone, and what would it take to hand it over?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Nobody bothers measuring a building that will never exist, so handing exact dimensions to a landless people works as a claim that God intends a real future with them.
Gates, courts, thresholds, and a boundary wall arrange the space by degrees of access, which teaches that coming near to God is an ordered thing rather than a casual one.

teaching_concepts.concept: A guide who explains very little
teaching_concepts.explanation: The bronze figure measures and names but seldom interprets, which leaves the reader standing where Ezekiel stands, given more than can be decoded in one pass.

teaching_concepts.concept: Seen in order to be told
teaching_concepts.explanation: The opening charge is to look, listen, and pay attention because that is the reason he was brought there, so the vision is entrusted to him for the people rather than for himself.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Ezekiel is told to do at the start of the vision and why, and state the reason given for the wall in Ezekiel 42:20.

comprehension_check.question: Three chapters of dimensions arrive with almost no explanation attached. What is the measuring itself saying to people in exile?
options: That the vision is mainly a memorial for the temple they lost
That God intends a real and ordered future for a landless people
That precise ritual detail matters to God more than people do
That God's presence now requires no place and no people at all
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 40:1-4 dates the vision fourteen years after the city was struck down and then hands the prophet a guide with a measuring rod, giving a homeless people the exact dimensions of a house.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 40:1-4 again. Notice where the exiles are in their own history when this vision arrives.

comprehension_check.question: The tour finishes outside, with a wall measured around the entire area. What does that final detail reveal about the design?
options: The wall was there to defend the sanctuary from foreign armies
The plan was meant chiefly to impress the surrounding nations
The space is graded so that nearness to God is ordered
The design keeps ordinary Israelites permanently outside the courts
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 42:20 gives the wall's purpose as separating the holy from the common, which is what the whole arrangement of courts, gates, and thresholds has been doing all along.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 42:15-20 again. Notice the reason given for the wall, then compare it with how the courts were laid out.

nodes.title: The Glory Returns and Worship Restored
nodes.summary: The vision reaches its point. Ezekiel is brought back to the east gate and the glory of the God of Israel comes from the east with a voice like rushing water, enters the temple through that gate, and fills the house. It is the same glory he watched leave in chapter 10, returning by the road it left on, and God calls the place his throne, where he will live among the Israelites forever. What follows orders the life that goes with that presence: the altar consecrated, the east gate shut behind him, priests charged to teach the difference between holy and common, the prince held to limits, and the festivals set out.
nodes.tradition_notes: Readings of the visionary temple and its ordinances divide across traditions rather than neatly between them: a literal future temple (held by some dispensationalist Protestants), an idealized pattern given to the post-exilic community, or a symbol of God's presence fulfilled in Christ and his people (the dominant Catholic, Orthodox, and Reformed reading, following Revelation 21-22's reuse of the vision).
nodes.discussion_prompt: Before God lets Ezekiel describe the design to Israel, he says to describe it so that they will be ashamed of what they have done, and then let them measure the plan. What does it do to a person to be shown something beautiful they had no hand in earning, and why might God put that before the rebuke instead of after it?
assessment_questions: Which direction does the glory come from in Ezekiel 43:2, and which gate does it enter the temple by?
The glory returns through the same gate it left by in chapter 10, and that gate is then shut behind it. What does that pairing say about what has changed and what has not?

Ezekiel 44:23 makes it the priests' job to teach people the difference between the holy and the common. Who taught you to tell that difference, and where in an ordinary week does the line get blurry for you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The glory that lifted off the threshold and went east comes back from the east through the same gate, so the vision resolves the loss the whole book has been carrying instead of changing the subject.
The moment God settles into the house the text turns to altars, priests, gates, and feasts, because a people living close to God need a shape for ordinary days.
Ezekiel is told to describe the design so Israel will be ashamed and then to let them measure the plan, which turns honest regret into a doorway rather than a dead end.
The ruler is given a real place in the worship and firm boundaries around his land and his conduct, which answers the abuses of Israel's kings from inside the new arrangement.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how chapter 43 answers chapter 10, and describe two ways the ordinances of chapters 44 through 46 shape daily life around God's presence.

comprehension_check.question: Chapter 43 is the vision's climax for anyone who watched the glory leave in chapter 10. What does the return settle?
options: That the exile was shorter than the prophets had originally warned
That God's judgment did not end his intention to dwell with them
That Israel had finally earned back the presence they had lost
That the old temple could be rebuilt exactly as it once stood
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 43:7 calls the place God's throne, where he will live among the Israelites forever, spoken over the very house the glory had abandoned.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 10:18-19 alongside Ezekiel 43:1-7. Notice the direction of travel each time, and what God says once he is inside.

comprehension_check.question: These chapters prescribe an altar, offerings, and festivals after the glory has returned, and Christians have long divided over that. What is the disagreement about?
options: Whether Ezekiel had authority to prescribe worship for a later age
Whether the vision replaces the covenant God made at Sinai
Whether the returning glory is the same glory that departed
Whether these offerings await a future temple or are fulfilled otherwise
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 43:18-27 sets out altar statutes inside a vision the New Testament later reads through Christ, and readers have placed the answer in a future temple, an ideal pattern, or a fulfillment in him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 43:6-11 and 43:18-27 again. Notice what is prescribed, who it is given to, and what the instructions are said to be for.

nodes.title: The River of Life and the City: The LORD Is There
nodes.summary: Water comes out from under the temple threshold and runs east, and the guide walks Ezekiel into it four times, a thousand cubits at a stretch: ankle deep, knee deep, waist deep, then a river too deep to cross. Where it arrives the Dead Sea turns fresh, fish fill it, and fishermen spread nets along a shore that never held any. Trees stand on both banks bearing fruit every month with leaves for healing, and the reason given is that the water comes out from the sanctuary. Then the land is shared out among the tribes, the city gates are named for them, and the book closes by renaming the city itself after the one who lives there.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The river starts as a trickle under a threshold and turns uncrossable within a short walk, with no stream anywhere joining it. What is that impossible growth claiming about where life comes from, and where would you most want to see something like it?
assessment_questions: How deep is the water at each of the four measurements in Ezekiel 47:3-5, and what happens to the Dead Sea once the river reaches it?
The water deepens with nothing feeding it and makes fresh a sea nothing lives in. What is that picture claiming about God's presence?
The last word of the book is the city's new name, that the LORD is there. If that were the true name of the place you live or work, what would you do differently tomorrow?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The river's source is under the sanctuary threshold, so the healing and abundance downstream are effects of God living there rather than features of the landscape.
The water rises at every measurement with no tributary anywhere in sight, which pictures a renewal that increases by its own nature instead of thinning out.

teaching_concepts.concept: The deadest place is the test case
teaching_concepts.explanation: The river runs into a sea famous for killing everything in it and makes the water fresh, so the vision picks the hardest possible ground to make its claim on.
Allotments and gates and measurements all end in a city renamed for God being there, which makes the restoration finally about who is present rather than what got built.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what happens to the river and to the Dead Sea in chapter 47, and explain what the city's new name in Ezekiel 48:35 claims about the future God intends.

comprehension_check.question: The guide walks Ezekiel into the water four times and it is deeper at every stop. What is the point of measuring it that way?
options: It shows a life that keeps increasing the further it goes
It shows how carefully the guide records every part of the vision
It shows the stages Israel must pass through to be restored
It shows how far Ezekiel had to walk to reach the sea
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 47:3-5 has the water rise from ankle deep to uncrossable across four short stretches with nothing flowing into it along the way.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 47:1-6 again. Notice where the water starts, and what does or does not join it as it runs.

comprehension_check.question: The book closes with tribal boundaries, then city gates, then a new name for the city. What does ending in that order claim about the restoration?
options: The rebuilt city will finally be secure against every enemy
The land divided fairly is what the exiles most needed
The point of it all is that God himself is present
The tribes are restored to the borders they held under David
comprehension_check.why: Ezekiel 48:35 names the city for God being there, so the last word of the whole book is his presence.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ezekiel 48:30-35 again. Notice what the final line names, and compare it with everything measured before it.

connections.reason: Revelation's measured city, river of life, and healing trees come straight from this vision — with one revision: no temple, for the Lamb is the temple.

nodes.title: Faithful in Babylon
nodes.summary: Four Judean teenagers are drafted into Nebuchadnezzar's re-education program — new names, new language, the king's food. Daniel draws one quiet line at the menu and thrives; the chapter is the Bible's primer on keeping faith inside a culture built to absorb you.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Daniel accepts a Babylonian name and a Babylonian education but draws the line at the king's food. How do you decide which pressures to absorb and where to quietly refuse, and what small line might God be asking you to hold right now?
assessment_questions: What test does Daniel propose to the chief official, and how do he and his friends compare to everyone else at the end of it?
Babylon renames the four young men and retrains them, yet Daniel resolves that he will not defile himself. Why does one small line at the menu carry so much weight for his identity?

Daniel serves a pagan government with excellence while keeping his deepest loyalty for God. Where do you live, study, or work inside a culture that pulls at your loyalty, and what would faithful excellence look like there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Regular ordinary decisions about food, habits, and discipline are what keep Daniel belonging to God inside an empire built to absorb him.

teaching_concepts.concept: God sustains the faithful in hostile places
teaching_concepts.explanation: God gives the four young men knowledge, skill, and favor, so their thriving in Babylon is his doing and honors their obedience.
Daniel excels inside a secular institution while keeping his ultimate loyalty for God, a model for faithful presence in any workplace or culture.
Daniel asks, negotiates, and proposes a test rather than staging a protest, showing that conviction and courtesy can work together.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of Daniel's food test and explain how it models keeping faith inside a culture built to absorb you.

comprehension_check.question: Babylon renames, reschools, and feeds the four young exiles. Within that program, what does the chapter present Daniel's food refusal as?
options: A public act of protest against the empire that deported him
A quiet line that keeps his loyalty from being absorbed
A rejection of all things Babylonian as defiling
A regimen to prove the exiles could outperform Babylon
comprehension_check.why: Daniel resolves not to defile himself yet serves the court with excellence, holding one line inside the program (Daniel 1:8).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 1:5-8 again. Notice how much of the program Daniel accepts, and the single point where he resolves to stop.

comprehension_check.question: By the chapter's end the four exiles surpass every expert in the kingdom. What is the chapter's explanation for their thriving?
options: The simple diet proved stronger than the king's fare
Their schooling back in Judah had outstripped Babylon's
God gave the learning, the skill, and the favor
The chief official had favored the four from the start
comprehension_check.why: The narrator credits God with granting the four their knowledge and skill in all learning (Daniel 1:17).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 1:9 and Daniel 1:17 again. Notice who is named as the giver of favor and learning in both verses.

connections.reason: Daniel and Esther are the Bible's paired diaspora manuals — faithfulness inside a pagan empire, one overt, one hidden.

nodes.title: The Statue and the Stone
nodes.summary: Nebuchadnezzar demands his dream be told and interpreted on pain of death; Daniel delivers both: a great statue of gold, silver, bronze, and iron — a parade of empires — shattered by a stone cut without hands that grows into a mountain filling the earth. History has a direction, and it isn't Babylon's.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The statue's metals get cheaper and weaker from head to foot, and one uncut stone shatters the whole thing. What is this dream claiming about where history is headed, and how would believing that change what you build your hopes on?
assessment_questions: What does Nebuchadnezzar demand of his wise men, and what does Daniel do with his friends before he answers the king?
The stone is cut without hands and grows into a mountain that fills the whole earth. What does the dream claim about God's kingdom compared with the empires in the statue?

Daniel's first response to a death sentence is prayer with his friends. When pressure hits you, where does your confidence actually turn first, and what would seeking God's wisdom before acting look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Daniel's prayer names it plainly: God removes kings and sets up kings, so even the mightiest empire is an instrument under his hand.
No human wisdom could tell the king his own dream, so the accurate telling of a secret authenticates Daniel's God as the one who reveals mysteries.
The metals decay in value down the statue and all of them shatter together, while the kingdom God sets up will never be destroyed.

teaching_concepts.concept: The stone read in more than one way
teaching_concepts.explanation: Christians differ on whether the mountain kingdom is already growing since Christ or awaits God's final act, and the dream's claim that God's kingdom wins stands in every reading.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the statue and the stone from memory and explain the dream's central claim about God's kingdom and human empires.

comprehension_check.question: In the dream, a stone no human hand cut shatters the statue of four metals and grows to fill the earth. What is the dream's central claim?
options: History will refine its empires until they deserve to last
Babylon's golden reign is promised a lasting preeminence
The empires will merge into one final, stable order
God's kingdom will end and outlast every human empire
comprehension_check.why: Daniel's interpretation ends with the God of heaven setting up a kingdom that will never fall to another people (Daniel 2:44).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 2:44 again. Notice what finally happens to all the kingdoms, and what never happens to the last one.

comprehension_check.question: Nebuchadnezzar demands the dream itself, not just an interpretation. In the story, what does that impossible demand end up proving?
options: That revelation is God's alone, beyond every sage
That the court's sages had been frauds from the start
That Daniel's training had surpassed his Chaldean teachers
That the king's cruelty had finally outrun his reason
comprehension_check.why: Daniel tells the king no wise man could show the mystery, but there is a God in heaven who reveals it (Daniel 2:27-28).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 2:27-28 again. Notice the contrast Daniel draws before he speaks a word of the dream.

connections.reason: Jesus' mustard-seed kingdom that grows to fill the garden echoes the stone that becomes a mountain.

nodes.title: The Fiery Furnace
nodes.summary: Three exiles refuse to bow to the golden image and answer the king with the Bible's finest statement of unconditional faith: 'Our God is able to deliver us — but if not, we will still not serve your gods.' Thrown in bound, they walk the flames with a mysterious fourth figure.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The three men tell the king that God is able to rescue them, and that even if he does not, they still will not bow. What kind of faith can say 'but if not,' and what would faith like that require of you when obedience gets expensive?
assessment_questions: What does Nebuchadnezzar see when he looks into the furnace, and how does he respond afterward?
The three refuse to bow before they know whether God will save them. What does their 'but if not' reveal about the difference between trusting God and bargaining with him?
Cultural pressure rarely looks like a golden statue today, yet it still demands a bow. Where are you being pressed to bow, and what would standing cost you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The three men's obedience does not hinge on a guaranteed rescue, since they trust God's worth even if the fire wins.

The mysterious fourth figure walking the flames shows God with his people inside the trial, and Christians have long pondered whether he is an angel or an appearance of Christ without the story settling it.
Whatever else exiles can absorb, faithful worship refuses idolatry under any threat, because only God may be bowed to.
Their stand moves a pagan king to praise their God, showing that costly faithfulness can speak louder than any argument.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the furnace story and explain what 'but if not' teaches about trusting God without conditions.

comprehension_check.question: The three tell the king their God is able to deliver them, and that they will not bow even if no rescue comes. What does that answer reveal about their obedience?
options: Doubt of God's power had tempered their expectations
Certainty of deliverance made the danger unreal to them
Obedience holds whether or not the rescue comes
Hope of reward made death a bargain worth striking
comprehension_check.why: They affirm that their God is able to deliver and refuse the image with no rescue guaranteed (Daniel 3:17-18).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 3:16-18 again. Notice the two halves of their answer, and what stays fixed in both.

comprehension_check.question: Nebuchadnezzar expects to watch three bound men burn and instead sees four walking free in the flames. What does the story show by placing the rescue inside the furnace rather than before it?
options: Courage can always count on rescue as its wage
God stands with his people inside the trial itself
The king's power to harm was never truly real
comprehension_check.why: The deliverance happens in the fire, where a fourth figure walks with the three (Daniel 3:25).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 3:24-25 again. Notice where the rescue takes place, and how many are walking there.

connections.reason: Hebrews' faith catalogue includes those who 'quenched the power of fire.'

nodes.title: Kings Humbled: The Writing on the Wall
nodes.summary: Nebuchadnezzar grazes like an ox until he learns that 'the Most High rules the kingdom of men'; Belshazzar toasts his idols from the temple's cups and reads his doom on the plaster — weighed and found wanting, the kingdom lost that night; and Daniel, by now an old man, prays through an open window and sleeps sound among lions.
nodes.discussion_prompt: A king grazes like an ox, another reads his doom on the wall, and an old man prays through an open window as if lions were nothing. Across these three stories, what does it look like to live under the truth that the Most High rules, and where does pride crowd that truth out of your own life?
assessment_questions: What happens to Nebuchadnezzar after his boast on the palace roof, and what does he confess when his sanity returns?
Belshazzar drinks from the temple's cups the very night his kingdom falls. What do the words 'weighed and found wanting' reveal about how God measures rulers?
Daniel keeps praying openly when prayer becomes a crime. What habit anchors your loyalty to God, and what would keep you practicing it under pressure?

teaching_concepts.concept: The Most High rules the kingdom of men
teaching_concepts.explanation: The refrain of these chapters is that every throne is on loan from God, who gives kingdoms to whomever he wills.
Nebuchadnezzar loses his mind until he lifts his eyes to heaven, and his restored confession shows that God's judgment can lead a proud man to worship.
Belshazzar knew his father's story and defied God anyway, so the writing on the wall judges knowing defiance rather than ignorance.
Daniel's habit of prayer, kept steady for decades, carries him through the lions' den and turns a trap into a testimony.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell one of the three stories in detail and explain what all three together teach about the sentence 'the Most High rules the kingdom of men.'

comprehension_check.question: Nebuchadnezzar grazes like an ox, Belshazzar reads his doom on the plaster, and Daniel outlasts the lions. What single claim do the three stories press?
options: Every throne is held on loan from the Most High
All pagan rule is illegitimate and doomed by its very nature
Faithful exiles will always rise inside the empire
Kingdoms endure by wisdom rather than by force
comprehension_check.why: The dream's decree and the humbled king's confession agree that kingship is heaven's to give (Daniel 4:17, Daniel 4:34-35).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 4:17 and Daniel 4:34-35 again. Notice the sentence the dream announces and the restored king repeats.

comprehension_check.question: Daniel retells Nebuchadnezzar's humbling to Belshazzar before reading the writing on the wall. Why does that reminder matter to the verdict?
options: It shows the dynasty was doomed no matter its conduct
It proves God judges sons for their fathers' pride
It marks how far Babylon's power had already sunk
It makes the sin knowing defiance instead of ignorance
comprehension_check.why: Daniel's charge turns on memory: Belshazzar had his father's story and defied heaven anyway (Daniel 5:22).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 5:18-23 again. Notice what Daniel says Belshazzar knew before the verdict is read.

nodes.title: The Son of Man and the Ancient of Days
nodes.summary: The statue dream returns as nightmare: four beasts from the churning sea, a boastful little horn — then thrones set, the Ancient of Days seated in fire, and 'one like a son of man' riding the clouds to receive everlasting dominion from him. This is the chapter behind Jesus' favorite self-title and his answer at his trial.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The empires look like beasts rising from a churning sea, while the everlasting kingdom goes to a human figure riding the clouds. What is this vision claiming about how power in history finally ends up, and how does that change whom you trust with your future?
assessment_questions: What does Daniel see after the four beasts rise from the sea, and who receives the everlasting dominion?
The beasts come up from the chaotic sea while the son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days. What is the vision claiming about beastly power and the kingdom God gives?

At his trial Jesus answered his judges with this scene, trusting his vindication to God's court. When you are wronged or afraid of the powers over you, what would it mean to wait for God's verdict instead of forcing your own?

teaching_concepts.explanation: History ends in God's courtroom, where the Ancient of Days sits and every violent, boastful power must answer.

teaching_concepts.concept: One like a son of man
teaching_concepts.explanation: A human figure receives everlasting dominion from God himself, and this scene stands behind Jesus' favorite title for himself and his answer at his trial.
The vision hands the kingdom to the holy people of the Most High as well, so God's future belongs to his oppressed people and never to the beasts.
Christians differ on which empires the beasts name and how the timeline runs, while the vision's core claim of God's final judgment and the son of man's kingdom holds in every reading.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the throne scene of Daniel 7 and explain why 'Son of Man' became Jesus' preferred title for himself.

comprehension_check.question: Daniel 7 sets beasts rising from a churning sea against a human figure coming with the clouds to God's throne. What is the vision claiming through that contrast?
options: History will cycle between beastly and humane ages forever
Beastly power faces judgment while lasting rule arrives as a gift
Empires slowly grow humane enough to inherit the earth
God's people must wrest the kingdom from the beasts by arms
comprehension_check.why: The court sits, the beasts lose their dominion, and everlasting kingship is given to the one like a son of man (Daniel 7:13-14).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 7:9-14 again. Notice how the son of man comes by his dominion, and what happens to the beasts' rule.

comprehension_check.question: The interpretation twice hands the everlasting kingdom to God's holy people. What does that add to the vision's claim?
options: The saints are spared the horn's war before it begins
The saints will wield the same rule the beasts once did
The court's ruling secures the future of the battered saints
The kingdom is the saints' reward for prevailing in battle
comprehension_check.why: After the horn wears the saints down, judgment is given for them and the kingdom becomes theirs (Daniel 7:22, Daniel 7:27).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 7:21-22 and Daniel 7:27 again. Notice what the saints endure first, and what the court's ruling hands them.

connections.reason: At his trial Jesus quotes this scene — 'you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds' — and is condemned for it.
Revelation's beast from the sea is Daniel 7's beasts fused into one.
John's opening vision of one 'like a son of man' with white hair fuses this chapter's two central figures.
Stephen's dying vision — 'the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God' — is Daniel 7 seen open-eyed.

nodes.title: The Sealed Visions
nodes.summary: Ram and goat empires collide; Daniel prays through Jeremiah's seventy years and receives the enigmatic 'seventy weeks'; a chapter-by-chapter preview of wars between north and south ends with a desolating sacrilege in the temple — and then the Old Testament's clearest resurrection promise: 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake.' Seal the book until the time of the end.
nodes.tradition_notes: The seventy weeks (9:24-27) is among the most variously interpreted passages in Scripture: fulfilled readings ending at Christ's first coming (common in Catholic, Orthodox, and Reformed exegesis), a gap-and-future-tribulation reading (dispensationalist Protestantism), and historical readings centered on Antiochus IV (much modern scholarship). The graph flags the divergence without ranking the options.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Daniel receives visions of wars he will never live to see, and the angel's closing word is to go his way and rest. What do these chapters claim about God's grip on a violent future, and how would that promise steady you in what feels uncertain right now?
assessment_questions: What does Daniel do at the start of chapter 9 after reading Jeremiah's prophecy, and what promise about those who sleep in the dust closes the book?

The visions preview persecution, a desolating sacrilege, and then an awakening to everlasting life. Whatever timeline a reader holds, what is the sealed book finally claiming about how God's story ends for his people?

Daniel responds to prophecy with confession and prayer rather than speculation. When the future feels dark, which do you reach for first, and what would praying like Daniel 9 sound like in your own words?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years and responds with confession and pleading for mercy, modeling that God's promises invite intercession rather than mere calculation.

teaching_concepts.concept: God numbers the days of evil
teaching_concepts.explanation: The visions show persecution as real and also bounded, since every tyrant in them runs to an appointed end that God has already set.
Daniel 12:2-3 gives the Old Testament's clearest resurrection promise, so the book's hope runs past political rescue to everlasting life.

Christians read the seventy weeks as fulfilled at Christ's first coming, as pointing to a future tribulation, or as centered on the Antiochus crisis, and the passage calls for humility rather than a forced verdict.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Daniel 12:2-3 promises and why it matters, and describe how Daniel 9 models responding to prophecy with prayer.

comprehension_check.question: The closing visions preview persecutions in exhausting detail and keep attaching set times to them. What is the detail doing for the faithful?
options: Equipping them to date the end once decoded rightly
Warning them the outcome still hangs on the wars ahead
Frightening them toward repentance before the crisis lands
Assuring them every tyrant's season is already bounded
comprehension_check.why: The visions keep saying the crisis runs to an appointed end fixed before it starts (Daniel 8:19, Daniel 11:35).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 8:19 and Daniel 11:35-36 again. Notice the word the visions keep attaching to the tyrant's time.

comprehension_check.question: After all the empires and wars, Daniel ends with the promise that the sleeping dead will awake. What does that promise do to the book's hope?
options: It carries the hope past any rescue history can give
It assures the faithful they will survive the persecution unharmed
It restates the hope of return from exile as a figure
It grants the wise a legacy that outlives their deaths
comprehension_check.why: The awakening of Daniel 12:2-3 reaches past political deliverance to life that death cannot end.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Daniel 12:1-3 again. Notice how long the promised awakening is said to last.

connections.reason: Jesus' Olivet Discourse cites 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet.'
Revelation's 42 months, 1,260 days, and sealed scroll take their vocabulary from these visions.
Daniel 9 opens with Daniel reading Jeremiah's seventy-years prophecy and praying over its meaning.

nodes.title: Marry a Woman Who Will Break Your Heart

comprehension_check.question: Why does the book open with God commanding Hosea to marry a woman who will be unfaithful?
options: So the prophet's marriage acts out God's bond with Israel
So Hosea's obedience can be proven by a costly command
So Israel receives a public warning against unfaithful spouses
So the prophet can suffer enough to earn his authority
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 1:2 ties the command to the land's own unfaithfulness to the LORD, making the marriage a lived picture of the covenant.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 1:2 again. Notice the reason God himself attaches to the command.

comprehension_check.question: After the judgment of chapter 2, Hosea is told to love and buy back his wife (Hosea 3:1-2). What does the act show about God's love?
options: It waits to receive the wayward once they have reformed
It overlooks betrayal rather than bringing it to judgment
It pursues and pays to recover the still unfaithful
It starts over with a new covenant on cleaner terms
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 3:1 commands love for a woman still loved by another, just as the LORD loves Israel while they turn away.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 3:1-2 again. Notice when the buying back happens, and what it costs.

nodes.summary: God commands his prophet to live the message: marry Gomer, who will be unfaithful, name the children Not-Loved and Not-My-People — and then buy her back from the auction block and love her again. Israel's idolatry is not law-breaking first; it is adultery against a husband who won't stop loving.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God asks Hosea to live out the pain of loving someone who keeps leaving. What does telling Israel's story as a marriage, rather than a courtroom case, change about how you understand sin, and what does it reveal about how God feels when people walk away from him?
assessment_questions: What does God command Hosea to do in chapter 1, and what names does he give the children?
In chapter 3 Hosea buys Gomer back and loves her again. Why does God choose a broken marriage, rather than a broken law, as the picture of Israel's idolatry?

Hosea 2 shows God leading his unfaithful people into the wilderness to speak tenderly to them. Where in your life have you treated God's love as something you can walk away from, and what would returning look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Hosea frames Israel's unfaithfulness as betrayal of a marriage, so sin wounds a living relationship rather than merely breaking a rule.

teaching_concepts.concept: Judgment is never the last word
teaching_concepts.explanation: The children's names of judgment get reversed into promises, showing that God's discipline aims at restoration.
God uses Hosea's real marriage as an enacted parable, teaching that lived drama can carry theological truth.
Hosea buys his wife back from the auction block, picturing a God whose love pursues the unfaithful at real cost.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of Hosea and Gomer and explain what it teaches about how God responds to his people's unfaithfulness.

connections.reason: Paul quotes 'Not-My-People will be called sons of the living God' for the Gentiles' inclusion.
Peter applies 'once you were not a people, but now you are God's people' to the church.

nodes.title: The Case Against Israel

comprehension_check.question: Israel in these chapters stays religiously busy, full of sacrifice and festival. Why does God's case against them still stand?
options: Their offerings prove God rejects sacrifice as a form of worship
Their offerings go on without steadfast love or knowledge of God
Their offerings are too irregular to meet the law's requirements
Their offerings ask for blessings instead of offering God praise
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 6:6 names what God desires above burnt offerings, a steadfast love and knowledge of himself that the busy worship lacks.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 6:4-6 again. Notice what God compares their devotion to just before he says what he wants.

comprehension_check.question: Hosea says the nation sows the wind and will reap the whirlwind (Hosea 8:7). What is he claiming about the coming disaster?
options: It is an arbitrary blow from a God whose patience ran out
It is the product of Assyrian ambition rather than divine judgment
It is proof the covenant between them has already ended
It is the grown harvest of what Israel itself has planted
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 8:7 speaks in farm logic, the storm they will harvest grew from the seed they sowed themselves.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 8:4-7 again. Notice what Israel has been making, and what the making grows into.

nodes.summary: The indictment in detail: priests who feed on sin, kings made 'but not through me,' loyalty like morning mist, and the line Jesus quoted twice — 'I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' They sow the wind and reap the whirlwind.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God says his people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and that he wants steadfast love more than sacrifice. What is the difference between knowing about God and actually knowing God, and where does your own loyalty look like morning mist?
assessment_questions: What charges does God bring against Israel's priests and kings in these chapters?
Hosea 6:6 says God desires steadfast love and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. Why would God reject worship from the very people busy performing it?
Israel sowed the wind and reaped the whirlwind. What habit or compromise in your life is quietly sowing something you do not want to harvest?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God wants faithful love and personal knowledge of himself, and ritual without them is judged as hypocrisy.
Corrupt priests and kings compound the nation's sin, so those who lead God's people carry heavier responsibility.
Sowing the wind reaps the whirlwind, because idolatry and injustice set real consequences in motion.
God prosecutes his people in order to call them back, so even the harshest charges serve covenant love.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words what Hosea 6:6 means and why God brings a legal case against a nation full of worship.

connections.reason: Jesus tells the Pharisees to 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice' — Hosea 6:6.
Hosea preached into exactly this collapse; the two texts narrate the same catastrophe from prophet's and historian's angles.

nodes.title: How Can I Give You Up?

comprehension_check.question: In Hosea 11:8-9 God recoils mid-judgment and refuses to fully destroy Ephraim. What grounds the refusal?
options: Israel's repentance arrives at the last possible moment
An intercessor steps in to turn the sentence aside
God's own nature as the Holy One among them
The punishment already suffered is counted as enough
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 11:9 roots the mercy in who God is, the Holy One dwelling in Israel's midst.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 11:8-9 again. Notice the reason God himself gives for holding back.

comprehension_check.question: Chapter 14 scripts words for Israel to carry when they return to the LORD. What does the shape of that return reveal?
options: God heals the turning away and loves them freely
Restoration waits until reformed conduct has proven the repentance
The years of exile themselves pay down the nation's debt
Only a carefully sifted remnant is offered the way back
comprehension_check.why: Hosea 14:1-4 asks Israel to return carrying only words, and God answers with healing and a love given freely.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hosea 14:1-4 again. Notice what Israel is told to bring, and what God promises to do.

nodes.summary: God remembers teaching Ephraim to walk, lifting the infant to his cheek — and breaks off mid-judgment: 'How can I give you up? … My heart recoils within me; I am God and not a man.' After a retelling of Jacob's wrestling and a last word against death itself, the book closes with a free-love promise: 'I will heal their apostasy.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: In chapter 11 God remembers teaching Ephraim to walk, then cries out that he cannot give his child up. What changes when you picture God as an anguished parent instead of a distant judge, and how does that picture hold together with the judgment all around it?
assessment_questions: What memories of Israel's childhood does God recall in chapter 11, and what promise closes the book in chapter 14?
God says his heart recoils within him because he is God and not a man. What does that line reveal about how divine mercy differs from human anger?
The book ends with God promising to heal their apostasy and love them freely. What would it mean for you to bring God your actual failures and let him do the healing?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God raised Israel like a parent teaching a toddler to walk, and the thought of abandoning that child causes him real anguish.
God punishes idolatry because it breaks covenant love, so his severity and his tenderness come from the same heart.
The retelling of Jacob at the Jabbok shows that honest struggle with God belongs to genuine faith.
Chapter 14 promises God will heal apostasy itself and love his people freely, so return stays possible at any point.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the picture of God in Hosea 11 and explain how the book holds his anguish, his judgment, and his promise to heal together.

connections.reason: 'Out of Egypt I called my son' (11:1) becomes Matthew's caption for the child Jesus' return from Egypt.
'O death, where are your plagues?' (13:14) resurfaces in Paul's resurrection taunt.
Hosea 12 retells Jacob's wrestling as a mirror for the nation named after him.

nodes.title: Joel: Locusts, the Day of the LORD, and the Spirit Poured Out
nodes.summary: A devastating locust plague becomes a window onto the Day of the LORD — 'rend your hearts and not your garments' — and past the judgment, the promise Pentecost claims: 'I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy… and everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Joel tells a devastated people to tear their hearts rather than their clothes. What separates real repentance from the performance of it, and what would wholehearted turning back to God look like in your week?
assessment_questions: What disaster strikes the land in Joel 1, and what does Joel call the people to do in response?
Joel promises that God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, sons and daughters alike. Why does it matter that the promise reaches everyone rather than only prophets and priests?
Joel says everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Who around you assumes God's mercy is out of their reach, and how does this promise change what you could say to them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The locust plague works as a warning that points forward to the far greater Day of the LORD.
God wants torn hearts rather than torn garments, because he judges the soul's posture over outward show.
Joel promises the Spirit poured out on all flesh, a new reality Peter announces as arriving at Pentecost.
The same God who warns also promises to repay the years the locusts ate, so his discipline intends renewal.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Joel moves from a locust plague to the Day of the LORD, and what he promises about the Spirit and about calling on the LORD's name.

comprehension_check.question: Joel 2:12-14 calls for torn hearts instead of torn garments. What does the call lean on for its hope?
options: The nation's covenant record, which earned another hearing
The known character of God, gracious and slow to anger
The completeness of the ritual, once done with full sincerity
The locusts' retreat, already visible as the sermon began
comprehension_check.why: Joel 2:13 grounds the summons in God's own character, the reason a return might be met with mercy.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joel 2:13-14 again. Notice the reason the prophet gives for returning, and the who-knows that follows it.

comprehension_check.question: Joel 2:28-29 promises the Spirit poured on sons, daughters, the old, the young, and servants. What is the promise announcing?
options: Israel will no longer need teachers or priests at all
The Spirit's nearness will make the day of the LORD safe
God's presence crossing every line of age, gender, and station
A restored order of prophets like Moses and Elijah
comprehension_check.why: Joel 2:28-29 stretches the gift across every category it names, the Spirit given without regard to age, sex, or status.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Joel 2:28-29 again. Notice which unlikely people the promise goes out of its way to include.

connections.reason: Peter's Pentecost sermon opens by quoting Joel 2 at length: 'this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel.'
'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' anchors Romans 10.

nodes.title: Let Justice Roll Down

comprehension_check.question: Amos 3:2 reasons that because God has known Israel out of all the families of earth, he will punish them. What is the logic?
options: Privilege with God carries obligation rather than exemption
Election was revoked, so Israel now counts as a foreign nation
Punishment falls only on the nations God has chosen to know
Being chosen shields Israel from the fate of the nations
comprehension_check.why: Amos 3:2 joins the knowing and the punishing in one sentence, privilege carrying responsibility with it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Amos 1:3-2:8 in outline, then Amos 3:2. Notice who else faces judgment, and what makes Israel's case sharper.

comprehension_check.question: In Amos 5:21-24 God says he despises Israel's feasts and offerings. What makes the worship hateful?
options: It proves sacrifice was never what God wanted from anyone
It is sincere in feeling but confused in its doctrine
It coexists with an injustice the worshipers intend to keep
It asks God for blessing instead of giving him praise
comprehension_check.why: Amos 5:24 names the missing thing, a justice that rolls through common life like a stream that does not fail.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Amos 5:21-24 again. Notice what God asks to have in place of the noise.

nodes.summary: A shepherd from Judah circles the nations with judgment oracles and then lands the hammer on prosperous Israel itself: the poor sold for sandals, worship divorced from justice. 'I hate, I despise your feasts… but let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Amos tells people who love their worship services that God despises them, because the poor are being crushed outside the sanctuary doors. What does it mean for justice to roll down like waters, and where would that stream have to run through your own community?
assessment_questions: How does Amos structure his opening oracles against the nations, and which nation does the final and longest judgment land on?

Amos 3:2 says that because God chose Israel out of all the families of the earth, he will punish them for their sins. Why does being God's people increase responsibility instead of granting exemption?
God rejects feasts and songs that coexist with injustice. What would change in how you worship if God measured it by how the vulnerable around you are treated?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The opening oracles hold every nation accountable for violence, so God's moral rule covers the whole world.
Being chosen exposes Israel to stricter judgment rather than shielding them from it.
God hates religious performance that lives comfortably beside oppression of the poor.
The fierce oracles are a summons to repent, since God announces judgment so that people can still turn.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Amos says God despises Israel's worship, and what Amos 5:24 demands instead.

nodes.title: The Plumb Line and the Rebuilt Booth

comprehension_check.question: Ordered by Amaziah to go earn his bread prophesying elsewhere, Amos answers with his own story (Amos 7:14-15). What is the force of the reply?
options: His guild credentials outrank a royal sanctuary's priest
The LORD who took him from the flock outranks Bethel
He will withdraw to Judah once this vision is delivered
Judah's king has granted him protection Bethel must honor
comprehension_check.why: Amos 7:15 rests the commission on the LORD taking him from behind the flock and sending him to prophesy to Israel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Amos 7:14-15 again. Notice what Amos denies being, and who he says sent him.

comprehension_check.question: After chapters of demolition, Amos ends with David's fallen booth rebuilt and nations bearing God's name (Amos 9:11-12). What does the ending do to the book?
options: It cancels the earlier judgments as threats never carried out
It repays the nation for repentance recorded in the visions
It restricts the promised restoration to David's royal line alone
It shows the tearing down served a rebuilding all along
comprehension_check.why: Amos 9:11-12 raises what fell and widens the rebuilt house to nations called by God's name.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Amos 9:11-12 again. Notice what is rebuilt, and who ends up inside it.

nodes.summary: Five visions of the end — plumb line, ripe fruit basket, the Lord beside the altar — and a showdown with the establishment priest of Bethel, who tells Amos to go prophesy somewhere else. The book that thunders judgment ends with David's fallen booth rebuilt and all the nations called by God's name.
nodes.discussion_prompt: God holds a plumb line against a wall his people built crooked. If God set that same measuring line against your community's life this week, what would it expose, and what does the rebuilt booth at the book's end say about why he measures at all?
assessment_questions: What visions does Amos see in chapters 7 through 9, and how does the priest Amaziah respond to his preaching?

Amaziah tells Amos to go prophesy somewhere else, and Amos answers that he was a shepherd whom God took from following the flock. What does their clash reveal about where prophetic authority comes from?
Amos warns of a famine of hearing the words of the LORD. What are you doing now with the access to God's word that others once starved for?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God measures his people against his own straight standard rather than their status or their rituals.
Amos confronts the establishment priest at Bethel because his commission comes from God rather than any institution.
Amos warns that persistently ignoring God's word can end in losing access to it altogether.
The fallen booth of David is raised and the nations included, so God's pruning aims at renewal.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the vision of the plumb line and the clash with Amaziah, and explain how a book of judgment can end with the booth of David rebuilt.

connections.reason: At the Jerusalem council, James quotes the rebuilt booth of David to justify welcoming the Gentiles.

nodes.title: Obadiah: The Doom of Edom
nodes.summary: The Old Testament's shortest book: judgment on Edom — Esau's descendants — for standing aloof and then joining in on the day Jerusalem fell. 'As you have done, it shall be done to you.' The ancient twin-brother rivalry of Jacob and Esau ends at the Day of the LORD, when 'the kingdom shall be the LORD's.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Edom watched from the cliffs while their brother's city burned, then came down to join the looting. Why does God treat standing by as taking part, and where might you be a bystander to harm you did not start?
assessment_questions: What did Edom do on the day Jerusalem fell, and what does God announce will happen to them?
Obadiah says the pride of Edom's heart deceived them in their rocky heights. How does pride convince people that they are safe from consequences?
The book says that as Edom has done, it shall be done to them. How does trusting God to repay betrayal change how you respond when it costs you to stand with someone?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God condemns Edom for gloating over kin, so kinship carries obligations that neutrality cannot cancel.
Edom trusted its mountain fortresses, and God brings down whatever arrogance builds its safety on.

teaching_concepts.concept: The Day of the LORD is universal
teaching_concepts.explanation: God holds every nation to the same moral standard, near to Israel or far from it.
The little book ends with God ruling over all, so history's last word belongs to him rather than to any empire.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why God judges Edom in Obadiah and what the closing line about the kingdom being the LORD's means for how the story of nations ends.

comprehension_check.question: Edom's first move on Jerusalem's worst day was simply to stand at a distance and watch. Why does the oracle count that as guilt?
options: Because Edom had secretly guided the invading armies in
Because standing aloof from a brother's ruin joins it
Because watching proved Edom planned the same crime
Because neutrality broke a formal treaty with Judah
comprehension_check.why: Obadiah 1:11 counts the day Edom kept its distance as the day Edom became one of the attackers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Obadiah 1:11-12 again. Notice how far the charges go before Edom ever lifts a hand.

comprehension_check.question: The oracle widens at Obadiah 1:15 from Edom to a day nearing all nations. What grounds the judgment there?
options: God's promise to avenge Israel on every rival nation
God's old preference for Jacob's line over Esau's
Edom's inherited share in its ancestor's ancient wrongs
Each nation's own deeds returning on its head
comprehension_check.why: Obadiah 1:15 announces one measure for all the nations, each repaid out of its own conduct.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Obadiah 1:15 again. Notice the rule the verse announces for every nation.

connections.reason: Psalm 137 remembers the same Edomite gloating: 'Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem.'

nodes.title: Jonah: The Prophet Who Ran
nodes.summary: Sent to Nineveh — capital of the empire brutalizing his people — Jonah sails the opposite direction, gets swallowed and returned, preaches five reluctant words, and watches the whole city repent. Then comes the real ending: Jonah sulking under a withered vine while God asks the question the book leaves hanging: 'Should I not pity Nineveh?'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jonah runs because he knows God is gracious and fears he will forgive Nineveh, and the book ends on God's unanswered question about pity. Who would you struggle to see God forgive, and what does your answer reveal about how you understand his mercy toward you?
assessment_questions: Where does God send Jonah, where does Jonah go instead, and what happens when he finally preaches to Nineveh?
Jonah quotes God's own creed, gracious and compassionate and slow to anger, as his reason for fleeing. What does that reveal about the real conflict of the book?
God asks Jonah whether he should not pity Nineveh, and the book never records an answer. How would you answer God's question about the people you find hardest to love?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God desires repentance even from Israel's worst enemies, so his compassion refuses the limits people set on it.
Jonah's flight exposes his own heart, showing that resistance to God's call reveals what we actually believe about him.
Storm, fish, plant, and worm all serve God's purpose, showing his rule over every means of pursuing a runaway.
Nineveh's turning averts the announced judgment, proving that God's warnings are invitations.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of Jonah and explain what God's final question teaches about his pity for people we would rather see judged.

comprehension_check.question: Jonah finally explains his flight in Jonah 4:2. What had he been running from?
options: The danger of preaching alone inside a brutal enemy capital
A mission he judged pointless, since Nineveh could not repent
The mercy he knew God would show if Nineveh turned
A word of judgment too harsh for him to deliver
comprehension_check.why: Jonah 4:2 gives his own reason, that he fled because he knew God to be gracious and ready to relent.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Jonah 4:1-3 again. Notice which attributes of God Jonah lists as his grievance.

comprehension_check.question: God's last word in Jonah is a question about pity, and the book ends without Jonah's answer. What does that ending do?
options: It leaves the question standing for readers who share the grudge
It implies Jonah repented, since silence signals his consent
It shows God abandoning the argument as beyond winning
It marks the story unfinished, its final scene lost to time
comprehension_check.why: Jonah 4:10-11 sets Jonah's pity for a plant against God's pity for a city, and the question is left open on purpose.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Jonah 4:10-11 again. Notice whose pity is compared with whose, and who never gets to reply.

connections.reason: Jesus gives 'the sign of Jonah' — three days and nights in the fish — as the one sign his generation will get.
Nahum announces doom on the same Nineveh that repented here; the two books are the Twelve's paired word on God's patience and its limit.

nodes.title: The Case Against Both Capitals
nodes.summary: A village prophet indicts Samaria and Jerusalem together: land-grabbers who lie awake devising evil, rulers who 'tear the skin off my people,' prophets who preach for pay. Micah says aloud what no one else dared — Zion will be plowed like a field.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Micah names people who lie awake at night planning how to seize fields, and prophets who tailor their message to whoever pays. What makes injustice by respectable people so hard to see from the inside, and who tells your community the truth when it profits no one?
assessment_questions: What groups does Micah accuse in chapters 2 and 3, and what does he say will happen to Zion?
Micah says he is filled with power and the Spirit of the LORD to declare Israel's sin, while other prophets preach for pay. What separates a true prophet from a false one in these chapters?

The land-grabbers coveted fields and seized them because it was in their power to do so. Where do you hold power that could be used to take advantage of someone, and what would using it justly look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Micah opens with God stepping forward as witness against both capitals, so no city stands above his court.
Coveting on the bed becomes seizing in the morning, showing how private desire matures into public oppression.
Leaders and preachers who twist truth for pay multiply the destruction of the very people they serve.
Micah dares to say Zion itself will be plowed like a field, proving no sacred status protects persistent injustice.

nodes.completion_criteria: Summarize Micah's charges against the leaders of Samaria and Jerusalem, and explain why his word about Zion being plowed was so shocking.

comprehension_check.question: In Micah 3:11, rulers, priests, and prophets all work for a price, yet lean on the LORD being among them. What is Micah exposing?
options: They kept the worship pure while letting the courts rot
They turned God's nearness into insurance against every judgment
They mistook the city's prosperity for proof of God's favor
comprehension_check.why: Micah 3:11-12 sets their confidence that no disaster can come beside the sentence that Zion will be plowed like a field.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Micah 3:9-12 again. Notice what the leaders say about the LORD, and what the very next verse announces.

comprehension_check.question: Micah 3:5-8 sets Micah against prophets who preach for pay. By his own account, what marks his word as the LORD's?
options: His forecasts come true where the paid prophets' visions fail
He refuses every fee so his message stays uncorrupted
He is filled with power to name Jacob's sin plainly
comprehension_check.why: Micah 3:8 grounds the difference in the Spirit of the LORD, power given for declaring to Jacob his transgression.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Micah 3:5 and Micah 3:8 again. Notice what shapes the hired message, and what fills Micah instead.

connections.reason: A century later, elders quote Micah's 'Zion plowed like a field' to save Jeremiah's life — proof one prophet's word protected another.

nodes.title: Bethlehem, the Mountain, and Who Is Like God?
nodes.summary: Swords to plowshares, a ruler from little Bethlehem 'whose origin is from of old,' the covenant lawsuit answered by the Bible's most quoted summary of true religion — 'do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God' — and a closing play on the prophet's own name: 'Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity?'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Micah answers the question of what the LORD requires with three plain things: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly with your God. Which of the three comes hardest for you, and what would practicing it cost you this month?
assessment_questions: What does Micah promise will come from Bethlehem, and what picture of the last days opens chapter 4?
In chapter 6 God puts his case to Israel by recounting what he has done for them, and the answer lands on Micah 6:8. Why does God want justice, mercy, and humility more than extravagant sacrifices?
Micah ends by marveling that God pardons iniquity and casts sins into the depths of the sea. How does being that fully forgiven change the way you treat people who wrong you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God promises a day when weapons become farm tools, so his future bends toward peace among the nations.
A deliverer whose origin is from of old comes from a small town, showing God working greatness through the overlooked.
Doing justice, loving mercy, and walking humbly summarize what God requires of a covenant people.
Micah's closing question, who is a God like you, celebrates a God whose delight is steadfast love and forgiveness.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Micah 6:8 requires in your own words, and how the book grounds it in the ruler from Bethlehem and the God who pardons.

comprehension_check.question: Micah 6:6-7 piles up offers, from burnt calves to rivers of oil to a firstborn child. What does the answer in Micah 6:8 do to that escalation?
options: It ends the escalation by setting sacrifice itself aside
It accepts the offerings but adds justice as a requirement
It scales the demand down to what the poor can afford
It turns the question from payment offered to a life walked
comprehension_check.why: Micah 6:8 answers the mounting bids with what the LORD seeks, justice done, mercy loved, a humble walk with God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Micah 6:6-8 again. Notice which direction the offers grow, and what kind of thing the answer asks for instead.

comprehension_check.question: Micah 7:18 asks who is a God like you. In the book's closing lines, what makes God beyond compare?
options: His pardon, passing over sin and delighting in mercy
His power, scattering every nation that tramples his people
His justice, repaying each wrong down to the last deed
His patience, delaying the judgment Israel had fully earned
comprehension_check.why: Micah 7:18-19 answers its own question with forgiveness, a God who lets anger go and casts sin into the sea.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Micah 7:18-19 again. Notice which divine actions the passage lists after asking its question.

connections.reason: The chief priests answer Herod's 'where will the Christ be born?' by quoting Micah 5:2 — Bethlehem.

nodes.title: Nahum: Nineveh's Hour Comes
nodes.summary: Roughly a century after Jonah, Nineveh's repentance is long dead and Assyria's atrocities have filled the ledger; Nahum announces the empire's end in some of the Bible's most vivid battle poetry. 'The LORD is slow to anger' — Jonah's creed — 'but great in power, and will by no means clear the guilty.' Patience is not indifference.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Nahum celebrates the fall of an empire whose cruelty was legendary, and the nations clap at the news. What does this book say to people suffering under powers too big to fight, and how do you hold onto hope for justice without becoming cruel yourself?
assessment_questions: What city does Nahum announce judgment against, and what had its empire done to deserve it?
Nahum repeats that the LORD is slow to anger, then adds that he will by no means clear the guilty. How does this book complete what Jonah showed about the same city?
Nahum 1:7 calls the LORD a stronghold in the day of trouble for those who take refuge in him. When injustice seems to be winning around you, what does taking refuge in God actually look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The LORD brings down powers that persist in violent pride, so even history's strongest remain accountable to him.
God's slowness to anger never means the guilty escape, so his mercy and his justice hold together.
Nineveh's fall is good news to its victims, showing that God sees atrocity and will vindicate the oppressed.
The city that repented under Jonah returned to cruelty, warning that a single turning cannot substitute for lasting faithfulness.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Nahum and Jonah together show God's patience and its limit, using the story of Nineveh.

comprehension_check.question: A century after Jonah, Nahum reworks the same creed about the same city, adding that the guilty are never simply cleared. What do the two books teach together?
options: God's patience is real and never indifference
God's mercy was withdrawn once Israel needed vengeance
God changed his mind about sparing Nineveh
God's warnings through Jonah failed and judgment followed
comprehension_check.why: Nahum 1:3 holds God's slowness to anger and his refusal to acquit persistent guilt in one sentence.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Nahum 1:3 again. Notice the two claims placed side by side in a single verse.

comprehension_check.question: Nahum ends with nations applauding Nineveh's fall, and near its start calls the LORD a refuge in distress. Who is this book good news for?
options: Any nation strong enough to replace the fallen empire
Israel alone, since judgment is reserved for foreigners
Every people crushed under a cruelty God has seen
Nobody, since it only celebrates an enemy's ruin
comprehension_check.why: Nahum 3:19 explains the applause: no nation escaped Assyria's cruelty, and Nahum 1:7 offers refuge to any who trust God.
