comprehension_check.hint: Read Nahum 3:19 again. Notice the reason the verse gives for the applause.

connections.reason: Nahum announces doom on the same Nineveh that repented here; the two books are the Twelve's paired word on God's patience and its limit.

nodes.title: Habakkuk: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
nodes.summary: A prophet argues with God: why do you tolerate Judah's violence — and worse, why answer it with Babylon, a nation more wicked still? The reply from the watchtower becomes one of the New Testament's load-bearing sentences: 'the righteous shall live by his faith.' The book ends with the Bible's greatest though-statement: though the fig tree does not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the LORD.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Habakkuk complains to God twice, and the answers make the problem harder before they make it better. What does his honest arguing teach about what faithful prayer can sound like, and what complaint would you bring to God if you believed he welcomed it?
assessment_questions: What two complaints does Habakkuk bring to God, and how does God answer each one?
God tells Habakkuk that the righteous shall live by his faith. In a book about waiting for justice that has not yet arrived, what does living by faith mean?
Habakkuk ends by rejoicing even if the fig tree fails and the fields produce nothing. What would it take for your joy to survive the loss of the things you currently count on?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Scripture models bringing honest anger and confusion directly to God, as the prophet does from his watchtower.
God may use even a wicked nation for his purposes without approving its evil, a mystery the book faces head on.
The righteous live by trusting God's promise before they can see it, a sentence the New Testament builds on three times.
The closing hymn shows worship that still stands when every visible blessing fails.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Habakkuk's two complaints and God's answers, and explain what the righteous living by faith means in that setting.

comprehension_check.question: Habakkuk asks why God would use Babylon and receives the watchtower answer in chapter 2. What does the answer give him instead of an explanation?
options: A promise the vision holds, and a way to live meanwhile
A defense of Babylon's role as a just instrument of discipline
A timetable naming when Babylon's turn to fall would come
A rebuke for daring to question the Judge of all
comprehension_check.why: Habakkuk 2:3-4 promises the vision will arrive at its appointed time and gives the righteous faith to live by until then.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Habakkuk 2:2-4 again. Notice what the waiting one is told to do while the vision lingers.

comprehension_check.question: Habakkuk ends with crops failed, flocks gone, and the prophet rejoicing anyway in 3:17-18. What holds that sentence together?
options: Confidence that the fields and flocks will shortly be restored
Joy anchored in God himself rather than in his gifts
Resignation that has stopped expecting anything from the land
Gratitude that Judah was spared the worst Babylon could do
comprehension_check.why: Habakkuk 3:18 fixes the rejoicing on the God of his salvation while every named support is stripped away.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Habakkuk 3:17-19 again. Notice what each though-clause removes, and what the yet-clause keeps.

connections.reason: 'The righteous shall live by faith' is the thesis-verse of Romans (1:17).
Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4 again in Galatians 3 against justification by law.
Hebrews 10 cites the same verse to steel a wavering church for endurance.

nodes.title: Zephaniah: The Day of the LORD and the Singing God
nodes.summary: The Day of the LORD at its darkest — 'a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish' sweeping from Judah across the nations — resolving into the Old Testament's tenderest picture of God: rejoicing over his remnant 'with gladness… exulting over you with loud singing.' Judgment and joy from the same throne.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Zephaniah paints the darkest Day of the LORD in the prophets, then ends with God singing loudly over his people. How can both scenes come from the same God, and which of the two pictures is harder for you to believe about him?
assessment_questions: What does Zephaniah say the Day of the LORD will be like, and who does he say may be hidden on that day?
Chapter 3 describes God rejoicing over his remnant with gladness and loud singing. What does it mean that this joy and the earlier judgment come from the same throne?
Zephaniah calls the humble of the land to seek the LORD, seek righteousness, seek humility. What would seeking humility on purpose look like in your habits this week?

teaching_concepts.concept: The day of wrath is real
teaching_concepts.explanation: God's holiness means idolatry and injustice face an actual day of reckoning that spares no nation.
The sweep of judgment starts with God's own people, so belonging to him brings scrutiny before it brings privilege.
God preserves a people marked by humility and honest speech, and he calls hearers to join them now.
The book resolves in God exulting over his people with loud singing, one of Scripture's tenderest pictures of his delight.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the Day of the LORD means in Zephaniah and how the book moves from a day of wrath to a God who sings over his people.

comprehension_check.question: Zephaniah opens with the fiercest day-of-wrath poetry in the prophets and closes with God rejoicing over his people in song. What does that movement claim?
options: God's anger burns itself out and gives way to relenting
The joy belongs to a new people replacing the judged
The singing repays those who endured their punishment well
The fire aims at a people God can delight in
comprehension_check.why: Zephaniah 3:17 shows the destination: the LORD at home among a humbled remnant, rejoicing over them with song.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zephaniah 3:17 again, with Zephaniah 1:14 in mind. Notice who stands beside God once the singing starts.

comprehension_check.question: Zephaniah 2:3 urges seeking the LORD, righteousness, and humility, yet attaches no guarantee to the shelter it holds out. What does the reservation teach?
options: That seeking God can never become a bargaining formula
That God had not yet decided Judah's final outcome
That most of those who seek will still be refused
That the prophet doubted his own message of rescue
comprehension_check.why: Zephaniah 2:3 leaves the shelter in God's free hands, so humility marks even the manner of hoping.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zephaniah 2:3 again. Notice the small word standing between the seeking and the shelter.

nodes.title: Haggai: Build the House
nodes.summary: Four dated sermons in four months, aimed at returnees living in paneled houses beside God's ruin: 'Consider your ways.' The people actually obey — rare among prophetic audiences — and to the elders who saw the first house and count this one as nothing comes the promise: 'The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: The returnees kept meaning to rebuild God's house once their own were settled, and eighteen years slipped by. What does it mean to consider your ways when your priorities have quietly drifted, and what rebuilding have you been postponing?
assessment_questions: What does Haggai tell the people to consider, and how do they and their leaders respond to his preaching?
The elders who remembered Solomon's temple wept at how small the new one looked. Why does God promise that the latter glory of this house will be greater than the former?
Haggai's audience lived in paneled houses beside God's ruin. Where does your calendar or budget show the same drift, and what one change would put first things first?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Living comfortably beside God's ruin exposed hearts that had quietly reordered God behind their own comfort.
Repentance in Haggai is practical, a concrete reordering of time, money, and labor around God's call.
The people actually listen and build, showing what a community's quick response to God's word can look like.
God promises the modest second temple a greater glory than the first, so present smallness never limits his future.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how Haggai restarted the temple work, and explain the promise God makes about the new house's glory.

comprehension_check.question: Haggai 1 connects thin harvests and wages in holed bags to the unbuilt house. What is the sermon saying through that link?
options: Prosperity reliably repays correct observance in every age
Their priorities had set them against the grain of blessing
Poverty came from Persia's taxes, which the temple would offset
The drought was random, but rebuilding would restore public morale
comprehension_check.why: Haggai 1:9-11 traces the scarcity to the Lord's own hand while his house lay in ruins and theirs did not.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Haggai 1:4-6 again. Notice the two kinds of houses the sermon sets side by side.

comprehension_check.question: Elders who saw Solomon's temple weep at the new foundation, and Haggai 2 answers them. Where does the promised greater glory come from?
options: From treasures the returning exiles would slowly accumulate
From craftsmanship surpassing Solomon's in the rebuilt courts
From God's own presence and promise, not the building's splendor
From the day the second house would host a restored monarchy
comprehension_check.why: Haggai 2:5-9 rests the promise on God's presence among them and his claim on all silver and gold.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Haggai 2:3-9 again. Notice what God keeps repeating to the discouraged builders, and what he claims as his own.

connections.reason: Haggai is one of the two prophets who restart this very construction project.

nodes.title: The Night Visions
nodes.summary: Eight surreal visions in one night for the rebuilding community: a horseman among myrtles, the high priest Joshua in filthy clothes acquitted before the accuser, a lampstand fed by living olive trees — 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.' A crown is set on a priest's head, fusing the two offices in a figure called the Branch.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The night visions keep answering discouragement: an accused priest is given clean clothes, and a governor is told the work will finish by God's Spirit rather than by might or power. What discouragement in your own work would these visions speak to, and what would relying on the Spirit change about how you carry it?
assessment_questions: What happens to Joshua the high priest in the vision of chapter 3, and what does the lampstand vision of chapter 4 promise Zerubbabel?
The visions were given to a small community rebuilding on ruins. Why does God answer their discouragement with pictures of cleansing, the Spirit, and a coming Branch?

God says the work will be done by his Spirit rather than by might or power. Which task in your life are you attempting entirely on your own strength, and what would depending on God's Spirit look like there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The visions promise God dwelling in Jerusalem again, so restoration means his presence even more than rebuilt walls.
Joshua's filthy clothes are removed at God's command, showing that acquittal is God's gift rather than the accused's achievement.
The rebuilding succeeds through God's Spirit rather than human strength, a word for every overwhelmed servant.
A crowned priest called the Branch fuses king and priest in one figure, a promise pointing beyond Zerubbabel's day.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe two of the night visions and explain the message they carried for the temple-rebuilding generation.

comprehension_check.question: The word to Zerubbabel in Zechariah 4:6-10 lands in a community embarrassed by its small work. What does it promise?
options: God's Spirit rather than human strength will finish the house
The rebuilt temple will outshine Solomon's once nations contribute
The work will pause until a worthier generation resumes it
The builders' own strength will grow to match the task
comprehension_check.why: Zechariah 4:6-9 puts the finishing of the house in the Spirit's power, and Zechariah 4:10 blesses the day of small things.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zechariah 4:6-10 again. Notice what the great mountain becomes, and whose hands are said to complete the work.

comprehension_check.question: Zechariah 3 puts the high priest, in filthy clothes, before the accuser. What does the scene teach about how his service can resume?
options: Joshua's humble silence in court disarms the accuser's charge
The sacrifices Joshua will offer once vested cleanse him
The people's repentance restores the priest who represents them
God's command removes the guilt and supplies clean robes
comprehension_check.why: Zechariah 3:4-5 has the angel of the LORD order the filthy clothes removed and iniquity taken away by his own word.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zechariah 3:1-5 again. Notice who speaks, who acts, and what Joshua himself contributes to the change.

connections.reason: Revelation's colored horsemen and two olive-tree witnesses come from these visions.
Zechariah's night visions encourage the same rebuilding community.

nodes.title: The King on a Donkey and the Pierced One
nodes.summary: The oracles the passion narratives quote again and again: a king coming humble and riding on a donkey, a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter, and the staggering 'they will look on me, on him whom they have pierced, and mourn.' A fountain opened for sin, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and finally the LORD king over all the earth.
nodes.discussion_prompt: These oracles give Israel a king who arrives humble on a donkey and a shepherd whose piercing the people will one day mourn. Why would God choose humility and wounds as the way his king wins, and what does that choice ask of anyone who wants to follow him?
assessment_questions: How does the king of Zechariah 9:9 arrive, and what price is the shepherd valued at in chapter 11?

In chapter 12 the people look on the one they pierced and mourn as for an only child, and in chapter 13 a fountain is opened for sin. What do these scenes together claim about how cleansing comes to God's people?
The oracles end with the LORD as king over all the earth. How does living under a humble, pierced king change what you expect power and victory to look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The promised ruler arrives righteous and lowly on a donkey, so God's kingship overturns every expectation of conquest.
A shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver shows God's chosen one suffering betrayal at his own people's hands.
Looking on the pierced one leads to grief, and grief leads to a fountain opened for sin, tying repentance to God's own provision.
The oracles resolve with God as king over the whole earth, holding the suffering scenes inside a certain victory.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the picture of the coming king and the pierced shepherd in these oracles, and how the section moves from betrayal to a fountain for sin to the LORD reigning over all the earth.

comprehension_check.question: Zechariah 9:9-10 announces a victorious king who arrives on a donkey and removes the war bow. What claim about his kingship is being made?
options: His humility is a disguise to be shed once enthroned
His poverty shows the kingdom will renounce ruling altogether
His victory comes in lowliness and issues in peace
His gentleness is for Israel and his sword for the nations
comprehension_check.why: Zechariah 9:10 has the king cut off chariot and bow and speak peace to the nations, ruling from sea to sea.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zechariah 9:9-10 again. Notice what is removed when this king arrives, and how far his rule still runs.

comprehension_check.question: Zechariah 12:10 has God pour out a spirit of grace before anyone looks on the pierced one and mourns. What does that order say about the mourning?
options: The mourning is what earns the cleansing fountain that follows
The grief itself is a gift awakened by poured-out grace
The sorrow is despair at a judgment already sealed
The weeping is a required public rite before restoration
comprehension_check.why: Zechariah 12:10 pours out grace and supplication first, and Zechariah 13:1 answers the mourning with a fountain opened for sin.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Zechariah 12:10 and Zechariah 13:1 again. Notice what God gives before the grief, and what the fountain is for.

connections.reason: Palm Sunday narrates Zechariah 9:9 verbatim — the king on a donkey's colt.
Thirty silver pieces, the potter's field, the shepherd struck — Matthew's passion quotes this oracle repeatedly.
John cites 'they will look on him whom they have pierced' at the spear-thrust on the cross.
Revelation 1:7 fuses Daniel's clouds with Zechariah's pierced one: 'every eye will see him, even those who pierced him.'

nodes.title: Malachi: The Old Testament's Last Word
nodes.summary: A disputation with a jaded post-exilic community — blemished sacrifices, broken marriages, 'it is vain to serve God' — answered by promise: 'Behold, I send my messenger to prepare the way before me, and the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.' The Old Testament closes waiting for Elijah to come 'before the great and awesome day of the LORD.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Malachi's audience keeps answering God's charges with the same weary question: how have we done that? What makes worship go stale without anyone deciding to quit, and where has your own service to God drifted into leftovers?
assessment_questions: What complaints does God raise against the priests and people in Malachi, and how do they keep responding to him?
God promises a messenger to prepare the way and describes the coming one as a refiner's fire. Why does the answer to half-hearted worship arrive as purification rather than simple punishment?
The people said it is vain to serve God because the arrogant seemed to prosper. When serving God feels pointless, what would it mean to keep bringing him your best anyway?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Blemished offerings insult God's honor, and he would rather have no fire on the altar than careless fire.
God counts broken marriages and injustice to workers as worship failures, since covenant faithfulness spans the whole of life.
God's coming purifies before it condemns, aiming to restore a people who can offer right worship again.
The Old Testament closes on a promised messenger and Elijah's return, leaving the story leaning forward to what comes next.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the disputation pattern of Malachi and explain the promise of the coming messenger that closes the Old Testament.

comprehension_check.question: Six times God states a charge and the people answer with the same weary question, asking how they have done any such thing. What does the pattern reveal about them?
options: They are openly defying God and proud of it
They are innocent and the charges are overstated
They never learned what the law actually required
Their drift has become invisible to them
comprehension_check.why: Malachi 1:6-7 shows priests serving contemptuously while genuinely unable to see it, a drift too slow to feel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Malachi 1:6-7 again. Notice what the priests are doing at the moment they ask their question.

comprehension_check.question: Malachi answers stale worship with the promise of one who comes like a refiner's fire. What is that fire for?
options: To sort out which worshipers deserve to survive the day
To purify a people until their offerings are right again
To frighten the careless back into proper observance
To repay the priests for years of contempt
comprehension_check.why: Malachi 3:2-3 sets the refiner over the priesthood until right offerings return, so the fire works restoration.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Malachi 3:2-3 again. Notice what the refiner is after in the silver.

connections.reason: The Gospels open where Malachi ends: John the Baptist is the promised messenger and the Elijah to come.
Gabriel describes John 'in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to children' — quoting Malachi 4.

nodes.title: The Genealogy and the Birth of the King
nodes.summary: Matthew opens the New Testament with a family tree — Abraham to David to exile to Jesus — announcing that every Old Testament thread lands here. Virgin birth, magi following a star, Herod's massacre, flight to Egypt: five fulfillment quotations in two chapters, each re-reading Israel's story around one child.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Matthew names Jesus Immanuel, God with us, and within two chapters that child is being hunted by a king. What do these chapters show about how God enters the world, and where would you expect to find him entering yours?
assessment_questions: Who travels to worship the child in chapter 2, and how does Herod respond to the news of a newborn king?
Matthew quotes the Old Testament five times in two chapters. What is he trying to convince his readers of by anchoring every scene in Israel's Scriptures?

The magi travel far on partial knowledge while Jerusalem's experts stay home with the full text. What keeps a person from acting on what they already know about God, and what would seeking like the magi look like for you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The genealogy runs from Abraham through David to Jesus, presenting him as the Messiah in whom the whole Old Testament account lands.

teaching_concepts.concept: The virgin birth is God's initiative
teaching_concepts.explanation: Conception by the Holy Spirit signals that this rescue begins with God stepping into history, since the child's very arrival is a divine act.
Gentile magi worship the child while Herod tries to kill him, so the kingdom meets both welcome and violence from its first pages.
The flight to Egypt shows God guarding his plan through tragedy and exile, guiding events even when they look like disaster.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Matthew begins with a genealogy, and what the names Jesus and Immanuel each claim about who this child is.

comprehension_check.question: Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy arranged from Abraham through David and the exile to the Christ. What is the family tree there to do?
options: Certify that Jesus' ancestry was morally worthy of the Messiah
Trace how the royal line held the throne until Jesus could claim it
Present Jesus as the destination of Israel's whole story
Prove that the records behind Matthew's account are reliable
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 1:17 counts the generations in three movements that all land on the Christ, reading Israel's whole history as one road that arrives at Jesus.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 1:17 again. Notice the three turning points Matthew counts by, and where the counting stops.

comprehension_check.question: In Matthew 2, foreign magi worship the child while Jerusalem's king plots to kill him. What is Matthew signaling from the start?
options: This king will draw outsiders' worship and rulers' violence
The stars can lead to God anyone who studies them
Israel as a nation had already refused its Messiah
God's plan advances only after its enemies are removed
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 2:11 shows gentiles kneeling and Matthew 2:16 shows the sitting king killing, the two receptions that will follow Jesus to the cross.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 2:11 and Matthew 2:16 side by side. Notice who kneels before this king and who reaches for a sword.

connections.reason: Balaam's 'star out of Jacob' stands behind the star the magi follow.
Rahab appears in Jesus' genealogy — the Canaanite convert becomes an ancestor of the Messiah.
Ruth the Moabite stands in Jesus' genealogy alongside Rahab — outsiders written into the messianic line.
Matthew's opening genealogy works the same way — using a family tree to claim the whole story for its subject.
Matthew's birth narrative quotes 'the virgin shall conceive… Immanuel' as fulfilled in Jesus.
'Out of Egypt I called my son' (11:1) becomes Matthew's caption for the child Jesus' return from Egypt.
The chief priests answer Herod's 'where will the Christ be born?' by quoting Micah 5:2 — Bethlehem.

nodes.title: Baptism and the Wilderness Test
nodes.summary: John the Baptist arrives in Elijah's camel hair announcing the kingdom; Jesus is baptized under an opened heaven — 'This is my beloved Son' — and then walks Israel's story backward: forty days in the wilderness, tempted where Israel fell for forty years, answering every test from Deuteronomy.
nodes.discussion_prompt: At his baptism Jesus hears the Father call him beloved Son, and the very next scene is forty days of hunger and testing. What do these chapters show about the connection between knowing who you are before God and facing temptation, and how would that change the way you meet your own tests?
assessment_questions: What happens when Jesus comes up out of the water at his baptism, and where does the Spirit lead him immediately afterward?
Jesus answers every temptation with words from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's wilderness years. What is Matthew showing us by having Jesus succeed exactly where Israel failed?
Each temptation offers Jesus a shortcut around the Father's plan. What shortcut looks most attractive in your own life right now, and what would refusing it the way Jesus did require?

teaching_concepts.explanation: At the baptism the Spirit descends and the Father speaks, announcing Jesus' identity before his ministry begins.
The sinless Jesus joins repentant sinners in the water to fulfill all righteousness, modeling humility from his first public act.

teaching_concepts.concept: The faithful Israel in the wilderness
teaching_concepts.explanation: Forty days replay Israel's forty years, and Jesus stands firm at every point where the nation once fell.
Jesus meets real spiritual conflict by answering with God's word, showing how the fight against temptation is actually won.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the baptism and temptation scenes, and explain how Jesus relives Israel's wilderness story without repeating its failure.

comprehension_check.question: John's baptism was for repentant sinners, and John himself objects to baptizing Jesus. Why does Jesus insist on it?
options: He wanted to test whether John would recognize him
He stood among the sinners he came to save
He needed the washing before his own ministry could begin
He was assuming command of John's renewal movement
comprehension_check.why: In Matthew 3:15 Jesus calls the baptism fitting to fulfill all righteousness, his first public act placing him with the people he came for.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 3:13-15 again. Notice whose company Jesus chooses to be found in at the Jordan.

comprehension_check.question: Matthew gives Jesus forty days in the wilderness answering every test from Deuteronomy. What is the pattern claiming?
options: Fasting builds the spiritual strength that ministry requires
Memorized scripture makes a person immune to temptation
The wilderness is where God is most reliably found
Jesus succeeds as faithful Israel where the nation fell
comprehension_check.why: The forty days replay Israel's forty years, and each answer in Matthew 4:4-10 comes from Deuteronomy, the wilderness book, obeyed this time.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 4:1-4 again. Notice how long Israel faced these same tests, and how that first testing went.

connections.reason: All three of Jesus' replies to Satan in the wilderness are quotations from Deuteronomy 6-8.
The Gospels open where Malachi ends: John the Baptist is the promised messenger and the Elijah to come.

nodes.title: The Sermon on the Mount
nodes.summary: From a mountainside, the kingdom's charter: blessed are the poor in spirit, salt and light, anger as murder's root, love for enemies, the Lord's Prayer, treasure in heaven, the golden rule, two houses on rock and sand. The most influential moral teaching ever delivered — and a deliberate echo of Sinai, spoken this time by the lawgiver in person.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus ends the Sermon with two builders, and the only difference between them is doing what they heard. Which of the Sermon's commands would cost you the most to actually practice, and what does that resistance reveal about where your foundation currently sits?
assessment_questions: How does the Sermon begin, and what two images does Jesus use for his disciples right after the Beatitudes?
Jesus repeatedly says you have heard it said, then traces each command down to anger, lust, and honesty in the heart. What is he claiming about where righteousness really lives?
Jesus commands love for enemies and prayer for persecutors. Who is the hardest person for you to want good for, and what small obedience would move you an inch toward that command?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The crowds notice that he speaks on his own authority, calling hearers into God's reign rather than offering moral advice.
God weighs motives as well as acts, so anger and lust already matter before murder and adultery ever happen.
Jesus raises the commands toward love, mercy, and truthful living instead of loosening them, fulfilling what the law was always after.
The two-builders ending makes obedience the test of whether the Sermon has taken root, since both builders heard the same words.

nodes.completion_criteria: Summarize the Sermon's picture of kingdom righteousness, and explain the difference between the two builders in your own words.

comprehension_check.question: In Matthew 5, Jesus sets anger beside murder and lust beside adultery. What is he teaching about God's commands?
options: They reach the motives underneath the acts they forbid
They were too harsh, and the kingdom now relaxes them
They are satisfied by sincerity even when behavior fails
They list the works that earn a place in the kingdom
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 5:21-22 and Matthew 5:27-28 move each command upstream to the anger and the look, where God has always weighed the heart.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 5:21-22 and Matthew 5:27-28 again. Notice where Jesus locates the sin before any act has happened.

comprehension_check.question: The Sermon ends with two builders who hear the same words. Why does Jesus close that way?
options: To reassure the crowd that careful listening lays a firm foundation
To promise that obedient disciples will be spared life's storms
To press hearers toward doing, since hearing alone builds nothing
To warn that storms fall hardest on those who build wrongly
comprehension_check.why: In Matthew 7:24-27 the same storm strikes both houses, and only acting on the words keeps a house standing.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 7:24-27 again. Notice what the two builders share, and the single verb that separates them.

connections.reason: James is essentially the Sermon on the Mount turned into pastoral instruction — hearing and doing.
The Beatitudes' 'blessed' opening and two-ways ending (rock vs. sand) mirror Psalm 1's architecture.
The Sermon on the Mount deliberately echoes Sinai — a mountain, a covenant people, the law's true depth.
Romans 12's bless-your-persecutors ethic is the Sermon on the Mount in epistle form.

nodes.title: Miracles and the Sending of the Twelve
nodes.summary: A rapid-fire run of miracles — leper, centurion's servant, storm stilled, paralytic forgiven, dead girl raised — then authority delegated: the Twelve sent out with the same message and power, warned to be 'wise as serpents and innocent as doves.' The kingdom in word (5-7) now moves in deed (8-9) and mission (10).
nodes.discussion_prompt: The centurion trusts Jesus to heal with a word from a distance, and Jesus calls it the greatest faith he has found in Israel. What do the healing stories in these chapters teach about what faith actually is, and where is Jesus' authority hardest for you to take at his word?
assessment_questions: Name three of the miracles in chapters 8 and 9, and describe what Jesus gives the Twelve when he sends them out in chapter 10.
Before healing the paralytic, Jesus first declares his sins forgiven and the scribes call it blasphemy. What does the healing that follows prove about who Jesus claims to be?
Jesus tells the disciples the harvest is plentiful and the workers few, then sends them into it. What need around you might be a harvest field you have prayed about without ever stepping into?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus' word commands sickness, demons, the sea, and sin itself, revealing an identity no prophet before him claimed.

teaching_concepts.concept: Faith takes Jesus at his word
teaching_concepts.explanation: The centurion and the bleeding woman receive healing by trusting what Jesus says and who he is, which is what Matthew means by faith.
Jesus hands his own authority to the Twelve, turning the kingdom into a movement that sends ordinary people out with his message.
The mission speech promises opposition and asks for a loyalty to Jesus that outranks safety, reputation, and even family approval.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe how the miracles of chapters 8 and 9 back up the Sermon's claims, and explain what Jesus commissions the Twelve to do.

comprehension_check.question: Matthew 8-9 runs together healings, a stilled storm, and a paralytic forgiven. What is the collection claiming?
options: Compassion for sufferers was the whole aim of the miracles
Healing is dispensed in proportion to the strength of faith
The signs were staged to draw crowds his teaching could not
One authority commands sickness, sea, spirits, and sin alike
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 9:6 makes the healing itself proof that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins, the claim beneath the whole sequence.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 8:26-27 and Matthew 9:6 again. Notice the question the disciples ask, and what any answer must cover.

comprehension_check.question: In Matthew 10, Jesus sends out the Twelve. What changes about the kingdom's work at that point?
options: It pauses while the Twelve complete their training safely
It becomes a movement carried by people Jesus sends
It passes to the Twelve so Jesus can withdraw
It shrinks to what the Twelve alone can manage
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 10:1 hands Jesus' own authority to the Twelve, and Matthew 10:7 gives them his own message to preach as they go.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 10:1 and Matthew 10:7 again. Notice whose authority and whose message the Twelve carry out the door.

connections.reason: Matthew reads the healings as Isaiah 53: 'He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.'
Jesus tells the Pharisees to 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice' — Hosea 6:6.

nodes.title: Opposition and Parables of the Kingdom
nodes.summary: Doubt from John in prison, sabbath showdowns, a blasphemy accusation — and Jesus shifts to parables: sower, weeds, mustard seed, hidden treasure, pearl. 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden.' Feeding five thousand and walking on the sea, he is misunderstood by crowds, Pharisees, and disciples alike.
nodes.discussion_prompt: In the middle of mounting rejection, Jesus invites the weary to come to him for rest. After watching crowds, Pharisees, and even John the Baptist wrestle with doubt in these chapters, what do you think keeps a heart soft toward Jesus, and what tends to harden yours?
assessment_questions: What question does John the Baptist send from prison, and how does Jesus answer it?
The parable of the sower describes four soils receiving the same seed. What is Jesus explaining about why the same message meets such different responses?
Jesus says of some hearers that their lips honor God while their hearts stay far away. Where does your own faith run on autopilot, and what would bringing your heart back near actually involve?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus points John's messengers to the healings and the good news itself, letting his works testify to his identity.
Mustard seed and leaven show God's reign growing quietly and surely long before its final harvest.
The same stories open the kingdom to receptive hearts and leave hardened hearers confirmed in their resistance.
The Canaanite mother keeps asking past every apparent refusal, and Jesus publicly praises her faith and grants her request.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Jesus shifts to teaching in parables in chapter 13, and what the parable of the sower says about hearing the kingdom's message.

comprehension_check.question: Asked why he teaches in parables, Jesus gives a surprising answer in Matthew 13. What does he say the stories do?
options: They simplify the kingdom so every hearer can grasp it
They shield the message from informers until the right time
They reveal to receptive hearts and conceal from hardened ones
They persuade by story where plain commands had failed
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 13:11-12 gives the kingdom's mysteries to some while even what others have is taken away, disclosure and judgment in one form of speech.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 13:10-13 again. Notice that Jesus names two audiences, and what the same stories do to each.

comprehension_check.question: The mustard seed and the leaven picture the kingdom in Matthew 13. What are those parables teaching about God's reign?
options: It begins almost invisibly and surely grows to fullness
It stays a small remnant until the very end
It arrives all at once in unmistakable public power
It grows exactly as fast as human effort feeds it
comprehension_check.why: In Matthew 13:31-33 the smallest seed becomes the largest garden plant and the leaven works through all the flour it touches.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 13:31-33 again. Notice the size of each start, and how far each finish reaches.

connections.reason: Jesus explains the parables' concealing effect by quoting Isaiah 6's hardening commission.
Jesus invokes this scene: 'the queen of the South came to hear Solomon — and something greater than Solomon is here.'
Jesus answers John the Baptist's doubts with Isaiah 35's checklist: the blind see, the lame walk.
Jesus' mustard-seed kingdom that grows to fill the garden echoes the stone that becomes a mountain.
Jesus gives 'the sign of Jonah' — three days and nights in the fish — as the one sign his generation will get.

nodes.title: The Confession, the Transfiguration, and the Community
nodes.summary: At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and immediately proves he doesn't understand it, rebuking the cross. Jesus shines with unveiled glory between Moses and Elijah, then teaches his new community the arithmetic of forgiveness: seventy times seven.
nodes.tradition_notes: Matthew 16:18 — 'you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church… I will give you the keys of the kingdom' — is the classic dividing text: Catholic teaching reads Peter and his successors (the papacy) as the rock; Orthodoxy honors Peter's primacy but locates it in his confession and rejects a universal Roman jurisdiction; most Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of Christ, or Peter as representative of all the apostles. Each reading is ancient; the graph reports, not referees.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Peter names Jesus as the Christ, then immediately tries to talk him out of the cross. What do these chapters suggest about the gap between saying the right thing about Jesus and understanding what it means, and where might that gap sit in your own faith?
assessment_questions: What does Peter say when Jesus asks who the disciples believe he is, and what happens on the mountain in chapter 17?

Right after the confession, Jesus begins predicting his suffering and Peter objects. Why does Jesus treat the objection so seriously, and what does the exchange reveal about the kind of Messiah he is?
Jesus tells Peter to forgive seventy times seven and backs it with the parable of the unforgiving servant. Who are you keeping count against, and what would losing count actually require of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Peter's declaration that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, names the claim the whole Gospel turns on.

Jesus promises to build his church on the rock of Matthew 16:18, words that Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant readers understand differently, while all agree on what he promises: a church that death itself cannot defeat.

teaching_concepts.concept: Glory confirms the road of suffering
teaching_concepts.explanation: The Transfiguration lets three disciples see the Son's unveiled glory so they can trust him through the cross he has just announced.
Chapter 18 gives concrete steps for reconciliation and a forgiveness that refuses to keep score, shaping how Jesus' people live together.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Peter's confession and the Transfiguration, and explain how chapter 18 describes life inside the community Jesus is building.

comprehension_check.question: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, then rebukes him for predicting the cross. What does that sequence show?
options: Peter's confession was a lucky guess he did not believe
Jesus withdrew the blessing once Peter opposed his plan
Titles for Jesus matter less than sincere devotion to him
The confession was right while Peter's expectations were still wrong
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 16:17 blesses the confession as revealed by the Father, and Matthew 16:21 begins teaching what kind of Christ has just been confessed.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 16:16-23 again. Notice what Jesus starts explaining from that time on, and how Peter receives it.

comprehension_check.question: Christian traditions famously part ways over Matthew 16:18. What exactly do they disagree about?
options: Whether the church Jesus builds can outlast death's assault
What the rock is and what authority follows from it
Whether Peter's confession truly came to him from God
Whether Jesus meant to found a lasting community at all
comprehension_check.why: The wordplay in Matthew 16:18 lets readers locate the rock in Peter himself, in his confession, or in his office, and the ancient traditions divide right there.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 16:17-19 again. Notice which word the promise is built on, and ask what it points back to.

connections.reason: Moses, once barred from the land, stands in it at the Transfiguration beside the prophet like him.
Elijah stands with Moses at the Transfiguration — the prophets personified beside the law.

nodes.title: The Road to Jerusalem and the Temple Cleared
nodes.summary: Hard teachings on the way up — marriage and divorce, the rich young man, vineyard laborers paid alike, 'the last will be first' — then Palm Sunday: the king on a donkey, the temple courts overturned, and parables (two sons, wicked tenants) aimed straight at the chief priests, who take the point.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The rich young man walks away sad, and days later Jerusalem cheers a king riding a donkey. What do these chapters say about what people want a king to be, and what would it cost you for Jesus to rule the part of your life you guard most?
assessment_questions: What does Jesus tell the rich young man to do, and what does Jesus do when he enters the temple courts?
In the vineyard parable of chapter 20, latecomers receive the same pay as all-day workers. What is Jesus teaching about how the kingdom measures reward?
Jesus says the last will be first, and he enters the city on a borrowed donkey. Where do you chase being first, and what would practicing his kind of downward greatness look like this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The entry on a donkey fulfills Zechariah's prophecy, presenting a Messiah whose power arrives in lowliness rather than conquest.
The rich young man and the welcomed children show that the kingdom is entered with empty hands, since salvation is possible only with God.
Clearing the temple and cursing the fig tree condemn religion that looks busy while producing nothing God is seeking.
The kingdom overturns human rankings of merit and status, so the last become first and greatness is redefined as service.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the rich young man's story and the triumphal entry each reveal about the kind of king Jesus is.

comprehension_check.question: In Matthew 19 a commandment-keeping rich man walks away while children are received. What is Matthew teaching about entering the kingdom?
options: It is received in dependence, since no one can achieve it
It is open to the poor and closed to the wealthy
It demands harder effort at the commands he already kept
It requires every disciple to sell all possessions first
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 19:26 grounds entry in what God alone can do, the same dependence the welcomed children of Matthew 19:14 picture.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 19:13-15 and Matthew 19:23-26 again. Notice what the children bring with them, and what the disciples ask.

comprehension_check.question: Matthew 21 stacks the temple clearing, the withered fig tree, and the tenant parable. What do the three announce together?
options: A ban on trade conducted anywhere near sacred space
A zeal meant to ignite an uprising against Rome
A judgment on religion that is busy but fruitless
A rejection of temple sacrifice as inherently corrupt
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 21:19 curses leaves without figs, and Matthew 21:43 gives the vineyard to those who will produce its fruit.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 21:12-19 and Matthew 21:33-43 again. Notice what the tree lacks, and what the tenants refuse to hand over.

connections.reason: Jesus' parable of the wicked tenants rebuilds Isaiah 5's vineyard song against the temple leadership.
Jesus quotes the temple sermon's 'den of robbers' as he overturns the money-changers' tables.
Palm Sunday narrates Zechariah 9:9 verbatim — the king on a donkey's colt.

nodes.title: Final Controversies and the Olivet Discourse
nodes.summary: Every faction takes a swing — taxes to Caesar, resurrection riddles, the greatest commandment — and Jesus answers all comers, pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees, and delivers the Olivet Discourse: the temple's doom, the Son of Man's coming, and three parables of readiness ending with sheep, goats, and 'as you did it to the least of these.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Asked for the greatest commandment, Jesus gives two that belong together, love of God and love of neighbor, then closes the discourse with sheep and goats separated by care for the least. What do these chapters teach about what God will actually weigh in the end, and how would living ready change your ordinary Tuesday?
assessment_questions: What two commandments does Jesus say the whole Law and the Prophets hang on, and what does he predict about the temple?
The seven woes target leaders who look righteous on the outside while the inside stays unclean. What is Jesus diagnosing about religion that manages appearances?
In the final parable, the King identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner. Who around you might be Christ in that disguise, and what would serving them cost you this month?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Love of God with everything and love of neighbor as yourself hold every other command together.
Jesus reserves his sharpest words for pious performance without inward repentance, warning that God sees past appearances.

The Olivet Discourse commands readiness and faithful stewardship rather than date-setting, and teachers still discuss how much of it aims at the temple's fall in AD 70 and how much at the end of the age.
The sheep and goats scene makes concrete care for the needy the evidence of real allegiance to the King.

nodes.completion_criteria: State the two greatest commandments, and explain what the parables of Matthew 25 say readiness for the King's return looks like.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus answers the law question by naming love of God and love of neighbor. What does he claim for those two commands?
options: They replace the older law, which is now retired
Every other command depends on them for its meaning
They give beginners the easiest place to start
They describe feelings that cannot really be commanded
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 22:40 makes every command in the Law and the Prophets depend on these two loves, the center holding the rest together.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 22:37-40 again. Notice the relationship the final verse sets up between these two commands and all the others.

comprehension_check.question: Across the Olivet parables in Matthew 24-25, what posture does Jesus command for the time the master is away?
options: Careful study of the signs until the date is fixed
Withdrawal from daily duties into watchful prayer
Confidence that the long delay means he is not coming
Faithful work precisely because the hour is unknown
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 24:42 and Matthew 25:13 command watch precisely because no one knows the day, and the parables fill the waiting with entrusted work.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 24:36 and Matthew 25:14-30 again. Notice what the master leaves behind, and what he checks on his return.

connections.reason: Jesus pairs Leviticus 19:18 with the Shema as the two commands on which everything hangs.
Jesus names the Shema as the first and greatest commandment.
Jesus silences his questioners with this psalm's riddle about David's son and Lord.
Jesus' Olivet Discourse cites 'the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet.'
The thief-in-the-night and stay-awake teaching echoes Jesus' Olivet parables of readiness.

nodes.title: The Passion and the Great Commission
nodes.summary: Betrayal for thirty silver pieces, a Passover meal become the Lord's Supper, Gethsemane, trials, Peter's denials, crucifixion under the cry of Psalm 22 — then the earthquake, the empty tomb, and the risen Jesus on a Galilean mountain: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: At the table Jesus calls the cup his blood of the covenant poured out for the forgiveness of sins, and on the mountain he claims all authority in heaven and on earth. Reading the passion and resurrection as one story, what did Jesus accomplish that no one else could, and what does his commission ask of you specifically?
assessment_questions: What does Jesus do with the bread and cup at the Passover meal, and what do the women find at the tomb on the first day of the week?
Jesus prays in Gethsemane for the cup to pass, then rises and walks toward his betrayer. What does that prayer reveal about how willingly Jesus went to the cross?

Peter denies Jesus three times, and the risen Jesus still includes him in the mission. What failure makes you feel disqualified, and what does the Great Commission's promise of Jesus' presence say back to it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Last Supper ties Jesus' coming death to the forgiveness of sins and gives his people an ongoing meal that points to it.
Gethsemane shows Jesus honestly dreading the cup and still choosing the Father's will with full knowledge of the cost.
Matthew presents the crucifixion as the decisive act where God's justice and mercy meet, the work the whole Gospel has been walking toward.
The risen Jesus claims all authority, sends his people to every nation, and promises his presence to the end of the age.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the passion story from the Last Supper to the empty tomb, and explain what the Great Commission sends disciples to do.

comprehension_check.question: In Gethsemane Jesus prays in open anguish, then rises to meet his betrayer. What does the scene show about his death?
options: He performed the dread to prepare his disciples
He hoped to escape and was simply overtaken
He chose the Father's will with full knowledge
He steadied himself once the disciples encouraged him
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 26:39 holds real dread and real surrender in one prayer, and Matthew 26:46 has Jesus rising to walk toward what he accepted.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 26:39-46 again. Notice how the prayer changes across its three rounds, and who is leading when it ends.

comprehension_check.question: On the mountain some worship and some doubt, and Jesus commissions them all anyway. What is the mission resting on?
options: His own complete authority and his continuing presence
The training the Eleven have now fully completed
The nations' proven readiness to hear the message
The disciples' need to repay their desertion of him
comprehension_check.why: Matthew 28:18 opens the commission with all authority given to Jesus, and Matthew 28:20 closes it with his presence to the end of the age.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Matthew 28:16-20 again. Notice the word that links the claim of authority to the command to go.

connections.reason: 'Make disciples of all nations' completes the promise that in Abraham's seed all nations would be blessed.
Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper at a Passover meal, casting his death as the new Passover.
The crucifixion narrative quotes and alludes to this psalm repeatedly — the cry, the mocking, the divided garments.
'When they had sung a hymn' after the Last Supper — the Passover Hallel; and 'the stone the builders rejected' frames the passion week.
At his trial Jesus quotes this scene — 'you will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds' — and is condemned for it.
Thirty silver pieces, the potter's field, the shepherd struck — Matthew's passion quotes this oracle repeatedly.
Matthew's fuller passion-and-resurrection account parallels Mark scene for scene and completes his abrupt ending.
The taunts against the righteous man ('let God deliver him, if he is his child') closely parallel the mockery at the cross.

nodes.title: The Kingdom Breaks In
nodes.summary: No genealogy, no nativity — Mark opens at a sprint: baptism, wilderness, and 'the kingdom of God is at hand.' Demons expelled, a paralytic forgiven and healed, sinners at the table, sabbath rules overruled; within three chapters the authorities are already plotting and his family thinks he's insane. The word is 'immediately,' more than forty times.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Mark's Jesus moves fast. Within three chapters he has forgiven sins, overruled sabbath custom, and been called insane by his own family. What makes his authority so unsettling to almost everyone in these chapters, and which of his claims would unsettle you most if you heard it fresh?
assessment_questions: What is Jesus' first announcement in Mark, and what do the friends of the paralyzed man do to get him to Jesus?
When Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are forgiven, the scribes object that only God can forgive sins. Why does Mark want the healing that follows to answer that objection?
Jesus says he came to call sinners, and the religious keep their distance from his table. Whose table would following him put you at, and what reputation would you risk by sitting there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus' opening summons is to repent and believe, because God's reign has come near in him.
The healings and exorcisms display power, and pronouncing forgiveness claims a prerogative that belongs to God alone.
The sabbath disputes show Jesus reading the law toward human need and mercy, which provokes the religiously rigid.
Fishermen leave their nets on the spot, and opposition gathers as fast as the crowds do.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe Jesus' opening announcement in Mark, and explain how the paralytic's healing backs his claim to forgive sins.

comprehension_check.question: In Mark 2:9-11 Jesus answers the charge against him by healing the paralytic. What is the healing meant to show?
options: Healing matters more to Jesus than debates about forgiveness
Visible power backs his invisible claim to forgive sins
The man's faith earned both his healing and his pardon
Jesus heals to prove the man's sickness came from sin
comprehension_check.why: Mark 2:10 states the purpose of the miracle, to show that the Son of Man really holds authority to forgive.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 2:5-12 again. Notice the question Jesus asks in Mark 2:9, and what the crowd can and cannot see.

comprehension_check.question: Mark opens with Jesus announcing that God's reign has drawn near. In Mark 1-3, where does that nearness actually show itself?
options: In the crowds, whose enthusiasm spreads the movement through Galilee
In a program of reform Jesus launches within the synagogues
In Jesus himself, whose word commands demons, disease, and disciples
In Rome's retreat, as political power begins changing hands
comprehension_check.why: In Mark 1:27 the crowd sees it, authority in Jesus' own word that even the unclean spirits obey.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 1:16-27 again. Notice what happens each time Jesus speaks, and to whom.

connections.reason: All four Gospels open Jesus' story with Isaiah 40's 'voice crying in the wilderness.'

nodes.title: Parables and Power
nodes.summary: The sower and the mustard seed by day; by night a storm silenced with two words while the disciples ask the Gospel's central question: 'Who then is this, that even wind and sea obey him?' Then a legion of demons, a hemorrhaging woman healed by a touch, and a dead twelve-year-old told to get up — talitha koum.
nodes.discussion_prompt: After the storm goes silent, the disciples are more afraid of Jesus than they were of the weather, asking who this is that wind and sea obey. As you watch him quiet a storm, free a tormented man, and raise a dead girl, how would you answer their question, and what would answering it honestly change for you?
assessment_questions: What are the four soils in the parable of the sower, and what does Jesus say to the storm?

In chapter 5 a desperate woman touches Jesus' cloak in a crowd and a synagogue ruler begs for his dying daughter. What do their two stories show about how Jesus treats faith that comes out of desperation?

The freed demoniac wants to leave with Jesus, and Jesus sends him home to tell what the Lord has done for him. What has God done in your life that someone at home has never heard, and what keeps the story untold?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The same seed lands on four soils, so receptivity determines whether the word bears fruit in a life.
The seed parables show God's reign advancing quietly and surely, even while the farmer sleeps.
A calmed storm and an expelled legion reveal an authority over creation and dark powers that Scripture reserves for God.
The bleeding woman and Jairus's daughter show Jesus honoring faith that simply reaches for him when everything else has failed.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the parable of the sower in your own words, and describe how chapters 4 and 5 answer the disciples' question about who Jesus is.

comprehension_check.question: In Mark 4:35-41 Jesus stills the storm with a word, yet the disciples end more afraid than before. What has frightened them?
options: They realize the storm was a punishment for their doubt
They fear Jesus will rebuke them as he rebuked the sea
They are ashamed their panic woke a sleeping teacher
They glimpse in their boat an authority Scripture gives God
comprehension_check.why: Mark 4:41 ties their great fear to the question of his identity, for only God commands the sea.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 4:39-41 again. Notice when the great fear arrives, before the calm or after it.

comprehension_check.question: In the parable of the sower in Mark 4, one sower and one seed meet four kinds of ground. What decides the harvest?
options: The kind of hearing the word meets in each person
The sower's care in choosing where his seed will land
The chance hazards of birds, sun, and crowding thorns
The amount of seed each patch of ground receives
comprehension_check.why: In Mark 4:20 the good ground is defined by how the word is heard and welcomed.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 4:14-20 again. Notice what stays the same in every scene, and what changes.

connections.reason: Psalm 107's sailors — 'he made the storm be still' — is the background that makes calming the sea a divine act.

nodes.title: Bread, Blindness, and the Turning Point
nodes.summary: Two feeding miracles bracket the disciples' incomprehension — 'do you not yet understand?' — with clean-and-unclean overturned ('thus he declared all foods clean') and a Syrophoenician mother out-arguing everyone in the book. A blind man healed in two stages becomes the parable of Peter, who sees ('You are the Christ') but only half.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus feeds thousands twice, and the disciples still worry about bread in the boat while a Gentile mother trusts him for crumbs. What do these chapters show about how spiritual sight comes gradually, and where might you be seeing Jesus only half clearly right now?
assessment_questions: How many people are fed in each of the two feeding miracles, and what does Peter say when Jesus asks who he is?
Jesus teaches that what defiles a person comes from within, and Mark adds that he declared all foods clean. What is Jesus relocating when he moves purity from the hands to the heart?

The blind man at Bethsaida first sees people like trees walking, and Jesus touches him a second time. What would asking Jesus for a second touch look like in the area where your understanding of him is still blurry?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Two feeding miracles show Jesus meeting real physical need with abundance, echoing God feeding Israel in the wilderness.
Jesus locates defilement in the heart's evils rather than in unwashed hands, so real holiness begins inside a person.
The Syrophoenician mother's faith wins her request, previewing a mission that reaches beyond Israel to the nations.
The two-stage healing mirrors Peter, who names Jesus as the Christ while still misunderstanding what kind of Christ he is.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the two-stage healing at Bethsaida, and explain how it pictures Peter's confession at the end of chapter 8.

comprehension_check.question: Mark places a two-stage healing of a blind man right before Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi. What is the placement doing?
options: It shows some ailments resist even Jesus at first
It teaches that healing arrives through repeated persistent prayer
It mirrors Peter, who sees Jesus truly but only in part
It shows Jesus carefully adapting his methods to each person's need
comprehension_check.why: Right after the healing Peter names Jesus the Christ in Mark 8:29, then fights the cross in Mark 8:32, sight still coming in stages.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 8:22-25 and then Mark 8:27-33 again. Notice what happens in stages in both scenes.

comprehension_check.question: Mark adds a note that Jesus' teaching in Mark 7 made all foods clean. Within Mark 6-8, what does that opening make way for?
options: Freedom from the law as a whole for everyone who follows
The mercy that reaches a Gentile mother in the next scene
A verdict that Israel was wrong to have kept such rules
Proof that ritual never mattered to God at all
comprehension_check.why: Straight after the saying Jesus goes to Tyre, and in Mark 7:29 a Gentile mother's plea is granted.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 7:19 and then Mark 7:24-30 again. Notice who Jesus meets right after the food saying, and how that meeting ends.

connections.reason: Jesus 'declared all foods clean' — a direct ruling on these chapters.

nodes.title: The Way of the Cross
nodes.summary: Transfiguration glory, then straight downhill toward Jerusalem as the passion predictions continue (the first came at 8:31; the second and third fall here) — and the disciples answer by arguing about greatness. The section's thesis is the Gospel's most famous sentence: 'The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.' Blind Bartimaeus — who actually sees — follows him on the way.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus keeps predicting his death, and the disciples keep responding with arguments about greatness. Why do you think glory feels easier to want than service, and where would serving instead of ranking change how you treat the people nearest you?
assessment_questions: Who appears with Jesus at the Transfiguration, and what does blind Bartimaeus do after receiving his sight?
Jesus says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. What does calling his death a ransom suggest about what it accomplishes for others?
James and John ask for the best seats, and Jesus points them to the servant's place. What position are you currently angling for, and what would deliberately taking the lower place look like there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Transfiguration confirms Jesus' unique Sonship, and the Father's voice steadies the disciples for the suffering ahead.
The repeated passion predictions redefine Messiah around the cross, against every expectation of earthly triumph.
In the kingdom rank is measured by serving and by welcoming the lowly, with a child as Jesus' object lesson.
Mark 10:45 compresses the meaning of the cross into one line, and Christians have spent centuries drawing out how the ransom works.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain Mark 10:45 in your own words, and describe how the disciples' arguments about greatness set up Jesus' teaching on service.

comprehension_check.question: Three times Jesus predicts his death, and each time the disciples respond with questions of rank. What does Mark build with the repetition?
options: The clash between his announced cross and their contest for rank
A proof that the Twelve were never sincere in following him
A lesson that the disciples needed clearer teaching to understand
A picture of a fate overtaking Jesus against his plans
comprehension_check.why: Mark 9:31-34 sets the pattern: he announces the cross, they argue over greatness, and he answers with service.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 8:31-33, Mark 9:31-34, and Mark 10:33-37 again. Notice what follows each prediction.

comprehension_check.question: Mark 10:45 sums up the Son of Man's mission in serving and a ransom. Within its scene, what work is the saying doing?
options: It explains the exact transaction by which the ransom works
It promises the Twelve the thrones they had been requesting
It sets a standard of service meant only for leaders
It roots the call to serve in Jesus' own mission
comprehension_check.why: Mark 10:43-45 turns from command to reason, greatness measured by service because the Son of Man himself came to serve.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 10:35-45 again. Notice what request starts the scene, and how the saying answers it.

connections.reason: 'A ransom for many' compresses the Suffering Servant's work into one line.

nodes.title: Jerusalem: The Fig Tree and the Temple
nodes.summary: The entry, the temple cleared — sandwiched inside a withered fig tree, Mark's trademark framing — then the vineyard parable, Caesar's coin, the widow's two copper coins, and the discourse on the temple's coming destruction: 'not one stone will be left on another.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Mark wraps the temple's clearing inside a fig tree that is all leaves and no fruit. What is that framing saying about worship that looks alive, and if the same fruit inspection came to your own practices of faith, what would it find?
assessment_questions: What does Jesus do in the temple courts, and whose offering does he single out for praise in chapter 12?
The fig tree withers on either side of the temple's clearing. Why does Mark frame the two stories together, and what does the pairing say about what God seeks in his house?

The widow gives two small coins, everything she has, while the wealthy give from their surplus. What would giving that actually costs you something look like in your money, your time, or your attention?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The entry fulfills Zechariah's picture of a king on a colt, announcing a kingship that reorders power instead of seizing it.
The fig tree and the temple clearing together warn that leaves without fruit invite God's verdict on corrupted worship.

teaching_concepts.concept: True giving is measured by cost
teaching_concepts.explanation: The widow's two coins outweigh the large gifts because she gives out of poverty and whole trust in God.
The discourse commands endurance and alertness through suffering, and teachers still discuss how its predictions divide between Jerusalem's fall and the end.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain Mark's fig-tree framing of the temple clearing, and describe what the Olivet Discourse tells disciples to do while they wait.

comprehension_check.question: Mark splits the fig tree story in two and sets the temple action inside it. What does the frame ask readers to see?
options: Jesus' hunger explains the anger he carries into the courts
The temple, leafy but fruitless, stands under the same verdict
The lesson is patience, since figs come only in their season
The cursing displays Jesus' power to punish whatever disappoints him
comprehension_check.why: Mark 11:20-21 shows the tree withered on the walk back from the temple, each half of the frame reading the other.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 11:12-21 as one piece. Notice what Jesus looks for at the tree in Mark 11:13, and what he looks for in the courts.

comprehension_check.question: The disciples ask when the temple will fall. What response does the discourse of Mark 13 actually ask of them?
options: Track the signs closely until the date becomes plain
Abandon ordinary work, since so little time remains
Stay awake and endure, since the hour stays unknown
Meet the upheavals with alarm, as signs of the end
comprehension_check.why: Mark 13:32-37 lands the discourse on one command, to keep watch, since the day and hour stay God's secret.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 13:5-7 and Mark 13:32-37 again. Notice which command keeps repeating, and what Jesus says about the timing.

nodes.title: The Passion According to Mark
nodes.summary: Anointed for burial by an unnamed woman, betrayed, abandoned by every disciple — Mark's passion is the starkest: darkness at noon, one loud cry, and the temple curtain torn top to bottom, while the first human in the book to call Jesus 'Son of God' is the Roman centurion watching him die. The oldest manuscripts end at the empty tomb with the women afraid.
nodes.tradition_notes: Mark 16:9-20 (the 'longer ending') is absent from the earliest manuscripts; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles retain it as canonical Scripture, and most Protestant translations print it with a bracket note. The difference is text-critical rather than doctrinal — no tradition builds unique teaching on it, though its snake-handling verse has produced fringe exceptions.
nodes.discussion_prompt: In Mark's telling every disciple fails, and the first person at the cross to call Jesus the Son of God is the Roman soldier who watched him die. What does this passion account say about who recognizes Jesus and how, and what does the tomb's message for Peter offer to anyone who has failed him?
assessment_questions: What happens to the temple curtain when Jesus dies, and what does the young man at the tomb tell the women?
The centurion who oversaw the crucifixion declares Jesus the Son of God at the moment of his death. Why does Mark give that confession to a Roman executioner rather than to a disciple?
The message at the tomb names Peter specifically, the disciple who denied Jesus three times. Where do you need to hear that failure did not get the last word, and who could you carry that word to?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Mark's whole Gospel drives toward Jesus freely giving his life, taking sin, suffering, and death into God's saving purpose.
Gethsemane shows Jesus genuinely dreading the cup and still choosing the Father's will, fully human in weakness and fully faithful in love.
The temple veil splitting from top to bottom signals a new access to God accomplished at the cross.
The disciples flee and Peter denies, yet the risen Lord sends word ahead to meet them in Galilee, so human failure never cancels God's purpose.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Mark's passion account from Gethsemane to the empty tomb, and explain what the torn curtain and the centurion's confession each declare.

comprehension_check.question: Mark waits until the moment of death to let a human call Jesus the Son of God, and the speaker is a Roman centurion. What is Mark saying by the timing?
options: Rome's power was already turning toward the new faith
Israel has been replaced by Gentiles as the seeing people
A dying man's courage can win respect from anyone
Who Jesus is comes fully into view at the cross
comprehension_check.why: Mark 15:39 ties the confession to watching Jesus die, with the curtain tearing in Mark 15:38 at the same moment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 15:37-39 again. Notice what the centurion is looking at when he finally speaks.

comprehension_check.question: In Gethsemane Jesus begs for the cup to pass, then goes to the cross anyway. What does Mark 14:32-42 show about his obedience?
options: He genuinely dreads the cup yet chooses the Father's will
His fear faded away once an answer came from heaven
He models how prayer removes the burden it names
His resolve shows the suffering never truly touched him
comprehension_check.why: Mark 14:36 holds the honest plea and the surrender inside a single prayer.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Mark 14:33-36 again. Notice how the prayer begins, and how it ends.

connections.reason: Matthew's fuller passion-and-resurrection account parallels Mark scene for scene and completes his abrupt ending.

nodes.title: The Songs of Christmas
nodes.summary: Two miraculous pregnancies, four songs — Mary's Magnificat, Zechariah's Benedictus, the angels' Gloria, Simeon's Nunc Dimittis — and a birth announced first to shepherds working the night shift. Luke's overture sounds every theme to come: the lowly lifted, the hungry filled, a light for the Gentiles.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Mary sings that God has brought down rulers and lifted the humble, and the first birth announcement goes to shepherds on the night shift. What do these chapters show about the kind of people God chooses to notice, and who would you expect God to overlook today?
assessment_questions: Who receives the angelic announcement of Jesus' birth, and what sign are they told to look for?
Mary's song praises God for filling the hungry and sending the rich away empty. Why does Luke open the story of Jesus with a song about reversal?

Simeon waited his whole life to see God's promise and finally held it as a baby in his arms. What promise of God would take patience like Simeon's for you to keep trusting, and what would that patience look like this year?

teaching_concepts.concept: The incarnation begins in real history
teaching_concepts.explanation: God enters the human condition in an actual birth, with a census, a manger, and a real family.
The songs of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon all praise God for keeping promises made to Israel centuries earlier.
The good news comes first to shepherds and to a young woman from a small town, showing that God's kingdom reverses worldly rankings.
Simeon names the child a light for the Gentiles, so from the first pages this salvation reaches past Israel to every nation.

nodes.completion_criteria: Name the four songs of Luke 1-2 and explain what the Magnificat says about how God treats the lowly and the proud.

comprehension_check.question: The songs of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon look backward as much as forward. What do the four songs of Luke 1-2 together claim about this birth?
options: God is rewarding two families for their faithful obedience
God is starting over, setting Israel's old story aside
God is keeping promises he made to Israel long ago
God is raising Israel to rule over the other nations
comprehension_check.why: Mary and Zechariah both end on Abraham and the covenant, and Simeon holds the long-promised consolation in his arms (Luke 1:54-55).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 1:54-55 and Luke 1:72-73 again. Notice whose names and promises close both songs.

comprehension_check.question: The first birth announcement goes to shepherds on a night shift rather than to Jerusalem's leading men. In Luke's telling, what does that choice signal?
options: It previews a kingdom that lifts up the lowly first
It honors the shepherds for humility the city lacked
It hides the child from rulers who would harm him
It shows the leaders had already refused God's messenger
comprehension_check.why: The sign matches the song: a baby laid in a manger fits the God who exalts the humble (Luke 1:52, Luke 2:12).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 1:52-53 and then Luke 2:8-12 again. Notice how the song's pattern plays out in who hears the news first.

connections.reason: Mary's Magnificat is modeled on Hannah's song; Luke writes Jesus' infancy against Samuel's.
Gabriel's words to Mary — 'the throne of his father David… his kingdom will never end' — quote this covenant.
Gabriel describes John 'in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to children' — quoting Malachi 4.

nodes.title: Baptism, Genealogy to Adam, and Nazareth
nodes.summary: Luke traces Jesus' line past Abraham all the way to 'Adam, the son of God' — this Messiah is for the human race. After baptism and wilderness testing, Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in his hometown synagogue — 'good news to the poor… today this scripture is fulfilled' — and the congregation tries to throw him off a cliff for mentioning God's history of blessing outsiders.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus announces good news to the poor and freedom for the oppressed, and his hometown cheers until he reminds them that God has a history of blessing outsiders. Why do you think the same message turned the crowd from admiration to fury, and where might it test you the same way?
assessment_questions: What happens at Jesus' baptism, and what does the voice from heaven say?
Luke traces Jesus' genealogy all the way back to Adam instead of stopping at Abraham. What is Luke saying about who this Messiah is for?
In the wilderness Jesus answers every temptation with Scripture. What would it take for God's word to be that ready in your own moments of testing?

teaching_concepts.explanation: At his baptism Jesus identifies with sinners, receives the Spirit, and hears the Father publicly claim him as Son.

teaching_concepts.concept: Son of Adam, Savior of all
teaching_concepts.explanation: By running the family line back to Adam, Luke presents Jesus as the Messiah for the whole human race.
Jesus resists the wilderness temptations with Scripture, refusing every shortcut to power that bypasses the Father's will.
Reading Isaiah 61, Jesus defines his mission as good news for the poor and freedom for the oppressed, and he declares it fulfilled that very day.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Jesus claims when he reads Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and why the congregation turns on him.

comprehension_check.question: Luke traces Jesus' family line back beyond Abraham, ending at Adam. What does that extra reach claim?
options: It secures the royal descent his throne required
It displays the thoroughness of Luke's historical research
