It roots the Messiah in Israel's deepest ancestry
It claims the Messiah for the human race
comprehension_check.why: The line ends at Adam, named the son of God, so this Messiah's reach is as wide as humanity (Luke 3:38).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 3:38 again. Notice where the list finally stops, and how its last name is described.

comprehension_check.question: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and tells the room it is coming true as they listen. What is he claiming?
options: The congregation must now enact the program Isaiah announced
The mission Isaiah promised has arrived in his own person
The synagogue's faithfulness has finally earned the promised visit
An end to poverty across the land has now begun
comprehension_check.why: He announces the scripture fulfilled in their hearing, locating Isaiah's anointed mission in himself (Luke 4:18, Luke 4:21).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 4:18-21 again. Notice who the Spirit-anointed speaker of Isaiah's lines turns out to be.

connections.reason: Jesus announces his ministry as 'the year of the Lord's favor' — Jubilee language from Leviticus 25 via Isaiah 61.
Jesus cites Naaman and the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth — God's pattern of blessing outsiders — and nearly gets thrown off a cliff for it.
Jesus reads Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and announces, 'Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.'

nodes.title: Galilee: Sinners Called, Storms Stilled
nodes.summary: Peter's boat-sinking catch ('depart from me, for I am a sinful man'), Levi's party, the sermon on the plain, a centurion's faith, a sinful woman forgiven at a Pharisee's table, and a widow's son raised. Luke's Jesus eats with everyone the righteous avoid — until the confession, the Transfiguration, and the hinge: 'he set his face to go to Jerusalem.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus keeps ending up at dinner tables with people the religious avoid, and the grumbling follows him from party to party. What do these meals say about what mercy actually looks like in practice, and whose table would it stretch you to share?
assessment_questions: Who does Jesus call from a tax booth, and what does the man do to celebrate?
When the sinful woman weeps at Jesus' feet, Jesus says her great love flows from great forgiveness. What does that scene teach about the connection between being forgiven and being able to love?
Jesus says anyone who wants to follow him must take up a cross daily. What is one comfort or ambition following him would actually cost you this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus calls Levi and forgives the sinful woman before either has anything to show, because his call creates the change it asks for.
The sermon on the plain blesses the poor and hungry and warns the rich, reversing every assumption about who is doing well.
A Roman centurion trusts Jesus' bare word and is praised above anyone in Israel, showing that faith counts for more than pedigree.
The Transfiguration reveals Jesus' glory just as he sets his face toward Jerusalem, so the shining and the cross belong to one mission.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell one table scene from these chapters and explain why eating with sinners was central to Jesus' mission.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus keeps sharing tables with tax collectors and sinners while the religious grumble. What do the meals themselves declare about his mission?
options: Acceptance is offered with nothing asked of anyone afterward
Mercy goes first to the sick to make them well
The meals reward repentance already completed in private
He turned to the sinners after the righteous refused him
comprehension_check.why: Jesus answers the grumbling by casting himself as a doctor whose place is with the sick he came to call (Luke 5:31-32).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 5:29-32 again. Notice the picture Jesus uses to explain why he sits at that table.

comprehension_check.question: At the Transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with the glorified Jesus about what he will accomplish at Jerusalem. What is Luke binding together?
options: The shining shows his death was never truly required
The shining marks the throne he will claim by force
The shining rewards the faithfulness of the Galilean years
The shining and the cross belong to a single mission
comprehension_check.why: Even in glory the subject is his departure at Jerusalem, and days later he sets his face toward it (Luke 9:31, Luke 9:51).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 9:28-31 and Luke 9:51 again. Notice what the glorified figures discuss, and where Jesus heads next.

nodes.title: On the Way: Samaritans, Prayer, and Banquets
nodes.summary: The travel narrative's first movement: seventy-two sent out, the Good Samaritan, Mary and Martha, the Lord's Prayer and the friend at midnight, the rich fool's barns, the narrow door, and a banquet where the invited make excuses and the poor and lame fill the hall. 'Count the cost' of following.
nodes.discussion_prompt: In these chapters God's invitation is wide open and the demands of following are steep. The banquet hall fills with the poor while the invited make excuses about fields and oxen. What separates the people who come from the people who excuse themselves, and which excuse sounds most like yours?
assessment_questions: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, who stops to help the wounded man, and who passes by?
The rich fool builds bigger barns and dies that night. What is Jesus warning about when he says life does not consist in an abundance of possessions?
Jesus tells would-be followers to count the cost like a builder planning a tower. What would an honest cost estimate of following Jesus include for you right now?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Good Samaritan makes mercy the measure of the Law and sends it across every ethnic and social boundary.
Mary sitting at Jesus' feet shows that attention to Christ comes before busy service, even good service.
The Lord's Prayer and the friend at midnight teach prayer as a child's persistent asking from a Father who loves to give.
The banquet is thrown wide to the poor and lame, yet Jesus insists that those who come must count the cost of discipleship.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the parable of the Good Samaritan and explain how these chapters hold together a wide-open invitation and a costly call to follow.

comprehension_check.question: Luke 14 throws a banquet open to the poor and, on the same journey, demands that followers count the cost. How do those fit together?
options: The feast is free to enter and claims everyone who comes
The cost is an entry fee the guests must pay first
The poor earned through hardship the places the rich forfeited
The demands fall on the twelve, the welcome on the crowd
comprehension_check.why: The hall fills with people who cannot repay, and the cost speech goes to the large crowds traveling with him (Luke 14:21, Luke 14:25-27).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 14:21-24 and Luke 14:25-28 again. Notice who fills the hall, and who is addressed by the sayings that follow.

comprehension_check.question: Right after teaching the Lord's Prayer, Jesus tells of a man pounding on a friend's door at midnight. What is the story teaching about prayer?
options: Keep on asking until God's reluctance finally gives way
Pray with exactly the right words to secure the answer
Ask boldly, for the Father gives more freely than friends
Prayers prevail by the proven merit of the one praying
comprehension_check.why: The argument runs from lesser to greater: if even a grudging neighbor gets up, how much more will the Father give (Luke 11:13).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 11:11-13 again. Notice what kind of father the story finally sets beside the sleepy friend.

nodes.title: The Lost and Found Chapters
nodes.summary: Luke's crown jewels: the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son with his fattened calf and furious older brother; then the shrewd manager, the rich man and Lazarus, the Pharisee and the tax collector, and little Zacchaeus up a tree — 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.' The journey ends riding into Jerusalem in tears.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The father in Luke 15 runs to one son and goes out to plead with the other. Which brother do you find easier to understand, the one who wasted everything or the one who resents the party, and what does the father's response to each one show about God?
assessment_questions: What three things are lost and found in Luke 15, and what happens each time the lost one is found?

The Pharisee thanks God for his own righteousness while the tax collector begs for mercy, and Jesus says the tax collector goes home justified. What does this parable teach about how a person becomes right with God?
Zacchaeus responds to Jesus by giving half his possessions to the poor and repaying fourfold what he stole. What would grace changing your relationship to money actually look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The shepherd, the woman, and the father all go after what is lost, and heaven celebrates every single recovery.
The prodigal is embraced before he can finish his rehearsed speech, and Zacchaeus shows that welcomed people start living differently.
The rich man steps past Lazarus every day without seeing him, a warning that comfort can blind a person to both neighbors and judgment.
The tax collector's plea for mercy makes him right with God, while the Pharisee's list of achievements earns nothing.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the parable of the prodigal son, including the older brother, and explain what Luke 19:10 says the Son of Man came to do.

comprehension_check.question: The parable of the prodigal son does not end with the feast. Why does Luke 15 close on the older brother standing outside?
options: It shows the years of obedience counted for nothing
It proves the father's heart belonged to the younger son
It concedes the father's welcome was unfair to the obedient
It turns the story toward the grumblers listening to it
comprehension_check.why: The chapter opens with the righteous grumbling over who Jesus welcomes, and the father goes out to plead with just such a son (Luke 15:1-2, Luke 15:28).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 15:1-2 and Luke 15:28-32 again. Notice whose complaint the older son is echoing.

comprehension_check.question: In Luke 18 the tax collector goes home justified and the Pharisee does not. What made the difference?
options: One pleaded for mercy, the other presented his record
One prayed sincerely, the other lied about his disciplines
One promised restitution, the other offered only his fasting
One prayed hidden and humble, the other for an audience
comprehension_check.why: Jesus gives the verdict to the man who would not look up but begged God for mercy as a sinner (Luke 18:13-14).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 18:11-13 again. Notice what each man's prayer is actually about, and who gets mentioned in it.

nodes.title: Questions in the Temple
nodes.summary: Teaching daily in the temple courts, Jesus fields the authorities' traps — his authority, Caesar's coin, the resurrection and seven brothers — and watches a poor widow out-give the wealthy. Then the temple's fate: 'not one stone,' Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and the call to 'straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus spends these chapters answering trick questions from powerful men, then points to a widow dropping two small coins as the moment worth noticing. What do you think Jesus sees in her gift that the wealthy givers missed, and what would giving that God notices look like from you?
assessment_questions: What question do the authorities ask about paying taxes to Caesar, and how does Jesus answer it?
When the Sadducees pose their riddle about seven brothers, Jesus answers that God is the God of the living. What does his answer reveal about the resurrection?
Jesus tells his disciples to stand up and raise their heads when frightening things happen, because redemption is drawing near. How would that posture change the way you face bad news?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Every trap set in the temple courts turns back on the questioners, because Jesus speaks with an authority they can neither match nor dismiss.
Giving Caesar his coin while giving God what bears God's image sets a limit on every earthly power's claim.
Jesus grounds resurrection hope in God's own character, since the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob keeps his people alive to him.
The temple's coming fall and the world's shaking call for prayerful alertness and lifted heads instead of panic.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Jesus handles the question about Caesar's coin and what the widow's offering teaches about how God measures a gift.

comprehension_check.question: Handed a trap question about the tribute tax, Jesus asks whose image the coin bears, then divides what belongs to Caesar from what belongs to God. What does his answer do?
options: It hands the state whatever it decides to demand
It pays the tax and limits Caesar's larger claims
It sidesteps a trap without teaching anything at all
It backs the protesters who refused the Roman tax
comprehension_check.why: The coin stamped with Caesar's image can go back to him, while what carries God's image belongs to God (Luke 20:24-25).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 20:23-26 again. Notice what Jesus asks to see, and what his question about its image implies.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus says the widow's two small coins amount to more than all the large gifts. What measure is he using?
options: It was multiplied by God beyond its face value
Her poverty made her offering more deserving of honor
It cost her everything she had to live on
She gave in secret while the rich gave for display
comprehension_check.why: Jesus points at the source of each gift, surplus for the rich and her whole living for her (Luke 21:4).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 21:1-4 again. Notice what Jesus says each gift came out of.

nodes.title: The Passion and Emmaus
nodes.summary: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood'; a sweat like drops of blood; 'Father, forgive them'; paradise promised to a dying thief. Then Luke's masterpiece ending: two heartbroken disciples on the Emmaus road, joined by a stranger who 'beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself' — and is known in the breaking of the bread.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The two on the Emmaus road knew every fact about the crucifixion and still walked away hopeless, until the stranger opened the Scriptures and broke the bread. What made the difference between knowing the story and recognizing him, and where do you go to have your own eyes opened?
assessment_questions: What does Jesus say about the bread and the cup at the Last Supper?
On the cross Jesus prays for the forgiveness of the men killing him and promises paradise to a dying thief. What do those two sayings show about what his death accomplishes?
On the Emmaus road Jesus explains that Moses and all the Prophets point to him. How would reading the Old Testament that way change the way you read the Bible this month?

teaching_concepts.explanation: At the table Jesus takes up Jeremiah's promised new covenant and locates it in his own body and blood given for his people.
In Gethsemane Jesus asks for the cup to pass and still surrenders to the Father's will, modeling honest prayer under dread.
Jesus dies praying for his executioners and welcoming a thief, so the cross itself becomes the place where forgiveness is spoken.

teaching_concepts.concept: The risen Lord opens the Scriptures
teaching_concepts.explanation: At Emmaus the whole Old Testament becomes a book about Christ, and the disciples recognize him in the breaking of the bread.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the Emmaus road story and explain why Jesus calls the cup the new covenant in his blood.

comprehension_check.question: On the Emmaus road the stranger chides the two disciples, then works through Moses and all the Prophets. What is he correcting?
options: Their neglect of the report the women brought back
Their knowledge of the week's events, which was incomplete
Their belief that the cross meant the hope had failed
Their grief, which had crowded out any room for hope
comprehension_check.why: He argues from all the Scriptures that the suffering was necessary on the way to the Messiah's glory (Luke 24:26-27).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 24:19-27 again. Notice what the two say they had been hoping, and what the stranger says was necessary.

comprehension_check.question: Luke's crucifixion scene shows Jesus praying for his executioners and promising paradise to a thief. What is Luke showing about the cross?
options: The cross is an injustice that only the resurrection will answer
The cross displays a calm his followers are to imitate
The cross ends his mission until God restores him
The cross itself is where he forgives and seeks the lost
comprehension_check.why: Dying, Jesus prays pardon for his killers and promises a criminal a place with him that very day (Luke 23:34, Luke 23:43).
comprehension_check.hint: Read Luke 23:34 and Luke 23:39-43 again. Notice what Jesus is doing for other people in his own dying hours.

connections.reason: Luke's second volume opens exactly where this ends — same author, same Jerusalem, the ascension told twice.
'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' — Jesus names his death in this chapter's terms.
Paul's account of the Supper's institution — the earliest written — matches Luke's wording.

nodes.title: The Word Became Flesh
nodes.summary: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' John's prologue rewrites Genesis 1 around Jesus, then the Baptist points — 'Behold, the Lamb of God' — and the first disciples start following. The Bible's deepest chapter is also one of its most readable.
nodes.discussion_prompt: John could have opened with Jesus' birth. Why do you think he starts 'in the beginning' instead?
assessment_questions: What does John say the Word was doing “in the beginning”?
John keeps insisting the Baptist “was not the Light.” What conclusion is he trying to prevent?
The chapter says those who received him became children of God. What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and receiving him?

teaching_concepts.explanation: John 1:1 places Jesus with God and as God before anything was made, the foundation of everything Christians believe about him.
All things were made through the Word, and he is the light that shines on every person who comes into the world.
God's glory, grace, and truth become visible in a real human life, so knowing Jesus is knowing God.
John the Baptist shows what faithful witness looks like by directing everyone to the Lamb of God instead of to himself.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words what John means by calling Jesus the Word, and why the prologue opens with an echo of Genesis 1.

comprehension_check.question: John 1 opens, “In the beginning was the Word.” What is the chapter’s central claim about the Word?
options: The Word is the greatest and first of all God’s creatures
The Word stands for the message God speaks through Scripture
The Word is the Baptist’s title for the prophet still to come
The Word is eternal God, maker of all, who became flesh
comprehension_check.why: The text says the Word was God, was with God in the beginning, made all things, and became flesh; “first creature” and “symbol” are the classic misreadings it closes off.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 1:1-3 and 1:14. Notice what the Word already was "in the beginning," before anything was made.

comprehension_check.question: Why does the chapter repeat that John the Baptist “was not the Light”?
options: To keep people from taking John himself for the Messiah
To reveal that John had begun to doubt his own calling
To expose a hidden failure in the Baptist’s character
To note that John was simply born before Jesus was
comprehension_check.why: John’s role is to witness to the Light, not to be it; the repetition guards against fixing on the messenger.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 1:6-8. Notice the difference John draws between himself and the Light he came to point to.

connections.reason: Wisdom with God at creation (Prov 8) is part of the Word's Old Testament pedigree.
'Full of grace and truth… no one has ever seen God' replays Moses' cleft-rock vision of the LORD's glory.
John deliberately reopens with 'In the beginning' — the Word present at creation is the same figure entering it.
'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' presents Jesus as the true temple — glory in a human body.
The Christ-hymn's creation-through-him theology parallels John's prologue — the New Testament's two summits of cosmic Christology.
Wisdom coming forth from God to 'tabernacle' in Israel (24:8) prefigures the Word made flesh who dwelt among us.

nodes.title: Water to Wine, New Birth, Living Water
nodes.summary: Wine at Cana, the temple cleared with a whip and a riddle ('destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up'), Nicodemus told he must be born again — with John 3:16 as the summary — and a five-times-married Samaritan woman becoming an evangelist to her whole town. Every scene replaces an old institution with Jesus himself.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Nicodemus the respected insider comes at night and leaves confused; the Samaritan woman, an outsider drawing water at noon, leaves as an evangelist. Comparing the two conversations, what does Jesus seem to be looking for in a person, and which of the two do you resemble more right now?
assessment_questions: What is Jesus' first sign at Cana, and who knows where the good wine actually came from?
Jesus tells Nicodemus that entering God's kingdom requires being born again by the Spirit. Why is birth, something no one accomplishes for themselves, the picture Jesus chooses?

Jesus offers the Samaritan woman living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life. What are you currently drinking from that keeps leaving you thirsty, and what would it mean to ask him for that water?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The miracle at Cana reveals Jesus' glory and invites trust in him as the giver of abundant life.
Clearing the temple, Jesus points to his own body as the real meeting place between God and people.
Entry into God's kingdom comes by the Spirit's re-creating work, and no amount of moral effort or religious status can substitute for it.
Jesus crosses barriers of ethnicity, gender, and reputation to offer a satisfaction that wells up from within, and the woman who receives it becomes a witness to her whole town.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the conversations with Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman, and explain what Jesus means by new birth and living water.

comprehension_check.question: Purification jars at Cana, the temple courts, Jacob's well. What is John doing as Jesus moves through these settings in chapters 2-4?
options: Presenting Jesus as what each institution was pointing toward
Showing Jesus abolish religion in favor of private spirituality
Proving Israel's worship had always been empty of God
Collecting early miracles in the order eyewitnesses recalled them
comprehension_check.why: John 2:21 makes the move explicit, the true temple is Jesus' own body, and John 4:14 offers him as the water that finally satisfies.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 2:19-21 and John 4:13-14. Notice what the temple saying and the well conversation each turn out to be about.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus tells Nicodemus, Israel's own teacher, that he must be born again (John 3:3, 3:10). What does that demand say about entering God's kingdom?
options: Entry takes deeper theological training than Nicodemus yet had
Entry takes a lifetime of obedience outweighing one's failures
Entry takes the Spirit's new work, beyond any credential
Entry takes abandoning Israel's Scriptures for Jesus' new teaching
comprehension_check.why: John 3:6 divides what flesh produces from what the Spirit produces, so entry rests on a birth only the Spirit can give.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 3:3-8. Notice which birth Jesus keeps naming, and where he says it comes from.

connections.reason: 'Born of water and the Spirit' draws on Ezekiel 36's clean water and new heart.
The Samaritan woman's 'our fathers worshiped on this mountain' runs back to the north's breakaway history.
Jesus makes the bronze serpent the picture of his own lifting up: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness…' (John 3:14).

nodes.title: The Great Claims: Bread, Light, I AM
nodes.summary: A healed man on the sabbath ignites the charge that Jesus 'makes himself equal with God' — and Jesus raises the stakes: 'I am the bread of life,' 'I am the light of the world,' and finally 'before Abraham was, I AM,' at which they pick up stones. The feeding of the five thousand becomes a sermon on eating his flesh that costs him most of his crowd.
nodes.tradition_notes: John 6's 'eat my flesh and drink my blood' divides eucharistic theology: Catholic and Orthodox readings take it as directly eucharistic and realist; many Protestant traditions read it as a metaphor for faith in Christ's death, with sacramental Protestants (Lutheran, Anglican) in between. All agree the chapter is about receiving Christ himself; the dispute is the mode.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Across these chapters Jesus keeps saying that what people ultimately need is him: bread that is his flesh, light for their darkness, the name I AM. The crowd wanted more miracle bread and walked away from the harder gift. What is the difference between wanting things from Jesus and wanting Jesus himself, and which are you actually after?
assessment_questions: After the feeding of the five thousand, what does the crowd want to do with Jesus, and what happens to that crowd by the end of the bread of life teaching?
When Jesus says 'before Abraham was, I AM,' his hearers pick up stones. What is Jesus claiming with those words, and why does the crowd hear it as blasphemy?

Jesus says that whoever comes to him will never hunger and whoever believes in him will never thirst. Where do you keep going back for satisfaction that does not last, and what would coming to him for it look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus claims to work as his Father works, to give life, and to judge, and his hearers rightly recognize this as a claim to equality with God.
Jesus offers himself as the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna, and receiving him is the way to eternal life.
In the temple courts Jesus claims to be the light that frees people from walking in darkness, a saving presence that also exposes.
'Before Abraham was, I AM' takes up the name God spoke from the burning bush, so Jesus is asserting eternal existence and divine identity.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why the claim 'before Abraham was, I AM' provoked stones, and what Jesus offers when he calls himself the bread of life.

comprehension_check.question: Twice in these chapters the hearers move to kill Jesus on the spot (John 5:18, 8:59). What have they understood his words to be?
options: He is breaking sabbath customs held sacred for generations
He is positioning himself to lead an armed uprising
He is dishonoring Abraham and the prophets by name
He is claiming what belongs to God alone
comprehension_check.why: John 5:18 states the charge plainly, equality with God, and the name Jesus takes up in John 8:58 answers to the burning bush.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 5:17-18 and John 8:58-59. Notice what Jesus says about himself immediately before each reaction.

comprehension_check.question: After the feeding, the crowd tracks Jesus down for more bread, and he offers them himself (John 6:26, 6:35). What is the exchange exposing?
options: Their hunger for ordinary bread was itself the sin
They want gifts from Jesus while missing the giver himself
They needed to work harder to deserve the next meal
They lacked the faith to expect a second multiplication
comprehension_check.why: John 6:35 turns the crowd from the loaves to the giver, Jesus offering his own person as the bread that ends the deeper hunger.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 6:26-29 and John 6:35. Notice what Jesus says the crowd is really after, and what he offers in its place.

connections.reason: Jesus' 'before Abraham was, I AM' takes the divine name revealed at the bush and applies it to himself.
Jesus' 'I am the bread of life' discourse is a running commentary on the manna.

nodes.title: Blind Eyes, the Good Shepherd, and Lazarus
nodes.summary: A man born blind sees while the seeing go blind — the Gospel's wittiest chapter — then 'I am the good shepherd' who lays down his life, and the sign that seals the plot: Lazarus, four days dead, walking out of his tomb at a shout. 'I am the resurrection and the life.' Mary anoints Jesus' feet; the hour has come.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The man born blind sees more clearly with every interrogation, while the trained experts go blind by insisting they already see. What makes a person able to see the truth about Jesus, and what might you be refusing to look at?
assessment_questions: How long has Lazarus been dead when Jesus arrives, and what does Jesus do at the tomb?
Jesus says 'I am the resurrection and the life' before he raises Lazarus. Why does he claim to be resurrection in person instead of simply promising a future event?
Mary pours out a year's wages of perfume on Jesus' feet and is criticized for the waste. What would costly devotion, the kind that looks wasteful to observers, look like in your life?

teaching_concepts.concept: Signs that reveal, division that follows
teaching_concepts.explanation: The healings and the raising of Lazarus point to who Jesus is, yet many witnesses still refuse him, so the signs invite faith without forcing it.
The blind man's growing insight and the Pharisees' hardening show that truly seeing Jesus is a matter of the heart before it is a matter of evidence.
Jesus lays down his life for the sheep willingly, defining his kingship as sacrificial care.
'I am the resurrection and the life' locates the defeat of death in Jesus himself, and Lazarus walking out of the tomb is the preview.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of the man born blind and explain what Jesus claims about himself at Lazarus's tomb.

comprehension_check.question: By the end of John 9 the blind beggar sees and worships, while Pharisees with perfect eyes are called blind (John 9:39-41). What is blindness here?
options: An ignorance that better religious education would have cured
A punishment handed down for someone's particular sin
A refusal of the light by those claiming sight
The honest doubt that comes from asking hard questions
comprehension_check.why: John 9:41 ties the guilt to the claim of sight, the certainty that keeps the Pharisees from the light standing in front of them.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 9:39-41 next to John 9:2-3. Notice who ends up blind, and what those people were sure of.

comprehension_check.question: Martha already believes her brother will rise at the last day (John 11:24). What does Jesus' answer add to that belief (John 11:25-26)?
options: Resurrection is a person, standing in front of her
Her brother's rising will prove her family's devotion earned it
Believers are exempted from ever undergoing bodily death
The general resurrection will happen sooner than she thinks
comprehension_check.why: In John 11:25 Jesus relocates resurrection from a far-off event into his own present person, life wherever he is trusted.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 11:23-26. Notice the difference between what Martha affirms and how Jesus answers her.

connections.reason: The good shepherd discourse claims the LORD-as-shepherd role of Psalm 23.
John 12 quotes Isaiah's hardening commission and says Isaiah 'saw his glory' — identifying the throne vision with Christ.
'I am the good shepherd' takes up Ezekiel 34: God himself, shepherding in person, against the false shepherds.
John 10's 'Feast of Dedication' is Hanukkah — Jesus walks the temple this book's victory rededicated.

nodes.title: The Upper Room
nodes.summary: The Lord washes feet, gives 'a new commandment — love one another as I have loved you,' promises the Spirit of truth, and speaks the vine-and-branches image of abiding. Then the Bible's holy of holies: Jesus' own prayer for his disciples and 'for those who will believe through their word' — that they may be one.
nodes.discussion_prompt: On his last night Jesus takes the servant's towel, then tells his friends that the world will identify them by their love for one another. If people judged whether Jesus is real by how his followers treat each other, what would they conclude from the Christians you know, and what part of that answer is yours to change?
assessment_questions: What does Jesus do with the basin and towel before the meal, and what does he tell the disciples to do for one another afterward?
Jesus says he is the vine and his followers are branches that can do nothing apart from him. According to his own words in John 15, what does abiding in the vine actually involve?
Jesus prays that his followers would be one so that the world would believe. What is one concrete step you could take toward unity with a believer you find difficult?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus washes feet on the night of his betrayal, making humble service the signature of anyone who follows him.
Mutual love, modeled on Jesus' own love, is the mark by which the world is meant to recognize his disciples.
The Spirit of truth continues Jesus' presence with his people, teaching, reminding, convicting, and giving courage.
Fruitfulness flows from staying connected to Christ, since apart from him the branches can do nothing.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the vine and branches image in your own words and describe what Jesus prays for his future followers in John 17.

comprehension_check.question: John stresses that Jesus washes feet knowing all things are in his hands (John 13:3-5). What does the scene teach about his authority?
options: He suspends his authority briefly to act as a servant
He performs the cleansing Passover required of every guest
He stages a final test to identify his betrayer
His lordship expresses itself in stooping to serve
comprehension_check.why: John 13:3-4 puts the towel into the hands that hold everything, and John 13:14-15 makes that downward movement the disciples' own pattern.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 13:3-5 and John 13:12-17. Notice what John says Jesus knew just before he reached for the towel.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus calls his own departure an advantage for the disciples (John 16:7). How can his leaving be better for them than his staying?
options: His mission had stalled and needed a fresh start
Through the Spirit his presence will reach them everywhere
Absence would train the disciples to stand on their own
The danger surrounding him had grown too great to stay
comprehension_check.why: John 14:16-18 promises the Spirit as an abiding Advocate, so the departing Jesus refuses to leave his people orphaned.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 16:7 and then John 14:16-18. Notice what the going away makes possible, and what Jesus promises it will never mean.

connections.reason: The promised Helper arrives at Pentecost — Acts 2 is the discourse's fulfillment.

nodes.title: The Passion and Resurrection According to John
nodes.summary: 'I AM' knocks the arresting party flat; Pilate asks 'what is truth?' with truth standing in front of him; 'it is finished' sounds from the cross like a completed mission, not a defeat. Then Mary Magdalene mistakes the risen Lord for the gardener, Thomas gets his scars-and-all proof — 'my Lord and my God!' — and Peter is restored over breakfast: 'do you love me? Feed my sheep.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: In John's telling Jesus is never a victim swept along by events. He announces himself in the garden, speaks truth to Pilate, and declares the work finished from the cross. How does it change the meaning of the cross to know Jesus laid his life down on purpose, and what would you say his finished work actually finished?
assessment_questions: What happens to the arresting party when Jesus says 'I am he,' and what are his final words on the cross?
Thomas demands to touch the wounds and ends by confessing 'my Lord and my God.' What does John want readers to learn from doubt turning into the Gospel's fullest confession?
Jesus asks Peter three times 'do you love me,' once for each denial, and gives him work to do. What failure in your past could God be turning into an assignment?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Before Pilate, Jesus claims a kingship that does not come from this world's power, and his calm authority dominates his own trial.
Jesus' final word declares his saving mission complete, an announcement of accomplishment spoken from the cross itself.

teaching_concepts.concept: The risen Lord meets people personally
teaching_concepts.explanation: Mary hears her name, Thomas gets his proof, and each encounter turns grief or doubt into faith and witness.
Peter's three denials are answered with three questions of love and a commission, showing that the risen Jesus rebuilds the people he sends.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell two of John's resurrection encounters and explain what 'it is finished' declares about Jesus' death.

comprehension_check.question: At the arrest the soldiers fall flat (John 18:6), before Pilate the question of authority flips (John 19:11), and the final word announces completion (John 19:30). What is John claiming about the cross?
options: A miscarriage of justice that only Easter set right
A fate Jesus accepted once escape became impossible
Jesus completing his mission, willing from first to last
A victory Rome and the priests shared between them
comprehension_check.why: John 10:18 presents Jesus' death as freely laid down under his own authority, and John 19:30 sounds from the cross like finished work.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 18:4-6 and John 19:10-11. Notice who actually holds control in each scene.

comprehension_check.question: Immediately after Thomas sees and believes, John explains why the book exists (John 20:29-31). What does that ending give every reader who was not there?
options: Written signs sufficient for believing without having seen
An apology for all the stories left unrecorded
Thomas' demand for proof as the model to copy
A blessing reserved for the eyewitness generation alone
comprehension_check.why: John 20:31 gives the purpose, testimony recorded precisely so later readers can come to faith and to the life Jesus gives.
comprehension_check.hint: Read John 20:29-31. Notice whom Jesus calls blessed, and whom John says the writing is for.

connections.reason: John cites 'they will look on him whom they have pierced' at the spear-thrust.
Not a bone broken, dying as the Passover lambs were slain — John times the crucifixion to Passover deliberately.

nodes.title: The Ascension and the Waiting Room
nodes.summary: The risen Jesus teaches for forty days, promises power 'when the Holy Spirit has come upon you… to the end of the earth' — the verse that is Acts' table of contents — and ascends while the disciples stare at the sky. A hundred and twenty believers wait, pray, and replace Judas.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Jesus gives the disciples a worldwide mission and then tells them to wait for power from the Spirit. Why do you think the power had to come before the witness, and what would waiting on God before acting look like in a decision you are facing right now?
assessment_questions: What promise does Jesus give the disciples before he ascends, and what does he tell them to do in Jerusalem?
The one requirement for Judas' replacement is that he must be a witness of the resurrection. Why does the church's message depend on people who saw what they proclaim?
The hundred and twenty spend the waiting days devoted to prayer together. When you face a season where you can only wait, what would waiting the way they did look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Jesus ascends to reign at God's right hand, and the angels promise he will return the same way he left.
The disciples must wait for the Holy Spirit because the church's witness runs on God's power rather than human effort.
Judas' replacement must have seen the risen Jesus, since the church's authority rests on eyewitness testimony to the resurrection.
The community chooses a leader through Scripture and prayer together, setting an early pattern for how the church decides.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Jesus promises in Acts 1:8 and how that one verse maps out the rest of the book of Acts.

comprehension_check.question: Jesus gives the disciples a mission reaching the end of the earth, then tells them to sit still in Jerusalem. Why must the waiting come first?
options: Their grief over his departure must settle before they can speak
Their witness will run on the Spirit's power, which has not yet come
Their obedience in a small command must be proven before a great one
Their message needs a plan for reaching so many distant nations
comprehension_check.why: Acts 1:4-5 gives the reason for the wait, the promised baptism with the Holy Spirit, and Acts 1:8 ties the witness to that power.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 1:4-8 again. Notice what Jesus says they are waiting for, and what he says will arrive with it.

comprehension_check.question: The one requirement for Judas' replacement is a man who was present from John's baptism to the ascension. What does that requirement show about the apostles' task?
options: Long loyalty through hard years has earned the man his office
Leadership must pass through those the community trusts most deeply
Only a full student of Jesus' teaching can explain it rightly
Their task is to testify to events they actually saw
comprehension_check.why: Acts 1:22 states the purpose of the office, that the man become a witness with them of the resurrection.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 1:21-22 again. Notice the words that name what the chosen man must become.

connections.reason: Luke's second volume opens exactly where this ends — same author, same Jerusalem, the ascension told twice.

nodes.title: Pentecost
nodes.summary: Wind, fire, and a congregation of pilgrims each hearing the gospel in their own language; Peter stands up with Joel 2 and Psalms 16 and 110 and cuts three thousand to the heart. The church is born devoted to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The crowd hears Peter and asks one question: what shall we do? After the wind, the fire, and a sermon built from old Scriptures, why does this message demand a response rather than just agreement, and what would responding that concretely ask of you?
assessment_questions: What signs accompany the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, and how does the crowd of pilgrims first react?
Peter announces that God has made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ. How do his quotations from Joel and the Psalms support that claim?
The first believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer. Which of those four would most change your week if you gave yourself to it, and why?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The outpoured Spirit turns a waiting room of disciples into a public witnessing community in a single day.
Peter reads Pentecost through Joel 2 to show that God is keeping an old promise on schedule.
Peter's sermon rests on events, the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Jesus, with the Spirit confirming the witnesses.
Peter calls the crowd to repent and be baptized, the doorway into forgiveness and the Spirit-filled community.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell what happened at Pentecost and explain how Peter uses Joel 2 to interpret it.

comprehension_check.question: A crowd gathers around a strange event, and Peter answers with Joel and two psalms. What is his sermon doing with those scriptures?
options: Showing the morning is God keeping promises made long ago
Borrowing familiar holy words to quiet a confused crowd
Proving the disciples now stand where the prophets once stood
Arguing that David wrote the psalms about his own rescue
comprehension_check.why: Acts 2:16 says the morning's events are what Joel foretold, so Peter reads Pentecost as an old promise kept on schedule.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 2:14-21 again. Notice the claim Peter makes just before he begins quoting Joel.

comprehension_check.question: The crowd hears the whole sermon, and only at its final claim do they cry out, asking what to do. What has landed on them?
options: The wonder of hearing Galileans speak in their own tongues
The fear that Joel's last days mean the world's quick end
The verdict that the man they crucified now reigns as Lord
The shame of being lectured by uneducated men in public
comprehension_check.why: Acts 2:36-37 sets the sermon's last claim, the crucified Jesus made Lord and Christ, right before the crowd's question.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 2:36-37 again. Notice which sentence comes immediately before the crowd finally speaks.

connections.reason: Peter's clincher is Psalm 110: David did not ascend, but his Lord sits at God's right hand.
Pentecost's many languages heard as one gospel is widely read as Babel's scattering reversed.
The Spirit poured out at Pentecost enacts Ezekiel 36-37's promise of God's Spirit within his people.
Peter's Pentecost sermon opens by quoting Joel 2 at length: 'this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel.'
The promised Helper arrives at Pentecost — Acts 2 is the discourse's fulfillment.

nodes.title: The Church in Jerusalem: Boldness and Purity
nodes.summary: A lame man leaps at the temple gate, Peter and John face the same council that condemned Jesus — 'we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard' — believers share everything, Ananias and Sapphira lie to the Spirit and drop dead, and the apostles leave a flogging 'rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Peter and John are ordered to stop speaking about Jesus and answer that they cannot help it. What made these ordinary men so sure of what they had seen, and what would it take for your convictions to hold that steady under pressure?
assessment_questions: What happens to the lame man at the Beautiful Gate, and who does Peter say deserves the credit?
Ananias and Sapphira die after lying about a gift no one forced them to give. What does their story teach about why truthfulness matters so much inside the church?
Threatened by the council, the believers pray for boldness instead of safety. When you face pressure for your faith, what do you usually pray for, and what would praying their prayer change?

teaching_concepts.concept: The healing points to the resurrection
teaching_concepts.explanation: Peter directs the amazed crowd from the healed man to the risen Jesus, so the miracle serves the message.
Unschooled men speak fearlessly before the council that condemned Jesus, because the Spirit supplies courage at the moment it is needed.
The believers' shared possessions make the gospel visible, showing a community being changed from the inside out.
The judgment on Ananias and Sapphira teaches that God takes truthfulness in his community with utter seriousness.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the healing at the temple gate and explain why Peter and John refuse the council's order to stay silent.

comprehension_check.question: Peter tells Ananias the land was his to keep and the money his to give. What, then, made the act deadly?
options: Staging a lie before the Spirit to look fully devoted
Holding back money that belonged to the common purse
Failing to match the full gift Barnabas had just given
comprehension_check.why: Acts 5:3-4 locates the offense in the falsehood itself, a lie told to God inside his own community.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 5:3-4 again. Notice what Peter says was freely theirs, and what he says the lie was aimed at.

comprehension_check.question: The apostles leave the council bleeding from a flogging, and Luke says they went out rejoicing. What understanding of suffering makes that joy possible?
options: Relief that the sentence stopped short of a death penalty
Confidence that public opinion would now swing to their side
Certainty that God would soon repay the council in kind
Conviction that dishonor for Jesus' name is itself an honor
comprehension_check.why: Acts 5:41 grounds the joy in being counted worthy to bear disgrace for the Name.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 5:40-42 again. Notice what the rejoicing is about, and what the apostles do the very next day.

connections.reason: Peter's temple sermon identifies Jesus as Deuteronomy 18's 'prophet like Moses.'
The early church prays Psalm 2 ('why do the nations rage?') as commentary on Jesus' crucifixion.

nodes.title: Stephen: The First Martyr
nodes.summary: The first deacon becomes the first martyr: Stephen retells Israel's whole story — Abraham, Joseph, Moses, the tabernacle — to argue that God has never been confined to one building and that Israel has always resisted the Spirit. Stoned, he sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand and dies with Jesus' words on his lips, while a young man named Saul holds the coats.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Stephen answers a charge about the temple by retelling Israel's whole story. What is he trying to show through that history, and how would believing that God's presence is never tied to one building change where you expect to meet him?
assessment_questions: Why are Stephen and the other six first chosen, and what accusation brings Stephen before the council?
Stephen recalls God meeting Abraham in Mesopotamia, Joseph in Egypt, and Moses in the wilderness. How does that pattern support his claim that the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands?
Stephen dies praying for the people killing him, echoing Jesus' own words. What would forgiving someone while the wound is still fresh require of you, and where could you start?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Stephen retells the national history to show that the gospel continues Scripture's plot to its climax.

teaching_concepts.concept: God is not confined to the temple
teaching_concepts.explanation: From Abraham to the tabernacle, God keeps meeting his people outside the land and the building, so his presence cannot be boxed in.
Stephen charges that rejecting Jesus repeats Israel's long pattern of resisting the Holy Spirit and his messengers.
Stephen is chosen to care for widows and ends his life forgiving his killers, holding practical service and costly testimony together.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the arc of Stephen's speech and explain why he argues that God has never been confined to the temple.

comprehension_check.question: Charged with speaking against the temple, Stephen answers with Abraham in Mesopotamia, Joseph in Egypt, and Moses at the bush. How does that history answer the charge?
options: It proves the nation's guilt is old enough to condemn the council
It shows his reverence for Moses, so the charge must be false
It shows God meeting his people everywhere, so no house contains him
It recalls the fathers' ways to argue nothing should ever change
comprehension_check.why: Acts 7:2, 7:9, and 7:30 find God active far outside the land, and Acts 7:48 draws the conclusion about houses built by hands.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 7:2, 7:9, and 7:30-33 again. Notice where God keeps showing up in each scene.

comprehension_check.question: Stephen lingers on Joseph and Moses, both refused by their own brothers before becoming their rescuers. Why does he build the speech on that pattern?
options: To show that suffering must season a leader before God can use him
To show that rejecting God's sent deliverer is Israel's oldest habit
To honor the patriarchs and soften the council before the hard rebuke
To explain why God kept moving his dwelling from place to place
comprehension_check.why: Acts 7:35 sharpens the pattern, the rejected Moses is the one God sent as ruler and redeemer, and Acts 7:51-52 lands it on the present.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 7:9, 7:35, and 7:51-52 again. Notice what happens each time God sends someone to rescue.

connections.reason: Stephen's dying vision — 'the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God' — is Daniel 7 seen open-eyed.
Stephen's speech retells Joseph as the pattern of the rejected deliverer whom God vindicates.
Stephen cites Deuteronomy 18's 'prophet like Moses' promise of Jesus (Acts 7:37), as Peter does in Acts 3:22.

nodes.title: Scattered Seed and the Damascus Road
nodes.summary: Persecution scatters the church, and the gospel goes with it: Philip in Samaria, then explaining Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official in a chariot. And on the Damascus road, the church's fiercest enemy meets a light and a voice — 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' — and becomes its greatest missionary.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Persecution meant to crush the church ends up spreading it, and the man leading the persecution becomes its missionary. What do these chapters suggest about who is actually directing this story, and how would trusting that direction change how you read a setback you are living through?
assessment_questions: What is the Ethiopian official reading when Philip meets him, and what happens by the end of their conversation?
Simon the magician offers money for the power of the Spirit, and Peter refuses him sharply. What does that exchange reveal about the difference between wanting God's gifts and wanting God?

Saul goes from breathing threats to preaching Jesus within days. What does his turnaround say about who is beyond God's reach, and how does that shape the way you pray for the hardest person you know?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The persecution that drives believers out of Jerusalem carries the gospel into Samaria and beyond, turning loss into mission.
Philip begins with the Isaiah passage the Ethiopian is already reading and shows how it points to Jesus, modeling how Scripture leads a seeker to faith.
Simon's attempt to buy spiritual power warns that being impressed by God is different from being changed by him.
Jesus personally claims his fiercest enemy on the Damascus road and names him a chosen instrument.

nodes.completion_criteria: Tell the story of Saul's conversion and explain how persecution ends up advancing the gospel in these chapters.

comprehension_check.question: Stephen's death sets off a persecution that empties Jerusalem of believers. How does Luke tell the story of that scattering?
options: As a sowing, the driven-out believers preaching wherever they land
As a retreat, the church protecting its message until safer days
As a pruning, the weaker believers falling away under pressure
As a rescue, God moving his people out before Jerusalem falls
comprehension_check.why: Acts 8:4 turns the flight into mission, the scattered announcing the word wherever they went.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 8:1-4 again. Notice what the scattered believers do as they go.

comprehension_check.question: Saul has been arresting believers, yet the voice on the road asks why Saul is persecuting him. What does that question reveal?
options: That Saul's raids were always secretly aimed at Jesus' own name
That heaven keeps watch whenever religion turns to violence
That Jesus counts harm to his people as harm to him
That the light means judgment has arrived for Saul's crimes
comprehension_check.why: Acts 9:4-5 has the risen Jesus name Saul's campaign against the church as an attack on himself.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 9:1-5 again. Notice whom Saul set out to seize, and whom the voice says he strikes.

connections.reason: The Ethiopian official is reading exactly this passage when Philip 'told him the good news about Jesus.'

nodes.title: Gentiles Receive the Spirit
nodes.summary: A Roman centurion's prayers and a sheet of unclean animals collide in Peter's vision — 'what God has made clean, do not call common' — and the Spirit falls on uncircumcised Gentiles mid-sermon — settling in practice what the church will formally deliberate at the Jerusalem council. Antioch becomes the first mixed church (where 'Christian' is coined), and James is martyred while Peter walks out of prison past the guards unnoticed.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Peter needs the same vision three times before he will walk into a Gentile's house. What had to be dismantled in him before the gospel could cross that threshold, and what assumption about who belongs might God need to unsettle in you?
assessment_questions: What does Peter see in his rooftop vision, and what happens while he is still preaching in Cornelius' house?
Peter concludes that God shows no partiality. How does the Spirit falling on uncircumcised Gentiles settle a question that argument alone could not?
Peter's critics in Jerusalem fall silent and glorify God once they hear what the Spirit did. When God's work challenges a boundary you hold, what would responding the way they did look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Spirit falls on Cornelius' household before anyone can object, confirming that God receives people from every nation by faith.
Peter's vision teaches that God himself decides who is clean, so the old boundary markers no longer draw the community's edge.
The first church of mixed Jews and Gentiles becomes a base for mission, and there believers are first called Christians.
James is killed and Peter walks free, and the church learns to pray earnestly while trusting the word of God to keep growing either way.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Peter's vision meant and how the events at Cornelius' house changed who the church understood the gospel to be for.

comprehension_check.question: While Peter is still speaking in Cornelius' house, the Spirit falls on everyone listening, before baptism and before any debate in Jerusalem. What does the timing accomplish?
options: It repays the centurion for his years of prayer and generous almsgiving
It marks the household as an exception God allowed only once
It shows baptism with water no longer matters for Gentile converts
It settles by God's own hand that Gentiles belong as they are
comprehension_check.why: Acts 11:17-18 draws the conclusion, God gave them the same gift, and the church can only recognize what God has done.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 10:44-48 and Acts 11:15-18 again. Notice the order things happen in, and who acts first.

comprehension_check.question: In one chapter Herod kills James, Peter walks free, and Herod dies. What is Luke teaching by telling all three together?
options: That rescue comes to churches whose prayers are free of doubt
That the word outruns kings, whether its servants live or die
That James' death was the cost of Peter's miraculous release
That bolder faith like Peter's is what makes deliverance possible
comprehension_check.why: Acts 12:24 closes the chapter with the word of God spreading and multiplying past every throne.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 12:1-5, then Acts 12:21-24 again. Notice how the chapter opens, and what is still standing when it ends.

connections.reason: Peter's vision of the sheet of unclean animals reworks Leviticus 11 to open the door to Gentiles.

nodes.title: The First Mission and the Jerusalem Council
nodes.summary: Antioch lays hands on Barnabas and Saul — henceforth Paul — for the first missionary journey: synagogue sermons, a stoning survived, churches planted and eldered. Then the watershed: must Gentiles be circumcised? The Jerusalem council answers no — salvation is 'through the grace of the Lord Jesus' for Jew and Gentile alike.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The early church nearly splits over what to require of Gentile converts. How does the council reach its answer, and what unofficial requirements for belonging might you be tempted to add to the gospel today?
assessment_questions: Who sends out Barnabas and Saul on the first journey, and what question later forces the church to gather in Jerusalem?
Peter argues that God cleansed Gentile hearts by faith and gave them the Spirit just as he did to Jewish believers. Why does that testimony carry decisive weight in the council's decision?

The council refuses to add requirements for salvation while asking Gentiles to avoid a few practices for the sake of fellowship. When would you give up a freedom so someone else could belong, and what would it cost you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Antioch fasts, prays, and releases its best teachers for mission, turning the church from a destination into a launching point.
The council concludes that Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, so no ethnic marker can be added as a condition.
The church settles its hardest dispute through testimony, Scripture, and shared discernment, concluding that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.
Paul is stoned at Lystra and returns anyway to strengthen the new churches, teaching that entering the kingdom involves many tribulations.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the question the Jerusalem council faced and how the church answered it, in your own words.

comprehension_check.question: At Antioch the Spirit speaks while the church worships and fasts, and Barnabas and Saul are sent out. Who is driving the mission as Luke tells it?
options: The Spirit initiates, and the church releases its best to obey
The church plans the journey, and the Spirit blesses it afterward
Barnabas and Saul volunteer, and the church confirms their ambition
Jerusalem's apostles direct Antioch to expand the work westward
comprehension_check.why: Acts 13:2-3 shows the order, the Spirit calls first and the church fasts, prays, and lets them go.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 13:1-3 again. Notice who speaks first, and what the church does in response.

comprehension_check.question: At the council, Peter's account of Cornelius' house carries the day. Why does that testimony settle a question this large?
options: Because the majority found his account the most persuasive offered
Because the Gentiles' upright conduct had proven them worthy at last
Because God had already given Gentiles the Spirit without added conditions
Because lived experience outweighs written Scripture when the two collide
comprehension_check.why: Acts 15:8-9 rests the case on God's own act, the same Spirit given and hearts cleansed by faith.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 15:7-11 again. Notice whose actions Peter recounts, and what he says would put God to the test.

connections.reason: Galatians is Paul's own furious account of the same circumcision controversy — the letter and the council interpret each other.
James settles the council by quoting Amos' rebuilt booth of David under which the nations seek the Lord.
Paul and Barnabas quote 'a light for the nations' as their marching orders to the Gentiles.

nodes.title: Into Europe: Philippi to Ephesus
nodes.summary: A vision calls Paul across to Macedonia: a businesswoman converted and a jailer baptized at midnight in Philippi, philosophers engaged on Mars Hill in Athens ('what you worship as unknown, this I proclaim'), eighteen months in Corinth, and a riot of silversmiths in Ephesus. The farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus is Paul's ministry in his own words.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul reasons with philosophers in Athens, sings in a Philippian jail, and weeps saying goodbye at Miletus. What do those scenes together show about carrying one message into very different rooms, and how would you translate the gospel for the rooms you walk into?
assessment_questions: How does the gospel first take root in Philippi, and who are the first two converts named there?
In Athens Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and quotes the Athenians' own poets. What does his approach show about how the gospel meets a culture that does not know Scripture?
At Miletus Paul says his life is worth nothing to him compared with finishing the ministry he received. What would treating your life as an assignment from God change about your current plans?

teaching_concepts.explanation: A night vision redirects Paul's route to Macedonia, and the message takes root in Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus.
On Mars Hill Paul builds from creation and the Athenians' own writers toward repentance and the resurrection, respecting his audience's starting point.
New believers in Ephesus burn their costly magic books, because following Jesus changes money, habits, and old allegiances.
Paul's farewell charges the Ephesian elders to guard the flock at personal cost, pointing to his own tears and labor as the pattern.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe Paul's approach on Mars Hill and explain one way these chapters show the gospel taking root in a new city.

comprehension_check.question: In Athens Paul opens with the city's own altar and quotes its poets, yet still ends at repentance and a risen judge. What is his method?
options: He blends Greek philosophy with the gospel until the two agree
He starts where Athens is and walks toward what it lacks
He hides the offensive parts of the message until trust is built
He proves the poets secretly worshiped Israel's God without knowing
comprehension_check.why: Acts 17:22-31 moves from their altar and poets to the call to repent, meeting the city without trimming the summons.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 17:22-31 again. Notice where Paul begins, and where the speech finally arrives.

comprehension_check.question: At Miletus Paul tells the elders his life has no value to him next to finishing the ministry received from the Lord Jesus. What view of ministry is he handing them?
options: Ministry is a career whose sacrifices deserve the church's honor
Ministry is measured by the number of churches one leaves behind
Ministry is safest when a shepherd avoids provoking the wolves
Ministry is a trust to be finished, whatever it personally costs
comprehension_check.why: Acts 20:24 stakes everything on completing the course and ministry received from Jesus, the assignment outranking the life that carries it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 20:22-24 again. Notice what Paul says he knows is coming, and what he says matters more.

connections.reason: The church founded in the Philippian jail receives Paul's most joyful letter.
The Corinth planted in Acts 18 is the church of the Corinthian letters.
The Ephesus of the riot and the Miletus farewell receives the letter to the Ephesians.
The Thessalonica of Acts 17 — three sabbaths and a riot — receives Paul's earliest surviving letter.

nodes.title: Arrest and the Defenses: Mob, Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus, Agrippa
nodes.summary: Warned at every port, Paul goes up to Jerusalem anyway, and a false rumor about the temple hands him to the mob. Roman custody becomes his platform: he answers the crowd, the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, and every defense turns into testimony that the resurrection hope of Israel is the real issue. The Lord stands by him at night and names Rome as the destination, so when the case stalls for two years Paul appeals to Caesar. Agrippa's parting verdict is Luke's quiet irony: this prisoner has done nothing deserving death or chains.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Agabus binds his own hands with Paul's belt to warn him, the believers weep and beg him to stay, and Paul goes to Jerusalem anyway, ready to be bound and even to die. When is refusing to be talked out of a course faithfulness rather than stubbornness, and how would you tell the difference in a decision you are facing?
assessment_questions: How does Paul end up in Roman custody in Jerusalem, and what appeal finally sends him toward Rome?
Before Agrippa, Paul insists he is saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would come. Why does he present his defense as the fulfillment of Israel's hope?
The Lord stands by Paul at night and tells him to take courage, for he must testify in Rome. When circumstances turn against you, how do you tell a closed door from a hard road you are meant to walk?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul answers mobs, governors, and a king with his own story, the Scriptures, and the resurrection, joining personal witness to public argument.
The Lord's night word after the Sanhedrin hearing turns custody into commission, and that one promise steadies Paul through every hearing that follows.
Paul frames every accusation as a question about the resurrection promised to the fathers, presenting the Way as the fulfillment of what his accusers already await.
Ambush plots, transfers, and a case stalled for two years all move Paul exactly where God said he would go, so even the chains serve the mission.

nodes.completion_criteria: Trace Paul's path from the temple mob to the appeal to Caesar, naming the audiences he answers, and explain why he keeps calling the resurrection the real issue.

comprehension_check.question: Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus, and Agrippa. Across these hearings, how does he present the charge against him?
options: He is on trial for the hope Israel itself has always held
He asks the courts to tolerate the Way as a new faith
He renounces his Pharisee past to prove he left Judaism behind
He admits fault but claims his citizenship shields him from punishment
comprehension_check.why: In Acts 23:6 and 26:6-8 Paul stakes his defense on the resurrection promised to the fathers, the hope his accusers themselves await.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 23:6, 24:21, and 26:6-8 again. Notice the one issue Paul names every time he explains why he stands accused.

comprehension_check.question: Agrippa concludes that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. What does Luke show the reader with that verdict?
options: Paul's rashness cost him a release the court was ready to grant
The charges were true but lay beyond what Rome could punish
His innocence stands on record while God's promise still points to Rome
Roman fairness, more than any providence, is what kept Paul safe
comprehension_check.why: Acts 23:11 already set Rome as the Lord's destination, and in Acts 26:31 the rulers themselves find nothing in Paul deserving death or chains.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 23:11, then Acts 26:30-32. Notice what the Lord says Paul must do, and what the rulers say Paul has done.

nodes.title: The Voyage, the Shipwreck, and Rome
nodes.summary: Luke sails with Paul and tells the voyage to Rome like a sea epic: contrary winds, an ignored warning, fourteen nights of storm, and a wreck off Malta that lands all two hundred seventy-six aboard alive, exactly as God promised. The prisoner is the steadiest man on the ship, urging courage and breaking bread because he believes God. After a winter of healings on Malta, Paul reaches Rome and spends two years under guard, welcoming everyone who comes. The book ends mid-stride, the kingdom proclaimed openly and the word unhindered, with no period on the story, on purpose.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul reaches Rome by way of arrest, storm, and shipwreck, yet the book ends on the word unhindered. Where do you see God steering events that look like disasters in these chapters, and what would trusting that steering mean in a season of your life that feels stalled?
assessment_questions: What does Paul tell the frightened crew in Acts 27:23-25 about what God has promised, and whom does the promise cover?
Paul relays a promise that no life will be lost, then stops the sailors from escaping and urges everyone to eat. What do his actions show about how he holds God's promise?

Paul believed God in the storm and still handed out bread and kept the crew at their posts. In a storm you are facing now, what is the promise you are holding, and what is the next ordinary step it asks of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The voyage Paul boards as a prisoner delivers him exactly where God said he would go, and the wreck itself becomes the road to Rome.
God grants every life on the ship, yet the rescue still runs through sailors kept at their posts and bread eaten before dawn, the promise carrying its own means.
In the storm, on Malta, and in his rented house in Rome, Paul keeps turning captivity into a platform, and the prisoner is the steadiest man in every scene.
Acts closes with the gospel preached openly in the empire's capital and no period on the story, handing the mission to the reader.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell how the promise of Acts 27:24 carries all aboard through the wreck to Malta and on to Rome, and explain why Acts ends without an ending.

comprehension_check.question: In the storm Paul announces that God has granted the lives of all aboard, then warns that no one is saved unless the sailors stay with the ship. How does the promise work?
options: Once God promised, nothing the crew did could matter to the outcome
The promise is certain, and it arrives through means people must take
The rescue was earned by the crew's careful obedience to Paul
Because Paul believed, the storm posed no real danger to anyone
comprehension_check.why: Acts 27:24 grants every life aboard, and Acts 27:31 still keeps the sailors at their posts, the sure promise moving through the steps it commands.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 27:22-25, then Acts 27:30-34. Notice what Paul says is already granted, and what he still tells people to do.

comprehension_check.question: Acts ends with Paul still a prisoner in Rome, while Luke's last note is that the preaching goes on freely. What is Luke saying by closing the book there?
options: Rome's official tolerance is what finally set the message free
The story closes because Paul's mission had reached its finish
Bold preachers are always given an open door in the end
The word's advance does not hang on its messenger's freedom
comprehension_check.why: Acts 28:30-31 sets the guarded house and the open proclamation side by side, the kingdom preached to all who come.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Acts 28:16-31 again. Notice what stays restricted in the final scene and what does not.

connections.reason: Paul wrote Romans on the eve of this journey; the letter announces the visit these chapters deliver in chains.
Acts leaves Paul under house arrest in Rome; this letter speaks from the harsher, final imprisonment tradition places after it.

nodes.title: The Righteousness of God Revealed
nodes.summary: Paul's most systematic gospel: all humanity — pagan and religious alike — is 'under sin,' and 'the righteous shall live by faith.' God justifies the ungodly through the redemption in Christ Jesus, 'a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith,' with Abraham as Exhibit A: he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness — before circumcision, before the law.
nodes.tradition_notes: Justification is the Reformation's fault line: Protestant traditions read Romans as teaching justification by faith alone, a declarative verdict; Catholic teaching (Trent, and the 1999 Joint Declaration with Lutherans narrowing the gap) holds justification includes inner transformation and is not by faith alone in the Reformation's sense; Orthodoxy frames salvation more as union with God (theosis) than courtroom acquittal. All three affirm salvation is by grace.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul works hard to show that religious people and pagans stand equally under sin before he announces any good news. Why does the diagnosis have to come first, and what would change if you stopped measuring yourself against other people and stood where Abraham stood, with nothing to offer except trust?
assessment_questions: What verdict does Paul reach about both Jews and Gentiles by the middle of chapter 3, and what evidence has he given?
Paul stresses that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed God, before circumcision and before the law existed. Why is that timing so important to his argument?

Paul says boasting is excluded because righteousness comes as a gift received by faith. Where does quiet boasting still live in your spiritual life, and what would resting in the gift look like instead?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul levels every human advantage, showing pagan and religious people alike without excuse before God.
God justifies the ungodly through the redemption in Christ Jesus, received by faith, so salvation is grace from start to finish.
Paul presents the cross as the place where God proves he is righteous at the very moment he justifies sinners.
Genesis 15:6 shows that being counted righteous through faith is Scripture's oldest pattern, standing long before Paul wrote.

nodes.completion_criteria: Walk through Paul's argument from universal sin to Abraham's faith, and explain why Genesis 15:6 carries so much weight in it.

comprehension_check.question: Paul spends over two chapters indicting pagans and the religious alike before announcing the gift of righteousness. What is that long indictment for?
options: To rank humanity's sins from mildest up to worst
To prove the Gentiles guiltier than the covenant people
To shut every route to acceptance based on merit
To move readers to reform their conduct before believing
comprehension_check.why: Romans 3:19-20 gathers the whole world guilty before God, so that righteousness can only arrive as his gift.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 3:19-20 again. Notice what the indictment leaves every mouth unable to do.

comprehension_check.question: Paul makes a point of asking when Abraham was counted righteous, before or after circumcision, in Romans 4:10. Why does the timing carry so much weight?
options: It proves the rite added nothing and should be dropped
It opens Abraham's family to everyone who shares his faith
It shows righteousness came easier before the law arrived
It honors Abraham's obedience as the ground of blessing
comprehension_check.why: Romans 4:11 draws the conclusion: counted righteous while uncircumcised, Abraham becomes father of all who believe.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 4:9-12 again. Notice the question Paul asks about the order of events in Abraham's life.

connections.reason: The sin-catalogue of Romans 3 is stitched from Psalms 14, 5, 10, and 36.
Paul's word for Christ as the 'place of atonement' (hilasterion) is the Greek name for the mercy seat of Leviticus 16.
Paul quotes Psalms 14 and 32 as core evidence in his argument about sin and forgiveness.
'The righteous shall live by faith' is the thesis-verse of Romans (1:17).
Paul wrote Romans on the eve of this journey; the letter announces the visit these chapters deliver in chains.
Romans is Galatians' argument rewritten at full length and lower temperature.
Romans 1's analysis of idolatry and its degradations tracks Wisdom 13-14 so closely that most scholars think Paul knew it.

nodes.title: Peace, Union, and No Condemnation
