nodes.summary: Justified, therefore peace with God: Adam's one trespass answered by Christ's one obedience, baptism as death and resurrection with him, the agonized 'I do not do what I want' of chapter 7 — and then Romans 8, by wide consent the greatest chapter in the Bible: no condemnation, the Spirit within, creation groaning toward glory, all things working for good, and nothing in all creation able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Chapter 7 gives voice to a person who keeps doing what he hates, and chapter 8 answers with no condemnation. How do these chapters hold honest ongoing struggle and real security together, and which of the two is harder for you to believe about yourself?
assessment_questions: What contrast does Paul draw between Adam and Christ in chapter 5, and what does each one's act bring to humanity?
Paul says those baptized into Christ were baptized into his death and raised to walk in newness of life. What does that union mean for sin's power over a believer?

Romans 8 ends with a list of everything that cannot separate us from God's love in Christ. What in your life feels most able to separate you, and what would it mean to read that promise against it by name?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Justification brings a settled relationship, so believers stand in grace secured by Christ rather than by their performance.
Paul reads all of history under two heads, where Adam's trespass brought condemnation and death, and Christ's obedience brings righteousness and life.
Baptism pictures believers dying and rising with Jesus, so sin's rule is broken and a new life led by the Spirit begins.
The Spirit confirms believers as adopted children, and Romans 8 stakes everything on the claim that no power in creation can separate them from God's love.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the Adam and Christ contrast of Romans 5, and describe what Romans 8 means by no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus.

comprehension_check.question: Romans 5:18-19 hangs the whole human story on two single acts, one trespass and one obedience. What is Paul's point in drawing the parallel?
options: Adam and Christ faced temptation with opposite results
Each person relives Adam's choice until choosing Christ's
The two acts cancel, leaving each person judged alone
One man's act can define the many under him
comprehension_check.why: Romans 5:19 sets one disobedience making many sinners against one obedience making many righteous, two heads carrying two humanities.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 5:18-19 again. Notice how many people each single act affects.

comprehension_check.question: Romans 8:31-34 answers fear with a string of questions about who could accuse or condemn. Where does Paul anchor the believer's assurance?
options: In what God has done and keeps doing in Christ
In the believer's daily progress against besetting sin
In the intensity of the believer's felt love for God
In the promise that hardship will soon pass
comprehension_check.why: Romans 8:32 argues from the greater to the lesser: the God who gave his own Son will not stop short of giving everything.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 8:31-34 again. Notice whose actions every answer points to.

connections.reason: Baptism into death and out again is the sea crossing's pattern — slaves brought through water into freedom.
The saints' reign with Christ and death's final defeat complete Romans 8's groaning-creation hope.

nodes.title: Has God's Word Failed? Israel and the Mystery
nodes.summary: Paul's anguish over Israel's unbelief drives the New Testament's deepest wrestling with election and faithfulness: the potter's freedom, 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,' the remnant, Gentile branches grafted into Israel's olive tree — and the doxology that ends the argument on its knees: 'Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!'
nodes.tradition_notes: Romans 9 is the proof-text battleground for predestination: Augustinian and Reformed readings find unconditional individual election; Arminian, Orthodox, and much Catholic exegesis read corporate election and foreseen faith, stressing 11's 'God has consigned all to disobedience that he may have mercy on all.' The chapter also anchors ongoing debate about Israel's future in God's plan.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul opens these chapters in anguish over his own people and closes them singing about the depth of God's wisdom. What happens across the argument to move him from grief to worship, and how do you respond when God's ways refuse to fit your categories?
assessment_questions: What image does Paul use in chapter 11 to picture Gentile believers joining Israel's story, and what warning comes attached to it?
Paul insists the word of God has not failed even though much of Israel has not believed. How does his appeal to the remnant support that claim?
Paul warns the grafted branches against pride toward the natural ones. Where does spiritual pride creep in for you, and what would it look like to stand in awe instead?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul argues from the remnant that God's promises to Israel still stand, because there have always been those within Israel who believed.
The potter imagery defends God's right to work out his purposes in history, and Paul says those purposes aim at mercy on all.
Gentile believers are wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree, so their standing rests on faith and leaves no room for boasting.
Paul closes the hardest argument in his letters with a doxology, showing that the right end of hard questions about God is awe.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Paul argues that God's word has not failed, and describe the olive tree picture and the warning it carries.

comprehension_check.question: Romans 9-11 opens with Paul's anguish over Israel and closes in doxology. What question drives the whole argument?
options: Whether individual believers can be sure they are elect
Whether the law still applies to Gentile converts
Whether God's promises to Israel have come to nothing
Whether evangelism matters if God has already chosen
comprehension_check.why: Romans 9:6 states the thesis under everything: the word of God has not failed, and three chapters defend it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 9:6 and Romans 11:1 again. Notice the question both verses are answering.

comprehension_check.question: After the hardest argument in his letters, Paul ends with worship instead of a tidy verdict in Romans 11:33-36. What does that ending say about the questions raised?
options: They dissolve for any reader who follows the argument closely
They run past tracing, and the right end is awe
They were improper questions believers should never have raised
They will be answered when Israel's hardening ends
comprehension_check.why: Romans 11:33 calls God's judgments unsearchable and his ways beyond tracing out, so the argument finishes on its knees.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 11:33-36 again. Notice what Paul says can and cannot be traced.

connections.reason: The seven thousand who never bowed to Baal are Paul's proof that a remnant always remains.
Paul builds his argument about God's electing freedom on 'the older will serve the younger' from Genesis 25.
Paul quotes 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy' from this scene as the cornerstone of Romans 9.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 30's 'the word is near you' as the voice of righteousness by faith.
Paul's potter-and-clay argument reworks Jeremiah 18's image of God's freedom over nations.
Paul quotes 'Not-My-People will be called sons of the living God' for the Gentiles' inclusion.
'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved' anchors Romans 10.

nodes.title: Living Sacrifices: The Gospel Embodied
nodes.summary: 'Therefore… present your bodies as a living sacrifice.' The doctrine becomes a way of life: sober self-assessment, genuine love, blessing persecutors, submission to governing authorities, love as the law's fulfillment, and patience across the strong/weak divide over food and days. Sixteen chapters end in a list of greeted names — the theology has faces.
nodes.discussion_prompt: After eleven chapters of doctrine Paul says therefore and turns to bodies, enemies, taxes, and dinner tables. Why does he ground everyday behavior in the mercies of God rather than in willpower, and which of his instructions would cost you the most this week?
assessment_questions: What does Paul urge believers to present as a living sacrifice, and what does he say must happen to their minds?
Paul tells the strong and the weak to stop despising and judging one another over food and days. What makes love a better guide than winning in disputes like these?
Paul says to bless persecutors and overcome evil with good. Who is the hardest person for you to bless right now, and what one concrete good could you do for them this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The living sacrifice makes everyday choices the arena of worship, and transformation begins with a renewed mind.
Paul turns love into specific practices, from honoring one another to feeding an enemy, because love is the fulfilling of the law.
Paul calls believers to honor governing authorities as instituted by God for order, a teaching Christians weigh carefully when rulers command what God forbids.
On disputable matters the strong bear with the weak, so no one's liberty is allowed to wreck another person's faith.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what presenting your body as a living sacrifice means, and give two concrete examples from these chapters of what that life looks like.

comprehension_check.question: Romans 12:1 turns from argument to instruction with an appeal grounded in the mercies of God. What does that grounding make of everything that follows?
options: A ladder of practices that secure God's mercy
An optional ideal for the most devoted believers
A stricter law replacing the one Moses gave
A response of worship to mercy already received
comprehension_check.why: Romans 12:1 grounds the appeal in God's mercies, so obedience is offered as living sacrifice, worship answering grace.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 12:1 again. Notice what the word therefore reaches back to.

comprehension_check.question: Food and holy days split the Roman church, and in Romans 14:5 Paul declines to hand down a ruling. What does he ask for instead of uniformity?
options: Patience while the scrupulous slowly mature into full freedom
Separate gatherings so neither side offends the other
Welcome across the divide, each conscience before its Lord
A council ruling to settle the disputed practices
comprehension_check.why: Romans 14:5 lets each be fully convinced in his own mind, and Romans 15:7 crowns the section with the command to welcome one another.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Romans 14:3-5 and 15:7 again. Notice the verbs Paul keeps commanding toward the other side.

connections.reason: Romans 12's bless-your-persecutors ethic is the Sermon on the Mount in epistle form.

nodes.title: The Foolishness of the Cross
nodes.summary: A gifted, quarreling church sorting itself by favorite preacher gets Paul's countermove: 'we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles' — God choosing the foolish, weak, and low to shame the impressive. Leaders are field hands and stewards; the church is God's temple; the Spirit alone knows the mind of God.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul says God chose the foolish and weak things of the world to shame the wise and strong. Where do you see people ranking each other by impressiveness, in church or anywhere else, and what would it cost you to start measuring by the cross instead?
assessment_questions: What slogans were the Corinthians using to divide themselves in chapter 1, and how does Paul respond to them?
Paul calls the message of the cross foolishness to those who are perishing and the power of God to those being saved. Why does a crucified Messiah overturn worldly ideas of wisdom and power?
Paul describes leaders as servants and stewards whom God alone will judge. How would seeing every leader you admire that way change the loyalty you give them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Christ crucified looks like folly to worldly reason, yet Paul insists it is the true wisdom and power of God.
Loyalty belongs to Christ rather than to favorite teachers, so party spirit in the church contradicts the gospel itself.
God deliberately works through the weak and unimpressive to shame the strong, which removes every ground for human boasting.
Christian leaders are field hands and household managers accountable to God, so ministry is service rather than a stage.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Paul answers the church's factions with the message of Christ crucified, and what that says about how God defines wisdom and power.

comprehension_check.question: Corinth ranked its teachers like rival philosophers. Why does Paul answer the factions with a message on the crucified Christ?
options: The cross gives every faction a symbol they already share
Paul wants loyalty transferred from Apollos back to himself
The cross overturns the status game the factions are playing
Eloquence itself is sinful, so plain speech alone pleases God
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 1:27-29 says God chose the low and despised so that no one could boast before him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 1:26-31 again. Notice what God's way of choosing does to boasting, then reread the slogans of 1 Corinthians 1:12.

comprehension_check.question: In 1 Corinthians 3:5-9 Paul reduces himself and Apollos to field hands in someone else's field. What does the picture do to the party slogans?
options: It sorts them, giving each teacher his own separate field
It ranks them, since planting must come before any watering
It excuses them, since quarrels are natural among fellow workers
It deflates them, since only God makes anything grow
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 3:7 locates all the increase with God, leaving no teacher worth a slogan.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 3:5-9 again. Notice what the workers share, and what belongs to God alone.

connections.reason: Paul's 'Christ the wisdom of God' takes up this book's central figure.
The Corinth planted in Acts 18 is the church of the Corinthian letters.

nodes.title: Bodies That Belong to the Lord
nodes.summary: Scandal ('a man has his father's wife'), lawsuits between believers, and prostitution answered by a bombshell premise: 'your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… you were bought with a price.' Then the Bible's longest treatment of marriage, singleness, and divorce — both states honored as callings.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul says you are not your own because you were bought with a price. If your body actually belongs to God, what changes about how you treat it and what you do with it, and which of your current habits would that force you to look at differently?
assessment_questions: What scandal does Paul confront in chapter 5, and what does he tell the church to do about it?
Paul calls the believer's body a temple of the Holy Spirit and says you were bought with a price. Why does belonging to Christ change what a person may do with their own body?
Paul honors both marriage and singleness as callings with real advantages. How does treating both as gifts change the way you view your own current season of life?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The church removes the unrepentant to protect its holiness and to wake the sinner up, so corrective love always hopes for a return.
The Holy Spirit lives in the believer's body, which makes sexual sin a betrayal of union with Christ rather than a private matter.
Believers settle grievances with one another inside the church, since dragging a brother before secular courts already means defeat.
Paul treats both states as gifts from God with distinct freedoms and duties, so neither is a lesser form of Christian life.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Paul means by calling the body a temple of the Holy Spirit, and how that premise drives his rulings on discipline, sexuality, and marriage.

comprehension_check.question: Paul answers sexual sin in Corinth by pointing to the Spirit's dwelling in the body and the price paid for it. What is his argument?
options: The body is a passing shell, so only the spirit's purity counts
The body is joined to Christ, so sin there denies him
Sexual sin is worse because it cannot be forgiven
Bodily desires are shameful and are best refused entirely
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 grounds the command: the Spirit indwells the body and God has paid for it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 6:13-20 again. Notice what Paul says the body is for, and whose it is.

comprehension_check.question: Paul orders the church to remove the unrepentant man in 1 Corinthians 5. What outcome is the removal aimed at?
options: The man's rescue and the church's protection from spreading sin
A public example deterring others from attempting similar sins
The permanent exclusion of a man now beyond recovery
Proof to outsiders that the church judges the world's morals
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 5:5 aims the act at the man's final salvation, and 1 Corinthians 5:6-7 at the health of the whole batch.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 5:4-7 and 1 Corinthians 5:12 again. Notice the two hoped-for results Paul names.

connections.reason: Paul says it directly: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.'

nodes.title: Freedom, Idol Feasts, and the Lord's Table
nodes.summary: May Christians eat meat sacrificed to idols? Paul's answer trains freedom on love: knowledge puffs up, love builds up; 'I have become all things to all people'; Israel's wilderness falls are 'examples for us.' It climaxes at the table: divisions at the Lord's Supper mean 'it is not the Lord's supper you eat' — discern the body.
nodes.tradition_notes: 1 Corinthians 10-11's eucharistic language ('a participation in the body of Christ,' 'discerning the body') is read with realist weight in Catholic and Orthodox theology and a spectrum of views among Protestants, from real presence (Lutheran, Anglican) to memorial (Zwinglian and much evangelicalism).
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul has the knowledge to eat anything with a clear conscience, yet he says he would never eat meat again if it made a brother stumble. When has your freedom collided with someone else's conscience, and what would laying down a real right for their sake cost you?
assessment_questions: What question about food runs through chapters 8 to 10, and which episodes from Israel's wilderness story does Paul hold up as warnings?
Paul says knowledge puffs up while love builds up. Why does he treat care for a weaker brother's conscience as more decisive than being correct about idols?
Paul tells the church to examine themselves before eating the bread and drinking the cup. What would honest self-examination before worship look like for you this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: A Christian's freedom bends whenever using it would wound another person's conscience or pull them back toward idols.
Food itself is morally neutral because an idol is nothing, yet conscience and context decide whether eating honors God or betrays him.
Paul gives up pay, comfort, and preference to win people for Christ, modeling that freedom is for service rather than self.
The Lord's Supper proclaims Christ's death and binds the church together, so divisions and selfishness at the table contradict the very thing it declares.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words how love limits Christian freedom across these chapters, from idol food to divisions at the Lord's Supper.

comprehension_check.question: In 1 Corinthians 8 Paul agrees that an idol is nothing, yet tells the knowing not to eat in certain settings. What governs his ruling?
options: Ritual defilement that idol meat carries in itself
The church's reputation among the pagan neighbors watching it
Moderation, since lawful pleasures corrupt when freely indulged
The conscience of the weaker brother watching him eat
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 8:9-12 moves the question from knowledge to the brother, since wounding his conscience is sin against Christ.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 8:9-13 again. Notice who keeps appearing in Paul's reasoning about whether to eat.

comprehension_check.question: Paul tells the Corinthians that when they gather, it is not really the Lord's supper they eat. What has emptied the meal?
options: Neglect of the appointed words over the bread and cup
The unworthiness of sinners daring to approach the table
A table split into factions, some feasting, some hungry
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 11:20-22 says a divided, humiliating meal contradicts the supper it claims to be.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 11:17-22 and 1 Corinthians 11:33 again. Notice what Paul tells them to do for one another when they gather.

connections.reason: Paul's account of the Supper's institution — the earliest written — matches Luke's wording.

nodes.title: One Body, Many Gifts — and the More Excellent Way
nodes.summary: Spiritual gifts distributed by one Spirit to one body — eye, hand, and unpresentable parts all indispensable — interrupted by the greatest thing Paul ever wrote: 'Love is patient and kind… the greatest of these is love.' Chapter 14 then referees tongues and prophecy: everything for building up, everything in order.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul says even the most spectacular gifts amount to nothing without love. Think about the abilities you most want to be known for. What would it look like to aim them at building someone else up, and would the people around you notice the difference?
assessment_questions: What image does Paul use in chapter 12 to describe how different gifts fit together in the church, and which members does he call indispensable?
Paul interrupts his teaching on gifts to say that tongues, prophecy, and knowledge without love are nothing. What does that placement reveal about what makes any gift valuable?
Paul's rule for worship is that everything be done for building up. Which of your abilities are you mostly using for yourself, and what would redirecting one of them toward others require this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Holy Spirit distributes different gifts to different believers on purpose, and every one of them exists for the common good.
Eye, hand, and the parts nobody showcases all belong together, so rivalry and shame both misread how God built the church.
Chapter 13 sits between the gifts chapters because self-giving love is what makes any gift count for anything lasting.
Public worship is ordered toward intelligibility and mutual edification, so everything done in the gathering should leave the church stronger.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe why chapter 13 sits between the two gifts chapters, and explain what makes any spiritual gift valuable in Paul's argument.

comprehension_check.question: Paul sets the love chapter between two chapters on spiritual gifts. What does the placement argue?
options: Without love the most impressive gifts amount to nothing
Love is itself the greatest of the spiritual gifts
The gifts caused the quarrels, so Paul quietly retires them
The gifts themselves divide the church while love unites it
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 13:1-3 weighs the showiest gifts and finds them worth nothing without love.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 12:31 and 1 Corinthians 13:1-3 again. Notice what Paul calls love, and what the gifts become without it.

comprehension_check.question: In the body imagery of 1 Corinthians 12, the foot wants to resign and the eye dismisses the hand. What do both mistakes miss?
options: That humbler parts should settle for a quieter, lesser place
That God arranged the body, and every part is needed
That maturity means every member doing every function
That belonging depends on how much a member contributes
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 12:18 grounds it: the members sit where God placed them, by his own design.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 12:14-26 again. Notice who did the arranging, and which parts get called indispensable.

connections.reason: Ephesians 4's gifts-for-building-the-body teaching parallels and extends this section.

nodes.title: The Resurrection Chapter
nodes.summary: The gospel 'of first importance' — died, buried, raised on the third day, seen by Cephas, the Twelve, five hundred at once — and the stakes stated baldly: 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile.' Christ the firstfruits, the last Adam, the trumpet, the mortal putting on immortality: 'O death, where is your sting?' Therefore: be steadfast; your labor is not in vain.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul ends the resurrection chapter with a command: be steadfast, because your labor in the Lord is not in vain. How does believing your body will actually be raised change what counts as wasted effort, and what would you pour yourself into if you believed it fully?
assessment_questions: What events does Paul list as the gospel of first importance, and who does he say saw the risen Christ?
Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. What does that harvest image claim about the connection between his resurrection and ours?
Paul answers the defeat of death with a call to steadfast work rather than relaxation. What work in your life would you approach differently if you were certain it carries into resurrection?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul stakes the whole faith on a historical claim with named witnesses, saying plainly that if Christ was not raised, faith is futile.
His rising is the first sheaf of a whole harvest, a guarantee that those who belong to him will be raised in their turn.
The raised body is both continuous with this one and profoundly changed, as the perishable puts on the imperishable.
Because death is already defeated in Christ, Christians can labor with steady courage, knowing nothing done in the Lord is lost.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Paul says everything depends on Christ's resurrection, and what the firstfruits image promises about believers who have died.

comprehension_check.question: Paul opens 1 Corinthians 15 with a list of witnesses who saw the risen Christ, many still living. What is the list doing?
options: Honoring the apostles in the order of their seniority
Showing that visions of Jesus continued long after Easter
Grounding the gospel in an event with living witnesses
Proving Paul's own encounter outranked the other appearances
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 15:6 notes that most of the five hundred remain alive, witnesses who could still be asked.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 again. Notice the detail Paul adds about the five hundred.

comprehension_check.question: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits. What does the image claim about believers who have died?
options: His rising was unique, a glory no one else will share
The dead are already raised, so nothing further remains
Their souls survive while their bodies stay behind forever
His rising begins a harvest that will include them
comprehension_check.why: 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 presents his resurrection as the first share of a harvest completed at his coming.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 again. Notice the order of events the farming image sets out.

connections.reason: 'Death is swallowed up in victory' quotes Isaiah 25's mountain feast.
'O death, where is your sting?' takes up Hosea 13:14's taunt.

nodes.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
nodes.summary: Paul's most personal theology of ministry: comfort multiplied through affliction, the new covenant's surpassing glory (a sustained reading of Moses' veil), treasure in clay jars, 'we walk by faith, not by sight,' and the great exchange — 'for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.' Be reconciled to God.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul says God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort others with the comfort we ourselves received. Think of the hardest thing you have walked through. How might it become equipment for someone else, and who around you might need it now?
assessment_questions: What image does Paul use in chapter 4 for carrying the gospel treasure, and what point does the image make about ministers?

Paul writes that God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. What exchange is Paul describing, and why does it ground his plea to be reconciled to God?
Paul calls believers ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us. Who in your life needs that appeal, and what would carrying it to them actually look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God comforts his people in affliction so the comfort keeps moving, turning every healed wound into ministry for someone else.
Paul's ministry runs on the Spirit who gives life, claiming Jeremiah's promised covenant with a glory that outshines Moses' veil.
The gospel's power sits in fragile human vessels on purpose, so that the surpassing power is seen to belong to God.
In Christ, God was reconciling the world to himself through the great exchange of 5:21, and he entrusts that message to his people.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the clay-jar picture in your own words, and describe how God's comfort in affliction becomes ministry to others.

comprehension_check.question: Paul says the gospel's treasure sits in jars of clay, and 2 Corinthians 4:7 adds the reason. Why does God choose fragile carriers?
options: So ministers remain too humble to boast in themselves
So no one confuses the power with the container
So suffering can purge the ministers' remaining sin
So churches learn to forgive their leaders' failures
comprehension_check.why: 2 Corinthians 4:7 gives the purpose: power this great in vessels this weak can only be credited to God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 4:7 again. Notice what the jar's weakness is meant to make plain about the treasure.

comprehension_check.question: In 2 Corinthians 5:18-20 Paul describes reconciliation between God and the world. Which way does the initiative run?
options: From God, who reconciles and then sends the appeal
From humanity, whose repentance moves God to make peace
From both sides at once, meeting through negotiated terms
From the church, whose ministry produces the reconciliation
comprehension_check.why: 2 Corinthians 5:18 traces the whole movement to God, reconciling the world through Christ and entrusting the message to messengers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 5:18-20 again. Notice who acts first and what role is left to the ambassadors.

nodes.title: The Grace of Giving
nodes.summary: The collection for Jerusalem's poor becomes the New Testament's fullest teaching on generosity: the Macedonians' overflowing joy in extreme poverty, and the pattern above every pattern — 'though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor.' God loves a cheerful giver; sow bountifully.
nodes.discussion_prompt: The Macedonians gave beyond their ability out of extreme poverty, and Paul calls it overflowing joy. What makes giving joyful for some people and grudging for others, and what would cheerful generosity actually cost you this month?
assessment_questions: Whose example of giving does Paul hold up in chapter 8, and what was surprising about their circumstances?
Paul grounds the whole appeal in Christ, who though he was rich became poor for your sake. How does that pattern turn giving from an obligation into a response?
Paul says God loves a cheerful giver and that each person should give as they decide in their heart. How would you decide what to give if you really trusted God to supply the seed?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Christian generosity answers the self-giving of Christ, who became poor so that others might become rich.
Paul refuses to coerce anyone, because God wants giving that comes freely from a decided and glad heart.
The collection moves abundance toward need so that no church has too much while another lacks, making giving an act of solidarity.
The giver depends on God who provides seed and multiplies the harvest, so generosity becomes an exercise of trust in his provision.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Paul grounds generosity in the grace of Christ, and describe what makes a giver cheerful in these chapters.

comprehension_check.question: Paul raises money for Jerusalem without issuing a command, and 2 Corinthians 8:8-9 shows his lever. What does he ground the appeal on?
options: The tithe commanded to Israel and carried forward
A promised return of greater wealth to generous givers
The apostles' authority to assess each church's share
The self-giving of Christ, who became poor for them
comprehension_check.why: 2 Corinthians 8:9 holds up the pattern beneath the appeal, Christ surrendering riches to enrich others, and giving follows that grace.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 8:8-9 again. Notice what Paul says he is not doing, and whose act he points to instead.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Corinthians 9:8-11 promises that the giver will be enriched. What is the enrichment for?
options: For personal comfort, God repaying faith with plenty
For savings, guarding the giver against future famine
For further giving, so generosity keeps circulating
For status, marking the giver's place among churches
comprehension_check.why: 2 Corinthians 9:11 completes the loop: enrichment comes so that generosity can overflow again into thanksgiving to God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 9:8-11 again. Notice what the abundance is said to be for.

nodes.title: Boasting in Weakness
nodes.summary: Forced by 'super-apostles' to compare résumés, Paul boasts backwards: beatings, shipwrecks, sleepless nights, a basket over a wall — then the vision he won't cash in and the thorn God refused to remove: 'My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.' The apostle's credentials are his scars.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul pleaded three times for the thorn to be removed and received a different answer: my grace is sufficient for you. Where in your life have you been asking God to take something away, and what would it mean to hear that answer there instead?
assessment_questions: What hardships does Paul list when he is forced to boast, and what unusual things does he choose to boast in?
God answers Paul's plea about the thorn by saying his power is made perfect in weakness. Why does Paul conclude that when he is weak, then he is strong?
Paul tells the church to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith. What honest test would show whether your confidence rests on Christ or on your own credentials?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul's right to speak rests on Christ's commission and God-given power, so eloquence, style, and crowd size prove nothing.
Paul boasts in beatings, escapes, and hardships because scars earned in service display Christ's power better than any resume.
The unremoved thorn teaches that God's grace can carry a person through what God chooses to leave in place.
False apostles can look impressive, so churches test leaders by fidelity to the gospel and the fruit of the Spirit rather than by persuasive polish.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of Paul's thorn in the flesh, and explain why he chose to boast in weakness against the super-apostles.

comprehension_check.question: Forced to compare credentials with the super-apostles, Paul lists beatings, escapes, and anxieties, and 2 Corinthians 11:30 states his policy. Why boast in exactly the wrong things?
options: Because weakness is where Christ's power shows itself
Because humility impresses churches more than strength
Because he lacked the eloquence to compete directly
Because suffering itself earns a higher apostolic rank
comprehension_check.why: 2 Corinthians 12:9 supplies the logic: Christ's power rests on the weak, so Paul's hardships are where that power is seen.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 11:30 and 12:9 again. Notice what Paul says his weaknesses make room for.

comprehension_check.question: Three times Paul begs for the thorn's removal, and in 2 Corinthians 12:8-9 the thorn stays. What does the answer he receives teach about unanswered prayer?
options: Persistence in prayer eventually secures what is asked
Suffering left in place signals hidden unconfessed sin
Stronger faith would have made the healing certain
Grace to endure is itself God's real answer
comprehension_check.why: In 2 Corinthians 12:9 the request is met with sufficient grace, an answer that carries Paul through what stays unchanged.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Corinthians 12:7-9 again. Notice what God gives in place of what Paul asked.

nodes.title: Galatians: No Other Gospel
nodes.summary: Paul's angriest letter — no thanksgiving, straight to 'I am astonished': teachers are requiring circumcision, and Paul treats it as a different gospel entirely. Abraham believed before the law existed; the law was a guardian until Christ; 'there is neither Jew nor Greek… for you are all one in Christ Jesus.' Freedom lands in the Spirit's fruit — love, joy, peace — against the flesh's works.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul writes with real heat because he believes the gospel itself is at stake. Why does adding requirements to grace change the message entirely, and where are you tempted to treat God's acceptance as something you have to earn?
assessment_questions: What are the teachers in Galatia requiring of Gentile believers, and how does Paul describe their message in chapter 1?
Paul points to Abraham, who believed God long before the law was given. How does Abraham's story support Paul's case about how people are made right with God?
Paul says freedom in Christ is given for serving one another in love. Where could you use your freedom to serve someone this week, and what would it cost you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul treats a message of Christ plus added requirements as a different gospel altogether, because it shifts the ground of salvation away from grace.
Right standing with God comes through trusting Christ, since no one can earn it by works of the law.
The law served as a guardian until Christ came, pointing forward to the faith and full sonship now given in him.
Christian freedom exists for love and the Spirit's fruit, so it looks like serving others rather than gratifying the flesh.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words why Paul insists there is no other gospel, and describe how the fruit of the Spirit shows what real freedom looks like.

comprehension_check.question: Paul calls the Galatian teaching a different gospel, though it kept Christ and added only circumcision. Why does the addition change everything?
options: Because a required addition moves the ground off Christ's work
Because the demand burdened converts Paul hoped to win more easily
Because the teachers lacked authorization from the apostles in Jerusalem
comprehension_check.why: Galatians 2:16 states the ground of justification, faith in Christ rather than works of law, which the added requirement overturns.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Galatians 1:6-9 and 2:16 again. Notice what Paul says is actually at stake in the addition.

comprehension_check.question: Galatians 5 announces freedom from the law and immediately warns against misusing it. What is the freedom for?
options: For each conscience to set its own standard of conduct
For enjoying what the law once denied, within sensible limits
For serving one another in love, walking by the Spirit
For proving to its critics that grace produces better conduct
comprehension_check.why: Galatians 5:13 turns freedom outward, a calling exercised in love and service toward one another.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Galatians 5:13-14 and 5:22-23 again. Notice what freedom produces when the Spirit is leading it.

connections.reason: Romans is Galatians' argument rewritten at full length and lower temperature.
'The righteous shall live by faith' does its work here as in Romans.
'Cursed is everyone hanged on a tree' (Deut 21) and the curse of the law (Deut 27) anchor Galatians 3.
Galatians is Paul's own furious account of the same circumcision controversy — the letter and the council interpret each other.

nodes.title: Every Spiritual Blessing: The Church in God's Plan

comprehension_check.question: Ephesians 1:4-5 speaks of God choosing and predestining his people in Christ before creation. Christian traditions all affirm the words and still divide over them. Where does the disagreement actually sit?
options: Over how God's choice and a person's faith fit together
Over whether the choosing took place before creation began
Over whether Gentiles are included among the chosen people
Over whether the choosing is located in Christ at all
comprehension_check.why: Ephesians 1:4-5 states the choosing plainly, and the church's long discussion concerns how that choice and human believing belong together.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ephesians 1:4-5 and then 1:13. Notice what the text asserts outright, and what it leaves the reader to fit together.

comprehension_check.question: Ephesians 2:8-10 places good works after salvation rather than before it. What role does that give them?
options: A ladder the diligent climb toward acceptance with God
An optional extra for the especially devoted believer
A prepared path the saved are created to walk
A debt repaid to God for the cost of grace
comprehension_check.why: Ephesians 2:10 makes good works the road God laid out in advance for people his grace has remade.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ephesians 2:8-10 again. Notice the order of saving and working, and who prepared what in advance.

nodes.summary: One long exhale of praise: chosen before the foundation of the world, dead in trespasses then made alive — 'by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works' — and the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile demolished into 'one new man.' The church, of all things, is how God's manifold wisdom is displayed to the cosmic powers.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul spends three chapters listing what God has already done for those in Christ before asking anything of them. As you trace that list, which blessing is hardest for you to believe applies to you, and how would really believing it change where you look for security?
assessment_questions: According to chapter 2, what was the condition of the Ephesians before Christ, and what did God do about it?
Paul says Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jew and Gentile to create one new humanity. Why does he treat this reconciliation as part of the gospel itself rather than a side effect?
Ephesians 2:10 says we are God's workmanship, created for good works God prepared beforehand. How does knowing the works were prepared for you change the way you look for them?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God blessed and chose his people in Christ before the world began, so Christian identity rests on God's eternal purpose rather than on human achievement.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith, and it produces the good works God prepared in advance for his people to walk in.
Christ's cross demolishes the wall between Jew and Gentile, reconciling both into a single new people at peace with God and each other.
God displays his manifold wisdom to the cosmic powers through the church, which makes the church central to his purpose rather than optional.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what it means to be saved by grace through faith, and describe the one new humanity God creates in Christ.

connections.reason: Acts 19-20 narrates Paul's years in Ephesus and his farewell to these elders.

nodes.title: Walk Worthy: Body, Household, Armor

comprehension_check.question: Ephesians 4:13-16 gives the aim of all the gifts Christ pours into the church. What is the growth toward?
options: A membership large enough to fill out the body's frame
A mature body, stable in truth and knit in love
A leadership strong enough to silence every rival teacher
A uniformity of practice enforced from the top down
comprehension_check.why: Ephesians 4:14-16 pictures the goal as a body no longer tossed by every wind, building itself up in love.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ephesians 4:13-16 again. Notice what the grown body can no longer be tossed by, and what each part contributes.

comprehension_check.question: Ephesians 6:12 relocates the believer's real struggle away from flesh and blood. What follows for how the fight is fought?
options: Fight hostile people harder, since dark powers drive them
Withdraw from society until the evil day has passed
Leave the contest to angels better matched to the enemy
Stand firm in God's own armor and keep praying
comprehension_check.why: Ephesians 6:13-18 turns the relocation into practice, armor from God, a repeated call to stand, and constant prayer.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Ephesians 6:13-18 again. Notice the verb the passage keeps repeating about what armored believers do.

nodes.summary: The calling walked out: one body with gifts for building itself in love, the old self put off like clothes, marriage mapped onto Christ and the church ('this mystery is profound'), children and parents, and the whole armor of God — 'for we do not wrestle against flesh and blood.' Stand, therefore.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul pictures the old way of life as clothes you take off and the new self as clothes you put on. What does that picture suggest about how change actually happens, and what would putting on the new self look like in one of your relationships this week?
assessment_questions: What pieces make up the whole armor of God in chapter 6, and what does Paul say the real struggle is against?
Chapters 4 through 6 open with a 'therefore.' How do the commands to walk worthy depend on everything God has already done in chapters 1 through 3?
Paul calls believers to speak the truth in love so the body builds itself up. Which half of that pairing do you tend to drop, and what would holding both together require of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Because believers share one Lord, one faith, and one baptism, their lives are to show humility, patience, and a hard-working unity.
Christ gives gifts to the church so the whole body grows up into maturity instead of being tossed around by every new teaching.

teaching_concepts.concept: Marriage points to Christ and the church
teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul reads Eden's one-flesh charter as a living picture of Christ's self-giving love for the church, which reorders every household relationship.
The struggle behind daily life is spiritual, so believers stand in God's own armor of truth, righteousness, faith, and prayer rather than fighting people.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what it means to put off the old self and put on the new, and explain what the armor of God is for.

connections.reason: The armor of God is borrowed from the LORD's own armor in Isaiah 59.
'The two shall become one flesh' — Paul quotes Eden's marriage charter and reads Christ and the church in it.
Ephesians 5's marriage-as-Christ-and-church gives the Song its long Christian allegorical afterlife.
Ephesians 4's gifts-for-building-the-body teaching parallels and extends this section.

nodes.title: Philippians: Joy from a Prison Cell
nodes.summary: Written in chains, saturated with joy: 'to live is Christ, to die is gain.' At its heart the Christ-hymn — equal with God, yet emptying himself to a slave's death on a cross, therefore exalted with the name above every name — and its famous exhales: rejoice always, be anxious for nothing, 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul writes about joy from a prison cell, with his life genuinely on the line. What does his joy rest on that his circumstances cannot touch, and what does your own joy currently rest on?
assessment_questions: Where is Paul when he writes this letter, and what does he say his imprisonment has actually done for the gospel?

The hymn in chapter 2 traces Christ from equality with God down to death on a cross and up to the name above every name. What does that downward and upward movement teach about how God defines greatness?

Paul says he has learned contentment in plenty and in hunger through Christ who strengthens him. What situation in your life most tests your contentment, and what would leaning on Christ's strength there look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Paul's joy rests on Christ and the gospel's advance, so even chains gain purpose instead of stealing his hope.
Union with Christ gives Paul a single center of meaning, so both living and dying become gain.
The Christ-hymn holds up self-emptying service as the shape of discipleship, with exaltation following humility rather than grasping.
Peace that passes understanding comes by handing every anxiety to God in prayer and trusting Christ's strength in any circumstance.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the Christ-hymn's movement from equality with God to the cross to exaltation, and explain how it shapes Paul's joy in prison.

comprehension_check.question: The hymn of Philippians 2 arrives right after a plea for humility and unity in the church. What is the hymn there to do?
options: To settle how the divine and human met in Jesus
To give the church the pattern its life should take
To assure them their suffering will earn the same exaltation
To warn that pride forfeits a place in the kingdom
comprehension_check.why: Philippians 2:3-5 asks for humility that puts others first, then holds up Christ as the shape that mindset takes.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Philippians 2:1-5 again. Notice what the church is asked to do just before the hymn begins.

comprehension_check.question: From prison Paul claims his chains have actually helped the gospel along. What lets him read his situation that way?
options: His confidence that the verdict will soon be overturned
His belief that suffering banks a greater final reward
His refusal to dwell on how serious things are
His single measure for everything, whether Christ gets proclaimed
comprehension_check.why: Philippians 1:12-18 measures the imprisonment by the gospel's progress, and by that measure the chains are working.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Philippians 1:12-18 again. Notice what Paul keeps counting while he sits in chains.

connections.reason: 'Every knee shall bow, every tongue confess' transfers Isaiah 45's oath to YHWH onto Jesus.
The church founded in the Philippian jail receives Paul's most joyful letter.

nodes.title: Colossians: Christ Over All
nodes.summary: Against a fog of add-on spirituality — visions, angel-veneration, ascetic rules — Paul answers with the highest Christology in his letters: 'the image of the invisible God… by him all things were created… in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell.' You died and rose with him; therefore seek the things above, and let every sphere of household life be 'in the Lord.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul answers teachers offering spiritual extras by describing who Christ actually is: creator, sustainer, the fullness of God in a body. Why does seeing Christ that clearly make the add-ons lose their pull, and what extras compete for your trust today?
assessment_questions: What titles and works does the hymn in Colossians 1:15-20 give to Christ?
Paul says believers died and were raised with Christ, and then tells them to seek the things above. How does what already happened to them explain what he now asks of them?

Chapter 2 warns against rules that look wise yet lack power to restrain the flesh. What practice or rule are you tempted to trust for spiritual standing, and what would trusting Christ's sufficiency there change?

teaching_concepts.concept: The image of the invisible God
teaching_concepts.explanation: In Christ God is truly revealed, since all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell in him bodily.
All things were created through Christ and for him, and through the blood of his cross God makes peace and reconciles all things.
Believers died and rose with Christ in baptism, so their identity and their ethics both flow from that union.
No vision, rule, or ritual adds anything to the fullness believers already have in Christ, which is why Paul refuses every substitute.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Colossians claims about who Christ is, and describe how dying and rising with him changes the way a believer lives.

comprehension_check.question: Colossians answers a spirituality of visions, rules, and angel-veneration with a soaring description of Christ. Why is that the letter's counter?
options: Because error yields best to worship rather than to argument
Because the fullness already theirs in Christ leaves nothing to add
Because the rules were good early practice outgrown by mature believers
Because visions are unreliable while doctrine can be tested
comprehension_check.why: Colossians 2:9-10 grounds the answer, the whole fullness dwelling in Christ and believers already complete in him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Colossians 2:8-10 again. Notice what the letter says believers already have in him.

comprehension_check.question: Colossians 3 grounds its commands in something already true, that believers died and were raised with Christ. What does that make of the Christian life?
options: A climb toward a standing believers do not yet possess
A repayment of the debt canceled at the cross
A withdrawal from earthly duties toward heavenly contemplation
A living out of an identity already given in Christ
comprehension_check.why: Colossians 3:1-4 issues its commands from a finished fact, a life already hidden with Christ in God.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Colossians 3:1-4 again. Notice which comes first, what has already happened or what they must now do.

connections.reason: The Christ-hymn's creation-through-him theology parallels John's prologue — the New Testament's two summits of cosmic Christology.
Philemon travels with this letter — Onesimus is named in Colossians 4 as 'one of you.'
Hebrews 1 and Colossians 1 are parallel summits of New Testament Christology.

nodes.title: 1 Thessalonians: Hope for Those Who Sleep
nodes.summary: Probably the earliest Christian document we possess: a young persecuted church praised for turning 'from idols to serve the living and true God,' taught to grieve with hope — the Lord will descend, the dead in Christ rise first — and to live ready: 'the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.' Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in everything.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul tells grieving believers that they do not sorrow like people who have no hope. What difference does the promise of resurrection make when you stand at a graveside, and who in your life needs that kind of comfort right now?
assessment_questions: What does Paul say happened when the Thessalonians received the gospel, and who are they now waiting for?

Paul calls dead believers those who sleep and promises they will rise first when the Lord comes. Why does he choose the picture of sleep, and what does it say about what death now is for those in Christ?
Paul says the day of the Lord comes like a thief, so believers should stay awake and sober. What does hopeful readiness look like in an ordinary week, and what would it change in yours?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Believers grieve real losses while holding the promise of resurrection and reunion at Christ's coming, so sorrow and hope live together.
For those in Christ death is temporary, a sleep from which the Lord himself will wake his people when he comes.
Paul gives no timetable for the day of the Lord, so its certainty calls for watchful, sober, loving lives instead of anxious calculation.
Waiting for Jesus shows itself in rejoicing always, praying without ceasing, honest work, and love that keeps growing.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Paul teaches the Thessalonians to grieve with hope, and describe what living ready for the Lord's coming looks like in practice.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Thessalonians 4:13 wants the church not to grieve like the rest, who have no hope. What exactly is Paul adjusting?
options: He forbids mourning as unbelief in the resurrection
He redirects their grief toward the living who remain
He leaves room to grieve while removing the despair
He postpones all comfort until the Lord's actual coming
comprehension_check.why: 1 Thessalonians 4:14-16 sets their dead inside Jesus' own death and rising, with the dead in Christ rising first.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 again. Notice which words describe the outsiders' grief, and what verse 18 says to do with the teaching.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Thessalonians 5:2-6 says the day comes like a thief, then says it will not surprise the readers that way. What makes the difference?
options: They have charted the signs well enough to date it
They already live awake in the light of that day
The thief comes only for the world, never near them
Their watchfulness has earned them an early private warning
comprehension_check.why: 1 Thessalonians 5:4-5 calls them children of light and of the day, and 1 Thessalonians 5:6 draws the conclusion, stay awake and sober.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Thessalonians 5:2-8 again. Notice the two groups in the passage and what each is doing when the day arrives.

connections.reason: The thief-in-the-night and stay-awake teaching echoes Jesus' Olivet parables of readiness.
The Thessalonica of Acts 17 — three sabbaths and a riot — receives Paul's earliest surviving letter.

nodes.title: 2 Thessalonians: The Day Has Not Arrived
nodes.summary: Someone convinced the church the day of the Lord had already come; Paul steadies them: first comes the rebellion and 'the man of lawlessness' who exalts himself in God's temple — mysterious verses that have generated two millennia of speculation — and meanwhile, no idle waiting: 'if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: The Thessalonians were shaken by a claim that the day of the Lord had already come, and Paul's remedy is to hold fast to what they were taught and keep working. Why do rumors about the end unsettle people so easily, and what does Paul's remedy say about what healthy hope looks like?
assessment_questions: What false claim had unsettled the church, and what does Paul say must happen before the day of the Lord arrives?
Paul reminds the church of a man of lawlessness and a restrainer without giving names or dates we can pin down. What is his main point in chapter 2, and how does it steady a shaken church?

Paul commands that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and tells the church not to grow weary in doing good. How can waiting for Christ slide into idleness, and what keeps your own hope productive?

teaching_concepts.explanation: God will repay the affliction of his people and give them relief at Christ's revealing, so present suffering is never the last word.
Paul's core correction is that the day of the Lord is still future, so believers should refuse every claim or rumor that it has already come.
The man of lawlessness and the restrainer are described without identities or dates we can fix, so Christians hold the details loosely while trusting the outcome.
Real expectation of Christ's return produces steady endurance and honest daily labor, never idle waiting or freeloading.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the error Paul corrects about the day of the Lord, and describe how he tells the church to live while it waits.

comprehension_check.question: 2 Thessalonians 2 answers a report that the day of the Lord had already come. What is Paul's steadying move?
options: He names what must come first, showing the day has not arrived
He denies the day can be discussed, ending all speculation about it
He moves their hope away from the day toward present endurance alone
comprehension_check.why: 2 Thessalonians 2:3 steadies the church by naming what precedes that day, so the alarming report collapses.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3 again. Notice the word Paul uses about deception, and what he says comes first.

comprehension_check.question: The letter moves from the day of the Lord to a command about earning bread in 2 Thessalonians 3. What links the two?
options: Work funds the mission that must be finished before the day
Labor makes amends for the alarm false teaching had spread
Busy hands keep the anxious from brooding on frightening prophecies
Faithful waiting looks like steady work, not abandoned daily life
comprehension_check.why: 2 Thessalonians 3:11-12 answers those who had quit working with a charge to quiet labor, part of readiness for the day.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12 again. Notice what some had stopped doing, and what Paul commands them in the Lord.

connections.reason: The lawless one and Revelation's beast are the New Testament's twin portraits of final anti-God power.

nodes.title: 1 Timothy: Order in God's Household
nodes.summary: Paul coaches his young delegate in Ephesus: silence the speculation-teachers, pray for kings, appoint overseers and deacons whose homes match their words, honor widows and elders, and flee the love of money — 'a root of all kinds of evils.' The church is 'the household of God… pillar and buttress of the truth,' and Christ Jesus came to save sinners, 'of whom I am the foremost.'
nodes.tradition_notes: The offices here (overseer/episkopos, deacon) ground divergent church polities: Catholic and Orthodox traditions read a threefold ministry (bishop, priest, deacon) in apostolic succession; presbyterian and congregational Protestants read overseer and elder as one office. 1 Tim 2:12 ('I do not permit a woman to teach') is the focal text in ongoing debates over women's ordination, read as universal by some traditions and as situational by others.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul insists that overseers and deacons be tested by the lives they already live at home. Why does the gospel's credibility ride so heavily on the character of the people who teach it, and whose life has made the faith believable to you?
assessment_questions: What kinds of qualifications does Paul give for overseers and deacons in chapter 3?
Paul says the aim of his charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. How does that aim separate sound doctrine from the speculation he tells Timothy to silence?
Paul calls godliness with contentment great gain and names the love of money a root of all kinds of evils. Where does money's pull show up in your own plans, and what would contentment change?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Sound teaching aims at love from a pure heart and a sincere faith, which is how Paul distinguishes it from clever speculation.
Paul holds up his own story as proof that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, so no one stands beyond mercy's reach.
Leaders in God's household are tested by proven character at home and in public, because their lives give the gospel its credibility.

teaching_concepts.concept: Contentment over the love of money
teaching_concepts.explanation: Godliness with contentment guards the heart, while craving wealth plants a root from which all kinds of evils grow.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe why Paul ties church leadership to tested character, and explain what he means by godliness with contentment.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Timothy 3:15 states the letter's purpose, conduct in the household of God, pillar and buttress of the truth. What does that image make of church order?
options: Ordered common life is part of how truth stands publicly
Order is itself the truth, so sound structure saves
Order is a discipline imposed until the false teachers leave
comprehension_check.why: 1 Timothy 3:15 makes the household the pillar holding the truth up, so its conduct is load-bearing for the gospel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Timothy 3:14-16 again. Notice what the household image is said to hold up, and the song that follows in verse 16.

comprehension_check.question: 1 Timothy 6:6-10 sets great gain beside ruin and piercing grief. Where does the passage locate the danger?
options: Money itself, which corrupts whoever handles it
Teaching for pay, which the church should never permit
Wealthy members, whose gifts distort the church's judgment
The craving to be rich, against contentment with enough
comprehension_check.why: 1 Timothy 6:9-10 traces the ruin to craving, the love of money that is a root of all kinds of evils.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 1 Timothy 6:6-10 again. Notice exactly what verse 10 calls a root, and who verse 9 says falls into the trap.

connections.reason: Titus is the same pastoral manual for Crete — the two letters share their elder-qualification lists.

nodes.title: 2 Timothy: Paul's Last Letter
nodes.summary: From a Roman death cell, abandoned by most, Paul writes his final charge: guard the deposit, suffer for the gospel, entrust the message to faithful men who can teach others — 'all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable.' The valediction is the most quoted deathbed text in Christian history: 'I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul writes his last letter from a death cell, abandoned by most of his friends, and still says he has finished the race. What does finishing well seem to mean to him, and what would it take to aim your life at that kind of finish line now?
assessment_questions: Where is Paul as he writes this letter, and what does he charge Timothy to do with the message entrusted to him?
Paul says all Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. What does that claim mean for how a believer approaches the Bible?
Paul tells Timothy to entrust the message to faithful people who can teach others also. Who passed the faith to you, and who could you begin passing it to?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The apostolic gospel is a trust to be kept intact and handed on, so every generation of believers is a link in a chain.
Paul frames faithful ministry with the images of a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer, all of whom endure hardship before the reward.
God's own breath stands behind Scripture, which makes it able to teach, correct, and train a person for every good work.
Paul measures his life by faithfulness to the end, keeping the faith through hardship rather than chasing ease or popularity.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what Paul means by guarding the deposit and passing it on, and retell how he describes his own finished race.

comprehension_check.question: Facing death, Paul tells Timothy in 2 Timothy 2:2 to entrust the message to people who can teach others. What does the charge assume about the gospel's future?
options: It rests on Timothy alone, the last man Paul can trust
It waits on fresh revelation to renew what the apostles taught
It depends on a relay of teaching passed person to person
It spreads by its own power, needing no human guarding
comprehension_check.why: 2 Timothy 2:2 lines up four generations in a single sentence, Paul to Timothy to faithful people to others still.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Timothy 2:2 again. Count how many handoffs the one sentence contains.

comprehension_check.question: Right after describing hard times and deceivers, 2 Timothy 3 points Timothy to the sacred writings. What is the point of that turn?
options: Scripture predicts each deceiver so the church can name them
Scripture equips God's servant fully for the work ahead
Scripture shields its readers from the suffering Paul has described
Scripture replaces human teachers, ending Timothy's need for guides
comprehension_check.why: 2 Timothy 3:16-17 traces the writings to God's own breath and aims them at a servant equipped for every good work.
comprehension_check.hint: Read 2 Timothy 3:14-17 again. Notice what Paul says the writings are able to do, and what they are for.

connections.reason: Acts leaves Paul under house arrest in Rome; this letter speaks from the harsher, final imprisonment tradition places after it.

nodes.title: Titus: Grace That Trains
nodes.summary: Titus is left in Crete — whose own poet called Cretans 'liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons' — to appoint elders and build a culture of good works on a foundation of pure grace: 'the grace of God has appeared… training us to renounce ungodliness,' and 'he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy.'
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul says the same grace that saves people also trains them to renounce ungodliness. How can kindness change a person's behavior in ways that rules alone cannot, and where have you seen that happen?
assessment_questions: Why did Paul leave Titus in Crete, and what did he tell him to do there?
Titus 3 says God saved us according to his own mercy, and a few verses later insists believers devote themselves to good works. How does the letter hold mercy and good works together?
Paul wants Christians in a culture famous for lying and laziness to be known for good works. What good work could make the gospel visible where you live, and what stops you from starting it?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Elders are judged by proven lives and faithful doctrine rather than charm, because false teaching corrupts whole households.
The grace that brings salvation also teaches believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, godly lives now.
Rescue comes from God's kindness and the Spirit's renewing work, never from works we perform to earn it.
Mercy received turns into visible good works, so the lives of believers adorn the teaching about God in public.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain how Titus holds together salvation by God's mercy and a life devoted to good works.

comprehension_check.question: Titus is told to build churches out of people famous for lying and laziness. Where does the letter say the changed life comes from?
options: From rules firm enough to restrain old habits
From godly training that earns saving grace
From leaders strict enough to model the standard
From the same grace that brought the salvation
comprehension_check.why: Titus 2:11-12 gives grace the teacher's chair: what appeared bringing salvation now trains believers out of the old life.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Titus 2:11-12 again. Notice what grace does after it brings salvation.

comprehension_check.question: Titus 2:10 gives ordinary working people a surprising power over the church's message. What can their conduct do?
options: Make the teaching about God credible to watching outsiders
Repay a portion of the mercy God has shown
Complete the salvation that mercy only began in them
Shield the young churches from imperial suspicion
comprehension_check.why: Titus 2:10 lets honest daily work put the teaching about God on public display at its most attractive.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Titus 2:9-10 again. Notice where the verse says the effect of honest work finally lands.

connections.reason: Titus is the same pastoral manual for Crete — the two letters share their elder-qualification lists.

nodes.title: Philemon: Receive Him as Me
nodes.summary: One page that quietly detonates under slavery: Onesimus, a runaway slave converted in Paul's prison, is sent home carrying this letter — 'no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother.' Paul offers to pay his debts himself: 'if he has wronged you, charge it to my account.' The gospel's logic of substitution and family, applied to one household.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Paul could command Philemon and chooses instead to appeal in love, even offering to pay Onesimus's debts himself. What does his approach show about how the gospel changes relationships, and who would it cost you something real to welcome as family?
assessment_questions: Who is Onesimus, and what does Paul ask Philemon to do when he arrives home carrying this letter?
Paul tells Philemon to charge any wrong to his own account. How does that offer echo what Christ has done, and why does it give the appeal its weight?
Paul asks Philemon to receive a runaway slave as a beloved brother. Where do social lines still decide how you treat people, and what would receiving someone as family cost you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The gospel moves from doctrine into one real household, where a wronged master is asked to welcome the man who wronged him.
Onesimus, once called useless, is now useful and a beloved brother, because conversion changes who a person is.
Paul persuades in love when he could give orders, modeling how the gospel reorders relationships through consent rather than force.
Paul's offer to put Onesimus's debt on his own account mirrors Christ taking the debt of sinners on himself.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Paul's appeal for Onesimus and explain how it shows the gospel reshaping a real relationship.

comprehension_check.question: Paul tells Philemon he has the standing to command him, then refuses to use it. What does the appeal make possible that an order could not?
options: A ruling Roman law would be forced to honor
A welcome that costs Philemon nothing he values
A goodness Philemon gives freely rather than under pressure
A precedent other slaveholders would have to follow
comprehension_check.why: Philemon 1:14 stakes everything on consent, wanting the good deed given freely instead of extracted by authority.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Philemon 1:14 again. Notice the kind of goodness Paul says he refuses to force.

comprehension_check.question: Paul writes that any wrong or debt of Onesimus should be put on his own account. What does that offer do for the reconciliation?
options: It settles the wrong so welcome need not pretend
It proves Onesimus never truly wronged his master
It pays Philemon off so he cannot refuse Paul
It satisfies the penalty Roman law laid on runaways
comprehension_check.why: Philemon 1:18 moves the real debt onto Paul instead of denying it, so the welcome starts with a clean ledger.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Philemon 1:17-19 again. Notice what Paul does with the debt rather than around it.

connections.reason: Philemon travels with this letter — Onesimus is named in Colossians 4 as 'one of you.'

nodes.title: Greater Than Angels and Moses; Enter the Rest
nodes.summary: An anonymous masterpiece opens with the New Testament's grandest sentence: the Son is the radiance of God's glory, upholding the universe by the word of his power. Greater than angels (a chain of psalm quotations), greater than Moses, he leads a new wilderness generation — 'Today, if you hear his voice' — toward a sabbath rest the first generation forfeited. The word is living, active, sharper than any two-edged sword.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Hebrews opens by saying God has spoken finally in a Son, then warns readers not to drift or harden their hearts. If Christ really is God's last word, what does drifting from him actually look like in an ordinary week, and what would 'Today, if you hear his voice' require of you before the day ends?
assessment_questions: According to Hebrews 1, what does the Son do in relation to creation, and where does he sit down after making purification for sins?
Hebrews 3 and 4 keep repeating the word 'Today' from Psalm 95. Why does the author treat a psalm written long after the wilderness generation as proof that God's rest is still open to enter?
The word of God is called living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword. What part of your life would change if you let that word examine you the way Hebrews 4:12 describes?

teaching_concepts.concept: God's final word is a Son
teaching_concepts.explanation: Christ is God's fullest and definitive revelation, greater than the prophets and the angels who carried God's word before him.
Moses served faithfully in God's house, while Christ is the faithful Son over the house, so his voice carries final authority.
God's promised rest remains available and is entered by trusting obedience, which is why the author keeps pressing the word 'Today.'
Unbelief hardens slowly, so the letter urges believers to exhort one another daily before neglect turns into refusal.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain why Hebrews calls the Son greater than the angels and Moses, and what it means to enter God's rest 'Today.'

comprehension_check.question: Hebrews 1 stacks quotation on quotation to raise the Son far above the angels. What is the letter doing with that height in Hebrews 2:1-3?
options: To prove the angel-carried law never truly bound Israel
To make neglecting the Son's message more dangerous than ever
To satisfy curiosity about the ranks of the heavenly court
To identify the Son as the highest of the angels
comprehension_check.why: Hebrews 2:2-3 argues from lesser to greater, so the salvation announced by the Son is more perilous to neglect than the word angels carried.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hebrews 2:1-3 right after chapter 1. Notice what the height of chapter 1 is suddenly used to urge.

comprehension_check.question: Hebrews insists that Joshua's conquest did not close the story of God's rest (Hebrews 4:7-8). What is the letter arguing?
options: The rest arrived in full once Israel possessed the land
The rest is simply the weekly sabbath Israel already kept
The psalm's warning expired with the wilderness generation
The promised rest still stands open, entered by faith now
comprehension_check.why: Hebrews 4:9-11 concludes that God's rest still waits for his people and urges every effort to enter it before hearts harden.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Hebrews 4:7-9. Notice what the letter concludes from God appointing a day so long after Joshua.

connections.reason: 'I will be to him a father' from the Davidic covenant opens the catena proving the Son's supremacy.
Hebrews 1 and Colossians 1 are parallel summits of New Testament Christology.
Hebrews 3-4 turns the Kadesh refusal into the standing warning: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.'
Hebrews 1 quotes Psalm 45's address to the king ('Your throne, O God, is forever') as speech about the Son.
Hebrews 3-4 builds its 'Today' warning on Psalm 95's Meribah rehearsal.
Hebrews' 'radiance of the glory of God' echoes Wisdom 7's 'pure emanation' vocabulary.

nodes.title: A Priest Forever: Melchizedek
nodes.summary: The argument nobody else in the New Testament attempts: Jesus is high priest not by Levitical descent but 'after the order of Melchizedek' — the king-priest who blessed Abraham, without recorded genealogy, greater than Levi who paid tithes 'in Abraham's loins.' A better hope, a better covenant, a priest who 'always lives to make intercession.' Includes the fearful warning about falling away and the anchor of hope behind the veil.
nodes.discussion_prompt: Hebrews says Jesus always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him. What difference would it make to your praying and your failing if you believed a living priest was speaking for you right now, and what keeps you from drawing near with that kind of boldness?
